docs.title: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
docs.text:
In short

A tiny computer inside the keyboard turns the keypress into a number, and USB carries it to the host. An interrupt makes the CPU drop what it's doing and run the kernel, which hands the event to user space. The application turns the number into the letter 'a' using the keyboard layout and draws it. Then the GPU sends the new frame to the monitor. All of this takes ~10–50 ms.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) MCU Microcontroller Unit Tiny computer inside the keyboard Scans the key matrix, debounces, builds HID reports HID Human Interface Device USB device class for keyboards and mice Sends fixed-format reports (8 bytes for a keyboard) USB Universal Serial Bus The cable/protocol between keyboard and PC Host polls devices at a fixed interval xHCI eXtensible Host Controller Interface The USB host controller chip Polls devices, DMAs data to RAM, raises interrupts DMA Direct Memory Access Device writes to RAM without the CPU Controller copies data while the CPU keeps working IRQ / MSI Interrupt Request / Message Signaled Interrupt A device's signal to the CPU MSI = a write to a special address that the APIC turns into an interrupt APIC Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller Routes interrupts to CPU cores Delivers a vector number to a core IDT / ISR Interrupt Descriptor Table / Interrupt Service Routine Table of handlers / the handler itself CPU looks up the vector in the IDT and jumps to the ISR Ring 0 / ring 3 — Kernel mode / user mode CPU privilege levels; syscalls and interrupts cross them evdev event device Linux's generic input event interface Queues key events on /dev/input/eventX Compositor — Display server combining windows (Wayland/X11) Reads input, sends it to the focused window, composes frames xkb X Keyboard Extension Keyboard layout database/library Maps keycode + layout + modifiers to a character GPU / framebuffer Graphics Processing Unit Graphics chip / memory holding the final frame Composes windows into the framebuffer, sent to the monitor vsync vertical synchronization The monitor's refresh tick New frames are shown only at each refresh (16.7 ms at 60 Hz)

docs.title: 🗺️ Big picture
docs.text: Reference setup: Linux + Wayland + USB keyboard. On Windows and macOS the layer names differ, but the logic is the same (see Other operating systems).

docs.title: 1 · Keyboard (hardware)
docs.text: # What happens Why it matters 1 The key switch closes: two metal contacts touch and complete a circuit. A keyboard has no idea what a "letter" is. It only knows which circuits are closed. 2 Key matrix: keys are wired into a rows × columns grid. The microcontroller drives each row in turn and checks which column responds (scanning). ~8 × 18 lines are enough for 100+ keys instead of 100+ wires. — Debounce: contacts physically bounce for a few ms. The MCU filters this so it counts as a single press. Without it, one press would type "aaaa". 3 The MCU converts the key into a code. On USB this is called a HID usage: “A” = 0x04. The code describes the key's position, not a letter. The same physical key sends the same code on any layout.

docs.title: 2 · USB transport
docs.text: # What happens 3 The MCU builds a HID report. In boot protocol it is 8 bytes: [modifiers, 0x00, k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k6]. Pressing A gives 00 00 04 00 00 00 00 00. 4 The keyboard never speaks first. The USB Host Controller (xHCI) on the computer asks it "anything new?" at a fixed interval (polling): 8 ms (125 Hz) on a normal keyboard, 1 ms (1000 Hz) on a gaming one. — When a new report arrives, xHCI writes it straight into RAM via DMA, without involving the CPU.

docs.title: 3 · Motherboard & CPU (assembly level)
docs.text:
# What happens 5 xHCI raises an interrupt to say "done". On modern systems this is a write to a special memory address (MSI). 6 The APIC (interrupt controller) delivers it to a CPU core as a vector number. — The CPU may be running something else, say Spotify. It finishes the current instruction and stops. 7 It looks up the handler address (ISR) for that vector in the IDT (Interrupt Descriptor Table). — So it can come back later, the CPU pushes RIP, CS, RFLAGS, RSP and SS onto the kernel stack (context save) and switches from ring 3 to ring 0 if needed. 8 It jumps to the handler. Kernel code is now running.

Through assembly eyes, simplified:

; --- The hardware does this automatically (no code from us) ---
; push SS, RSP, RFLAGS, CS, RIP   → "where the interrupted program was"
; RIP ← IDT[vector].handler        → jump to the handler

xhci_isr:
    push rax                    ; save the registers we will use
    push rdi
    ; ... (in Linux this calls into C: xhci_irq())
    mov  dword [lapic_eoi], 0   ; tell the APIC "interrupt handled" (End Of Interrupt)
    pop  rdi
    pop  rax
    iretq                       ; restore saved state → Spotify resumes where it was

Remember this

An interrupt is how hardware says "listen to me" to the CPU. The CPU drops everything, saves its state, runs the kernel, and returns with iretq. Every I/O device works this way: network cards, disks, keyboards.

docs.title: 4 · Kernel space (ring 0)
docs.text:
# What happens 8 xhci_irq() reads the event from RAM and tells the usbhid driver "your report arrived". 9 The HID layer parses the report: HID usage 0x04 maps to the Linux key code KEY_A = 30. The input core and evdev queue it as an event on /dev/input/eventX: EV_KEY, KEY_A, 1 (pressed) followed by EV_SYN.

Linux's "everything is a file" idea applies here too: the keyboard is a file, and keypresses are records you read from it.

docs.title: 5 · User space (ring 3)
docs.text: # What happens 10 The compositor (Mutter on GNOME, KWin on KDE) was waiting on that file through libinput with epoll. It wakes up and fetches the event with the read() syscall. This is the dashed line in the diagram: ring 0 → ring 3. 11 libinput processes the event: is it a shortcut, a key repeat, and so on. 12 The compositor knows which window has keyboard focus and sends the event to that app over the Wayland protocol: wl_keyboard.key(key=30, state=pressed).

docs.title: 6 · Application
docs.text: # What happens 13 The app's event loop (GTK or Qt) receives the message. 14 xkbcommon translates code 30 using the keyboard layout: 30 → keysym 'a' → Unicode U+0061. With Shift held it would be 'A'; on a French AZERTY layout the same key gives 'q'. This is the first moment a "letter" exists. 15 The character is inserted into the text buffer and the widget marks itself "needs redraw". The font engine (HarfBuzz + FreeType) turns the shape of 'a' (glyph) into pixels. 16 The app draws the new frame into a buffer and hands it to the compositor with wl_surface.commit.

docs.title: 7 · Display
docs.text: # What happens 17 The compositor uses the GPU to combine all windows into a single frame in the framebuffer. 18 On the monitor's next refresh (vsync, every 16.7 ms at 60 Hz) the frame is sent over HDMI/DP, the pixels change, and 'a' appears.

docs.title: How does an interrupt work?
docs.text: The CPU is busy running a program. A device raises an IRQ; at the next instruction boundary the CPU saves RIP/RFLAGS/RSP on the kernel stack, switches to ring 0, looks up the vector in the IDT and jumps to the ISR. The handler does the minimum (acknowledge the device, queue work), then iretq restores the saved state and the program continues as if nothing happened.

docs.title: Where does the latency come from? (~10–50 ms)
docs.text:
Source Typical Debounce + MCU 1–5 ms USB polling 1–8 ms Interrupt + kernel + compositor + app < 1–5 ms Waiting for the next frame (60 Hz) 0–16.7 ms Monitor processing + pixel response 2–15 ms

DevOps connection: an HTTP request's latency budget works exactly the same way. The total is the sum of every hop, and the slowest hop sets what users feel.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: one core drowning in interrupts
docs.text:
The alarm

After a traffic increase, p99 latency of a busy API node doubles. Average CPU is only 35%, but top shows one core at 100% si, and ksoftirqd/0 sits at the top of the process list.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

/proc/interrupts: the NIC's queue interrupts all increase only in the CPU0 column; the other 15 columns barely move.

🔍 Clue 2

ethtool -l eth0 shows Combined: 1: the NIC runs with one queue. systemctl status irqbalance → not installed in the minimal image.

🎯 Root cause

All packet processing (hard IRQ + NET_RX softirq) lands on a single core. That core saturates while the others idle, so packets wait in the queue and latency climbs, even though average CPU looks fine.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Enable multiple queues (ethtool -L eth0 combined 8), spread their IRQs (irqbalance or smp_affinity), and consider RPS/RFS. Lesson: average CPU hides per-core saturation; check mpstat -P ALL and the si column.

docs.text: Page What's inside 1.1 — Interrupts & device drivers What interrupts are and why they exist, polling vs interrupts vs DMA, MSI/MSI-X and IRQ affinity, top and bottom halves, how drivers are matched and loaded, and how this shows up in production (softirq, irqbalance, NIC queues). 1.2 — USB & HID How USB works (host-driven polling, enumeration, descriptors, endpoints and transfer types), the HID class and report descriptors, the 8-byte keyboard report, polling rate and latency, and USB in servers, VMs and containers. 1.3 — The Linux input stack evdev and input events, libinput, the compositor and Wayland vs X11, keyboard focus, keymaps with xkbcommon (keycode → keysym → character), key repeat, input methods, and how browsers turn it into KeyboardEvent.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 01-keypress (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces.

On a Mac, run these labs in a Linux VM (UTM, Multipass) or on a Linux machine.

# 1) Check your keyboard's polling interval (bInterval)
lsusb                                   # find the keyboard's Bus/Device numbers
sudo lsusb -v -s <bus>:<dev> | grep -E "bInterval|bInterfaceProtocol"

# 2) Watch the interrupt counter climb while you type
watch -n0.2 "grep -i xhci /proc/interrupts"

# 3) See what the kernel produces (step 9): you'll see MSC_SCAN 70004 and KEY_A
sudo evtest                             # pick your keyboard, press A

# 4) Events as libinput sees them (steps 10–11)
sudo libinput debug-events

# 5) What the application receives (steps 12–14)
wev        # Wayland: key 30 → sym: a, utf8: 'a'
xev        # X11:     keycode 38 (= 30 + 8) → keysym 0x61, a

Exercise: in the evtest output, find the press (value 1), hold/repeat (value 2) and release (value 0) events for A. Think about who is responsible for key repeat.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Key → circuit closes → matrix scan → MCU: HID usage 0x04
   → USB HID report (8 bytes) → xHCI polling + DMA → RAM
   → MSI interrupt → APIC → CPU: stop, save, IDT → ISR (ring 0)
   → xhci → usbhid → KEY_A(30) → evdev /dev/input/eventX
   → [syscall read()] → libinput → compositor → wl_keyboard.key(30)
   → app event loop → xkbcommon (layout) → 'a' U+0061
   → text buffer → glyph → buffer commit → GPU compose → vsync → monitor
  • The keyboard sends a position, not a letter. The letter only appears at the keymap inside the app.
  • A USB keyboard never speaks first. The host polls it.
  • Interrupt = grabbing the CPU's attention. It saves state, runs the handler, and returns with iret.
  • The ring 0 / ring 3 boundary is crossed with a syscall.

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. If you switch from QWERTY to AZERTY, does the code sent over USB change for the same physical key?

No. The code (0x04) describes the key's position. Translating it to a character is done by the OS or the app, using the layout.

2. With 8 ms polling, how long can a keypress wait in the worst case?

About 8 ms. If you press right after a poll, the report waits until the next one.

3. What happens to the program the CPU was running when the interrupt arrived?

The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the program's state (RIP, RFLAGS, …) on the stack, runs the handler, and resumes the program exactly where it was with iretq. The program never notices.

4. Why don't applications read the keyboard directly from /dev/input?

Security and focus. If every app could read every key, every app would be a keylogger. The compositor only delivers events to the focused window.

5. Why is the 'A' keycode 38 on X11 but 30 on Wayland?

For historical reasons X11 adds 8 to the evdev code (30 + 8 = 38). Wayland sends the evdev code as is.

docs.title: ✍️ My notes
docs.text: After reading, explain this chapter in your own words in 5 lines. The parts you can't explain are the parts you don't understand yet.

docs.title: 1.1 — Interrupts & device drivers
docs.text:
In short

Devices are slow and unpredictable. So instead of the CPU constantly asking "anything new?", a device interrupts the CPU when something happens. A small kernel interrupt handler runs and defers the heavy work to a bottom half. A device driver, matched to the hardware by its IDs, turns the device's raw registers into a standard interface programs can use.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Interrupt — Signal that makes the CPU pause and run a handler Hardware raises it; CPU jumps via the IDT IRQ Interrupt Request An interrupt line/number cat /proc/interrupts lists them Polling — CPU repeatedly checks a device Wastes CPU when idle; great at very high load DMA Direct Memory Access Device copies data to RAM itself Driver gives it buffer addresses (rings) MSI / MSI-X Message Signaled Interrupts Interrupt sent as a memory write One vector per queue, can target any core APIC Advanced Programmable Interrupt Controller Delivers interrupts to cores Local APIC per core + I/O APIC ISR / top half Interrupt Service Routine Code run immediately on the interrupt Must be very short, can't sleep Bottom half — Deferred part of interrupt work softirq, tasklet, workqueue, threaded IRQ softirq software interrupt Kernel's high-priority deferred work si in top; NET_RX, BLOCK, TIMER Driver — Kernel code for one kind of device probe() when matched, then serves a subsystem Kernel module — Loadable piece of the kernel (.ko) modprobe, lsmod udev userspace device manager Reacts to kernel device events Loads modules, creates /dev nodes, names devices IRQ affinity — Which cores handle an IRQ /proc/irq/N/smp_affinity, irqbalance NAPI New API Network drivers switch to polling under load Interrupt once, then poll a batch of packets

docs.title: What is the problem?
docs.text:
A keyboard sends maybe 10 events per second; a 100 Gbit NIC can deliver millions of packets per second. The CPU can't know when data arrives. It has three options:

Approach How it works Good for Bad for Polling CPU checks a status register in a loop Very high, steady load (DPDK, NVMe at high queue depth) Burns a core while idle Interrupts Device signals; CPU runs a handler Low/irregular load, latency-sensitive input Interrupt storms at very high rates DMA + interrupts Device writes data to RAM itself, then interrupts once per batch Disks, NICs, GPUs Needs careful buffer management

Real systems mix them: Linux network drivers use NAPI, which takes one interrupt, disables it, and then polls a batch of packets until the queue is empty.

docs.title: 2 · How an interrupt is delivered
docs.text:
1. The device raises an interrupt. Modern PCIe devices use MSI-X: they write a small message to a special address, and the APIC turns it into an interrupt vector on a chosen core.
  2. The core finishes its current instruction, saves state, switches to kernel mode and jumps to the handler listed in the IDT for that vector (chapter 1 diagram).
  3. The handler runs, acknowledges the device, and returns with iret.

Each NIC queue or NVMe queue gets its own MSI-X vector, so work can be spread across cores. /proc/interrupts shows the per-core counters.

docs.title: Why split?
docs.text:
While the top half runs, other interrupts on that core are blocked and the handler cannot sleep. So it does only the minimum (acknowledge, grab data pointers) and schedules the rest:

  • softirq / tasklet: runs soon after, with interrupts enabled, still can't sleep. Network receive (NET_RX) and block I/O completion live here.
  • workqueue / threaded IRQ: runs in a kernel thread (kworker, irq/42-…), can sleep, can be scheduled like any thread.

When the softirq load is too high, the kernel hands it to the ksoftirqd/N threads; seeing them at the top of top means the box is drowning in interrupt work.

docs.title: 4 · Drivers: how the right code gets loaded
How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The bus (USB, PCIe, I²C) enumerates devices and reads their IDs (vendor, product, class).
  2. The kernel sends a uevent; udev looks up the matching module by its modalias and runs modprobe.
  3. The driver's probe() runs: map device registers, allocate DMA rings, request_irq().
  4. It registers with a subsystem (input, net, block, DRM). The subsystem gives a standard interface: a keyboard becomes /dev/input/eventN, a NIC becomes eth0, a disk becomes /dev/nvme0n1.

That's why user space never talks to hardware directly: it uses the same read() / ioctl() for every keyboard, whatever the brand.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• High si / ksoftirqd on a network-heavy node → spread queues across cores (RSS, ethtool -L), check IRQ affinity and irqbalance, consider RPS/RFS.
  • IRQs pinned to one core → that core is saturated while others idle. Compare columns in /proc/interrupts.
  • Latency-sensitive workloads (trading, real-time, some GPU nodes) pin IRQs away from application cores (isolcpus, CPU manager in Kubernetes).
  • Drivers in containers: containers share the host kernel and its drivers. GPU drivers, RDMA and special NICs must be on the node (that's what the NVIDIA GPU Operator installs).
  • SR-IOV lets one NIC present many "virtual functions" with their own queues and interrupts, passed directly to VMs or pods.

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can't an interrupt handler sleep or do heavy work?

It runs with interrupts (at least on that line/core) blocked and outside any process context; sleeping would freeze that core's interrupt handling. Heavy work goes to a bottom half.

2. What does NAPI do and why?

After the first interrupt it disables the NIC's interrupt and polls batches of packets until the queue is empty, avoiding an interrupt storm at high packet rates.

3. How does Linux know which driver to load for a newly plugged device?

The bus reads the device IDs, the kernel emits a uevent with a modalias, udev matches it to a module and runs modprobe; the driver's probe() then claims the device.

4. A node shows one core at 100% in si while others are idle. What do you check?

/proc/interrupts: NIC queue IRQs probably land on one core. Add queues / RSS, fix IRQ affinity or enable irqbalance, consider RPS.

5. Why must GPU drivers be installed on the node and not just in the container?

Drivers are kernel code. Containers share the host kernel; they only carry user-space libraries that talk to the host's driver.

docs.title: 1.2 — USB & HID
docs.text:
In short

USB is a host-driven bus: the computer discovers each device (enumeration), reads its descriptors to learn what it is, assigns it an address, and then polls it on a schedule. A keyboard belongs to the HID class, which describes its data with a report descriptor. Every time you press or release a key it answers the next poll with a small report listing which keys are currently down.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) USB Universal Serial Bus Host-controlled peripheral bus Host schedules all traffic; devices only answer Host controller (xHCI) eXtensible Host Controller Interface Chip that runs the USB bus Executes transfer rings in RAM, raises interrupts Hub — Port multiplier Reports attach/detach to the host Enumeration — Discovering a newly attached device Reset → descriptors → address → configuration Descriptor — Self-description data a device returns Device, configuration, interface, endpoint, HID report VID / PID Vendor ID / Product ID 16-bit IDs of maker and model 046d:c31c = Logitech keyboard Endpoint — A data channel on a device EP0 control + others (IN/OUT) Transfer types — Control, interrupt, bulk, isochronous Keyboard: interrupt; disk: bulk; audio: isochronous Polling interval — How often the host asks an interrupt endpoint 1–8 ms for keyboards (125–1000 Hz), faster for gaming HID Human Interface Device Device class for input devices Self-describing reports, no special driver needed Report descriptor — Describes the layout of the device's reports Usage pages, sizes, counts Usage — Meaning of a field (e.g. "Keyboard A") Numbers from the HID Usage Tables Boot protocol — Fixed simple 8-byte keyboard format Works in BIOS/UEFI without parsing descriptors NKRO N-Key RollOver Any number of simultaneous keys Uses a bitmap report instead of 6 slots

docs.title: 1 · What makes USB different: the host asks
docs.text:
On USB, devices never talk first. The host controller (xHCI) keeps a schedule of transfers in RAM and works through it:

  • Control transfers (endpoint 0): setup and configuration, used during enumeration.
  • Interrupt transfers: small, periodic, guaranteed latency. Keyboards, mice. ("Interrupt" here only means "polled regularly"; the device doesn't interrupt anything.)
  • Bulk transfers: large, whenever bandwidth is free. Storage, printers.
  • Isochronous transfers: fixed bandwidth, no retries. Audio, webcams.

When an interrupt endpoint has nothing new, it answers NAK. When it has a report, the controller DMAs it into RAM and raises a real CPU interrupt (MSI) to tell the kernel.

docs.title: 2 · Enumeration: how the host learns what you plugged in
docs.text:
1. Attach: the hub sees a voltage change on a port and tells the host.
  2. Reset: the host resets the port; the device answers at address 0 and its speed is detected.
  3. Device descriptor: VID, PID, USB version, device class.
  4. SET_ADDRESS: the device gets a unique address (1–127 per bus).
  5. Configuration, interface and endpoint descriptors: for a keyboard, an interface with class 3 (HID) and an interrupt IN endpoint with a polling interval.
  6. HID report descriptor: the exact layout of the reports.
  7. The kernel matches the usbhid driver by class; it hands reports to the HID core, which creates an input device (/dev/input/eventN).

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text: HID devices describe themselves. The report descriptor says, for example: "8 one-bit fields for modifier keys, 1 reserved byte, 6 byte-sized key slots from usage page Keyboard". So one generic driver handles every keyboard, mouse, game pad and barcode scanner.

docs.title: How does a key press look?
docs.text:
Action Report bytes Nothing pressed 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 a pressed 00 00 04 00 00 00 00 00 Shift + a 02 00 04 00 00 00 00 00 Released 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
  • 0x04 is the HID usage for the key in the "A" position, not the letter. The layout (US, Turkish-Q, AZERTY) is applied much later, by xkb (1.3).
  • The report lists keys currently down; a release is just a report without that key. Key repeat is generated by software, not the keyboard.
  • The 6 slots mean the boot protocol supports 6 simultaneous keys (6KRO); gaming keyboards use a bitmap report for NKRO.

docs.title: 4 · Polling rate and latency
docs.text: At 125 Hz polling the host asks every 8 ms, so a press waits 0–8 ms (avg 4 ms) just to leave the keyboard. At 1000 Hz it's 0–1 ms; some gaming devices go to 8000 Hz. Add the keyboard's own matrix scan + debounce (often 1–10 ms) and you have most of the "keyboard latency" before the OS even sees the event.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Servers and VMs: BMC/IPMI virtual consoles and hypervisors (KVM/QEMU, VMware) emulate USB HID keyboards/tablets; "typing into the console" goes through this same HID path.
  • USB passthrough: usbip, QEMU -device usb-host, or VM "USB redirection" forwards a real device into a VM. In Kubernetes, USB devices reach pods via device plugins or hostPath device mounts (rarely, e.g. HSMs, licence dongles, edge sensors).
  • Security: a malicious "keyboard" (BadUSB, Rubber Ducky) can type commands. Hardened hosts use USBGuard to allow-list devices, and many cloud images disable USB storage.
  • Troubleshooting edge devices: dmesg -w while plugging tells you whether enumeration fails (power, cable, descriptor errors) or the driver is missing.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
lsusb                                   # devices with VID:PID
lsusb -t                                # tree: bus, port, speed, driver
sudo lsusb -v -d 046d: 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'bInterfaceClass|bEndpointAddress|bInterval|wMaxPacketSize'
sudo dmesg -w                           # plug in a USB device and watch enumeration
sudo usbhid-dump -m 046d 2>/dev/null | head   # raw report descriptor (package: usbutils/usbhid-dump)
sudo evtest                             # pick your keyboard; see EV_KEY events per press
ls /sys/bus/usb/devices/                # sysfs view of the bus

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Concept Remember Who starts transfers Always the host Keyboard transfer type Interrupt IN, polled every 1–8 ms Device class HID = class 3 Report 1 modifier byte + 1 reserved + 6 key usages 0x04 Key in "A" position, layout comes later Release / repeat New report without the key / done in software

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. If USB devices can't speak first, how does a key press reach the computer?

The host polls the keyboard's interrupt endpoint every 1–8 ms; the next poll after the press returns a report instead of NAK.

2. Why does one generic driver work for almost every keyboard and mouse?

HID devices describe their report layout in a report descriptor, so the HID core can parse any of them.

3. Does the keyboard send the letter 'a'?

No. It sends usage 0x04, a key position. The layout (xkb in user space) decides it means "a", "q" or something else.

4. How much latency can a 125 Hz polling rate add?

Up to 8 ms (average ~4 ms) before the host even sees the report.

5. Why do some hardened servers block unknown USB devices?

A device can claim to be a keyboard and type commands (BadUSB). Allow-listing with USBGuard prevents that.

docs.title: 1.3 — The Linux input stack
docs.text:
In short

The kernel turns the keyboard report into an evdev event (KEY_A pressed). The compositor reads it through libinput, decides which window has keyboard focus, and sends that window a raw keycode over the Wayland protocol. The app's xkbcommon applies the keymap (layout + modifiers) to get a keysym and the text "a", and the toolkit or browser delivers it to your code as a key event.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Input subsystem — Kernel layer for all input devices Drivers report events; it fans them out evdev event device Generic interface /dev/input/eventN struct input_event: time, type, code, value EV_KEY / EV_SYN — Event types Key press/release/repeat; "end of this batch" Keycode — Number for a physical key KEY_A = 30 in Linux (+8 in xkb) libinput — Library handling input devices Device setup, pointer accel, gestures, key state Compositor — Display server in Wayland (GNOME Mutter, KDE KWin, Sway) Owns input + output, composes windows Wayland / X11 — Display protocols Wayland: compositor routes input; X11: X server does Focus — Which surface receives keyboard input Chosen by the compositor Keymap — Rules from keycodes to symbols Layout, variant, options (e.g. tr, us, caps:escape) xkbcommon X Keyboard Extension common library Keymap engine used by apps and compositors Tracks modifier state, returns keysym + UTF-8 Keysym key symbol Meaning of a key in a layout XKB_KEY_a, XKB_KEY_A, XKB_KEY_Return Modifier / level — Shift, AltGr, Ctrl… / which symbol on a key Shift = level 2, AltGr = level 3 IME Input Method Editor Composes text for complex scripts ibus/fcitx via text-input protocol KeyboardEvent — Browser's key event key (meaning), code (physical position)

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Every input device gets a /dev/input/eventN file. Reading it returns fixed-size input_event records:

time        type     code       value
...123456   EV_MSC   MSC_SCAN   0x70004     (raw HID usage)
...123456   EV_KEY   KEY_A      1           (1 = press)
...123456   EV_SYN   SYN_REPORT 0           (end of batch)
...223401   EV_KEY   KEY_A      0           (0 = release)

The kernel doesn't know about layouts or text: KEY_A only means "the key in the A position". Anyone with read access to these files could log every keystroke, so they're root/input-group only.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
• On Wayland, the compositor (GNOME Shell/Mutter, KDE KWin, Sway, Hyprland) opens the evdev devices through libinput (with permission from logind, which hands them over for the active session).
  • It handles global shortcuts first (Super, Alt+Tab, screenshot).
  • Then it sends the event only to the focused surface: wl_keyboard.key(serial, time, keycode, pressed). When focus changes, the new window gets enter with the set of keys already down.
  • It also sends the keymap once (as a file descriptor) and modifiers events, so the app and compositor agree on layout and Shift/Caps state.

On X11, the X server did this, but any X client could listen to all keystrokes, which is a big reason for the move to Wayland.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Keycode 30 (+8 = xkb keycode 38, named <AC01>).
  2. The keymap for layout tr says <AC01> has symbols [ a, A ] on levels 1–2.
  3. xkbcommon looks at the current modifier state (Shift? Caps Lock? AltGr?) to pick the level → keysym a or A.
  4. xkb_state_key_get_utf8() returns the text "a".

That's why the same physical key gives a on US-QWERTY and q on AZERTY, and why ı/i on the Turkish layout just works: it's all in the keymap. Dead keys and compose sequences (´ + e = é) are handled at this layer; full input methods for Chinese/Japanese use an IME via the text-input protocol.

Key repeat is generated by the client/toolkit using the rate and delay the compositor advertises (repeat_info), not by the keyboard.

docs.title: 4 · In the toolkit and the browser
docs.text:
GTK, Qt and Chromium wrap all of the above. In the browser your JS sees a KeyboardEvent:

Field Shift + key in "A" position (Turkish Q layout) Meaning event.code "KeyA" Physical position (layout-independent) event.key "A" What it means in the current layout event.shiftKey true Modifier state event.repeat false Auto-repeat?

Use code for game controls ("WASD" positions), key for shortcuts and text, and the input event (not keydown) for text fields so IMEs and paste work.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Remote desktops / VDI / browser consoles (noVNC, cloud serial consoles) translate keycodes between layouts; "wrong characters in the console" is usually a keymap mismatch between client and server. Typing passwords with special characters there is risky.
  • Headless servers: localectl set-keymap / set-x11-keymap configure layouts for the console and for X/Wayland sessions; loadkeys for the TTY.
  • Kiosks and test automation inject input with uinput (a virtual evdev device), ydotool (Wayland) or xdotool (X11).
  • Security model: on Wayland apps can't read other windows' keys or inject input globally; tools that need that (screen sharing, automation) must go through portals.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
sudo evtest                                 # raw evdev events of one device
sudo libinput debug-events                  # what libinput sees (needs libinput-tools)
echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE                      # wayland or x11
localectl status                            # current console and X/Wayland layouts
xkbcli compile-keymap --layout tr | grep -A3 '<AC01>'   # keymap entry for the "A" key (libxkbcommon-tools)
xkbcli interactive-wayland 2>/dev/null || xkbcli interactive-evdev   # keycode → keysym → UTF-8 live

// Browser console: watch code vs key
addEventListener('keydown', e => console.log(e.code, e.key, e.shiftKey, e.repeat));

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Layer Knows Example Keyboard (HID) Key position usage 0x04 Kernel (evdev) Linux keycode KEY_A = 30 Compositor Which window, shortcuts wl_keyboard.key 30 pressed xkbcommon Layout + modifiers keysym A, text "A" Browser Both code: "KeyA", key: "A"

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Where does the letter (as opposed to the key position) get decided on a Wayland desktop?

In the application, by xkbcommon applying the keymap the compositor sent, using the current modifier state.

2. Why are /dev/input/event* files not readable by normal users?

Reading them would let any program capture every keystroke system-wide (a keylogger).

3. Why could any X11 app capture your passwords, but not on Wayland?

X11 let any client listen to all input; on Wayland the compositor only sends input to the focused surface.

4. A game should use WASD on every layout. Which KeyboardEvent field should it read?

event.code, the physical key position, not event.key.

5. Who generates key repeat when you hold a key down?

The client/toolkit, using the rate and delay advertised by the compositor; the keyboard only reports that the key is still down.

docs.title: Chapter 2 — CPU & Assembly
docs.text:
In short

A CPU is a very fast, very simple machine. It fetches the instruction that the RIP register points to, decodes it, executes it on values held in registers, writes back the result and moves on to the next one, billions of times per second. Everything else (caches, RAM, disk) exists to keep it fed with data.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CPU Central Processing Unit The processor running your code Fetches, decodes and executes instructions ISA Instruction Set Architecture The instructions a CPU understands (x86-64, ARM64) Compilers translate code into this instruction set Register — Tiny storage slots inside the core The only place math happens directly RIP / RSP Instruction Pointer / Stack Pointer Next instruction address / top of stack Updated by every instruction, call, ret and push/pop ALU Arithmetic Logic Unit The part that does math and logic Adds, compares, shifts values from registers Cache line — 64-byte unit moved between RAM and caches Reading one byte loads its 63 neighbours too L1 / L2 / L3 Level 1/2/3 cache On-chip memories, smaller = faster Keep recently used data close to the core Pipeline — Overlapping fetch/decode/execute of several instructions Keeps every stage busy every cycle Branch prediction — Guessing which way an if goes Wrong guess → pipeline flush, wasted cycles Stack frame — A function's area on the stack Holds return address, saved registers, locals ABI Application Binary Interface Binary-level rules between compiled code Which registers hold args/return values, stack layout GHz gigahertz Clock frequency 3 GHz = 3 billion cycles per second

docs.title: 🗺️ Big picture
docs.text: Reference: x86-64 (Intel/AMD) on Linux. ARM (Apple M-series, AWS Graviton) has different register names but the same ideas.

docs.title: 1 · From C to bytes (build time)
docs.text:
The CPU never sees your C, Go or Python. It only sees machine code: bytes that encode instructions.

int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel add.c produces:

add:
    lea  eax, [rdi + rsi]   ; eax = a + b   (a arrives in RDI, b in RSI)
    ret                     ; return to caller, result is in EAX

objdump -d add.o shows the actual bytes: 8d 04 37 (lea) and c3 (ret). Four bytes, and that's the whole function.

On Ubuntu you'll also see endbr64 (f3 0f 1e fa) first. It's a security landing marker (Intel CET) the compiler adds by default; you can ignore it here.

Step Tool Output Compile gcc -S Assembly text (human-readable instructions) Assemble as Object file (machine code + symbols) Link ld Executable ELF file on disk (Chapter 4 goes deep here)

Calling convention (System V, Linux x86-64)

Arguments go in RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, the return value comes back in RAX. This is an agreement between compilers, so code compiled by GCC can call code compiled by Clang or Rust.

docs.title: 2 · Registers: the CPU's hands
docs.text:
Registers are a handful of tiny storage slots inside the CPU core. They are the only place the CPU can do math on directly.

Register Role RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI, R8–R15 General purpose, 64-bit each. EAX is the lower 32 bits of RAX. RIP Instruction pointer: the address of the next instruction. "Where am I in the program?" RSP Stack pointer: the top of the stack. RBP Frame pointer (optional): the base of the current function's stack frame. RFLAGS Result flags: zero? negative? overflow? Used by if (cmp + je/jne).

Chapter 1 link: when an interrupt arrives, the CPU saves exactly these (RIP, RFLAGS, RSP, …) so it can resume later.

docs.title: 3 · The memory hierarchy
docs.text:
The CPU is much faster than memory. To hide that gap, data moves through layers that get smaller but faster closer to the core.

Level Typical size Typical latency In CPU cycles (3 GHz) Register ~16 × 8 bytes ~0.3 ns 1 L1 cache (per core, split L1i/L1d) 32–64 KB ~1 ns ~4 L2 cache (per core) 1–2 MB ~4 ns ~12 L3 cache (shared) 16–100+ MB ~10–20 ns ~40 RAM GBs ~80–100 ns ~300 NVMe SSD TBs ~20–100 µs ~100,000
  • Data moves between RAM and caches in cache lines of 64 bytes. Reading one byte brings its 63 neighbours along.
  • That's why arrays are fast (neighbours are already in cache) and linked lists are slow (every node is a new trip to RAM).

Remember this

If L1 were 1 second, RAM would be ~1.5 minutes and an SSD read would be ~1 day. Most "performance work" is really "stop waiting for memory" work.

docs.title: 4 · The instruction cycle
docs.text:
# Stage What happens 9 — RIP points at the next instruction in memory (via L1i cache). 10 Fetch Read the instruction bytes at RIP: 8d 04 37. 11 Decode Work out what they mean: lea eax, [rdi+rsi]. Modern x86 cores translate this into simpler internal micro-ops. 12 Execute The ALU (arithmetic logic unit) computes 2 + 3. — Write back Store the result in a register: EAX = 5. Advance RIP by the instruction's length and start again.

Real cores do this as a pipeline: while one instruction executes, the next is decoding and the one after is being fetched. They also execute out of order and predict branches to stay busy. When a prediction is wrong, the pipeline is flushed and work is wasted. That's why unpredictable ifs in hot loops cost performance.

docs.title: 5 · The stack: how functions call each other
docs.text:
Unoptimized (-O0), the same add shows the stack at work:

add:
    push rbp                    ; save caller's frame pointer on the stack
    mov  rbp, rsp               ; my frame starts here
    mov  DWORD PTR [rbp-4], edi ; store a in my frame
    mov  DWORD PTR [rbp-8], esi ; store b in my frame
    mov  edx, DWORD PTR [rbp-4]
    mov  eax, DWORD PTR [rbp-8]
    add  eax, edx               ; eax = a + b
    pop  rbp                    ; restore caller's frame pointer
    ret                         ; pop return address into RIP → jump back
  • call add pushes the return address (the instruction after the call) onto the stack and jumps to add.
  • The stack grows downward in memory: push decreases RSP, pop increases it.
  • ret pops that address back into RIP, and execution continues in the caller.
  • Every function call gets its own stack frame. Infinite recursion keeps adding frames until it runs out of space: a stack overflow.

docs.title: How does the stack work during a call?
docs.text: call pushes the return address and jumps. The prologue saves the old frame pointer and reserves space for locals. The epilogue undoes that, and ret pops the return address into RIP. Every call grows the stack downward; every return shrinks it back.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the service that only crashes on new nodes
docs.text:
The alarm

The platform team adds a new node pool with a cheaper instance type. Pods scheduled there die instantly with exit code 132; the same image runs fine on the old nodes.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

132 = 128 + 4 → SIGILL, illegal instruction. dmesg on the node: traps: app[...] trap invalid opcode.

🔍 Clue 2

The Dockerfile builds with -march=native on a CI runner with AVX-512. grep -o avx512f /proc/cpuinfo on the new nodes → nothing.

🎯 Root cause

The compiler emitted AVX-512 instructions because the build machine had them. The new CPUs don't implement those instructions, so the first one executed traps.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Build for a baseline (-march=x86-64-v3, or v2), or ship variants and select at runtime; use node affinity if you truly need AVX-512. Lesson: the ISA is a contract: binaries must target the oldest CPU they may run on.

docs.title: 🧭 Go deeper

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 02-cpu (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) See your CPU: cores, cache sizes, flags
lscpu
lscpu -C                          # cache sizes per level

# 2) C → assembly → bytes
echo 'int add(int a,int b){return a+b;}' > add.c
gcc -O2 -S -masm=intel add.c && cat add.s
gcc -O0 -S -masm=intel add.c -o add-O0.s && cat add-O0.s   # with the stack frame
gcc -O2 -c add.c && objdump -d -M intel add.o              # the real bytes

# 3) Count instructions and cache misses of a command
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses ls -R /usr > /dev/null

# 4) Step through instructions and watch registers change
gcc -g -O0 -o add add.c -x c - <<< 'int add(int,int);int main(){return add(2,3);}'
gdb -q ./add -ex 'break add' -ex 'run' -ex 'layout asm' -ex 'info registers rip rsp rdi rsi'

Exercise: in gdb, run stepi a few times inside add and watch RSP decrease after push rbp and RIP jump back after ret.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
C → compiler → assembly → assembler → machine code (bytes) → ELF file on disk
   → loaded into RAM → cache lines (64 B) → L3 → L2 → L1 → registers
   → FETCH (at RIP) → DECODE → EXECUTE (ALU) → WRITE BACK → RIP += len → repeat
  • The CPU only understands bytes. Assembly is a human-readable spelling of them.
  • Registers are where work happens. RIP = where am I, RSP = top of stack.
  • Memory is a hierarchy: smaller = faster. Locality (nearby data) is king.
  • call / ret use the stack to remember where to return.
  • Args in RDI, RSI, …, return value in RAX (System V calling convention).

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is iterating over an array faster than over a linked list with the same number of elements?

The array's elements sit next to each other, so one 64-byte cache line brings several of them at once and the prefetcher can guess what comes next. Linked-list nodes are scattered, so each one may need a ~100 ns trip to RAM.

2. What does the RIP register hold, and who changes it?

The address of the next instruction. It normally advances by the instruction's length. Jumps, call, ret and interrupts change it directly.

3. What does ret actually do?

It pops the return address that call pushed onto the stack and puts it into RIP, so execution continues right after the call.

4. Why can a program compiled with GCC call a library compiled with Clang?

Both follow the same calling convention (System V ABI): which registers carry arguments and return values, and which registers each side must preserve.

5. Roughly how many CPU cycles does one RAM access cost at 3 GHz?

About 300 cycles (~100 ns × 3 cycles/ns). During that time the core could have executed hundreds of instructions.

docs.title: 2.1 — Instruction sets & assembly
docs.text:
In short

An ISA is the contract between software and a CPU: the instructions, registers and rules the chip promises to understand. Compilers turn your code into those instructions, and the assembler encodes them into bytes. The calling convention (part of the ABI) says how functions pass arguments and results. That's what you need to read compiler output, perf profiles and crash dumps.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) ISA Instruction Set Architecture The instructions + registers a CPU family understands x86-64, ARM64 (AArch64), RISC-V CISC / RISC Complex / Reduced Instruction Set Computer Two design philosophies Many variable-length instructions vs few fixed-length ones Opcode operation code The bytes that say which instruction 8d = LEA, c3 = RET Operand — What an instruction works on Register, memory address, immediate value Addressing mode — How a memory operand is computed [base + index*scale + disp] ModRM / SIB Mod-Reg-R/M / Scale-Index-Base x86 bytes encoding operands Pick registers and address form Immediate — A constant inside the instruction mov eax, 42 Flags (RFLAGS) — Bits set by arithmetic ZF (zero), CF (carry), SF (sign), OF (overflow) Jump / branch — Changes RIP jmp, conditional je, jne, jl … after cmp SIMD Single Instruction, Multiple Data One instruction on many values SSE, AVX2, AVX-512 (x86); NEON, SVE (ARM) µop micro-operation Internal simpler operation x86 decodes instructions into µops ABI Application Binary Interface Binary-level rules between compiled code Calling convention, struct layout, syscalls Calling convention — How args/returns/registers are handled in calls System V on Linux/macOS, Microsoft x64 on Windows Disassembler — Turns bytes back into assembly objdump -d, gdb, Compiler Explorer

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
The ISA is the visible interface of a CPU: registers, instructions, memory model, privilege levels. Any chip implementing it (Intel, AMD, different generations) runs the same binaries, even though their insides differ completely. That's why you build separate images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

x86-64 ARM64 (AArch64) RISC-V Style CISC RISC RISC (open standard) Instruction length 1–15 bytes always 4 bytes 4 (2 with compressed ext.) General registers 16 (RAX…R15) 31 (X0…X30) 31 (x1…x31) Memory operands Most instructions can use memory Only load/store touch memory Load/store only Where Most servers, PCs Phones, Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton, Ampere, NVIDIA Grace Embedded, growing

Inside, modern x86 cores decode instructions into RISC-like µops, so the difference today is mostly about decoding cost, ecosystem and power efficiency.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
return a + b; compiles (with -O2) to lea eax, [rdi+rsi] / ret, which becomes 8d 04 37 c3:

Byte Field Meaning 8d opcode LEA (load effective address, used here as a fast add) 04 ModRM destination register EAX; memory operand uses a SIB byte 37 SIB base = RDI, index = RSI, scale = 1 c3 opcode RET

On x86 the CPU must find where each instruction ends before decoding the next (lengths vary), which is why x86 front ends are complex and cache decoded µops. ARM64's fixed 4-byte instructions make decoding many at once simpler.

docs.title: 3 · Reading assembly: the 15 instructions you'll see most
docs.text:
Instruction Does mov dst, src Copy lea dst, [addr] Compute an address (often arithmetic) add / sub / imul / xor Arithmetic (xor eax, eax = set to 0) cmp a, b / test a, b Set flags only je / jne / jl / jg / jmp (Conditional) jump call f / ret Push return address & jump / pop & return push / pop Stack syscall Enter the kernel nop Nothing (alignment) endbr64 CET landing pad for indirect jumps (security)

Intel vs AT&T syntax: objdump defaults to AT&T (lea (%rdi,%rsi),%eax, source first); add -M intel for the order used above.

docs.title: 4 · The calling convention
docs.text:
• Integer/pointer arguments: RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9, then the stack. Floats in XMM0–7.
  • Return value in RAX (and RDX for 128-bit), floats in XMM0.
  • Callee-saved (RBX, RBP, R12–R15): a function that uses them must restore them. Caller-saved: may be overwritten by any call.
  • The stack must be 16-byte aligned at each call (SIMD instructions rely on it).
  • Syscalls use a slightly different set: number in RAX, args in RDI, RSI, RDX, R10, R8, R9.

ARM64 is similar: args in X0–X7, return in X0, return address in the link register X30.

docs.title: 5 · SIMD: one instruction, many values
docs.text: AVX2 registers hold 256 bits = 8 floats; AVX-512 holds 16. One vaddps adds 8 pairs at once. Compilers auto-vectorize simple loops at -O2/-O3; libraries (BLAS, simdjson, compression, crypto, NumPy) use it heavily. Containers built with -march=native can crash with "illegal instruction" on older CPUs that lack those extensions.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Multi-arch images: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 + a manifest list. ARM nodes (Graviton etc.) are often 20–40% cheaper per performance; a wrong-arch image fails with exec format error.
  • illegal instruction (SIGILL) after moving to new or older hardware: the binary uses AVX-512/AVX2 the CPU doesn't have. Build for a baseline (x86-64-v2/v3) or check /proc/cpuinfo flags.
  • Reading crash dumps: in a core dump or gdb backtrace, the first arguments of the crashed function are in RDI/RSI/RDX; info registers + disassemble tells you which instruction faulted.
  • Profiling: perf annotate shows which instructions are hot; you don't need to write assembly, but recognizing call, loops and div helps.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
cat > add.c <<'EOF'
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
int sum(int *v, int n) { int s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) s += v[i]; return s; }
EOF
gcc -O2 -c add.c && objdump -d -M intel add.o          # see lea/ret and the bytes
gcc -O3 -mavx2 -S -masm=intel -o - add.c | grep -E 'vpadd|ymm' | head   # auto-vectorized loop
grep -o -w -E 'avx2|avx512f|sse4_2' /proc/cpuinfo | sort -u           # SIMD the CPU supports
/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --help 2>/dev/null | grep supported      # x86-64-v2/v3/v4 levels
uname -m; docker buildx ls 2>/dev/null | head -3
# Online: https://godbolt.org (Compiler Explorer) — paste C, Go or Rust and see the assembly

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Remember Args (Linux x86-64) RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9 Return RAX Syscall syscall, number in RAX, 4th arg in R10 Args (ARM64) X0–X7, return X0, LR = X30 Zero a register xor eax, eax Disassemble objdump -d -M intel, gdb disassemble, godbolt

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does an amd64 image fail on a Graviton node?

Graviton is ARM64; the binary's instructions belong to a different ISA. The kernel refuses to execute it (exec format error).

2. Why is decoding x86 harder than ARM64?

x86 instructions are 1–15 bytes long, so the CPU must find instruction boundaries first; ARM64 instructions are always 4 bytes.

3. In a gdb session a function crashed. Where do you find its first two arguments?

In RDI and RSI (System V calling convention), if they haven't been overwritten yet.

4. A program dies with SIGILL after migrating to another VM type. What's a likely cause?

It was compiled for CPU extensions (AVX-512, AVX2) the new CPU doesn't support.

5. What does xor eax, eax do and why do compilers prefer it?

Sets EAX to zero; it's shorter than mov eax, 0 and recognized by the CPU as a dependency-breaking zero idiom.

docs.title: 2.2 — Caches & the memory hierarchy
docs.text:
In short

A CPU core can do several instructions per nanosecond but RAM takes ~100 ns to answer, so chips put small, fast caches (L1, L2, L3) between them and move memory in 64-byte cache lines. Programs that access memory sequentially and compactly stay in cache and run fast, while scattered access, false sharing between cores and remote NUMA memory can make the same algorithm many times slower.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Cache — Small fast memory holding recent data Checked before going to the next, slower level L1 / L2 / L3 (LLC) Level 1/2/3 (Last-Level Cache) Cache levels L1/L2 per core, L3 shared by cores Cache line — Unit of transfer: 64 bytes Reading 1 byte loads its whole line Hit / miss — Found / not found in a cache Miss → ask the next level Locality — Temporal (reuse soon) + spatial (neighbours) Caches exploit both Prefetcher — Hardware that guesses the next lines Great for sequential/strided access Associativity — Where a line may live in a cache 8-way = one of 8 slots in its set Coherence / MESI Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid Keeping cores' copies consistent Writing invalidates other cores' copies False sharing — Different variables in the same line written by different cores The line ping-pongs between cores NUMA Non-Uniform Memory Access Each socket has its "own" RAM Remote memory is slower than local TLB Translation Lookaside Buffer Cache of virtual→physical translations Misses cost a page-table walk Huge pages — 2 MB / 1 GB pages instead of 4 KB Fewer TLB entries needed Memory bandwidth — GB/s RAM can deliver Often the real limit for data-heavy code Cache-miss / IPC Instructions Per Cycle Key perf counters perf stat shows both

docs.title: What is the problem?
docs.text: At 3 GHz one cycle is 0.33 ns. A DRAM access is ~100 ns, so ~300 cycles; a modern core could have executed 1000+ instructions in that time. Without caches every core would be idle almost all the time.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The core asks for an address. L1 (32–64 KB, ~4–5 cycles) is checked first.
  2. On a miss, L2 (1–2 MB, ~14 cycles), then the shared L3 (tens to hundreds of MB, ~40–70 cycles), then DRAM.
  3. The whole 64-byte line comes back and is kept in the caches. Something else is evicted (roughly least-recently used).
  4. The prefetcher notices patterns (i, i+1, i+2…) and fetches lines before you ask.

docs.title: 2 · Locality: why data layout matters
docs.text:
Pattern Cache behaviour Example Sequential array scan Excellent: every line fully used, prefetcher helps for i in range(n): sum += a[i] Strided access Wastes most of each line Column-wise walk of a row-major matrix Pointer chasing Every step can be a full DRAM miss Linked lists, trees, hash maps of pointers Small hot working set Stays in L1/L2 Lookup tables, small dicts

That's why arrays beat linked lists, why "struct of arrays" helps analytics, and why columnar formats (Parquet, ClickHouse) are fast: they read only the needed columns, sequentially.

docs.title: 3 · Coherence and false sharing
docs.text: Every core has its own L1/L2, so the hardware keeps copies consistent (MESI): before a core writes a line, all other copies are invalidated. If two threads write different variables that sit in the same 64-byte line, the line bounces between cores on every write; each bounce costs ~50–100 ns. Adding threads makes the program slower. Fixes: pad/align hot per-thread data to 64 bytes, or keep per-thread counters and sum at the end.

docs.title: 4 · NUMA, TLBs and bandwidth
docs.text:
• NUMA: in a 2-socket server each socket has its own memory controllers. Accessing the other socket's RAM is ~1.3–2× slower. The kernel tries to allocate memory on the node where the thread runs; moving threads across sockets hurts.
  • TLB: every access needs a virtual→physical translation (chapter 3). The TLB caches a few thousand of them. With 4 KB pages a 100 GB heap needs 25 million entries; huge pages (2 MB / 1 GB) cut that drastically. Databases and JVMs often benefit; Transparent Huge Pages can also cause latency spikes, so many DBs tune it.
  • Bandwidth: a server socket gives ~200–500+ GB/s of DRAM bandwidth. Streaming workloads (analytics, AI inference on CPU) hit this limit long before running out of cores. GPUs use HBM for the same reason (10.2).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Noisy neighbours: pods on the same node share L3 and memory bandwidth. A batch job can slow a latency-sensitive service without touching its CPU limit. Intel RDT / AMD QoS (cache allocation, memory bandwidth allocation) can partition them.
  • Kubernetes Topology Manager + CPU Manager (static) pin Guaranteed pods to cores on one NUMA node together with their devices (GPU, NIC).
  • numactl --hardware, lscpu show the layout; databases often need numactl --interleave=all or NUMA-aware settings.
  • CPU limits ≠ cache: two pods with the same CPU quota can perform very differently depending on what shares their L3.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
lscpu | grep -iE 'model name|socket|numa|L1d|L2|L3'
numactl --hardware 2>/dev/null | head
getconf -a | grep -i CACHE_LINESIZE

# Row-wise vs column-wise: same work, very different speed
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import numpy as np, time
a = np.random.rand(4000, 4000)
t = time.perf_counter(); s = sum(a[i, :].sum() for i in range(4000)); r = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter(); s = sum(a[:, j].sum() for j in range(4000)); c = time.perf_counter() - t
print(f"rows {r:.3f}s   columns {c:.3f}s   ({c/r:.1f}x slower)")
PYEOF

perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses -- sleep 1 2>&1 | tail -12
cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Level Latency Size L1 ~1 ns 32–64 KB / core L2 ~4 ns 1–2 MB / core L3 ~10–20 ns 32–512 MB / socket DRAM (local / remote NUMA) ~80–100 / ~130–150 ns GB–TB NVMe ~10–100 µs TB Smell Likely cause More threads → slower False sharing / lock contention High LLC misses, low IPC Working set > L3, pointer chasing Slower on 2-socket box Remote NUMA memory Latency spikes on big heaps TLB misses / THP compaction

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does reading one byte from RAM cost as much as reading 64?

Memory moves in 64-byte cache lines; the whole line is fetched either way.

2. Why is iterating a linked list much slower than an array of the same length?

Each node can be anywhere in memory, so each step can be a cache miss and the prefetcher can't predict the next address.

3. Two threads increment two different counters and get slower than one thread. Why?

The counters share a cache line (false sharing); each write invalidates the other core's copy.

4. What does NUMA mean for a database on a 2-socket server?

Memory attached to the other socket is slower; threads and their data should stay on the same node (or memory interleaved).

5. Why do huge pages help large heaps?

One TLB entry covers 2 MB (or 1 GB) instead of 4 KB, so far fewer TLB misses and page-table walks.

docs.title: 2.3 — Pipelines, branch prediction & speculation
docs.text:
In short

A modern core doesn't run one instruction at a time: it pipelines them, executes several per cycle out of order as soon as their inputs are ready, and guesses the outcome of branches so it can keep going. Correct guesses make code fast, wrong ones throw work away, and the traces left by that speculative work are what Spectre-style attacks exploit.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Pipeline — Splitting execution into stages Each stage works on a different instruction each cycle Superscalar — Several instructions per cycle Multiple decoders and execution units OoO Out-of-Order execution Run instructions when inputs are ready, not in program order Results committed in order later ROB ReOrder Buffer Tracks in-flight instructions Retires them in program order Register renaming — Mapping architectural to physical registers Removes false dependencies Dependency chain — Instructions that need each other's results Limits parallelism IPC / CPI Instructions Per Cycle / Cycles Per Instruction Efficiency measure perf stat reports it Branch predictor — Hardware that guesses branch direction and target Learns from history Misprediction — Wrong guess Pipeline flush, ~15–20 cycles lost Speculative execution — Running the predicted path before it's confirmed Discarded if wrong Spectre / Meltdown — Side-channel attacks on speculation Secrets leak through cache timing SMT / Hyper-Threading Simultaneous Multi-Threading Two hardware threads share one core Fills idle units; a vCPU is often one of these Turbo / DVFS Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling Clock speed changes with load and heat Fewer active cores → higher boost Top-down analysis — Classify cycles: frontend, bad speculation, backend, retiring perf stat --topdown

docs.title: 1 · Pipelining: an assembly line for instructions
How does it work?
docs.text:
Like a car factory: while one instruction executes, the next is being decoded and the one after is being fetched. A simple 5-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write-back) can finish one instruction per cycle even though each takes 5 cycles.

Modern cores go much further:

  • Wide: fetch/decode 4–8 instructions per cycle, with many execution units (ALUs, load/store, vector).
  • Out of order: a scheduler holds hundreds of instructions and runs any whose inputs are ready, hiding cache-miss latency behind other work.
  • In-order retirement: results become visible in program order, so the program behaves as if executed sequentially.

What limits it: dependency chains (each step needs the previous result), cache misses that stall everything, and branches.

docs.title: Why guess?
docs.text: A pipeline is 15–20 stages deep. When it fetches an if, the condition won't be known for many cycles. Waiting would empty the pipeline on every branch (and code has a branch every ~5 instructions). So the CPU predicts the direction (taken/not taken) and the target (for indirect calls, virtual methods, switch) using history tables, and is right >95% of the time.

docs.title: What does a misprediction cost?
docs.text: All speculative work after the branch is thrown away: ~15–20 cycles. A branch that's random (50/50) costs a lot in a hot loop. Classic demo: summing values > 128 in an array is several times faster if the array is sorted first, because the branch becomes predictable. Compilers sometimes turn branches into branch-free code (cmov), and likely()/unlikely() hints help.

docs.title: 3 · Speculation and Spectre
docs.text:
The CPU executes predicted paths before checks are done, including bounds checks and (in Meltdown's case) permission checks. Results are discarded, but cache state is not rolled back. An attacker can train the predictor so the victim speculatively reads a secret and touches a cache line that depends on it, then measure which line is fast to load.

  • Meltdown (2018): user code could read kernel memory on affected Intel CPUs → fixed with KPTI (separate kernel page tables), now mostly fixed in hardware.
  • Spectre variants: still a class of issues; mitigations include retpolines, IBRS/eIBRS, barriers, and process/VM isolation.
  • Cost: mitigations make syscalls and context switches more expensive; check /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/.

docs.title: 4 · SMT, frequency and what a "vCPU" is
docs.text:
• SMT / Hyper-Threading: one physical core runs two hardware threads, sharing execution units and caches. It gives maybe +10–30% throughput, not 2×. In most clouds, 1 vCPU = 1 hardware thread, so 2 vCPUs may be one physical core.
  • Security-sensitive environments sometimes disable SMT (cross-thread side channels) or schedule only same-tenant workloads on sibling threads.
  • Turbo/boost: clock speed rises when few cores are busy and drops under all-core load or heat; benchmarks on an idle laptop don't predict a busy server.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• CPU limits and throttling: in Kubernetes a CPU limit is a CFS quota of time per 100 ms period. Multithreaded apps can burn the quota early in the period and then be throttled for the rest; that shows up as latency spikes with low average CPU. Watch container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total; many teams set requests but no limits for latency-sensitive services.
  • Sizing: 4 vCPU on SMT hardware = 2 physical cores. For CPU-bound work, compare instance types by real benchmarks, not vCPU count.
  • Kernel mitigations cost a few % on syscall-heavy workloads; the trade-off is a security decision (mitigations= boot parameter), usually keep them on in multi-tenant environments.
  • Profiling: low IPC (<1) means the CPU is waiting (memory, mispredictions); high IPC (>2–3) means you're compute-bound and need a better algorithm or more cores.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
lscpu | grep -E 'Thread|Core|Socket|MHz'          # SMT: "Thread(s) per core: 2"
grep -r . /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/ | sed 's#.*/##'

# Branch prediction demo: same data, sorted vs unsorted
cat > branch.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <time.h>
int cmp(const void*a,const void*b){return *(int*)a-*(int*)b;}
int main(int c,char**v){int n=1<<24,*a=malloc(n*4);srand(1);
 for(int i=0;i<n;i++)a[i]=rand()%256; if(c>1)qsort(a,n,4,cmp);
 clock_t t=clock(); long s=0;
 for(int r=0;r<10;r++)for(int i=0;i<n;i++)if(a[i]>=128)s+=a[i];
 printf("sum=%ld loop=%.2fs\n",s,(double)(clock()-t)/CLOCKS_PER_SEC);}
EOF
gcc -O0 branch.c -o branch   # -O0 keeps the real branch; at -O1+ gcc may emit branch-free cmov
./branch; ./branch sorted    # e.g. loop=0.86s vs loop=0.28s
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branches,branch-misses ./branch        2>&1 | grep -E 'branch|insn|elapsed'
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,branches,branch-misses ./branch sorted 2>&1 | grep -E 'branch|insn|elapsed'
perf stat --topdown -a sleep 2 2>/dev/null | tail -6    # where cycles go (if supported)

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Metric Healthy Suspicious IPC 2–4 (compute) < 1 (stalled) Branch-miss rate < 1–2% > 5% in hot code Cache-miss rate (LLC) low high + low IPC → memory-bound CFS throttled periods ~0 rising → CPU limit too low / bursty threads

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. How can a CPU finish one instruction per cycle if each takes 15+ cycles?

Pipelining: many instructions are in different stages at the same time.

2. Why does sorting an array make a branchy loop over it faster?

The if becomes predictable (all false, then all true), so mispredictions and pipeline flushes nearly disappear.

3. What does Spectre exploit?

Speculative execution leaves traces in the cache that aren't rolled back; timing cache accesses reveals data read speculatively.

4. Your cloud VM has 8 vCPUs. How many physical cores is that likely to be?

Usually 4 physical cores with SMT (2 hardware threads each), depending on the provider and instance type.

5. A pod with low average CPU shows latency spikes and rising cfs_throttled_periods. What's happening?

Its threads use up the CPU limit's quota early in each 100 ms period and are throttled until the next one. Raise or remove the limit, or reduce thread bursts.

docs.title: Chapter 3 — The operating system
docs.text:
In short

The operating system kernel is the referee. It gives every program the illusion of its own CPU (scheduler), its own memory (virtual memory) and simple access to devices (files, sockets). At the same time it makes sure no program can touch what isn't its own. Programs ask it for anything they need through syscalls.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) OS / kernel Operating System The software that manages hardware and programs Runs in ring 0, everything else asks it via syscalls Process / PID Process ID A running program with its own memory Created by fork/clone + execve Thread — A worker sharing a process's memory Own stack and registers, scheduled independently Scheduler — Decides which task runs on which core Time slices + timer interrupts + context switches EEVDF / CFS Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First / Completely Fair Scheduler Linux's scheduler algorithms Give each task a fair share, weighted by nice Context switch — Switching the CPU from one task to another Save registers, load the next task's, maybe switch page tables Virtual memory — Each process's private view of memory Page tables map virtual pages to physical frames MMU / TLB Memory Management Unit / Translation Lookaside Buffer Hardware doing translation / its cache Translates every address, caches recent ones Page fault — Access to an unmapped page Kernel maps or loads it, then the instruction retries Syscall System call A request from a program to the kernel Number in RAX, args in registers, syscall instruction fd file descriptor Small integer handle to an open file/socket/pipe Index into the process's fd table VFS Virtual File System Kernel layer giving one API for all file types Routes read/write to the right filesystem or driver Signal — A notification sent to a process SIGTERM (polite), SIGKILL (final), SIGINT (Ctrl+C) cgroup / OOM control group / Out Of Memory Resource limits for groups of processes / memory exhaustion Exceeding a memory cgroup limit triggers the OOM killer

docs.title: 1 · Process: a running program
docs.text:
A process is a program loaded into memory and running, with everything the kernel tracks about it:

Part What it is PID Process ID, a number. PID 1 is the first process (systemd, or your app inside a container). Address space Its own private view of memory (see virtual memory below). File descriptor table Open files and sockets: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr, then 3, 4, … Registers + state Saved RIP, RSP, … when it's not running. State: running, sleeping, stopped, zombie. Credentials User/group it runs as, capabilities. Parent Every process has a parent. New processes are created with fork() (copy me) + execve() (become another program).

Memory layout of a process (low → high addresses):

[ text: machine code ][ data/bss: globals ][ heap → grows up ]  …  [ mmap: libraries ]  …  [ ← stack grows down ]

docs.title: 2 · Thread: a second worker inside the same process
docs.text:
• Threads of one process share its memory and open files, but each has its own stack and registers.
  • That's why threads are cheap to communicate between (shared memory) but need locks to avoid stepping on each other.
  • On Linux, process and thread are both a task to the kernel. A thread is a task that shares memory with others.

docs.title: 3 · The scheduler: sharing the CPU
docs.text:
There are more runnable tasks than cores. The scheduler decides who runs next and for how long.

  • Each task gets a time slice of a few milliseconds. A timer interrupt (Chapter 1 again!) lets the kernel take the CPU back.
  • Context switch: save the current task's registers, load the next one's, and switch page tables if it's a different process. Cost: ~1–5 µs plus the caches going cold.
  • Linux's scheduler is EEVDF (since kernel 6.6, replacing CFS). It tries to give each task its fair share, adjusted by priority (nice).
  • Load average = how many tasks are running or waiting to run, on average.

DevOps connection: a Kubernetes CPU limit is enforced by the scheduler through cgroups. When a container uses its quota early in the period it is throttled until the next period, even if the node has idle cores.

docs.title: 4 · Virtual memory: everyone gets their own address space
docs.text:
Every process thinks it has a huge, private memory starting near address 0. The kernel and the CPU's MMU make this true:

Concept Meaning Page Memory is handled in 4 KB chunks. Page table Per-process map: virtual page → physical frame in RAM. The kernel builds it, the MMU reads it on every memory access. TLB A cache of recent translations inside the CPU, so lookups stay fast. Page fault Access to a page that isn't mapped yet. The kernel maps it (minor fault) or reads it from disk (major fault), then the instruction is retried. Copy-on-write After fork(), parent and child share pages until one of them writes. Only then is a copy made. OOM killer When memory runs out, the kernel kills a process to survive.

Why this matters: process A cannot even name process B's memory. Isolation comes for free from the page tables.

DevOps connection: OOMKilled in Kubernetes means the container hit its memory cgroup limit and the kernel's OOM killer stopped it.

docs.title: How does address translation work?
docs.text: Every memory access uses a virtual address. The MMU first checks the TLB; on a hit the physical address is ready in about one cycle. On a miss it walks the 4-level page table. If there is no valid entry, the CPU raises a page fault and the kernel maps (or loads) the page and retries the instruction.

docs.title: 5 · Syscalls: the only door into the kernel
docs.text:
A program in ring 3 can't touch hardware. It asks the kernel with a system call:

# Step 1 Your code calls printf("hi\n"). 2 libc formats the text and calls write(1, "hi\n", 3). 3 The write wrapper puts the syscall number in RAX (1 = write on x86-64) and arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, then runs the syscall instruction. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel's entry point. 4 The kernel looks up fd 1 → it's a terminal, a file or a pipe. VFS routes the call to the right driver. The result (bytes written, or a negative error) returns in RAX, and the CPU goes back to ring 3.

Common syscalls: read, write, openat, close, mmap, clone (fork/threads), execve, socket, connect, accept, epoll_wait, exit_group.

docs.title: 6 · "Everything is a file"
docs.text: Files, terminals, pipes, sockets and devices (/dev/input/event3 from Chapter 1) are all accessed through file descriptors with the same read/write calls. /proc is a fake filesystem where the kernel shows its internal state as files.

docs.title: 7 · Signals: the kernel taps a process on the shoulder
docs.text:
Signal Meaning SIGINT (2) Ctrl+C SIGTERM (15) "Please shut down." Can be caught for a graceful shutdown. SIGKILL (9) "You're dead now." Cannot be caught. SIGCHLD A child process exited.

DevOps connection: on pod deletion Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to PID 1 of each container, waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30 s), then sends SIGKILL. If PID 1 is a shell script that doesn't forward signals, your app never gets the SIGTERM.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: p99 spikes with 30% CPU
docs.text:
The alarm

A Go API has p99 latency spikes of 80–100 ms every few seconds. Dashboards show 30% average CPU of its 2-CPU limit. Adding replicas doesn't help.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total rises constantly: the container is throttled in most 100 ms periods.

🔍 Clue 2

The node has 64 cores; the Go version is older than 1.25, so GOMAXPROCS=64: 64 threads burn the 200 ms quota in ~3 ms.

🎯 Root cause

The CPU limit is a quota per 100 ms period across all threads. With 64 runnable threads the quota is exhausted almost immediately, then the whole container is frozen until the next period: average usage stays low, tail latency explodes.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Set GOMAXPROCS to the limit (automaxprocs, or upgrade to Go 1.25+), or remove the CPU limit and rely on requests. Lesson: watch throttling, not average CPU, for latency-sensitive services.

docs.text: Page What's inside 3.1 — Processes & threads What a process and a thread are, fork/exec and copy-on-write, process states, PID 1, zombies and orphans, signals and graceful shutdown, and why this matters for containers and Kubernetes. 3.2 — The scheduler & CPU time How Linux decides which task runs where, run queues and EEVDF, preemption and context switches, nice and real-time priorities, load average, CPU affinity, and how cgroup CPU weights, quotas and Kubernetes requests/limits really work. 3.3 — Virtual memory & memory management The process address space, pages and page tables, demand paging and page faults, RSS vs VSZ, the page cache, mmap, swap, memory pressure and reclaim, the OOM killer, cgroup memory limits and why containers get OOMKilled. 3.4 — Syscalls, I/O & filesystems How system calls work, file descriptors and "everything is a file", the read/write path through VFS, page cache, filesystem and block layer, fsync and durability, blocking vs epoll vs io_uring, inodes, filesystems and storage in containers. 3.5 — Namespaces, cgroups & container isolation The Linux kernel features that make containers - the seven namespaces, cgroups v2 controllers, capabilities, seccomp and LSMs, user namespaces and rootless containers - and how runc builds a container from them.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 03-os (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) Processes and threads
ps -eo pid,ppid,nlwp,stat,cmd | head      # nlwp = number of threads
cat /proc/$$/status | grep -E "Pid|PPid|Threads|VmRSS"

# 2) The memory map of your shell (text, heap, libraries, stack)
cat /proc/$$/maps

# 3) Watch syscalls happen
strace -e trace=write echo hi             # write(1, "hi\n", 3) = 3
strace -c ls / > /dev/null                # syscall summary table

# 4) Context switches and the scheduler
vmstat 1 5                                # cs = context switches per second
perf stat -e context-switches,page-faults sleep 1

# 5) Signals
sleep 300 &  kill -TERM $!                # polite
kill -l                                   # list all signals

Exercise: run strace -f -e trace=clone,execve bash -c 'ls' and find the fork (clone) and execve that turn your shell into ls.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Process = PID + own address space + fd table + saved registers
Thread  = shares the process's memory, own stack + registers
Scheduler: time slices → timer interrupt → context switch (save/restore registers)
Virtual memory: virtual page --(page table, MMU, TLB)--> physical frame (4 KB)
Syscall: libc → RAX = nr, args in RDI/RSI/RDX → `syscall` → ring 0 → result in RAX
Everything is a file: fd 0/1/2, sockets, pipes, devices, /proc
Signals: SIGTERM (polite, catchable) → SIGKILL (final)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Two threads of the same process and two separate processes both run in parallel. What is the key difference?

Threads share one address space (memory, open files) and can read each other's data directly. Separate processes have separate page tables and cannot see each other's memory without explicit sharing (pipes, sockets, shared memory).

2. Why can't a buggy process overwrite another process's memory?

Each process has its own page table. Its virtual addresses can only map to the physical frames the kernel gave it, and the MMU enforces this on every access.

3. What happens, step by step, when your program calls write()?

libc puts the syscall number in RAX and arguments in RDI/RSI/RDX, executes syscall, the CPU switches to ring 0, the kernel's VFS finds what fd refers to and calls the right driver, the result comes back in RAX, and the CPU returns to ring 3.

4. A container keeps getting killed with OOMKilled. Which kernel mechanism is doing it?

The memory cgroup limit plus the kernel's OOM killer. The container used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed a process inside it.

5. Why should your container's PID 1 handle SIGTERM?

Kubernetes sends SIGTERM first to allow a graceful shutdown (finish requests, close connections). If PID 1 ignores it, the pod waits out the grace period and is then killed with SIGKILL, dropping in-flight work.
