docs.title: ✍️ My notes
docs.text: Explain the difference between a process and a thread, and what a syscall is, in your own words in 5 lines.

docs.title: 3.1 — Processes & threads
docs.text:
In short

A process is a running program with its own memory, file descriptors and identity (PID). A thread is a worker inside a process that shares that memory but has its own stack and registers. Processes are born with fork/clone + execve, move between running and sleeping, and end with exit, after which the parent must wait() for them. In a container your app is usually PID 1, which gives it special duties.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Process — A program in execution Own address space, fds, credentials PID / PPID / TID Process ID / Parent PID / Thread ID Numeric identities Every thread has a TID; the main thread's TID = PID Thread — Execution context inside a process Shares memory, own stack + registers fork() / clone() — Create a new process/thread clone flags decide what is shared COW Copy-On-Write Lazy copying after fork Pages are shared until one side writes execve() — Replace the program in a process Same PID, new code and memory wait() / waitpid() — Parent collects a child's exit status Removes the zombie Zombie — Exited process whose status isn't collected Holds only a PID and exit code Orphan — Process whose parent died Re-parented to PID 1 (or a subreaper) PID 1 / init — First process in a PID namespace Must reap orphans; default signal handling differs Signal — Asynchronous notification SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGINT, SIGCHLD, SIGHUP Exit code — Number returned at exit 0 = OK; 128+N = killed by signal N (137 = SIGKILL) State codes — R, S, D, Z, T in ps Running, Sleeping, Uninterruptible, Zombie, Stopped

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. fork() (actually clone() on Linux) creates a child that is a copy of the parent. Thanks to copy-on-write, memory isn't copied: both share the pages read-only, and a page is copied only when one side writes to it. That's why forking a 10 GB process is fast (and why Redis can snapshot with fork).
  2. The child usually calls execve(): the kernel throws away its memory and loads a new program (chapter 4). PID stays the same; open fds stay too unless marked close-on-exec.
  3. The parent continues, and later calls wait() to collect the child's exit code.

A shell running ls is exactly this: fork, exec ls in the child, wait in the parent.

docs.title: 2 · Processes vs threads
docs.text:
Process Thread Memory Separate (isolated) Shared with other threads Create / switch cost Higher Lower Communication Pipes, sockets, shared memory Just read/write shared variables (with locks) One crashes Others survive The whole process dies Examples nginx/Postgres workers, Python multiprocessing JVM, Go runtime, Chrome renderer threads

On Linux both are "tasks" created by clone(); the flags (CLONE_VM, CLONE_FILES …) decide how much is shared. ps -eLf or top -H show threads.

docs.title: 3 · States, zombies and orphans
docs.text:
• R running or runnable · S sleeping (interruptible, e.g. waiting on a socket) · D uninterruptible sleep (usually disk/NFS I/O; can't be killed until the I/O returns) · Z zombie · T stopped.
  • A zombie has exited but its parent hasn't called wait(). It uses no memory, only a PID slot. Thousands of zombies mean a parent with a bug, and you can run out of PIDs (pids.max).
  • An orphan (parent died first) is adopted by PID 1, which is expected to reap it.

docs.title: 4 · Signals and graceful shutdown
docs.text:
Signal Default Typical use SIGTERM (15) terminate "Please shut down" (Kubernetes, systemd, docker stop) SIGKILL (9) kill, can't be caught Last resort; no cleanup SIGINT (2) terminate Ctrl+C SIGHUP (1) terminate Terminal closed; many daemons reload config SIGCHLD ignore A child changed state (parent should wait()) SIGSEGV (11) core dump Invalid memory access

Graceful shutdown = on SIGTERM: stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, flush, close connections, exit 0.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• PID 1 in containers: the kernel doesn't apply default signal actions to PID 1, so an app that doesn't install a SIGTERM handler ignores docker stop / pod deletion and gets SIGKILLed after the grace period (30 s by default). It also must reap zombies. Use tini / docker run --init / shareProcessNamespace, or make the app handle it.
  • Shell form vs exec form: CMD python app.py runs /bin/sh -c … as PID 1; sh may not forward SIGTERM. Use exec form CMD ["python","app.py"] or exec in entrypoint scripts.
  • Kubernetes termination: pod marked terminating → removed from Endpoints (asynchronously!) → preStop hook → SIGTERM → terminationGracePeriodSeconds → SIGKILL. A short preStop sleep avoids dropping requests that still arrive.
  • Exit codes in pod status: 137 = SIGKILL (often OOMKilled), 143 = SIGTERM, 139 = SIGSEGV, 1 = app error.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,nlwp,cmd --forest | head -30     # tree with state and thread count
ps -eLf | head; top -H                                # threads
cat /proc/self/status | grep -E 'Pid|PPid|Threads|State'

# Make a zombie for 30 s and look at it
python3 -c 'import os,time; os.fork() or os._exit(0); time.sleep(30)' &
sleep 1; ps -o pid,ppid,stat,cmd --ppid $!

# Does PID 1 ignore SIGTERM? Compare:
docker run --rm -d --name noinit alpine sleep 300 && time docker stop noinit      # ~10 s (SIGKILL after timeout)
docker run --rm -d --name withinit --init alpine sleep 300 && time docker stop withinit   # instant

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Meaning docker stop / pod delete takes exactly the grace period PID 1 ignores SIGTERM Exit code 137 SIGKILL (OOM or timeout after SIGTERM) Many Z processes Parent doesn't wait() / no init in container Processes in D state, load avg high Stuck I/O (disk, NFS) fork: Resource temporarily unavailable PID / thread limit (pids.max, ulimit -u)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is fork() fast even for a process with gigabytes of memory?

Copy-on-write: parent and child share pages until one of them writes; only page tables are copied up front.

2. What's the difference between a zombie and an orphan?

A zombie has exited but hasn't been reaped by its parent. An orphan is still running but its parent died; it gets adopted by PID 1.

3. Your pod always takes 30 s to stop. Why?

The app (PID 1) doesn't handle SIGTERM, so nothing happens until the kubelet sends SIGKILL after the grace period.

4. What does exit code 137 mean?

128 + 9: the process was killed by SIGKILL, commonly by the OOM killer or after the termination grace period.

5. When would you use processes instead of threads?

When you need isolation (a crash or memory leak shouldn't take everything down) or to avoid a lock like Python's GIL.

docs.title: 3.2 — The scheduler & CPU time
docs.text:
In short

The scheduler decides, many times per second on every core, which task gets the CPU next. Linux keeps a run queue per CPU and uses EEVDF to give each task a fair, weighted share. It preempts tasks on timer ticks and wake-ups and balances load between cores. Containers add cgroup weights and quotas on top, which is exactly how Kubernetes CPU requests and limits work.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Scheduler — Kernel code choosing the next task Runs on tick, wake-up, block, yield Run queue — Per-CPU list of runnable tasks Tasks waiting for that CPU EEVDF Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First Linux's default fair scheduler since 6.6 Picks the eligible task with the earliest virtual deadline CFS Completely Fair Scheduler The previous default (2007–2023) Picked the task with the least virtual runtime Time slice — How long a task may run before re-evaluation A few ms, depends on load Preemption — Taking the CPU away from a running task On tick or when a more deserving task wakes Context switch — Switching the CPU from one task to another Save/restore registers, maybe change page tables nice — User priority −20…19 Changes the task's weight (~1.25× per step) RT policies Real-Time (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, SCHED_DEADLINE) Strict priority classes Always run before normal tasks Load average — Average number of runnable + D-state tasks 1, 5, 15-minute values Affinity — Which CPUs a task may run on taskset, cpusets cpu.weight / cpu.max — cgroup v2 CPU share / hard quota Weight under contention / quota per period Throttling — Pausing a cgroup that used its quota Until the next period (default 100 ms) PSI Pressure Stall Information How long tasks waited for CPU/memory/IO /proc/pressure/cpu

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Each CPU has a run queue of tasks that are ready to run. Sleeping tasks (waiting on I/O, locks, timers) aren't in it.
  2. EEVDF gives each task a weighted fair share. Tasks that received less than their share are eligible; among them, the one with the earliest virtual deadline runs next. Short-sleeping, latency-sensitive tasks get to run quickly after waking.
  3. The current task runs until its slice ends, it blocks (e.g. read() on a socket), or a wake-up of a more deserving task preempts it.
  4. Every switch is a context switch: save registers, load the next task's, and if it's another process, switch page tables (TLB impact). A few microseconds each; tens of thousands per second per core is normal.
  5. Periodically and when a CPU goes idle, load balancing moves tasks between CPUs, considering cache and NUMA topology.

docs.title: 2 · Priorities
docs.text:
• nice −20 (most) to 19 (least): each step changes CPU share by about 10%. Background jobs: nice -n 19.
  • Real-time (SCHED_FIFO, SCHED_RR, SCHED_DEADLINE) always beat normal tasks. Powerful and dangerous: a busy RT task can starve the system.
  • I/O priority is separate: ionice.

docs.title: 3 · Load average is not CPU %
docs.text: Load average = runnable tasks + tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D), averaged over 1/5/15 minutes. On an 8-core box, a load of 8 means "fully busy". A high load with low CPU% usually means tasks stuck in D state (slow disk, hung NFS). For a better signal use PSI: /proc/pressure/cpu says what percentage of time tasks were waiting for a CPU.

docs.title: 4 · cgroups: weights and quotas
docs.text:
Kubernetes cgroup v2 file What it does resources.requests.cpu: 500m cpu.weight Share under contention: when the node is busy, you get CPU in proportion to your request. When it's idle, you can use more resources.limits.cpu: 1 cpu.max = 100000 100000 Hard cap: 100 ms of CPU per 100 ms period, across all your threads. Exceeding it → throttled until the next period Guaranteed QoS + static CPU manager cpuset Exclusive whole cores (pinning)

The trap: a service with 8 threads and limit: 1 can use its 100 ms of quota in the first 12.5 ms of each period and then freeze for 87.5 ms. Average CPU looks low, p99 latency is terrible. Watch nr_throttled in cpu.stat / container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Requests drive scheduling and fairness; limits drive throttling. Many teams set CPU requests on everything and avoid CPU limits on latency-sensitive services (memory limits stay).
  • Runtimes must know their CPU budget: JVM (container-aware since JDK 10, sizes GC/JIT threads from the quota), Go (since 1.25 GOMAXPROCS follows the cgroup CPU limit), Node/Python worker counts, nginx worker_processes auto (sees host cores!).
  • Noisy neighbours without limits are handled by weights; high kube_pod_container_resource_requests accuracy matters more than limits.
  • High context-switch rate (vmstat cs) or run-queue length (r) > cores = CPU saturation.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
nproc; uptime                                   # cores and load average
vmstat 1 5                                      # r = run queue, cs = context switches/s
cat /proc/pressure/cpu                          # PSI: % time waiting for CPU
pidstat -w 1 3 2>/dev/null | head -15           # context switches per process (sysstat)
chrt -p $$; nice -n 19 sleep 1                  # scheduling policy, niceness
cat /sys/kernel/debug/sched/features 2>/dev/null | tr ' ' '\n' | head -3  # (root) scheduler features

# Throttling inside a container
docker run --rm --cpus=0.5 alpine sh -c 'yes > /dev/null & sleep 3; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat'

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Question Look at Is the CPU saturated? vmstat r > cores, PSI cpu some Is my container throttled? cpu.stat nr_throttled / throttled_usec High load, low CPU% Tasks in D state (ps -eo stat,cmd | grep ^D) Make a job polite nice -n 19, ionice -c3 Pin to cores taskset -c 2,3, Kubernetes static CPU manager

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What happens to a task that calls read() on a socket with no data?

It blocks: leaves the run queue and sleeps until data arrives; the scheduler runs something else.

2. Load average is 16 on a 16-core server but CPU is 20%. What's going on?

Load includes D-state tasks; many tasks are probably stuck in uninterruptible I/O (disk, NFS).

3. What's the difference between a CPU request and a CPU limit in Kubernetes?

Request sets cpu.weight (share under contention, used for scheduling); limit sets cpu.max (hard quota, causes throttling).

4. Why can a CPU limit hurt latency even when average CPU usage is well below it?

Multiple threads can burn the whole period's quota early, then the container is throttled for the rest of the period.

5. Why should runtimes like the JVM or Go know the container's CPU limit?

They size thread pools and GC workers from the number of CPUs; seeing 64 host cores with a 2-CPU limit causes heavy throttling.

docs.title: 3.3 — Virtual memory & memory management
docs.text:
In short

Every process sees its own huge, private virtual address space. The kernel maps it page by page (4 KB) to physical RAM only when touched (demand paging) and fills free RAM with page cache. When memory runs short it reclaims cache and swaps if allowed. As a last resort the OOM killer kills a process: in a container, that's the famous OOMKilled at the cgroup memory limit.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Virtual address — Address a program uses Translated by the MMU on every access Page / frame — 4 KB unit of virtual / physical memory Page tables map pages to frames Page table — Per-process mapping tree (4–5 levels) Walked by the MMU on a TLB miss Page fault — Access to a page that isn't mapped (yet) Kernel maps it (minor) or reads it from disk (major) Demand paging — RAM assigned on first touch malloc(1 GB) uses ~0 RSS until written VSZ / RSS Virtual Size / Resident Set Size Reserved address space / pages in RAM RSS is what costs memory PSS / USS Proportional / Unique Set Size RSS with shared pages divided / only private pages Fairer per-process accounting Anonymous memory — Heap, stacks: not backed by a file Can only go to swap Page cache — File data cached in RAM Reclaimable; "buff/cache" in free mmap memory map Map a file or anonymous memory into the address space Lazy loading, shared libraries, databases Swap / zswap — Disk (or compressed RAM) for anonymous pages Slows things down but avoids OOM Reclaim — Freeing memory under pressure Drop clean cache, write dirty pages, swap OOM killer Out Of Memory Kernel kills a process to free memory Chooses highest oom_score memory.max / memory.high — cgroup v2 hard limit / throttle point Kubernetes memory limit → memory.max

docs.title: 1 · Pages, page tables and page faults
How does it work?
docs.text:
The address space is cut into 4 KB pages. A page table (a 4- or 5-level tree per process) maps virtual pages to physical frames, with permission bits (read/write/execute, user/kernel). The MMU walks it on every TLB miss (diagram in chapter 3).

When a program touches a page with no mapping, the CPU raises a page fault:

  • Minor fault: the data is already in RAM (fresh zero page, shared library already cached) → just add the mapping. Microseconds.
  • Major fault: data must be read from disk (a file mapped with mmap, or swapped-out memory). Milliseconds.
  • Invalid access (no mapping allowed, wrong permission) → SIGSEGV ("segmentation fault").

That's why malloc(1 GB) returns instantly and RSS only grows as you write to the memory.

docs.title: 2 · Reading memory numbers correctly
docs.text:
$ free -h
               total   used   free   shared  buff/cache  available
Mem:            62Gi   18Gi   2.1Gi   1.0Gi       42Gi       43Gi
  • "free" is small and that's fine: Linux uses spare RAM as page cache. Look at available (free + reclaimable cache).
  • VSZ can be huge (Go and JVM reserve lots of address space); it costs nothing. RSS is real usage, but shared libraries are counted in every process; PSS splits them fairly.
  • Container memory (memory.current) includes page cache from files the container read/wrote. Kubernetes uses the working set (usage minus inactive file cache) for eviction decisions.

docs.title: 3 · When memory runs out
docs.text:
1. Reclaim: kswapd drops clean page cache (cheap, just re-read later), writes back dirty pages, and swaps anonymous pages if swap exists.
  2. Thrashing: if the working set doesn't fit, the system spends its time paging; everything is slow but alive. PSI memory shows it.
  3. OOM: if reclaim can't free enough, the kernel's OOM killer picks the process with the highest oom_score (mostly by memory usage, adjusted by oom_score_adj) and sends SIGKILL.
  4. In a cgroup the same happens inside the limit: when a container exceeds memory.max, only processes in that cgroup are candidates. Kubernetes reports OOMKilled, exit code 137.

docs.title: 4 · mmap and the page cache
docs.text:
• read() copies from the page cache into your buffer; mmap() maps the cached pages directly into your address space, no copy. Databases (LMDB, older MongoDB), search engines and model loaders (llama.cpp loads weights with mmap) use it.
  • Writes go to the page cache first (dirty pages) and are flushed later; fsync() forces them to disk. Losing power before that loses data, which is why databases call fsync.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Kubernetes memory: requests are used for scheduling; the limit is a hard wall (memory.max) → OOMKilled. Unlike CPU, memory can't be throttled, only reclaimed or killed. Set limit ≈ request for predictable services.
  • Runtime heap vs limit: JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, Go GOMEMLIMIT, Node --max-old-space-size. Leave headroom for off-heap memory, thread stacks, page cache, native libs.
  • Node-pressure eviction: the kubelet evicts pods (BestEffort first, then Burstable over their request) when node memory.available drops below a threshold; that's different from the cgroup OOM kill.
  • Swap in Kubernetes: supported (NodeSwap, LimitedSwap for Burstable pods) but off by default on most clusters.
  • Memory leaks vs cache: a growing memory.current might just be page cache from log files; check memory.stat (anon vs file).

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
free -h; cat /proc/meminfo | head -20
cat /proc/self/maps | head -20                 # this shell's address space
pmap -x $$ | tail -3                           # mapped size vs RSS
grep -E 'VmSize|VmRSS' /proc/$$/status
cat /proc/pressure/memory                      # memory PSI

# Demand paging: reserve 1 GB, watch RSS grow only when written
python3 -c "
import mmap, os, time
m = mmap.mmap(-1, 1<<30)
print('after reserve:', open('/proc/self/status').read().split('VmRSS:')[1].split()[0], 'kB')
for i in range(0, 1<<30, 4096): m[i] = 1
print('after touching:', open('/proc/self/status').read().split('VmRSS:')[1].split()[0], 'kB')"

# OOM in a container
docker run --rm -m 64m python:3.12-alpine python -c "x = bytearray(200*1024*1024)"; echo "exit=$?"   # 137

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Metric Meaning available (free) What you can still use without swapping VSZ Reserved address space (ignore) RSS / PSS Real memory (PSS shares counted fairly) memory.current / memory.stat Container usage, split into anon and file major faults Disk reads due to paging (bad if high) OOMKilled / 137 Hit memory limit or node OOM

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. A process allocates 4 GB but RSS is only 50 MB. Is something wrong?

No. Pages are only backed by RAM when touched (demand paging); untouched allocations cost nothing.

2. free shows 1 GB free on a 64 GB server. Should you worry?

Look at available. Most RAM is probably page cache, which the kernel drops when applications need memory.

3. What's the difference between a minor and a major page fault?

Minor: the data is already in RAM, only a mapping is added. Major: the data must be read from disk.

4. Why did my JVM pod get OOMKilled even though -Xmx is below the limit?

The JVM uses memory outside the heap (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, JIT code, native libs); heap + all that exceeded memory.max.

5. Why can't Kubernetes throttle memory the way it throttles CPU?

CPU time can be delayed; memory already in use can't be taken back without reclaiming (cache/swap) or killing the process.

docs.title: 3.4 — Syscalls, I/O & filesystems
docs.text:
In short

Programs can only touch files, sockets and devices by asking the kernel through system calls. The kernel gives them file descriptors and routes each read()/write() through the VFS, the page cache, the filesystem and the block layer. It also offers different ways to wait: blocking, epoll and io_uring. That choice separates a server handling 100 connections from one handling 100,000.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Syscall system call Request from user space to the kernel syscall instruction, number in RAX vDSO virtual Dynamic Shared Object Kernel code mapped into user space gettimeofday without a real syscall fd file descriptor Small integer for an open file/socket/pipe Index into the process's fd table VFS Virtual File System Common layer for all filesystems Same API for ext4, xfs, NFS, procfs, sockets Inode index node A file's metadata (size, owner, blocks) Names (dentries) point to inodes Dentry directory entry Name → inode link, cached Path lookup cache Page cache — File data cached in RAM Reads hit it; writes go there first fsync — Force a file's data to stable storage Durability; slow on purpose Block layer (blk-mq) multi-queue block layer Queues and merges I/O requests One queue per CPU to the device Journal — Filesystem's write-ahead log Consistency after a crash IOPS / throughput / latency I/O operations per second Storage performance numbers Small random vs big sequential I/O epoll — Wait for many fds at once Kernel tells you which are ready io_uring — Shared-ring async I/O interface Submit and complete I/O with few syscalls OverlayFS — Union filesystem used by container images Read-only layers + one writable layer

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. libc's read(fd, buf, n) puts the syscall number (0 for read on x86-64) in RAX and arguments in RDI, RSI, RDX, then executes the syscall instruction.
  2. The CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel's entry point, which looks up the handler in the syscall table.
  3. The kernel checks the arguments (is buf really in your memory?), does the work, puts the result (or -errno) in RAX and returns with sysret.

A syscall costs ~0.1–1 µs (more with Spectre mitigations), so hot paths batch work (readv, sendmmsg, io_uring) and some calls avoid the kernel entirely via the vDSO (clock_gettime).

docs.title: 2 · File descriptors: "everything is a file"
docs.text:
open(), socket(), pipe(), epoll_create(), eventfd(), memfd_create() all return an fd, and you read()/write()/close() them the same way. 0/1/2 are stdin/stdout/stderr. /proc/<pid>/fd shows them all.

Limits: each process has a max (ulimit -n, often 1024 soft by default); servers with many connections need it raised (LimitNOFILE in systemd). "Too many open files" = hit the limit or leaking fds.

docs.title: 3 · The read and write path
docs.text:
• Read: VFS resolves the fd to an inode → page cache lookup. Hit = copy from RAM (µs). Miss = filesystem maps the file offset to disk blocks → block layer queues a request → NVMe driver → DMA + interrupt → page cached → copy (~100 µs on NVMe, ms on network disks).
  • Write: data is copied into the page cache and marked dirty; write() returns immediately. Background writeback flushes it later. fsync() waits until it's on stable storage. Databases call it on every commit; that's why disk fsync latency often decides database performance.
  • Direct I/O (O_DIRECT) skips the page cache; databases with their own cache (Postgres doesn't, MySQL InnoDB can) use it.

docs.title: 4 · Waiting for I/O at scale
docs.text:
Model How Used by Blocking + thread per connection Each thread sleeps in read() Classic Apache, JDBC, simple servers Non-blocking + epoll One thread asks "which of my 10,000 sockets are ready?" nginx, Node.js (libuv), Redis, Go netpoller, Netty io_uring Submit many operations into a ring, collect completions High-performance storage, newer databases and proxies

Go goroutines and Java virtual threads let you write blocking-style code while the runtime uses epoll underneath.

docs.title: 5 · Filesystems you'll meet
docs.text: Filesystem Where Note ext4 / xfs Linux root and data disks xfs common for large files/DBs overlayfs Container images Copy-up on first write to a lower-layer file tmpfs /dev/shm, emptyDir: {medium: Memory} Lives in RAM, counts toward memory limit procfs / sysfs / cgroupfs /proc, /sys Kernel state as files NFS / EFS / CephFS Shared network storage Higher latency, D-state hangs if server disappears Block volumes (EBS, PD) PersistentVolumes IOPS/throughput limits by volume type and size

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• "Disk full" but df says space is left → out of inodes (df -i), often millions of tiny files. Space not freed after deleting a log → a process still holds it open (lsof +L1).
  • Container writes to the overlay layer are slow and vanish with the container: use volumes for data, stdout for logs.
  • Cloud disks have IOPS/throughput caps; a database "randomly slow" may be throttled at the volume level. Check iostat -x (await, %util) and the provider's metrics.
  • emptyDir on memory and /dev/shm count against the pod's memory limit (e.g. PyTorch DataLoader workers need a larger /dev/shm).
  • Too many open files in high-connection services → raise LimitNOFILE / container ulimits.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
strace -c ls > /dev/null                        # syscall summary of a command
strace -e trace=openat,read,write -f cat /etc/hostname
ls -l /proc/$$/fd; ulimit -n                    # fds and the limit
df -h; df -i                                    # space and inodes
iostat -x 1 3 2>/dev/null                       # per-device latency and utilization (sysstat)
cat /proc/pressure/io

# Page cache in action: second read is from RAM
dd if=/dev/urandom of=/tmp/big bs=1M count=512 status=none
sync; echo 3 | sudo tee /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches > /dev/null
time cat /tmp/big > /dev/null; time cat /tmp/big > /dev/null

# fsync cost
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/f bs=4k count=1000 oflag=dsync 2>&1 | tail -1

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Check Too many open files ulimit -n, /proc/PID/fd count, leaks Disk full, df shows space df -i (inodes) Deleted file still uses space lsof +L1 Slow DB commits fsync latency, volume IOPS caps, iostat -x await Process stuck in D state Storage/NFS hang Syscall-heavy CPU strace -c, perf top (sys %)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What happens between calling read() and the kernel running its code?

libc sets the syscall number and args in registers and executes syscall; the CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel entry, which dispatches to the read handler.

2. write() returned success. Is the data on disk?

Not necessarily: it's in the page cache as a dirty page. Only after fsync() (or writeback) is it on stable storage.

3. How does nginx handle 50,000 connections with a few worker processes?

Non-blocking sockets + epoll: each worker waits for readiness on all its sockets and only handles the ready ones.

4. You deleted a 20 GB log but the disk is still full. Why?

A process still has the file open; the inode isn't freed until the last fd is closed. Restart/reload the process or truncate via /proc/PID/fd.

5. Why can /dev/shm usage cause an OOMKill in a pod?

It's tmpfs, i.e. RAM, and counts against the container's memory cgroup.

docs.title: 3.5 — Namespaces, cgroups & container isolation
docs.text:
In short

A container is not something the kernel knows about. It's an ordinary process that a runtime (runc, crun) starts in its own namespaces, which limit what it can see: PIDs, network, mounts, hostname. A cgroup limits what it can use: CPU, memory, I/O. Its root filesystem comes from the image, and reduced capabilities, a seccomp filter and an LSM profile limit what it can do.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Namespace — A private view of one kernel resource Created with clone()/unshare() flags pid ns — Own PID numbering Container's first process is PID 1 net ns — Own interfaces, routes, iptables, ports Connected via veth pairs / CNI mnt ns — Own mount table pivot_root into the image filesystem uts / ipc ns UNIX Time-Sharing / Inter-Process Communication Own hostname / own SysV IPC & POSIX queues hostname inside ≠ host user ns — Own UID/GID mapping Root inside = unprivileged user outside cgroup control group Group of processes with resource limits Files under /sys/fs/cgroup cgroup v2 — Unified hierarchy (modern default) cpu.max, memory.max, io.max, pids.max Capabilities — Root's powers split into ~40 pieces CAP_NET_ADMIN, CAP_SYS_ADMIN… dropped by default seccomp secure computing mode Syscall filter (BPF) Blocks dangerous syscalls (kexec_load, mount…) LSM Linux Security Module Mandatory access control AppArmor profiles, SELinux labels OCI runtime Open Container Initiative Program that creates the container runc, crun, gVisor (runsc), Kata Rootless — Containers run entirely as a normal user User namespaces + slirp4netns/pasta Privileged — Container with nearly all protections off Effectively root on the host

docs.title: 1 · Namespaces: what a process can see
How does it work?
docs.text:
clone() and unshare() accept flags like CLONE_NEWPID, CLONE_NEWNET, CLONE_NEWNS. Each creates a fresh instance of that resource for the new process:

Namespace Isolates Inside the container you see… pid Process IDs Your app as PID 1, no host processes net Network stack Only lo and eth0 (one end of a veth pair) mnt Mount points The image's /, your volumes uts Hostname The pod name ipc Shared memory, semaphores Only your own user UID/GID mappings "root", mapped to an unprivileged host UID cgroup cgroup tree view Your cgroup as the root time Some clocks (rarely used)

In Kubernetes all containers in a pod share the net (and ipc, uts) namespace, which is why they can talk over localhost; the pause container holds the namespaces.

docs.title: 2 · cgroups v2: what a process can use
docs.text:
Each container (and each pod) gets a directory under /sys/fs/cgroup/. Writing to files there sets limits; reading gives usage:

File Meaning From Kubernetes cpu.weight Share under contention CPU request cpu.max Hard CPU quota CPU limit memory.max Hard memory limit → OOM Memory limit memory.high Soft limit, throttles reclaim (MemoryQoS feature) io.max / io.weight Disk bandwidth / IOPS (rarely set) pids.max Max processes/threads podPidsLimit cpu.stat, memory.stat, memory.events Usage, throttling, OOM events Read by cAdvisor/kubelet metrics

docs.title: 3 · Hardening: capabilities, seccomp, LSMs
docs.text:
• Capabilities: containers start with a small default set (no CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN…). Best practice: drop: ["ALL"] and add back only what's needed (e.g. NET_BIND_SERVICE).
  • seccomp: the RuntimeDefault profile blocks ~50 dangerous syscalls. Kubernetes: securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
  • AppArmor / SELinux: restrict file and network access by policy, even for root inside.
  • User namespaces: root inside maps to an unprivileged UID on the host, so an escape isn't host root. Kubernetes supports it with hostUsers: false.
  • privileged: true disables almost all of this; with it (or CAP_SYS_ADMIN, host mounts of /, or the Docker socket) a container can usually take over the node.

docs.title: 4 · How runc builds a container
docs.text:
1. containerd unpacks the image layers and prepares an overlayfs rootfs, writes an OCI config.json.
  2. runc clone()s with the namespace flags, creates and joins the cgroup, sets limits.
  3. Inside: mounts /proc, /sys, /dev, volumes; pivot_root into the rootfs; sets hostname.
  4. Drops capabilities, applies seccomp and AppArmor/SELinux, switches to the configured user.
  5. execve() your entrypoint. From here it's a normal process on the host: visible in ps on the node.

Stronger isolation when tenants don't trust each other: gVisor (user-space kernel), Kata Containers / Firecracker (lightweight VMs per pod).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Pod Security Standards (restricted profile) enforce: non-root, no privilege escalation, drop ALL capabilities, seccomp RuntimeDefault.
  • Debugging from the node: nsenter -t <pid> -n ip addr enters a container's network namespace with host tools; crictl inspect gives the PID.
  • Container sees host resources in /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/meminfo (not namespaced!) → apps must read cgroup files (or use LXCFS) to know their limits.
  • Breakouts almost always come from privileged containers, host mounts, the Docker socket, or kernel bugs, not from namespaces themselves being "weak".

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
ls -l /proc/$$/ns                                 # namespaces of this shell
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash -c 'ps aux; echo "I am PID $$"'   # new PID namespace
sudo unshare --net bash -c 'ip addr'              # empty network namespace (just lo, down)
sudo unshare --uts bash -c 'hostname inside; hostname'; hostname              # host unchanged
unshare --user --map-root-user bash -c 'id'       # "root" without real root (user namespace)

cat /proc/self/cgroup; ls /sys/fs/cgroup | head
docker run --rm --memory 100m --cpus 0.5 --pids-limit 50 alpine \
  cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max
docker run --rm alpine sh -c 'grep Cap /proc/self/status'     # capability bitmasks
capsh --decode=00000000a80425fb 2>/dev/null                   # decode the default set

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Want Use Hide host processes pid namespace Own IP/ports net namespace (+ CNI) Limit RAM / CPU / PIDs cgroup memory.max / cpu.max / pids.max Root inside ≠ root outside user namespace (hostUsers: false) Block dangerous syscalls seccomp RuntimeDefault Least privilege capabilities: drop: [ALL], runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem Enter a container's network nsenter -t PID -n

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Is a container a lightweight VM?

No. It's a regular process on the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups. A VM runs its own kernel.

2. Why can two containers in the same pod reach each other on localhost?

They share one network namespace (held by the pause container).

3. Which kernel feature enforces a memory limit, and what happens when it's exceeded?

The memory cgroup (memory.max); the OOM killer kills a process inside that cgroup.

4. Why is privileged: true dangerous?

It gives all capabilities, disables seccomp/AppArmor confinement and exposes host devices; the container can usually control the host.

5. An app inside a container reads /proc/meminfo and sees 256 GB on a 2 GB limit. Why?

/proc/meminfo isn't namespaced; the app must read the cgroup files (memory.max) to learn its real limit.

docs.title: Chapter 4 — How a program runs
docs.text:
In short

A toolchain turns your source code into an ELF file on disk. When you type ./app, the shell forks, the child calls execve, the kernel maps the file into a fresh address space, the dynamic linker pulls in shared libraries, and finally your main() runs. Java, Python and Node.js add a runtime/VM in between.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Compiler — Translates source code to assembly/machine code Parses, type-checks, optimizes, emits code Preprocessor — Text-level step before compiling (C/C++) Expands #include and #define Assembler — Assembly → object file Encodes instructions into bytes, records symbols Linker — Combines object files and libraries Resolves symbols, writes the executable ELF Executable and Linkable Format Linux's binary file format Header + segments to load + sections Static / dynamic linking — Copy libraries in / load them at start Dynamic: ld.so maps .so files and fixes addresses ld.so dynamic linker/loader Program that loads shared libraries Named in PT_INTERP, runs before main() fork / execve — Copy the process / replace its program Shell forks a child, child execs the new program libc C standard library Wrappers for syscalls + standard functions printf, malloc, open → syscalls underneath Bytecode — Portable intermediate code for a VM Run by an interpreter or JIT (JVM, CPython, V8) JIT / AOT Just-In-Time / Ahead-Of-Time Compile while running / before running JIT compiles hot code at runtime; AOT produces native binaries VM Virtual Machine (language runtime) Runtime executing bytecode JVM, CPython VM, V8 engine

docs.title: 1 · Build: from main.c to an executable
docs.text:
gcc main.c -o app        # one command, four stages:
# Stage Tool Input → output What it does 1 Preprocess cpp main.c → main.i Pastes #include files in, expands #define macros. Still C. 2 Compile cc1 main.i → main.s C → assembly. Type checks, optimizations (-O2) happen here. 3 Assemble as main.s → main.o Assembly → machine code. Calls to printf are left as unresolved symbols ("fill this address in later"). 4 Link ld main.o + libs → app Combines object files, resolves symbols, writes the final ELF.

Static vs dynamic linking

Static Dynamic (default for C on Linux) Library code Copied into the binary Loaded at start from libc.so.6 Binary size Larger Smaller Security updates Rebuild everything Update the .so, all programs benefit Runs on a minimal system Yes, even FROM scratch Needs the right libraries present

DevOps connection: Go builds static binaries by default (with CGO_ENABLED=0), which is why Go apps fit in tiny scratch or distroless images.

docs.title: 2 · The ELF file
docs.text:
ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the file format for programs on Linux. It starts with the magic bytes 7f 45 4c 46 (.ELF).

Part Contains ELF header Architecture (x86-64, arm64), entry point address Program headers (segments) What to load where: code (R-X), data (RW-), plus PT_INTERP = path of the dynamic linker Sections .text (code), .rodata (constants, strings), .data (initialized globals), .bss (zeroed globals), .dynamic (needed libraries)

docs.title: 3 · Start: ./app
docs.text: # Step 6 You type ./app. The shell calls fork(): a copy of the shell process is created (cheaply, with copy-on-write, Chapter 3). 7 The child calls execve("./app", argv, envp). The kernel checks permissions, reads the ELF header, throws away the shell's memory, maps the segments into a new address space and builds the initial stack (argc, argv, environment variables, auxiliary vector). 8 Because the ELF has a PT_INTERP entry, the kernel first jumps to the dynamic linker /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2, not to your code.

docs.title: 4 · Inside the new process
docs.text:
# Step 9 The dynamic linker reads the NEEDED list (libc.so.6, …), finds the libraries, mmaps them in, and fixes up addresses (relocations, GOT/PLT). 10 It jumps to the program's entry point _start, which calls __libc_start_main, which calls main(argc, argv). — When main returns, exit() flushes buffers and calls the exit_group syscall. The parent shell receives SIGCHLD, collects the exit code with wait(), and you see it as $?.

Remember this

A running program = kernel loader (execve) + dynamic linker (ld.so) + libraries + your code. Two classic container errors come from this chain: exec format error = the binary is for a different CPU architecture (arm64 vs amd64), and no such file or directory for a file that clearly exists = its dynamic linker is missing (e.g. a glibc binary on Alpine, which uses musl).

docs.title: 5 · Other languages: same OS, different runtimes
docs.text:
Language What you ship What runs Speed trick C / C++ / Rust / Go Native ELF binary The CPU directly Ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation Java / Kotlin .class/.jar bytecode The JVM (itself an ELF) interprets bytecode JIT: hot methods are compiled to machine code at runtime (HotSpot) JavaScript (Node.js) .js source V8 parses to bytecode (Ignition) JIT: hot functions are optimized to machine code (TurboFan) Python .py source CPython compiles to bytecode (.pyc) and runs it in an interpreter loop Mostly interpreted, so CPU-heavy work goes to C extensions (NumPy, PyTorch)

In every case, what the kernel actually starts with execve is an ELF: your binary, or java, node, python3.

docs.title: How do AOT, interpreters and JIT differ?
docs.text: AOT compilers (C, Go, Rust) produce machine code before you run it: fast start, nothing to warm up. Interpreters (CPython) execute bytecode one instruction at a time: flexible but slower. JIT runtimes (JVM, V8) start interpreting, profile which code is hot, then compile just that to machine code while running.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: “no such file or directory” for a file that exists
docs.text:
The alarm

To shrink images, a team switches the runtime stage from debian:bookworm-slim to alpine. The new pods crash-loop with exec /app/server: no such file or directory, yet ls -l /app/server inside the image shows the file.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

file /app/server → dynamically linked, interpreter /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2.

🔍 Clue 2

ls /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 in the Alpine image → missing. Alpine uses musl and its loader is /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1.

🎯 Root cause

execve succeeds in finding the file, but the kernel must start the ELF's interpreter (PT_INTERP) first, and that path doesn't exist. The error refers to the missing loader, not to your binary.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Build statically (CGO_ENABLED=0 for Go, musl targets for Rust), or use a glibc-based slim/distroless base. Lesson: a dynamic binary drags its loader and libc ABI with it; check with readelf -l and ldd.

docs.title: 🧭 Go deeper
docs.text: Page What's inside 4.1 — Compiling & linking What compilers do inside (front end, IR, optimizer, back end), optimization levels, object files and symbols, static vs dynamic linking, LTO, cross-compilation, reproducible builds and build caching, with Go, Rust and C examples. 4.2 — ELF & the program loader The ELF file format (header, segments, sections), what execve does, ASLR and PIE, the dynamic loader ld.so, library search paths, PLT/GOT and lazy binding, LD_PRELOAD, security hardening flags, and the classic "not found" and "symbol not found" errors. 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go What a language runtime adds to a process - interpreters and JIT compilers, garbage collection, threading models (GIL, event loop, goroutines, virtual threads) - and how to size and tune JVM, Node.js, Python and Go services in containers.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 04-program (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

cat > main.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { printf("hello\n"); return 0; }
EOF

# 1) The four stages, one at a time
gcc -E main.c -o main.i && wc -l main.i     # preprocessed: hundreds of lines
gcc -S main.c && cat main.s                 # assembly
gcc -c main.c && nm main.o                  # 'U puts' = undefined symbol
gcc main.o -o app && ./app

# 2) Look inside the ELF
file app
readelf -h app | grep -E "Class|Machine|Entry"
readelf -l app | grep -A1 INTERP            # the dynamic linker path
ldd app                                     # shared libraries it needs

# 3) Watch the start-up
strace -f -e trace=execve,openat,mmap ./app
LD_DEBUG=libs ./app 2>&1 | head

# 4) Other runtimes
file $(which python3) $(which node) 2>/dev/null   # interpreters are ELF too
python3 -c "import dis; dis.dis(lambda a, b: a + b)"

Exercise: build once with gcc main.c -o app and once with gcc -static main.c -o app-static. Compare ls -lh, ldd and readelf -l | grep INTERP for both.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
main.c → cpp (main.i) → cc1 (main.s) → as (main.o) → ld (+libc) → ELF ./app
./app → shell fork() → child execve() → kernel maps ELF segments + builds stack
      → PT_INTERP: ld-linux.so → mmap libc.so → relocations → _start → main()
      → return → exit_group → parent wait() → $?
JVM / V8 / CPython = an ELF that runs bytecode, often with a JIT

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. At which stage does printf get its real address?

Not in the compiler or assembler. Those leave an undefined symbol. With static linking the linker fills it in; with dynamic linking the dynamic linker resolves it at start-up (or lazily on first call).

2. What's the difference between fork() and execve()?

fork() creates a new process that is a copy of the current one. execve() replaces the current process's program with a new one (same PID, new memory). Starting a program = fork + execve.

3. Your image runs fine on your laptop but fails on the cluster with exec format error. Why?

The binary was built for a different CPU architecture, e.g. arm64 (Apple Silicon) vs amd64 nodes. Build multi-arch images (docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64).

4. Why can a Go binary run in a FROM scratch image but a typical C program can't?

A static Go binary contains everything it needs and has no PT_INTERP. A dynamically linked C program needs ld-linux.so and libc.so.6, which a scratch image doesn't have.

5. What does a JIT compiler do?

It watches which code runs often ("hot") and compiles that bytecode into native machine code while the program is running, so those parts run at near-native speed.

docs.title: 4.1 — Compiling & linking
docs.text:
In short

A compiler reads source code, checks it, turns it into an intermediate representation (IR), optimizes it and emits machine code for one target into object files. The linker then resolves the symbols between those files and libraries and lays everything out into one executable, either copying libraries in (static) or leaving them to be loaded at run time (dynamic).

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Compiler — Translates source to machine code gcc, clang/LLVM, rustc, go build, javac (to bytecode) AST Abstract Syntax Tree Tree form of the parsed code Built by the parser, type-checked IR Intermediate Representation Language- and CPU-neutral code LLVM IR, GCC GIMPLE, Go SSA SSA Static Single Assignment IR form where each variable is assigned once Makes optimizations simpler Optimization level — How hard the compiler optimizes -O0 debug … -O2 default … -O3, -Os size Object file (.o) — Machine code + symbols + relocations One per source file Symbol — Named function or variable Defined (T) or undefined (U) Relocation — "Patch this address later" note Filled in by the linker or loader Linker — Combines objects into an executable ld (bfd), gold, lld, mold Static library (.a) archive Bundle of .o files copied in at link time Bigger binary, no runtime dependency Shared library (.so) shared object Loaded at run time, shared in memory Smaller binaries, update libs separately LTO / PGO Link-Time Optimization / Profile-Guided Optimization Whole-program / data-driven optimization Faster binaries, slower builds Cross-compiling — Building for another OS/CPU GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64, --target Reproducible build — Same source → bit-identical output Needed for verifying supply chains

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Front end: the lexer splits text into tokens, the parser builds an AST, semantic analysis resolves names and checks types. Your compile errors come from here.
  2. Middle end: the AST is lowered to IR (often SSA). Dozens of passes optimize it: constant folding, dead-code elimination, inlining, loop unrolling, vectorization, escape analysis (Go: does this value need the heap?).
  3. Back end: instruction selection for the target ISA, register allocation, instruction scheduling, then emitting machine code into an object file.

Because front ends and back ends are separate, LLVM compiles C, C++, Rust, Swift, Zig and more to x86, ARM, RISC-V, WebAssembly and GPUs with one optimizer.

docs.title: 2 · Object files, symbols and the linker
docs.text:
$ nm hello.o
                 U puts        # undefined: needed from somewhere else
0000000000000000 T main        # defined here, in .text

The linker:

  1. Collects all .o files and libraries (-lssl, .a, .so).
  2. Resolves symbols: every U must match exactly one definition. "undefined reference to …" = missing library or wrong order; "multiple definition" = defined twice.
  3. Lays out sections (.text, .rodata, .data, .bss) into segments and applies relocations.
  4. Writes an ELF executable (4.2).

docs.title: 3 · Static vs dynamic linking
docs.text:
Static Dynamic Libraries Copied into the binary Loaded by ld.so at start Binary size Larger Smaller Runtime deps None (just the kernel) Matching .so versions must exist Security patches Rebuild every binary Update the library once Containers Perfect for FROM scratch / distroless Needs a base image with libc Examples Go (CGO_ENABLED=0), Rust with musl Most C/C++ programs, Python, Node

glibc vs musl: Alpine uses musl; binaries built against glibc won't run there ("not found" for an existing file = missing loader). Go with cgo disabled sidesteps it entirely.

docs.title: 4 · Making builds fast and trustworthy
docs.text:
• Incremental + cached builds: ccache/sccache for C/C++/Rust, Go's build cache, Bazel/Buck2 remote caches, Docker layer caching in CI.
  • Faster linkers: mold or lld can cut link time from minutes to seconds on big C++/Rust projects.
  • LTO / PGO: optimize across files and with real profiles; Go supports PGO from default.pgo (often 2–14% faster).
  • Reproducible builds: pin toolchains, strip timestamps/paths (-trimpath, SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH), so anyone can verify that a binary matches its source. A foundation of SLSA supply-chain levels.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Multi-stage Dockerfiles: compile in a big builder image, copy just the static binary into scratch/distroless → tiny images with no shell and few CVEs.
  • Cross-compiling in CI (GOARCH=arm64, cargo build --target, docker buildx) is much faster than emulating ARM with QEMU.
  • Debug symbols: strip them from release images (-ldflags="-s -w", strip) but keep them (separate debuginfo) to symbolize crash dumps and profiles.
  • SBOMs (syft, go version -m) list what got linked in: essential for answering "are we affected by CVE-X?".

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
cat > hello.c <<'EOF'
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) { puts("hello"); return 0; }
EOF
gcc -E hello.c | tail -3                         # after the preprocessor
gcc -O2 -S hello.c -o - | head -20               # assembly
gcc -c hello.c && nm hello.o                     # symbols: U puts, T main
gcc hello.o -o hello-dyn && ldd hello-dyn        # dynamic: needs libc.so.6
gcc -static hello.o -o hello-static 2>/dev/null && ls -lh hello-dyn hello-static && ldd hello-static
clang -O2 -S -emit-llvm hello.c -o - 2>/dev/null | head -20   # LLVM IR (if clang is installed)

# Go: static, cross-compiled, stripped, with embedded build info
# CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o app-arm64 .
# go version -m app-arm64

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Error / need Meaning / fix undefined reference to X Missing library or link order multiple definition of X Symbol defined twice (e.g. in a header) cannot find -lfoo Install libfoo-dev, check -L Binary "not found" on Alpine glibc binary on musl → build static or use glibc base Smaller image Static binary + FROM scratch/distroless Faster C++/Rust links mold / lld

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What does the compiler's IR make possible?

One optimizer for many languages and many targets; front ends and back ends can be mixed (LLVM).

2. What does U puts in nm output mean?

The object file uses puts but doesn't define it; the linker (or loader) must find it, here in libc.

3. Why are Go binaries popular for FROM scratch images?

With CGO_ENABLED=0 they're statically linked: no libc or loader needed, only the kernel.

4. A security fix lands in OpenSSL. What's the difference for statically vs dynamically linked apps?

Dynamic: update the shared library (base image) once. Static: every binary must be rebuilt and redeployed.

5. Why do reproducible builds matter for supply-chain security?

Anyone can rebuild from source and check the binary is bit-identical, proving nothing was injected during the build.

docs.title: 4.2 — ELF & the program loader
docs.text:
In short

An executable on Linux is an ELF file: a header, segments that say what to map into memory with which permissions, and sections for tools. execve() makes the kernel map those segments at a randomized address (ASLR) and start the dynamic loader ld.so. The loader finds the shared libraries, fixes up addresses through the GOT/PLT, runs constructors and finally calls main().

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) ELF Executable and Linkable Format Linux/BSD format for executables, .o and .so Magic bytes 7f 45 4c 46 ("\x7fELF") ELF header — First bytes: class, ISA, entry point, table offsets readelf -h Segment (program header) — What the loader maps (PT_LOAD, PT_INTERP, PT_DYNAMIC…) readelf -l Section — What tools/linker use (.text, .data, .symtab, .debug_*) readelf -S Entry point — First instruction executed (_start) Not main PT_INTERP program interpreter Path to the dynamic loader /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 ld.so dynamic linker/loader Loads shared libraries at start Configured by RPATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, ld.so.cache DT_NEEDED — List of required libraries readelf -d GOT / PLT Global Offset Table / Procedure Linkage Table Indirection tables for library addresses Filled lazily or at start ASLR Address Space Layout Randomization Random base addresses each run Makes exploits harder PIE Position-Independent Executable Executable that can load anywhere Needed for full ASLR RELRO / NX / stack canary RELocation Read-Only / No-eXecute Hardening features Protect GOT, stack, data pages soname shared object name Library ABI identity (libssl.so.3) Major version in the file name LD_PRELOAD — Force-load a library first Override functions (tracing, mocks, also attacks)

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
$ readelf -l /usr/bin/ls   (simplified)
Type     Offset    VirtAddr  Flags  Meaning
PHDR     ...                 R      the program headers themselves
INTERP   ...                 R      "/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2"
LOAD     0x000000  0x000000  R      headers, read-only data
LOAD     0x004000  0x004000  R E    code (.text)
LOAD     0x01b000  0x01b000  R      constants (.rodata)
LOAD     0x022000  0x023000  RW     globals (.data, .bss), GOT
DYNAMIC  ...                 RW     list of needed libraries, symbol tables
GNU_STACK                    RW     stack is NOT executable
  • Segments are what the kernel maps: each LOAD becomes a memory region with exactly those permissions (code is never writable, data is never executable).
  • Sections (.text, .rodata, .symtab, .debug_info) are for the linker, debuggers and profilers. You can strip them without breaking the program.

docs.title: 2 · execve(): the kernel's part
docs.text:
1. Open the file, check the magic (\x7fELF) or a #! line (then run the interpreter it names instead).
  2. Throw away the old address space, create a new one.
  3. Map each PT_LOAD segment at a random base (ASLR, if the binary is PIE), set up the stack with argc, argv, envp and the auxiliary vector (page size, entry point, random bytes…).
  4. If there's a PT_INTERP, map ld.so too and jump to its entry point; otherwise (static binary) jump straight to _start.

docs.title: 3 · ld.so: the dynamic loader's part
docs.text:
1. Read DT_NEEDED (e.g. libssl.so.3, libc.so.6) and search for each: RPATH/RUNPATH in the binary → LD_LIBRARY_PATH → /etc/ld.so.cache → /lib, /usr/lib.
  2. Map each library (each with its own random base) and recursively load their dependencies.
  3. Relocate: fill the GOT with real addresses of external functions and variables. With lazy binding, calls go through the PLT stub and are resolved on first call; with -z now (full RELRO) everything is resolved up front and the GOT is made read-only.
  4. Run constructors (.init_array, C++ static constructors), then _start → __libc_start_main → main(argc, argv, envp).

LD_DEBUG=libs ./app prints this whole search.

docs.title: 4 · Hardening flags you can check
docs.text:
Feature Protects against Check PIE + ASLR Hard-coded addresses in exploits file says "pie executable" NX (non-executable stack/data) Injected shellcode GNU_STACK without E Stack canary Stack buffer overflows __stack_chk_fail symbol Full RELRO GOT overwrites BIND_NOW + GNU_RELRO CET (IBT/SHSTK) ROP/JOP gadget chains endbr64 instructions FORTIFY_SOURCE Unsafe libc calls __*_chk symbols

Distro and most language toolchains enable these by default; hand-written Makefiles sometimes don't.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• exec /app: no such file or directory for a file that exists = the interpreter in PT_INTERP doesn't exist in the image (glibc binary on Alpine, or wrong arch). Check with readelf -l / file.
  • error while loading shared libraries: libX.so.N = a DT_NEEDED library is missing in the runtime image (forgotten in a multi-stage copy).
  • GLIBC_2.38 not found = built on a newer distro than the runtime image. Build on the oldest base you support (or link statically).
  • Distroless images contain only the loader, libc and certificates: no shell, smaller attack surface; debug with kubectl debug ephemeral containers.
  • LD_PRELOAD is used by profilers/allocators (jemalloc, tcmalloc) and by attackers; it's ignored for setuid binaries.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
file /usr/bin/ls
readelf -h /usr/bin/ls | grep -E 'Class|Machine|Type|Entry'
readelf -lW /usr/bin/ls | grep -E 'INTERP|LOAD|GNU_STACK|GNU_RELRO' -A1 | head -20
readelf -d /usr/bin/ls | grep NEEDED
ldd /usr/bin/ls
LD_DEBUG=libs /usr/bin/true 2>&1 | head -15      # watch the loader search
cat /proc/self/maps | grep -E 'ls|cat|libc|ld-'  # where things got mapped (run twice: ASLR)
hexdump -C /usr/bin/ls | head -2                 # 7f 45 4c 46 = \x7fELF
# checksec --file=/usr/bin/ls                    # hardening summary (checksec package)

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Tool Shows file Arch, PIE, static/dynamic, stripped readelf -h / -l / -S / -d Header / segments / sections / dynamic deps ldd Resolved libraries (don't run on untrusted binaries) LD_DEBUG=libs Loader search path in action nm -D Dynamic symbols a library exports/needs objdump -d Disassembly

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What's the difference between ELF segments and sections?

Segments describe what the loader maps into memory and with which permissions; sections are for the linker, debuggers and tools and can be stripped.

2. Is main the first code that runs in a C program?

No. ld.so runs first (for dynamic binaries), then _start → __libc_start_main and constructors, then main.

3. A container fails with exec /app: no such file or directory but /app exists. Why?

Its interpreter (PT_INTERP, e.g. glibc's ld-linux) isn't in the image, or it's built for another architecture.

4. What is ASLR and why does it need PIE?

Randomizing where code, heap, stack and libraries load each run; the executable itself can only move if it's position-independent.

5. What does full RELRO protect?

It resolves all symbols at start and makes the GOT read-only, so an attacker can't overwrite function pointers in it.

docs.title: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
docs.text:
In short

Except for C/C++/Rust, your program doesn't run "alone": a runtime lives inside the process and decides how code is executed (interpreter or JIT), how memory is freed (garbage collector) and how work is scheduled (threads, event loop, goroutines). Knowing those three choices for the JVM, V8/Node.js, CPython and Go explains most of their performance, memory and container-sizing behaviour.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Runtime — Code that runs alongside your program Memory, threads, compilation, standard library Bytecode — Portable instruction format for a VM .class, .pyc, V8 Ignition bytecode Interpreter — Executes bytecode instruction by instruction Simple, slower JIT Just-In-Time compiler Compiles hot code to machine code at run time Needs warm-up; uses profiling data AOT Ahead-Of-Time Compile to native before running Go, Rust, GraalVM native-image GC Garbage Collector Frees memory no longer reachable Mark live objects from roots, reclaim the rest Stop-the-world pause — All app threads paused for GC Shows up as latency spikes Generational GC — Separate young and old objects Most objects die young GIL Global Interpreter Lock CPython lock: one thread runs Python at a time Free-threaded builds since 3.13 remove it Event loop — One thread running callbacks Node.js (libuv), Python asyncio Goroutine — Go's lightweight thread (~2 KB stack) M:N scheduled on OS threads Virtual threads — JVM lightweight threads (Java 21+) Blocking code without OS-thread cost Heap limit — Max managed memory -Xmx, --max-old-space-size, GOMEMLIMIT Warm-up — Slow period before JIT optimizes Affects autoscaling and cold starts

docs.title: 1 · Executing code: interpret, JIT or AOT
docs.text: Runtime How code runs Consequence JVM (HotSpot) Interpreter → C1 (quick JIT) → C2 (optimizing JIT) for hot methods Slow first minute, then very fast; CDS/AOT cache and CRaC reduce warm-up V8 (Node, Chrome) Ignition interpreter → Sparkplug/Maglev → TurboFan optimizing JIT Deoptimizes if types change ("monomorphic" code is faster) CPython Bytecode interpreter (3.13+ has an experimental JIT) Pure-Python loops are slow; heavy work goes to C extensions (NumPy, PyTorch) Go AOT-compiled native binary with the runtime linked in Fast start, no warm-up, predictable

docs.title: 2 · Memory: garbage collection
docs.text:
• JVM: G1 (default, balanced), ZGC (sub-millisecond pauses, large heaps), Parallel (throughput). Heap = -Xmx or -XX:MaxRAMPercentage. Plus off-heap: metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, code cache.
  • V8: generational (Scavenger for young, Mark-Compact for old), --max-old-space-size (MB). Exceeding it → "JavaScript heap out of memory".
  • CPython: reference counting (objects freed immediately when the count hits 0) + a cycle collector. Memory often isn't returned to the OS (fragmentation).
  • Go: concurrent, non-generational mark-and-sweep, very short pauses. Tunables: GOGC (how much growth before the next GC) and GOMEMLIMIT (soft memory limit, set it ~90% of the container limit).

docs.title: 3 · Concurrency models
docs.text:
Runtime Model Parallel CPU use? JVM OS threads + virtual threads (Java 21+) Yes, all cores Node.js One JS thread + event loop; libuv thread pool for fs/DNS/crypto Only via worker threads or multiple processes (cluster/pods) CPython OS threads but the GIL lets one run Python at a time; asyncio for I/O Multiprocessing, C extensions, or the free-threaded 3.13+ build Go Goroutines on GOMAXPROCS OS threads, netpoller for I/O Yes, all GOMAXPROCS

A blocking call (sync file read, CPU-heavy JSON parse) on Node's event loop freezes every request on that process.

docs.title: 4 · Runtimes in containers
docs.text:
The runtime must see the cgroup limits, not the host:

Runtime CPU Memory JVM (≥ 11) Container-aware: derives CPU count from cgroup (override -XX:ActiveProcessorCount) -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 (default is only 25%) Go (≥ 1.25) GOMAXPROCS follows the cgroup CPU limit by default GOMEMLIMIT ≈ 90% of the limit Node.js One thread anyway; scale with replicas --max-old-space-size ≈ 75% of the limit Python Worker count (gunicorn/uvicorn) from limit, not os.cpu_count() Watch RSS growth; restart workers (max_requests)

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Warm-up vs autoscaling: new JVM pods are slow for a minute; use readiness probes that pass only when warm, startup probes, gradual traffic shifting, or AOT/CDS/CRaC.
  • OOMKilled with "plenty" of heap left → off-heap memory (JVM metaspace/threads, native libs, Python C extensions) exceeded the container limit.
  • GC pauses as p99 spikes → GC logs (-Xlog:gc, GODEBUG=gctrace=1, --trace-gc), right-size heap, choose a low-pause GC.
  • Node.js CPU at 100% on one core of a 4-core pod → it can only use one; run more, smaller pods.
  • Python web servers: process-based workers (gunicorn), async (uvicorn), and careful worker counts per pod.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# JVM: what does it think its limits are inside a container?
docker run --rm -m 512m --cpus 2 eclipse-temurin:21-jre \
  java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'MaxHeapSize|ActiveProcessorCount|UseG1GC'

# Node: heap limit
docker run --rm -m 512m node:22-alpine node -e "console.log(require('v8').getHeapStatistics().heap_size_limit/1048576,'MB')"

# Python: the GIL in action (threads don't speed up CPU work)
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
import time, threading
def work(): sum(i*i for i in range(5_000_000))
t=time.time(); work(); work(); print("sequential", round(time.time()-t,2))
t=time.time(); a=[threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(2)]; [x.start() for x in a]; [x.join() for x in a]
print("2 threads ", round(time.time()-t,2))
PYEOF

# Go: GC trace
# GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./your-go-app

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: JVM Node.js CPython Go Execution JIT JIT Interpreter AOT GC G1 / ZGC Generational Refcount + cycles Concurrent M&S Uses all cores ✅ ❌ (1 JS thread) ❌ (GIL) / ✅ processes ✅ Memory knob MaxRAMPercentage --max-old-space-size worker count GOMEMLIMIT Warm-up Yes Some No No

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why are JVM services slow for the first minute after a deploy?

Code starts interpreted; the JIT compiles hot methods only after profiling them (warm-up).

2. Why doesn't adding threads speed up CPU-bound pure-Python code?

The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time (except in the free-threaded build).

3. A Node.js pod has a 4-CPU limit but never goes above 1 CPU. Why?

JavaScript runs on one thread; use worker threads or more, smaller replicas.

4. What should GOMEMLIMIT be set to in a container with a 1 GiB limit, and why?

Around 900 MiB: the GC then works harder before reaching the limit, avoiding OOMKills, while leaving headroom for non-heap memory.

5. The JVM's default max heap is 25% of the container memory. What do you change?

Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (e.g. 70–75%), leaving room for off-heap memory.

docs.title: Chapter 5 — Networking fundamentals
docs.text:
In short

Your data gets wrapped in layers of headers (TCP → IP → Ethernet). A switch delivers it inside your local network using MAC addresses. A router moves it between networks using IP addresses, and NAT swaps your private IP for a public one. Then dozens of routers forward it hop by hop until it reaches the server, which unwraps the layers in reverse.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) OSI / TCP/IP model Open Systems Interconnection Layered models of networking Each layer solves one problem and adds one header MAC address Media Access Control 48-bit hardware address on a local link Used by switches to deliver frames IP address Internet Protocol Address of a host on the internet (IPv4 32-bit, IPv6 128-bit) Routers forward packets by destination IP Port — 16-bit number selecting a program on a host TCP/UDP header carries source and destination ports Subnet / CIDR Classless Inter-Domain Routing A block of IPs like 192.168.1.0/24 /24 = first 24 bits are the network part Default gateway — The router for everything outside your subnet Frames for remote IPs go to its MAC ARP Address Resolution Protocol Finds the MAC for an IP on the local network Broadcast 'who has X?', owner replies, result cached Switch — L2 device forwarding frames by MAC Learns which MAC is behind which port Router — L3 device forwarding packets between networks Longest-prefix match in the routing table, TTL−1 NAT Network Address Translation Rewrites private addresses to a public one Remembers each connection in a conntrack table MTU Maximum Transmission Unit Largest payload per frame (usually 1500 bytes) Bigger data is split into several packets TTL Time To Live Hop counter in the IP header Each router decrements it; 0 = drop (prevents loops) BGP / AS Border Gateway Protocol / Autonomous System How networks on the internet share routes Each AS announces the IP ranges it can reach VPC Virtual Private Cloud A private network in a cloud Subnets, route tables, gateways, security groups in software

docs.title: 1 · Layers: each one solves one problem
docs.text:
Layer (OSI #) Name Problem it solves Address Device Examples 7 Application What do the bytes mean? URL, hostname — HTTP, DNS, SSH 4 Transport Which program on the machine? Reliable or fast? Port (16-bit) — (end hosts) TCP, UDP 3 Network Which machine in the world? IP (IPv4 32-bit, IPv6 128-bit) Router IP, ICMP 2 Data link Which machine on this cable / Wi-Fi? MAC (48-bit) Switch, AP Ethernet, Wi-Fi 1 Physical Turn bits into signals — Cable, radio Copper, fibre, 2.4/5 GHz

OSI layers 5 and 6 exist on paper. In practice TLS and the application cover them.

docs.title: 2 · Encapsulation: envelopes inside envelopes
docs.text:
[ Ethernet 14 B | [ IP 20 B | [ TCP 20 B | [ HTTP data … ] ] ] | FCS 4 B ]
  • Going down the stack, each layer adds its header. Going up at the receiver, each layer removes its own.
  • The maximum frame payload on Ethernet is usually 1500 bytes (MTU). Bigger data is split into multiple TCP segments.
  • MAC addresses change at every hop, IP addresses do not (except where NAT rewrites them). The IP is the final destination; the MAC is just "the next device".

docs.title: 3 · Your local network: subnet, ARP, switch
docs.text:
Your laptop has 192.168.1.23/24. The /24 (subnet mask 255.255.255.0) means "the first 24 bits are the network": everyone from 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.255 is on my local network.

The laptop asks itself one question for every packet:

Destination on my subnet? Then Yes (e.g. 192.168.1.50) Send the frame directly to that machine's MAC. No (e.g. 93.184.215.14) Send the frame to the default gateway (the router, 192.168.1.1).

To get a MAC from an IP, it uses ARP:

Broadcast: "Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.23"
Reply:     "192.168.1.1 is at a4:2b:b0:12:34:56"     → cached in the ARP table

A switch (or Wi-Fi access point) learns which MAC lives behind which port and forwards frames only there. It never looks at IP addresses.

docs.title: How does ARP work?
docs.text: To send a frame on the LAN you need the destination's MAC. If it is not in the cache, the host broadcasts who has 192.168.1.1?; every device hears it, only the owner replies with its MAC. The answer is cached (ip neigh) and frames can flow.

docs.title: 4 · The router and NAT
docs.text:
# What happens 4 The frame arrives at the router because its destination MAC is the router's MAC. 5 The router strips the Ethernet header, reads the destination IP, checks its routing table (longest matching prefix wins; 0.0.0.0/0 = "everything else → ISP"), decrements TTL, and builds a new frame for the next hop. — NAT: 192.168.x.x addresses are private (also 10.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12). They're not routable on the internet, so the router rewrites the source to its public IP and a port, and remembers the mapping in a connection tracking table so replies can find their way back.

That's also why someone on the internet can't simply connect to your laptop: there is no NAT entry until you start the conversation (unless you add port forwarding).

docs.title: How does NAT work?
docs.text: On the way out, the router replaces the private source IP:port with its public IP and a free port, and writes the mapping into conntrack. When the reply arrives at that public port, it looks up the mapping and rewrites the destination back to the private address.

docs.title: 5 · The internet: a network of networks
docs.text:
• Your ISP, the cloud providers and big companies each run their own networks, called autonomous systems (AS).
  • They tell each other which IP ranges they can reach using BGP. That's how a router in Istanbul knows where to send a packet for an address in Virginia.
  • Every router on the way repeats the same job: read the destination IP, look up the table, forward, TTL − 1. traceroute makes these hops visible by sending packets with TTL 1, 2, 3, …

docs.title: 6 · At the destination
docs.text:
The server's NIC accepts the frame because it's addressed to its MAC. The kernel removes the Ethernet and IP headers, uses the destination port (443) to find the socket that the web server is listening on, and hands the data to the process.

DevOps connection: an AWS/GCP VPC is this exact model in software: subnets (CIDR blocks), route tables (0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway), a NAT gateway so private subnets can reach out, and security groups acting as per-instance firewalls on IP + port. Kubernetes adds its own pod CIDR on top.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: peering that broke half the cluster
docs.text:
The alarm

A new VPC peering to the data team's VPC goes live. Minutes later, some pods can no longer reach each other, and the data team can reach some of your services but not others.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

Your cluster's pod CIDR is 10.244.0.0/16. The data VPC is 10.244.0.0/16 too (both teams used a common default).

🔍 Clue 2

ip route get 10.244.3.8 on a node now picks the peering route for part of the range: longest-prefix match prefers the more specific routes that were just added.

🎯 Root cause

Overlapping address ranges make routing ambiguous: packets for pod IPs are sent to the other VPC (and vice versa), depending on which route is more specific.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Remove the peering, renumber one side (new pod CIDR or secondary VPC CIDR), and keep a central IPAM plan. Lesson: VPC, pod, service, on-prem and peered CIDRs must never overlap; plan them before the first cluster.

docs.text: Page What's inside 5.1 — Ethernet, ARP & VLANs (Layer 2) How Ethernet frames, MAC addresses and switches work, MAC learning and flooding, ARP and its cache, broadcast domains and VLANs (802.1Q), MTU and jumbo frames, loops and STP, and how Layer 2 appears in Linux bridges, Docker and Kubernetes CNIs. 5.2 — IP addressing, subnets & routing IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, CIDR and subnet math, private ranges, routing tables and longest-prefix match, default gateways, ICMP, traceroute, TTL, fragmentation and PMTU, and how routing works between Kubernetes pods and across VPCs. 5.3 — NAT, firewalls & conntrack Stateless vs stateful firewalls, netfilter hooks, iptables vs nftables, connection tracking, SNAT, DNAT and masquerading, port exhaustion, how kube-proxy implements Services with NAT, eBPF alternatives (Cilium), NetworkPolicies and cloud security groups. 5.4 — Cloud networking (VPC) How cloud networks are built on SDN, VPCs, subnets and availability zones, route tables, internet and NAT gateways, security groups and NACLs, private endpoints, peering, transit gateways, VPN and Direct Connect, cloud load balancers, egress costs and Kubernetes networking in the cloud.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux / macOS)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 05-network (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) Your addresses, subnet and MAC
ip addr                     # macOS: ifconfig
ip route                    # 'default via 192.168.1.1' = your gateway
ip neigh                    # ARP table: IP → MAC   (macOS: arp -a)

# 2) Is it local or through the gateway?
ip route get 192.168.1.50
ip route get 8.8.8.8

# 3) Hops to a server, live
traceroute example.com      # or: mtr example.com

# 4) Watch ARP and ping on the wire (Ethernet headers included)
sudo tcpdump -n -e -i any 'arp or icmp'   # in another terminal: ping -c 3 192.168.1.1

# 5) Your public IP (what NAT turns you into)
curl -s https://ifconfig.me ; echo

# 6) Open sockets: local IP:port ↔ remote IP:port
ss -tn

Exercise: compare the IP you see in ip addr with the one from ifconfig.me. Which device is rewriting it, and where is that mapping stored?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
L7 data → L4 +TCP header (ports) → L3 +IP header (IPs) → L2 +Ethernet (MACs) → L1 signals
Same subnet? → ARP for target MAC → switch delivers
Other subnet? → ARP for gateway MAC → router → routing table → next hop (TTL−1)
Private IP → NAT (conntrack) → public IP → ISP → BGP-routed internet → server
MAC changes every hop, IP stays (except NAT). Port picks the program.
MTU 1500 · /24 = 256 addresses · private: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. A packet goes through 12 routers. How many times does the destination IP change? And the destination MAC?

The destination IP stays the same the whole way (ignoring NAT on the server side). The destination MAC changes at every hop, because each L2 frame only goes to the next device.

2. Your laptop wants to reach 192.168.1.50 and 8.8.8.8. Which MAC address does it put on each frame?

For 192.168.1.50 (same /24): that machine's own MAC, found via ARP. For 8.8.8.8 (outside the subnet): the gateway's MAC.

3. What does a switch look at, and what does a router look at?

A switch looks at MAC addresses (L2). A router looks at IP addresses (L3) and its routing table.

4. Why can't a server on the internet open a connection to your laptop at home?

Your laptop only has a private IP behind NAT. The router only knows where to send incoming packets for conversations your side started (conntrack entries). Unsolicited inbound traffic has no mapping, unless you configure port forwarding.

5. What is the AWS equivalent of your home router's NAT?

A NAT gateway: instances in a private subnet send outbound traffic through it, and it rewrites their private IPs to a public one.
