docs.title: 5.1 — Ethernet, ARP & VLANs (Layer 2)
docs.text:
In short

Inside one local network, data moves as Ethernet frames addressed by MAC addresses. Switches learn which MAC sits behind which port and forward frames only there, or flood them when unsure. ARP finds the MAC for an IP on the same subnet, and VLANs split one physical network into separate broadcast domains. The same ideas reappear as Linux bridges, veth pairs and CNI plugins on every Kubernetes node.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) L2 Layer 2 (data link) Delivery within one local network Frames addressed by MAC Frame — L2 packet: dst MAC, src MAC, EtherType, payload, FCS FCS = checksum; bad frames are dropped MAC address Media Access Control 48-bit NIC address aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, first half = vendor (OUI) EtherType — Which protocol is inside 0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP Switch — Device that forwards frames by MAC Learns source MACs into a MAC table Flooding — Sending a frame out all ports For broadcast and unknown destinations Broadcast domain — Set of hosts that receive each other's broadcasts One VLAN / one subnet ARP Address Resolution Protocol IPv4 → MAC lookup on the LAN Broadcast question, unicast answer, cached NDP Neighbor Discovery Protocol IPv6's replacement for ARP Uses ICMPv6 multicast GARP Gratuitous ARP Unasked ARP announcing "this IP is at my MAC" Used for failover (VIP moves) VLAN / 802.1Q Virtual LAN Logical L2 network on shared hardware 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID Trunk / access port — Carries many tagged VLANs / one untagged VLAN Switch-to-switch vs switch-to-host MTU Maximum Transmission Unit Largest payload per frame 1500 standard, 9000 "jumbo" STP Spanning Tree Protocol Blocks redundant links to prevent loops Elects a root, disables loop ports

docs.title: 1 · Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
docs.text:
| dst MAC (6) | src MAC (6) | [802.1Q tag (4)] | EtherType (2) | payload (46–1500) | FCS (4) |
  • Every NIC has a MAC address (virtual NICs get generated ones). It only matters on the local link: routers rewrite both MACs at every hop (chapter 5 diagram).
  • Broadcast = ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, delivered to everyone in the broadcast domain.
  • MTU is the max payload (1500 bytes). Bigger IP packets must be fragmented or (normally) the sender lowers its segment size via Path MTU discovery.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A frame arrives on port 3 with source aa:…. The switch learns: "aa:… is behind port 3" (entries age out after ~5 minutes).
  2. It looks up the destination MAC. Known → send it out only that port. Unknown or broadcast → flood to all other ports in the same VLAN.
  3. Replies teach it the other direction, so after the first exchange traffic is unicast.

Unlike an old hub, a switch doesn't send everything everywhere, so hosts only see their own traffic plus broadcasts.

docs.title: 3 · ARP: from IP to MAC
docs.text:
1. Host A wants to send to 192.168.1.20 (same subnet). Its ARP cache has no entry.
  2. It broadcasts "Who has 192.168.1.20? Tell 192.168.1.10".
  3. Only .20 answers (unicast) with its MAC. A caches it (ip neigh) for minutes.
  4. For an IP outside the subnet, A ARPs for the default gateway instead (5.2).

Gratuitous ARP ("192.168.1.100 is now at my MAC") is how keepalived/VRRP and MetalLB L2 mode move a virtual IP between machines. ARP has no authentication, so on a shared L2 network ARP spoofing lets an attacker intercept traffic.

docs.title: 4 · VLANs
docs.text:
A VLAN makes one physical switch behave like several separate ones. Frames between switches carry an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN ID (1–4094) on trunk links; hosts on access ports never see tags. Different VLANs can only talk through a router (or L3 switch), which is where firewalls and policies sit.

Data centres moved from big stretched VLANs to routed (L3) fabrics with overlays like VXLAN (L2 frames inside UDP, 24-bit IDs → 16 million segments), which is also what many CNIs and cloud networks use under the hood.

docs.title: 5 · Loops and STP
docs.text: Two links between the same switches create a loop: a broadcast circulates forever (frames have no TTL), multiplying until the network melts (broadcast storm). STP detects loops and blocks redundant ports; modern designs prefer link aggregation (LACP) and routed fabrics instead.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Linux is a switch too: docker0 / cni0 are Linux bridges; each container gets a veth pair (one end in its network namespace as eth0, the other on the bridge). Flannel/Calico/Cilium use bridges, routes, VXLAN/Geneve or eBPF.
  • MTU mismatches with overlays: VXLAN adds 50 bytes, so pod MTU must be ~1450 on a 1500 network. Symptom: small requests work, big responses hang (TLS handshakes, large JSON).
  • MetalLB L2 mode / keepalived use gratuitous ARP; failover takes as long as clients' ARP caches to update.
  • Cloud VPCs are not real L2: no broadcast, ARP is answered by the hypervisor, so "layer 2 tricks" (GARP failover, multicast) usually don't work; use cloud load balancers or route-based failover.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
ip -br link                                   # interfaces with MACs and state
ip neigh                                      # ARP / NDP cache
sudo tcpdump -eni any arp -c 6                # -e shows MACs; ping a neighbour meanwhile
ping -c1 $(ip route | awk '/default/{print $3}'); ip neigh | head -3
bridge link 2>/dev/null; ip -d link show type bridge 2>/dev/null | head   # Linux bridges (docker0, cni0)
ip -d link show | grep -E 'vxlan|mtu' | head  # overlay devices and MTUs
ping -M do -s 1472 -c1 1.1.1.1               # 1472+28 = 1500: does a full-size packet pass without fragmenting?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Large transfers hang, small ones work MTU mismatch (overlay, VPN) Duplicate IP warnings / flapping Two hosts claim the same IP (ARP conflict) Network meltdown, LEDs solid L2 loop / broadcast storm VIP failover slow Stale ARP caches Pods on same node can talk, not across nodes Overlay/routing (VXLAN port, routes)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC it hasn't learned?

It floods it to all ports in that VLAN except the one it came in on.

2. You ping 8.8.8.8. Whose MAC address does your laptop ARP for?

The default gateway's; MACs only matter on the local link.

3. Why do VXLAN overlays usually need a smaller MTU?

VXLAN encapsulation adds ~50 bytes of headers; inner packets must shrink so the outer packet still fits in 1500.

4. Why doesn't gratuitous-ARP failover usually work in AWS/GCP VPCs?

The cloud network isn't a real L2 segment; the SDN controls which IP belongs to which interface and ignores GARP.

5. What problem does STP solve?

It blocks redundant links so broadcasts can't loop forever and cause a broadcast storm.

docs.title: 5.2 — IP addressing, subnets & routing
docs.text:
In short

IP gives every host an address that's meaningful across networks. A CIDR prefix like /24 says which part is the network. Every host and router keeps a routing table, picks the longest matching prefix for each destination and forwards the packet to the next hop, decrementing the TTL. The same few rules run your laptop, the internet core and your cluster's pod network.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) IP Internet Protocol L3: addressing and forwarding between networks Best-effort, no delivery guarantee IPv4 / IPv6 — 32-bit / 128-bit addresses 10.0.1.5 / 2001:db8::5 CIDR Classless Inter-Domain Routing address/prefix-length notation /24 = first 24 bits are the network Subnet mask — Same as prefix, dotted /24 = 255.255.255.0 Network / broadcast address — First / last address of an IPv4 subnet Not usable by hosts Private ranges RFC 1918 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 Not routed on the internet → need NAT CGNAT range Carrier-Grade NAT 100.64.0.0/10 ISPs, also used for pod CIDRs Routing table — List of prefix → next hop / interface ip route Longest-prefix match — Most specific route wins /32 beats /24 beats /0 Default route — 0.0.0.0/0 (::/0) "Everything else → gateway" TTL / hop limit Time To Live Counter decremented per router 0 → drop + ICMP "time exceeded" ICMP Internet Control Message Protocol Errors and diagnostics ping (echo), unreachable, time exceeded PMTUD Path MTU Discovery Finding the smallest MTU on a path Relies on ICMP "fragmentation needed" BGP Border Gateway Protocol Exchanges routes between networks Internet, also Calico/MetalLB/cloud routers

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
10.0.16.0/20 means: the first 20 bits are the network, the last 12 bits are hosts → 2¹² = 4096 addresses (10.0.16.0–10.0.31.255).

Prefix Addresses Typical use /32 1 A single host route /28 16 Tiny subnet (AWS minimum) /24 256 Classic LAN / small subnet /20 4,096 Kubernetes node subnet /16 65,536 A VPC /8 16.7 M 10.0.0.0/8 private range

Two addresses are on the same subnet if their network bits match (ip & mask). Clouds also reserve a few addresses per subnet (AWS: 5).

IPv6 works the same way with 128 bits: a /64 per subnet (18 quintillion addresses), no NAT needed, NDP instead of ARP, and every interface also has a link-local fe80::/10 address.

docs.title: 2 · Routing: longest-prefix match
docs.text:
$ ip route
default via 192.168.1.1 dev wlan0
10.20.5.0/24 dev eth1 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.5.2
10.0.0.0/8 via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0
172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0

For 10.20.5.9: three routes match (/0, /8, /24); the longest prefix (/24) wins → send directly on eth1 (ARP for 10.20.5.9 itself). For 8.8.8.8, only default matches → ARP for 192.168.1.1 and send it there.

Every router does the same, decrements TTL, recomputes the header checksum and rewrites the L2 header. The IP addresses don't change along the way (unless NAT, 5.3).

docs.title: 3 · ICMP, ping and traceroute
docs.text:
• ping sends ICMP echo requests; a reply means L3 reachability (not that the app or port works).
  • traceroute / mtr sends packets with TTL 1, 2, 3…; each router that drops one returns "time exceeded", revealing the path. * * * lines just mean that hop doesn't answer.
  • Blocking all ICMP breaks things: PMTU discovery needs "fragmentation needed" messages; without them, large packets silently vanish (black-hole connections).

docs.title: 4 · Routing in Kubernetes and clouds
docs.text:
• Each node gets a pod CIDR (e.g. 10.244.3.0/24); pods get IPs from it. The CNI makes every pod reachable from every other pod without NAT: by routes (Calico BGP, cloud route tables, AWS VPC CNI giving pods real VPC IPs) or an overlay (VXLAN/Geneve).
  • Service CIDR (e.g. 10.96.0.0/12) is virtual: no route exists, kube-proxy/eBPF rewrites the destination (5.3).
  • CIDR planning matters: pod, service, VPC, on-prem and peered VPC ranges must not overlap, or traffic goes to the wrong place and peering is refused. Plan with room to grow.
  • VPC route tables decide where a subnet's traffic goes: local, internet gateway, NAT gateway, peering, transit gateway, VPN.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• "Can't reach X" checklist: DNS → ip route get <ip> (which route?) → ping gateway → traceroute → security groups/NACLs → is the service listening.
  • Overlapping CIDRs are a top cause of failed VPC peering, VPN and cluster merges. Keep an IPAM sheet.
  • IP exhaustion with AWS VPC CNI: every pod uses a VPC IP; small subnets run out. Use prefix delegation, secondary CIDRs (100.64.0.0/10) or an overlay.
  • Asymmetric routing (reply takes a different path) breaks stateful firewalls and NAT.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
ip -br addr; ip route                          # addresses and routing table
ip route get 8.8.8.8                           # which route/interface/source would be used
ip -6 route 2>/dev/null | head -5
python3 -c "import ipaddress as i; n=i.ip_network('10.0.16.0/20'); print(n.num_addresses, n[0], n[-1], i.ip_address('10.0.20.7') in n)"
ping -c3 1.1.1.1
traceroute -n 1.1.1.1 2>/dev/null || tracepath -n 1.1.1.1
mtr -rwc 10 1.1.1.1 2>/dev/null | head -15     # loss/latency per hop
kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,PODCIDR:.spec.podCIDR 2>/dev/null

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Command / rule Which route is used ip route get <ip> Host count of /n 2^(32−n) (minus 2 for IPv4 hosts) Same subnet? ip & mask equal Path to a host traceroute -n, mtr Never overlap VPC, pod, service, on-prem, peered CIDRs Don't block ICMP type 3 code 4 (frag needed)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. How many addresses are in a /22, and what range does 10.1.4.0/22 cover?

1024 addresses: 10.1.4.0 – 10.1.7.255.

2. A host has routes for 10.0.0.0/8 via A and 10.0.5.0/24 via B. Where does 10.0.5.20 go?

Via B: the /24 is the longest matching prefix.

3. Do the source and destination IPs change as a packet crosses routers?

No (without NAT). Only TTL/checksum and the L2 (MAC) header change at each hop.

4. Why can blocking all ICMP break HTTPS for some users?

PMTU discovery depends on ICMP "fragmentation needed"; without it, big packets are dropped silently and connections hang.

5. Why must pod CIDRs not overlap with your corporate network?

Routes would be ambiguous: traffic to corporate IPs would be sent into the cluster (or vice versa) and peering/VPN can't be set up.

docs.title: 5.3 — NAT, firewalls & conntrack
docs.text:
In short

The Linux kernel's netfilter framework lets rules inspect every packet at fixed hooks. Conntrack remembers each connection, so firewalls can be stateful ("allow replies") and NAT can rewrite addresses consistently. SNAT shares one public IP; DNAT sends traffic for a virtual IP to a real backend. That's exactly how Docker port publishing and Kubernetes Services work.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Firewall — Allows or blocks traffic by rules Match on IP, port, protocol, state, interface Stateless / stateful — Judges each packet alone / knows connections Stateful allows replies automatically netfilter — Kernel packet-processing framework Hooks: PREROUTING, INPUT, FORWARD, OUTPUT, POSTROUTING iptables / nftables — User tools for netfilter rules nftables is the modern replacement conntrack connection tracking Table of active flows States: NEW, ESTABLISHED, RELATED, INVALID NAT Network Address Translation Rewriting IPs/ports in packets Reverse rewrite on replies via conntrack SNAT / MASQUERADE Source NAT Change the source address Many private hosts behind one IP DNAT Destination NAT Change the destination address Port forwarding, Service VIP → pod Port exhaustion — Running out of source ports for SNAT ~64K per (src IP, dst IP, dst port) kube-proxy — Implements Services on each node iptables / IPVS / nftables modes eBPF extended Berkeley Packet Filter Programs run safely in the kernel Cilium replaces kube-proxy and iptables NetworkPolicy — Kubernetes pod-level firewall Enforced by the CNI Security group / NACL — / Network Access Control List Cloud firewall per interface / per subnet Stateful / stateless

docs.title: 1 · Stateless vs stateful filtering
docs.text:
A stateless rule looks at one packet: "allow TCP to port 443". Replies from the server go out to random high ports, so a stateless firewall needs a second wide rule for them (cloud NACLs work this way).

A stateful firewall uses conntrack: the first packet of a flow is NEW; if allowed, everything belonging to that flow (ESTABLISHED, RELATED like ICMP errors or FTP data) is allowed automatically. One rule ct state established,related accept + rules for NEW is the classic pattern. Security groups and almost every host firewall are stateful.

docs.title: 2 · netfilter hooks and tables
docs.text:
Hook Sees Typical use PREROUTING Every incoming packet, before routing DNAT (port forwarding, Service VIPs) INPUT Packets for this host Host firewall FORWARD Packets being routed through Router / container / pod traffic OUTPUT Locally generated packets Local DNAT, egress filtering POSTROUTING Every outgoing packet, after routing SNAT / MASQUERADE

iptables organises rules in tables (filter, nat, mangle, raw) and chains; nftables (nft) is the modern, faster replacement with one syntax and sets/maps. Both drive the same netfilter hooks.

docs.title: How does SNAT work?
docs.text:
1. A pod 10.244.1.7:51544 connects to 93.184.215.14:443.
  2. POSTROUTING / MASQUERADE rewrites the source to the node IP 10.0.16.5:40001 and stores the mapping in conntrack.
  3. The reply comes to 10.0.16.5:40001; conntrack finds the flow and rewrites the destination back to 10.244.1.7:51544.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• conntrack table full (nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet) → new connections dropped. Tune nf_conntrack_max, reduce short-lived connections.
  • SNAT port exhaustion: one public IP can hold ~64K connections to the same destination IP:port. Many pods calling one API through one NAT IP hits this (cloud NAT gateways show "port allocation errors").
  • UDP and conntrack races caused the infamous 5-second DNS delays in Kubernetes (5.2/6.2).

docs.title: 4 · How Kubernetes Services use NAT
docs.text:
A ClusterIP like 10.96.12.7:80 exists on no interface. kube-proxy (iptables mode) writes rules:

  1. PREROUTING/OUTPUT: packets to 10.96.12.7:80 jump to the Service chain.
  2. The chain picks one endpoint at random (probability rules) and DNATs to e.g. 10.244.2.15:8080.
  3. conntrack remembers it, so the whole connection sticks to that pod and replies are un-NATed.
  4. NodePort / LoadBalancer add DNAT on node ports, and SNAT if the backend is on another node (unless externalTrafficPolicy: Local, which preserves the client IP).

Scaling: thousands of Services = tens of thousands of iptables rules evaluated linearly. IPVS mode, nftables mode, or eBPF (Cilium, replacing kube-proxy with hash-map lookups) scale much better.

docs.title: 5 · NetworkPolicies and cloud firewalls
docs.text:
• NetworkPolicy: "pods labelled app=api accept traffic only from app=web on 8080". Default is allow-all; once any policy selects a pod, everything not allowed is denied. Enforced by the CNI (Calico, Cilium); flannel alone doesn't.
  • Security groups: stateful, attached to instances/ENIs, can reference other groups. NACLs: stateless, per subnet, ordered rules.
  • Layers stack: SG → NACL → node firewall → NetworkPolicy → app auth. Debug from the outside in.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Client IP lost behind Services/LBs → SNAT. Use externalTrafficPolicy: Local, proxy protocol, or X-Forwarded-For (6.1).
  • Intermittent connection failures at scale → conntrack table full or NAT port exhaustion; check conntrack -S, dmesg, cloud NAT metrics.
  • Start NetworkPolicies with default-deny per namespace, then allow DNS (port 53 to kube-dns!) and required flows.
  • Docker publishes ports by inserting iptables rules that bypass ufw on many distros — a common surprise.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
sudo iptables -t nat -S | head -30             # NAT rules (Docker, kube-proxy)
sudo nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | head -40   # nftables view
sudo conntrack -L 2>/dev/null | head           # tracked connections (conntrack-tools)
sudo conntrack -S 2>/dev/null | head -3        # stats: drops, insert_failed
cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max 2>/dev/null

# A Kubernetes Service, as kube-proxy sees it (iptables mode)
sudo iptables -t nat -S KUBE-SERVICES 2>/dev/null | head
kubectl get svc,endpointslices -n default 2>/dev/null | head

# Docker port publishing = DNAT
docker run -d --rm -p 8080:80 --name web nginx:alpine && sudo iptables -t nat -S DOCKER; docker stop web

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Mechanism Many hosts share one public IP SNAT / MASQUERADE Expose an internal port DNAT (port forward) Allow replies automatically conntrack established,related Pod-to-pod firewall NetworkPolicy (CNI) Keep client IP on NodePort/LB externalTrafficPolicy: Local Huge clusters, fast Services IPVS / nftables / eBPF (Cilium)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does a stateful firewall need only one rule for HTTPS while a NACL needs two?

conntrack lets replies of an allowed flow through automatically; a stateless NACL must explicitly allow the return traffic to ephemeral ports.

2. How does a packet to a ClusterIP reach a pod when no interface has that IP?

kube-proxy rules DNAT the destination to a chosen pod IP in PREROUTING/OUTPUT; conntrack keeps the mapping for the connection.

3. Many pods call one external API through a NAT gateway and get random connection timeouts. Likely cause?

SNAT source-port exhaustion to that single destination IP:port. Add NAT IPs, reuse connections, or spread destinations.

4. What happens to other traffic once a NetworkPolicy selects a pod for ingress?

All ingress not explicitly allowed by some policy is denied for that pod.

5. Why does externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserve the client IP?

Traffic only goes to pods on the node that received it, so no SNAT to another node is needed.

docs.title: 5.4 — Cloud networking (VPC)
docs.text:
In short

A VPC is your own private, software-defined network inside a cloud region. You choose an IP range and split it into subnets per availability zone. Route tables decide whether each subnet reaches the internet directly (internet gateway), only outbound (NAT gateway) or not at all. Security groups guard every interface, and peering, transit gateways, VPN or Direct Connect link you to other networks.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) VPC / VNet Virtual Private Cloud / Virtual Network Isolated network in a region AWS/GCP call it VPC, Azure VNet SDN Software-Defined Networking Network implemented in hypervisors/NICs No real L2; the cloud decides who reaches whom Region / AZ — / Availability Zone Geographic area / isolated data centre(s) in it Subnets live in one AZ (AWS) Subnet (public / private) — Slice of the VPC CIDR "Public" = has a route to an internet gateway Route table — Per-subnet routing rules 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-… or → nat-… IGW Internet Gateway Connects the VPC to the internet 1:1 NAT for public IPs NAT gateway — Outbound-only internet for private subnets Managed SNAT, charged per GB ENI Elastic Network Interface Virtual NIC attached to an instance Has IPs and security groups Security group (SG) — Stateful firewall on ENIs Can allow traffic "from SG X" NACL Network Access Control List Stateless subnet firewall Ordered allow/deny rules VPC endpoint / PrivateLink — Private access to cloud services S3, ECR, APIs without NAT/internet Peering / TGW — / Transit Gateway Connect two VPCs / hub for many VPCs + on-prem Peering is non-transitive VPN / Direct Connect — Encrypted tunnel / private fibre to the cloud Hybrid connectivity Egress — Traffic leaving a region/cloud Usually the expensive direction

docs.title: 1 · How is a VPC different from a physical network?
How does it work?
docs.text:
There are no real switches or broadcast domains. Every packet leaving a VM is captured by the host (hypervisor / smart NIC such as AWS Nitro), checked against your security groups, route tables and NACLs, encapsulated and sent across the provider's fabric to the destination host. Consequences:

  • No broadcast/multicast, no gratuitous ARP: the SDN answers ARP for you (5.1).
  • Source/destination checks: an instance only receives traffic for its own IPs unless you disable the check (needed for NAT instances, some CNIs).
  • Per-instance limits on bandwidth, packets per second and connections tracked.

docs.title: 2 · Subnets, route tables and gateways
docs.text:
Subnet type Default route Use for Public 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway Load balancers, bastions, NAT gateways Private 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway App servers, Kubernetes nodes Isolated none Databases, sensitive workloads

Spread subnets across ≥ 3 AZs for availability; put one NAT gateway per AZ (otherwise one AZ's outage or cross-AZ data charges hit everyone).

docs.title: 3 · Security groups vs NACLs
docs.text:
Security group NACL Attached to ENI / instance Subnet State Stateful Stateless (allow return ports!) Rules Allow only Allow and deny, ordered Reference Other SGs ("from sg-web") CIDRs only

Typical design: SGs do the real work (least privilege by role), NACLs stay mostly open or block known-bad ranges.

docs.title: 4 · Connecting networks
docs.text:
• VPC peering: private routing between two VPCs; not transitive (A↔B and B↔C doesn't give A↔C). CIDRs must not overlap.
  • Transit gateway / Cloud Router / Virtual WAN: a hub that connects many VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connects with route tables.
  • Site-to-site VPN (IPsec over the internet) or Direct Connect / Interconnect / ExpressRoute (private links, stable latency).
  • PrivateLink / Private Service Connect: expose a service (yours or the cloud's) into another VPC as a private IP, without routing whole networks.
  • VPC endpoints for S3/ECR/DynamoDB: avoid NAT gateway charges and keep traffic private.

docs.title: 5 · Cloud load balancers
docs.text:
Type Layer Notes AWS NLB / GCP passthrough L4 TCP/UDP, preserves client IP, static IPs, very high scale AWS ALB / GCP HTTP(S) LB / Azure App Gateway L7 Host/path routing, TLS, WAF, HTTP/2/3 Global anycast LBs (GCP, Cloudflare, Front Door) L7 One IP worldwide, routes to nearest healthy region

In Kubernetes, Service type: LoadBalancer or Ingress/Gateway objects create these through the cloud controller / load balancer controller.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Kubernetes in the cloud: AWS VPC CNI gives pods real VPC IPs (watch IP exhaustion, use prefix delegation); GKE uses alias IP ranges; AKS Azure CNI overlay or Cilium. Pods can then be targeted directly by LBs (target-type: ip).
  • Costs: NAT gateway processing per GB, cross-AZ traffic, internet egress and inter-region traffic often dominate the network bill. Use VPC endpoints, keep chatty services in one AZ where it's safe, cache at the CDN.
  • IaC: build VPCs with Terraform/OpenTofu modules; plan CIDRs centrally (IPAM) so future peering and acquisitions don't collide.
  • Debugging: VPC Flow Logs (accepted/rejected flows), Reachability Analyzer / Connectivity Tests, then node-level tools.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# AWS examples (read-only)
aws ec2 describe-vpcs --query 'Vpcs[].{id:VpcId,cidr:CidrBlock}' --output table
aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].{id:SubnetId,az:AvailabilityZone,cidr:CidrBlock,free:AvailableIpAddressCount}' --output table
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --query 'RouteTables[].Routes[]' --output table | head -30
aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids sg-xxxx --query 'SecurityGroups[].IpPermissions'
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --query 'NatGateways[].{id:NatGatewayId,subnet:SubnetId,state:State}'

# From inside an instance: metadata about its network (IMDSv2)
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X PUT http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token -H 'X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60')
curl -s -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/network/interfaces/macs/

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Want Use Internet-facing LB Public subnets + IGW Private servers that download updates Private subnets + NAT gateway (per AZ) Reach S3/ECR without NAT Gateway / interface VPC endpoints Allow app → DB DB SG allows port 5432 from app SG Connect many VPCs + on-prem Transit gateway (hub-and-spoke) See dropped traffic VPC Flow Logs

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What makes a subnet 'public'?

Its route table has a default route to an internet gateway (and instances have public IPs).

2. Instances in a private subnet can't download packages. What do you check?

The subnet's route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → a NAT gateway in a public subnet, the NAT gateway is healthy, and SG/NACL allow outbound + return traffic.

3. VPC A is peered with B, and B with C. Can A reach C?

No. Peering isn't transitive; use a transit gateway or peer A and C directly.

4. Why is it better to reference security groups than CIDRs in rules?

Rules follow roles, not IPs: any instance (or pod with SG-for-pods) in the app SG is allowed, even as IPs change with autoscaling.

5. Your NAT gateway bill is huge. What's a common fix?

Add VPC endpoints for S3/ECR/other AWS services so that traffic bypasses the NAT gateway.

docs.title: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
docs.text:
In short

The browser turns a name into an IP with DNS and opens a reliable TCP connection to it. It wraps the connection in TLS so nobody can read or change it. Then it speaks HTTP over it: "GET / please" → "200 OK, here's the HTML". Each step costs round trips, and round trips are what you feel as latency.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) URL Uniform Resource Locator Address of a resource scheme://host:port/path?query DNS Domain Name System Turns names into IP addresses Recursive resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative TLD Top-Level Domain The last label of a name (.com, .org, .tr) TLD servers point to each domain's authoritative servers TTL (DNS) Time To Live How long a DNS answer may be cached Lower it before migrations TCP Transmission Control Protocol Reliable, ordered byte stream 3-way handshake, ACKs, retransmits, flow + congestion control UDP User Datagram Protocol Fire-and-forget datagrams No handshake, no retransmits; base of DNS and QUIC RTT Round-Trip Time Time for a message to go and come back Every handshake step costs about one RTT TLS Transport Layer Security Encryption + server authentication Key exchange (ECDHE) + certificate check, then symmetric encryption CA / certificate Certificate Authority Trusted issuer / signed proof of a domain's key Browser checks the chain up to a trusted root CA SNI / ALPN Server Name Indication / Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation TLS extensions Which hostname / which protocol (h2, h3) inside ClientHello HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol Request/response protocol of the web Method + path + headers → status + headers + body HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 / QUIC — / — / Quick UDP Internet Connections Multiplexed HTTP over TCP / over QUIC (UDP) Many streams on one connection; QUIC removes TCP head-of-line blocking TTFB Time To First Byte Time until the first response byte arrives DNS + TCP + TLS + server processing

docs.title: 0 · Before anything: parse the URL
docs.text: https://example.com/ → scheme https (so port 443 and TLS), host example.com, path /. The browser first checks its own caches: a cached DNS answer, an open connection it can reuse, or an HSTS rule that forces HTTPS.

docs.title: 1 · DNS: from name to IP
docs.text:
# Who What happens 1 Browser → OS "What's the IP of example.com?" The OS checks /etc/hosts and its own cache. 2 OS → recursive resolver Asks your configured resolver (your ISP's, or 1.1.1.1 / 8.8.8.8) over UDP port 53. 3 Resolver → root servers "Who handles .com?" The root replies with a referral to the .com servers. 4 Resolver → TLD (.com) "Who handles example.com?" Another referral: ns1.example.com. 5 Resolver → authoritative server "What is example.com?" Final answer: A 93.184.215.14, valid for its TTL (e.g. 300 s). 6 Back down the chain Every layer caches the answer for the TTL, so the next lookup is usually instant. Record Meaning A / AAAA Name → IPv4 / IPv6 address CNAME Name → another name (an alias) NS Which servers are authoritative for this zone MX Mail servers for the domain TXT Free text: domain verification, SPF, DKIM

DevOps connection: lower the TTL before a migration, so clients pick up the new IP quickly. "It's always DNS" is a joke because it's so often true.

docs.title: 2 · TCP: a reliable pipe
docs.text:
Step Packet Meaning 1 Client → SYN "I want to talk. My sequence numbers start at x." 2 Server → SYN-ACK "OK. Mine start at y, and I got your x." 3 Client → ACK "Got your y." The connection is open.

That costs 1 round trip (RTT) before any data is sent. After that, TCP gives you:

  • Reliability: every byte is acknowledged. Lost packets are retransmitted.
  • Ordering: sequence numbers put bytes back in the right order.
  • Flow control: the receiver advertises how much it can accept (the window).
  • Congestion control: the sender speeds up slowly and backs off when packets are lost, so the network isn't flooded.

A connection is identified by its 4-tuple: client IP : client port ↔ server IP : server port. The client port is a random ephemeral port.

UDP has none of this: no handshake, no retransmission, no ordering. It's just "send this datagram". That makes it good for DNS, video and games, and it's the base for QUIC.

docs.title: 3 · TLS 1.3: make the pipe private and authentic
docs.text:
Step What happens ClientHello Supported cipher suites, a key share (an ephemeral public key, ECDHE), and SNI (which hostname you want, so one IP can host many sites). ServerHello The server picks a cipher, sends its key share. Both sides can now compute the same session key. Everything after this is encrypted. Certificate + CertificateVerify The server proves it is example.com: a certificate signed by a CA, and a signature made with the matching private key. Client verifies Is the chain signed by a trusted root CA in my trust store? Is the hostname in the certificate? Is it still valid? Finished Both sides confirm the handshake wasn't tampered with.
  • Asymmetric crypto (ECDHE, RSA/ECDSA signatures) is used only to agree on keys and prove identity. It's slow, so it's used once.
  • Symmetric crypto (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) encrypts the actual data. It's fast.
  • TLS 1.3 needs 1 RTT (TLS 1.2 needed 2). Resumed connections can even send data in 0-RTT.

docs.title: 4 · HTTP: the conversation
docs.text:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
Accept: */*

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=UTF-8
Cache-Control: max-age=604800
Content-Length: 1256

<!doctype html> …
Status Meaning Examples 2xx Success 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content 3xx Go elsewhere 301 permanent redirect, 304 Not Modified (use your cache) 4xx You made a mistake 400, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404, 429 rate-limited 5xx The server failed 500, 502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 gateway timeout Version Transport Key idea HTTP/1.1 TCP Text. One request at a time per connection, so browsers open ~6 connections per site. HTTP/2 TCP Binary, many parallel streams on one connection, header compression. Negotiated during TLS via ALPN (h2). One lost TCP packet still stalls all streams (TCP head-of-line blocking). HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP TLS 1.3 built into the transport, streams are independent (no head-of-line blocking), faster set-up, connections survive network changes (Wi-Fi → 4G).

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text:
With a 50 ms round trip to the server and nothing cached:

Step Cost DNS (resolver walks root → TLD → authoritative) 0 to several RTTs, cached afterwards TCP handshake 1 RTT = 50 ms TLS 1.3 handshake 1 RTT = 50 ms HTTP request → first byte 1 RTT + server time = 50 ms +

That's ~150–200 ms before the first byte of HTML, which is why connection reuse, HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 and CDNs (putting servers close to users, Chapter 7) matter so much.

DevOps connection: TLS is often terminated at the load balancer or ingress, using certificates from Let's Encrypt via cert-manager. Behind it, traffic may be plain HTTP or re-encrypted (mTLS in a service mesh).

docs.title: How do the handshakes add up?
docs.text: Before the first byte of HTML: one RTT for the TCP handshake, one for the TLS 1.3 handshake, one for the HTTP request/response (plus DNS if not cached). On a 50 ms RTT link that is already ~150 ms. HTTP/3 over QUIC merges the transport and TLS handshakes.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the mysterious +5 seconds
docs.text:
The alarm

Calls from pods to an external payment API sometimes take exactly 5 seconds longer than usual. It's random, about 1 in 50 requests, and never happens from developers' laptops.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

The extra time is spent before the TCP connect: it's DNS. /etc/resolv.conf in the pod: options ndots:5, timeout:5 is the resolver default.

🔍 Clue 2

conntrack -S on the nodes shows insert_failed increasing. The resolver sends the A and AAAA queries in parallel over the same UDP socket.

🎯 Root cause

Two parallel UDP DNS packets with the same 5-tuple race in conntrack; one gets dropped, and the client waits the full 5 s timeout before retrying. ndots:5 multiplies the number of lookups, so the race happens often.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Run NodeLocal DNSCache, use FQDNs with a trailing dot or lower ndots, and/or single-request-reopen. Lesson: exact multiples of a timeout (5 s, 1 s, 3 s) are a fingerprint: find the timeout, then find what's being dropped.

docs.title: 🧭 Go deeper
docs.text: Page What's inside 6.1 — HTTP headers deep dive What an HTTP header is, how a message is built, and what headers do for routing, content negotiation, caching, authentication, cookies, security, CORS, proxies and tracing. 6.2 — DNS deep dive How DNS resolution works, record types, TTL and caching, DNS in Kubernetes, DNSSEC, encrypted DNS and the DNS problems DevOps engineers meet most. 6.3 — TCP deep dive TCP connection lifecycle and states, sequence numbers and ACKs, flow control and congestion control (CUBIC, BBR), keep-alive and connection reuse, and the TCP problems seen in production. 6.4 — TLS & certificates deep dive What TLS protects, how the TLS 1.3 handshake and key exchange work, certificates and chains of trust, revocation, short-lived certificates and automation with ACME and cert-manager, mTLS, and post-quantum TLS. 6.5 — HTTP/2 & HTTP/3 deep dive Why HTTP/1.1 needed replacing, how HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, how QUIC and HTTP/3 remove TCP head-of-line blocking, and what this means for load balancers, gRPC and Kubernetes. 6.6 — Methods, status codes & API styles HTTP methods and their safety and idempotency, every status code family that matters in operations, and how REST, gRPC, GraphQL, WebSockets and SSE use HTTP, plus versioning, pagination, retries and rate limits.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 06-internet (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) DNS
dig example.com                 # answer + TTL
dig +short AAAA example.com     # IPv6
dig +trace example.com          # walk root → .com → authoritative yourself
resolvectl status 2>/dev/null | head   # which resolver your Linux uses

# 2) The whole conversation, verbose
curl -v https://example.com -o /dev/null

# 3) Timing of each phase
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n' https://example.com

# 4) TLS details: certificate chain, protocol, cipher
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | head -25

# 5) Watch the TCP handshake on the wire
sudo tcpdump -n -i any 'tcp port 443 and (tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn) != 0)'   # then run curl in another terminal

Exercise: run the timing command twice in a row against the same site. Which phases get faster the second time, and why?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
URL → scheme/host/port/path
DNS: browser → OS (/etc/hosts, cache) → recursive resolver → root → TLD → authoritative → A record (TTL cached)
TCP: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK (1 RTT) · reliable, ordered, flow + congestion control · 4-tuple
TLS 1.3: ClientHello (key share, SNI) → ServerHello + cert + Finished (1 RTT) → symmetric keys
HTTP: request line + headers → status + headers + body · 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx
HTTP/1.1 (text, 1 req/conn) → HTTP/2 (streams on 1 TCP) → HTTP/3 (QUIC on UDP)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Your recursive resolver already knows .com's servers. Does it still ask the root for example.com?

No. It caches the root's referral (the .com NS records) for their TTL and goes straight to the .com servers. The root is only asked when that cache has expired.

2. Why does a new HTTPS request cost at least 2 RTTs before any HTTP data flows (TLS 1.3 over TCP)?

1 RTT for the TCP handshake, then 1 RTT for the TLS 1.3 handshake. Only then can the HTTP request be sent. HTTP/3 merges the transport and TLS handshakes to save one of them.

3. How does the browser know the server really is example.com and not an attacker?

The server sends a certificate for example.com signed by a CA the browser trusts, and proves it holds the matching private key (CertificateVerify). The browser checks the chain, the hostname and the validity dates.

4. What is SNI and why is it needed?

Server Name Indication: the hostname sent in ClientHello. One IP (a load balancer, a CDN) can serve thousands of sites, so it needs to know which certificate to present before encryption starts.

5. 502 vs 504 from your load balancer: what's the difference?

502 Bad Gateway: the LB got an invalid or no response from the backend (crashed, connection refused). 504 Gateway Timeout: the backend didn't answer in time.

docs.text: Explain what happens between pressing Enter and receiving the first byte of HTML, in your own words in 5 lines.

docs.title: 6.1 — HTTP headers deep dive
docs.text:
In short

A header is a Name: value line of metadata that travels with every HTTP request and response. The body is the content. The headers say who it is for, what format it is in, how long it may be cached, who is asking, what the browser is allowed to do with it, and which hops it passed through. Most of what CDNs, load balancers, ingress controllers, auth and browser security do is driven by headers.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Header (field) — A Name: value line of metadata Names are case-insensitive; sent before the body Request / response header — Metadata sent by the client / by the server Accept, Authorization vs Content-Type, Set-Cookie Start line / status line — First line of a request / response GET /path HTTP/1.1 / HTTP/1.1 200 OK MIME type Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions Format label like application/json Put in Content-Type and Accept Content negotiation — Client says what it can take, server picks Accept-* in, Content-* + Vary out Hop-by-hop / end-to-end — Headers for one connection / for the final recipient Proxies strip hop-by-hop ones (Connection, Keep-Alive) Cache-Control — Caching rules for browsers and CDNs max-age, no-store, private, s-maxage … ETag Entity Tag Version id of a response Client sends it back in If-None-Match; unchanged → 304 Cookie / Set-Cookie — Small state the browser stores and sends back Server sets it; browser adds Cookie to matching requests Authorization / Bearer — Credentials for a request Authorization: Bearer <token>; missing/invalid → 401 CORS Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Browser rule for cross-origin reads API answers with Access-Control-Allow-* headers Origin — scheme + host + port of a page https://app.example.com ≠ https://api.example.com HSTS HTTP Strict Transport Security "Always use HTTPS for this site" Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=… CSP Content Security Policy Allow-list of where scripts/styles may load from Browser blocks everything else (stops most XSS) XSS Cross-Site Scripting Attacker's script running in your page Prevented by escaping output + CSP X-Forwarded-For (XFF) — Original client IP behind proxies Each proxy appends the address it received from traceparent W3C Trace Context Distributed-trace id passed between services 00-<trace-id>-<span-id>-<flags> HPACK / QPACK — Header compression in HTTP/2 / HTTP/3 Static + dynamic tables replace repeated headers with indexes Pseudo-header — HTTP/2+ fields that replace the start line :method, :path, :authority, :scheme, :status

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
An HTTP message has four parts: a start line, a block of headers, an empty line, and an optional body. The headers are metadata: they describe the body and the request, and they tell every hop what to do.

POST /api/cart HTTP/1.1
Host: shop.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 11
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi…
Accept: application/json

{"sku": 42}

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
• Format: Name: value, one per line, ending with \r\n. An empty line ends the header block; then come exactly Content-Length bytes of body (or chunked pieces).
  • Names are case-insensitive: content-type = Content-Type. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 require them lowercase on the wire.
  • Repeated headers can be merged with commas (Accept: a, b), except Set-Cookie, which must stay one per line.
  • HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 don't send text lines. The start line becomes pseudo-headers (:method: POST, :path: /api/cart, :authority: shop.example.com), and all headers are compressed with HPACK / QPACK, so a repeated Cookie or User-Agent costs only a few bytes after the first request.
  • Size limits exist. Servers and proxies cap header size (nginx: large_client_header_buffers, default 4 × 8 KB). Too-large cookies or JWTs give 400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large or 431 Request Header Fields Too Large.
  • Custom headers: just pick a name (X-Tenant-Id, Acme-Feature-Flag). The X- prefix is an old convention and is no longer recommended for new standards, but it's still common.

docs.title: 2 · The header families
docs.text: Family Request headers Response headers Used for Routing Host (:authority in h2/h3) Location (with 3xx / 201) Virtual hosting, ingress rules, redirects Content negotiation Accept, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language Content-Type, Content-Encoding, Content-Language, Vary JSON vs HTML, gzip/br/zstd, language Body framing Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding same Where the body ends Connection Connection, Upgrade Connection, Keep-Alive Keep-alive, WebSocket upgrade (hop-by-hop) Caching Cache-Control, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, Age, Expires Browser and CDN caching Auth Authorization, Cookie WWW-Authenticate, Set-Cookie Logins, API tokens, sessions Security Origin, Sec-Fetch-* Strict-Transport-Security, Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy Telling the browser how to protect the user CORS Origin, Access-Control-Request-* Access-Control-Allow-* Cross-origin API calls from JS Proxies X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, Forwarded, Via Via Real client IP and scheme behind LBs Observability X-Request-ID, traceparent, tracestate X-Request-ID, Server-Timing Correlating logs and traces Rate limiting — Retry-After (+ RateLimit-* drafts) Telling clients when to retry after 429 / 503

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The client lists what it accepts: Accept: application/json, Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd, Accept-Language: tr, en;q=0.8 (q = preference weight).
  2. The server picks one and labels the response: Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8, Content-Encoding: br.
  3. It adds Vary: Accept-Encoding so caches know the URL has several versions and must key on that header too. A missing Vary is a classic CDN bug: users get a compressed (or wrong-language) copy meant for someone else.

DevOps note

A wrong Content-Type breaks things quietly: JSON served as text/html, or JS as text/plain is blocked when X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff is set. Check it with curl -sI.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text:
Caching headers tell browsers and CDNs whether they may keep a copy, for how long it stays fresh, and how to check whether it has changed.

Cache-Control directive Meaning max-age=3600 Fresh for 3600 s; use it without asking s-maxage=600 Same, but only for shared caches (CDN); overrides max-age there no-cache You may store it but must revalidate before every use (not "don't cache"!) no-store Never store it (bank pages, personal data) private / public Only the browser may cache it / CDNs may too immutable Will never change during its lifetime; don't revalidate even on reload stale-while-revalidate=60 Serve the stale copy for up to 60 s while fetching a new one in the background

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
• Freshness: while max-age hasn't expired, the cache answers on its own, without any request.
  • Revalidation: after that, the cache sends a conditional request with If-None-Match: "<etag>" (or If-Modified-Since). If nothing changed the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body, and the copy is fresh again.
  • The common pattern: HTML gets no-cache (always check), static assets with a hash in the file name get max-age=31536000, immutable (cache forever; a new deploy means a new file name).

docs.title: How does Authorization work?
docs.text:
The client sends credentials on every request: Authorization: Bearer <token> (OAuth/JWT) or Authorization: Basic <base64(user:pass)>. If they are missing or invalid, the server answers 401 Unauthorized with WWW-Authenticate saying which scheme to use. 403 Forbidden means "I know who you are, but you're not allowed."

Warning

Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Basic auth and bearer tokens are only safe over HTTPS, and they must never be logged.

docs.title: How do cookies work?
docs.text:
1. The server sends Set-Cookie: session=abc123; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=86400.
  2. The browser stores it, and on every later request to a matching site and path it adds Cookie: session=abc123.
Attribute What it does HttpOnly JavaScript can't read it, so XSS can't steal the session Secure Only sent over HTTPS SameSite=Lax / Strict / None Whether it's sent on cross-site requests (CSRF protection). None requires Secure Domain / Path Which hosts and paths receive it Max-Age / Expires Lifetime; without them it's a session cookie __Host- name prefix Forces Secure, Path=/ and no Domain (strongest scoping)

docs.title: 6 · Security headers
docs.text:
These headers ask the browser to enforce rules that protect the user:

Header Example Protects against Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains Downgrade to HTTP, SSL stripping Content-Security-Policy (CSP) default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' cdn.example.com XSS, injected scripts X-Content-Type-Options nosniff The browser guessing a file's type X-Frame-Options / CSP frame-ancestors DENY / frame-ancestors 'none' Clickjacking (your page inside an iframe) Referrer-Policy strict-origin-when-cross-origin Leaking full URLs to other sites Permissions-Policy camera=(), geolocation=() Pages using powerful browser features

X-XSS-Protection is obsolete; modern browsers ignore it. Use CSP instead.

docs.title: What is it?
docs.text: Browsers apply the same-origin policy: JavaScript from https://app.example.com can't read responses from https://api.example.com (a different origin), unless the API explicitly allows it. CORS is how the API gives that permission, using headers.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
• Simple requests (GET/POST with basic content types) go straight out with an Origin header. The browser lets JS read the response only if it contains a matching Access-Control-Allow-Origin.
  • Other requests (PUT/DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, custom headers) first send an OPTIONS preflight. The API answers with the allowed origin, methods and headers; Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser cache that answer.
  • With cookies (credentials: 'include'), Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is not allowed: name the exact origin and add Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
  • CORS is enforced only by browsers. It is not authentication, and it doesn't protect your API from curl or scripts.

docs.title: How does X-Forwarded-For work?
docs.text:
Behind a load balancer, your app sees the LB's IP, not the user's. So each proxy appends the address it received the connection from:

X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, 10.0.1.12
X-Forwarded-Proto: https
X-Forwarded-Host: shop.example.com

The leftmost value is the client as claimed. A client can send a fake X-Forwarded-For, so configure your app or ingress to trust only your own proxies' entries (nginx set_real_ip_from + real_ip_header, Express trust proxy). The standard form is Forwarded: for=203.0.113.7;proto=https.

docs.title: How does traceparent work?
docs.text:
The first service (or the ingress) creates a trace id. Every service passes it on in outgoing calls and adds its own span id:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             ver ── trace-id (16 bytes) ───────── parent span ─── sampled

OpenTelemetry SDKs read and write this header automatically, so one request can be followed across the LB, the services and the database calls. X-Request-ID is the simpler version: one id to grep for in all logs.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Ingress / nginx: proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;. Add security headers with add_header … always; so they're present on error pages too.
  • WebSockets through nginx need proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";, because these are hop-by-hop headers and aren't forwarded by default.
  • "Login loops behind the LB" usually mean the app thinks the request is http because it ignores X-Forwarded-Proto, so it redirects forever or sets Secure cookies wrongly.
  • CDN hit ratio depends on Cache-Control, Vary and cookies. A Set-Cookie on a static response, or Vary: User-Agent, can make it uncacheable.
  • Big JWTs or many cookies hit header size limits on ingress or the LB. Raise the buffers or slim the tokens.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# 1. Only the response headers (HEAD request)
curl -sI https://github.com | head -25

# 2. Everything: request headers (>) and response headers (<)
curl -sv https://example.com -o /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E '^[<>]'

# 3. Content negotiation and compression
curl -sI -H 'Accept-Encoding: br, gzip' https://www.wikipedia.org | grep -iE 'content-(type|encoding)|vary'

# 4. Conditional request: get the ETag, then ask "changed?"
URL=https://www.wikipedia.org/portal/wikipedia.org/assets/img/Wikipedia-logo-v2.png
ETAG=$(curl -sI $URL | grep -i '^etag' | cut -d' ' -f2 | tr -d '\r')
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "If-None-Match: $ETAG" $URL   # → 304

# 5. A CORS preflight by hand
curl -si -X OPTIONS https://api.github.com/user \
  -H 'Origin: https://example.com' -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET' | grep -i '^access-control'

# 6. See exactly what a server receives
python3 - <<'PYEOF'
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        print(self.requestline); print(self.headers)
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header('Content-Type','text/plain'); self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b'ok\n')
HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 8080), H).handle_request()
PYEOF
# in another terminal: curl -H 'X-Hello: world' http://127.0.0.1:8080/

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: I want to… Header Route by hostname Host Say what the body is Content-Type Compress responses Accept-Encoding → Content-Encoding + Vary Cache static files forever Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable Always revalidate HTML Cache-Control: no-cache + ETag Never store a response Cache-Control: no-store Send an API token Authorization: Bearer … Keep a safe session cookie Set-Cookie: …; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax Force HTTPS Strict-Transport-Security Block injected scripts Content-Security-Policy Allow a front-end on another origin Access-Control-Allow-Origin (+ preflight) Know the real client IP X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded (from trusted proxies only) Follow a request across services traceparent, X-Request-ID

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What does Cache-Control: no-cache actually mean?

The response may be stored, but it must be revalidated with the server (e.g. If-None-Match) before each use. To forbid storing, use no-store.

2. Your API works with curl but the browser shows a CORS error. Why, and where is the fix?

CORS is enforced only by browsers. The API (or the ingress in front of it) must return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin, and answer the OPTIONS preflight with the allowed methods and headers.

3. Behind your load balancer every log line shows the same client IP. What's wrong?

The app logs the TCP peer (the LB). Read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded, and trust only entries added by your own proxies.

4. Why must a CDN see Vary: Accept-Encoding?

The same URL exists in several encodings (br, gzip, none). Without Vary the CDN may serve a brotli body to a client that can't decode it.

5. Which cookie attributes stop JavaScript from reading a session cookie and stop it being sent over HTTP?

HttpOnly (no JS access) and Secure (HTTPS only). Add SameSite=Lax or Strict against CSRF.

docs.title: 6.2 — DNS deep dive
docs.text:
In short

DNS is the internet's distributed phone book. A recursive resolver walks from the root to the TLD to the domain's authoritative servers to turn a name into records: IP addresses, aliases, mail servers, text. Every answer is cached for its TTL. That makes DNS fast, and it's also why DNS changes "take time".

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) DNS Domain Name System Distributed database of names Hierarchy of zones, each served by its own name servers Zone — The part of the tree one operator controls example.com zone holds its records and delegations Stub resolver — The small resolver in your OS Asks one recursive resolver, caches answers Recursive resolver — Server that does the lookup for you Walks root → TLD → authoritative, caches everything Authoritative server — Server that holds the zone's real answers Answers with the AA (authoritative answer) flag Root / TLD Top-Level Domain Top of the tree / .com, .org, .tr Root points to TLD servers; TLD points to domain NS Record (RR) Resource Record One entry: name, type, TTL, value shop.example.com. 300 IN A 93.184.215.14 TTL Time To Live Seconds an answer may be cached Lower TTL = faster changes, more queries Negative caching — Caching "this name doesn't exist" (NXDOMAIN) Lasts the zone's SOA minimum TTL Glue record — IP of a name server, stored in the parent Breaks the loop when NS is inside its own zone DNSSEC DNS Security Extensions Signatures on DNS records Resolver validates a chain of keys from the root DoH / DoT DNS over HTTPS / DNS over TLS Encrypted DNS Hides queries from the network path CoreDNS — Kubernetes' cluster DNS server Answers *.svc.cluster.local, forwards the rest ndots — resolv.conf option Names with fewer dots than this try search domains first

docs.title: 1 · How does resolution work?
docs.text:
1. Your app calls getaddrinfo("shop.example.com"). The OS checks /etc/hosts, then its own cache (systemd-resolved, mDNSResponder on macOS).
  2. On a miss it asks the recursive resolver configured in /etc/resolv.conf (your router, ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or the VPC resolver in the cloud).
  3. If the resolver has nothing cached, it asks a root server: "where is .com?" The root answers with a referral to the .com TLD servers.
  4. It asks a TLD server: "where is example.com?" It gets a referral to ns1.example.com (plus glue IPs).
  5. It asks the authoritative server and gets the final answer: A 93.184.215.14, TTL 300.
  6. Every step is cached. The next lookup for anything under .com skips the root, and the next lookup for shop.example.com within 300 s is answered from cache in under a millisecond.

DNS mostly uses UDP port 53 (one packet each way). Large answers and zone transfers use TCP 53.

docs.title: 2 · Record types
docs.text: Type Holds Example Used for A / AAAA IPv4 / IPv6 address 93.184.215.14 / 2606:2800::1 The basic name → IP CNAME Alias to another name www → shop.example.com. Pointing at a CDN or LB hostname. Not allowed at the zone apex ALIAS / ANAME Provider-specific apex alias example.com → lb-123.elb.amazonaws.com CNAME-like behaviour at the apex (Route 53 alias) NS Name servers of a zone ns1.example.com. Delegation SOA Zone metadata serial, refresh, negative TTL Zone management MX Mail servers + priority 10 mx1.example.com. Email delivery TXT Free text v=spf1 …, google-site-verification=… SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification, ACME DNS-01 SRV host + port of a service _sip._tcp 10 5 5060 sip.example.com. Service discovery (also in Kubernetes) CAA Which CAs may issue certs 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" Certificate security HTTPS / SVCB Connection hints alpn="h3,h2" Advertise HTTP/3, ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) PTR IP → name 14.215.184.93.in-addr.arpa. Reverse DNS, mail server reputation

docs.title: 3 · TTL and caching: why "DNS takes time"
How does it work?
docs.text:
Every resolver and stub caches each answer for its TTL. If a record had TTL 86400 and you change it, some users keep the old IP for up to a day. There is no "propagation"; old copies just expire.

  • Before a migration, lower the TTL (e.g. to 60) at least one old-TTL period ahead. Do the switch, check, then raise it again.
  • Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached too. If you query a name before creating it, you may keep seeing "doesn't exist" for the SOA's negative TTL.
  • Applications cache too. The JVM (networkaddress.cache.ttl), some HTTP clients and connection pools keep IPs far longer than the TTL. That is a classic cause of "we failed over but traffic still goes to the old IP".

docs.title: 4 · DNS inside Kubernetes
docs.text:
• Every Service gets a name: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local → its ClusterIP. Headless Services (clusterIP: None) return the pod IPs directly.
  • Pods get /etc/resolv.conf with nameserver <kube-dns IP>, a search list (<ns>.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local) and ndots:5.
  • ndots:5 means any name with fewer than 5 dots is first tried with every search suffix. api.stripe.com (2 dots) becomes api.stripe.com.shop.svc.cluster.local, api.stripe.com.svc.cluster.local … before the real query, so one lookup costs 4–5 round trips (×2 for A and AAAA).
  • Fixes: use FQDNs with a trailing dot (api.stripe.com.), set dnsConfig.options: ndots: "2" on the pod, and run NodeLocal DNSCache so lookups are answered on the node.
  • Intermittent 5-second delays usually point to UDP conntrack races or packet loss to CoreDNS. Check the CoreDNS metrics and logs.

docs.title: 5 · Security: DNSSEC and encrypted DNS
docs.text:
• DNSSEC signs records. Each zone's key is vouched for by its parent (DS record), up to the root. A validating resolver rejects forged answers. It proves authenticity, not privacy.
  • DoT (TCP 853) and DoH (HTTPS 443) encrypt the query between you and the resolver, so the network path can't read or change it. Browsers and phones increasingly use them by default.
  • DNS is an attack surface: dangling CNAMEs to deleted cloud resources allow subdomain takeover; open resolvers are used for amplification attacks; and registrar or DNS-provider accounts deserve MFA.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Cloud: private hosted zones and the VPC resolver (AWS .2 address, Route 53 Resolver endpoints for hybrid), split-horizon DNS (different answers inside and outside).
  • ExternalDNS watches Services and Ingresses and writes records to Route 53, Cloud DNS, Cloudflare and others, so DNS becomes part of GitOps.
  • Health-checked / weighted / geo DNS is a cheap global load balancer, but clients only notice changes as fast as TTLs (and app caches) allow.
  • "It's always DNS": when something fails intermittently, check resolution first (dig from inside the pod, not from your laptop).

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
dig shop.example.com +short             # just the answer
dig example.com +trace                  # walk root → TLD → authoritative yourself
dig example.com NS +short               # who is authoritative
dig example.com MX TXT CAA              # several record types
dig @1.1.1.1 example.com +stats         # ask a specific resolver, see query time
dig cloudflare.com HTTPS +short         # HTTP/3 hints in DNS
dig -x 1.1.1.1 +short                   # reverse lookup (PTR)
resolvectl status                       # which resolver your Linux box uses

# Inside Kubernetes
kubectl run -it --rm dnstest --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sh -c \
  'cat /etc/resolv.conf; nslookup kubernetes.default'

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Check Change not visible Old TTL still cached dig +ttlid, query the authoritative NS directly Works on laptop, not in pod Search domains / ndots / CoreDNS cat /etc/resolv.conf in the pod NXDOMAIN right after creating a record Negative caching SOA minimum TTL Traffic still hits old IP after failover App-level DNS cache JVM TTL, connection pools Random 5 s delays UDP loss / conntrack race CoreDNS metrics, NodeLocal DNSCache Can't put CNAME on example.com Apex restriction Use ALIAS/ANAME or A records

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Who actually walks the root → TLD → authoritative chain: your laptop or the resolver?

The recursive resolver. Your laptop's stub resolver sends one query and gets the final answer.

2. You changed an A record with TTL 3600 ten minutes ago. Why do some users still see the old IP?

Resolvers that cached it before the change keep it until their copy's TTL expires (up to an hour), and some apps cache even longer.

3. Why can a pod's lookup of api.stripe.com be slow, and what are two fixes?

ndots:5 makes it try every search suffix first, each for A and AAAA. Use the FQDN with a trailing dot, lower ndots, and/or run NodeLocal DNSCache.

4. What does DNSSEC protect against, and what doesn't it protect?

Forged or modified answers (authenticity and integrity). It doesn't hide which names you look up; that's DoH/DoT.

5. What is a subdomain takeover?

A CNAME still points at a cloud resource (bucket, app, CDN) that was deleted. An attacker claims that resource name and now serves content on your subdomain.

docs.title: 6.3 — TCP deep dive
docs.text:
In short

TCP turns unreliable IP packets into a reliable, ordered byte stream between two sockets. It opens with a 3-way handshake, numbers every byte and resends what isn't ACKed. It slows the sender down when the receiver (flow control) or the network (congestion control) can't keep up. It closes with FIN packets.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) TCP Transmission Control Protocol Reliable byte stream over IP Handshake, sequence numbers, ACKs, retransmits Socket — An endpoint: IP + port (+ protocol) A connection = 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port) Segment — One TCP packet Header (20+ bytes) + payload SYN / ACK / FIN / RST synchronize / acknowledge / finish / reset Header flags Open / confirm / close politely / abort Sequence number — Byte offset of the segment's data Lets the receiver reorder and detect gaps MSS Maximum Segment Size Largest payload per segment Usually 1460 bytes (1500 MTU − 40 bytes of headers) rwnd receive window Free buffer space at the receiver Flow control: sender may not exceed it cwnd congestion window Sender's estimate of what the network can take Grows on ACKs, shrinks on loss RTT / RTO Round-Trip Time / Retransmission TimeOut Measured delay / timer for resends RTO adapts to the measured RTT CUBIC / BBR — / Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT Congestion control algorithms Loss-based (Linux default) / model-based TIME_WAIT — State after an active close Keeps the 4-tuple reserved ~60 s on Linux Keep-alive — Reusing a connection for many requests (HTTP) or probing idle ones (TCP) Saves handshakes / detects dead peers Backlog — Queue of connections waiting for accept() Full queue → dropped SYNs, slow connects Ephemeral port — Random client-side port Range 32768–60999 on Linux

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The client sends SYN with a random initial sequence number x.
  2. The server answers SYN-ACK: its own number y, and ack = x+1.
  3. The client sends ACK with ack = y+1. Both sides are now ESTABLISHED.

It costs one RTT before any data can flow. On the server, the kernel completes handshakes by itself and puts finished connections in the accept queue (the backlog) until the app calls accept(). If the app is too slow, the queue fills and new SYNs are dropped, which looks like "random 1 s / 3 s connect delays".

docs.title: 2 · Sending data: sequence numbers, ACKs and windows
docs.text:
• Every byte has a sequence number. The receiver ACKs "I have everything up to byte N", and reorders out-of-order segments.
  • Retransmission: if an ACK doesn't arrive before the RTO, or three duplicate ACKs say "still waiting for byte N", the segment is resent.
  • Flow control: each ACK carries the receiver's free buffer (rwnd). A slow reader shrinks it to zero and the sender pauses.
  • Throughput limit: at most window / RTT. A 64 KB window over a 100 ms path gives only ~5 Mbit/s, which is why window scaling exists and why long-distance transfers need big buffers.

docs.title: 3 · Congestion control
docs.text:
The network has no "slow down" message, so the sender guesses:

  • Slow start: begin with ~10 segments and double cwnd every RTT.
  • Congestion avoidance: past a threshold, grow more carefully.
  • Loss = congestion: on loss, cut cwnd (CUBIC multiplies by 0.7) and grow again.
  • BBR (Google) instead measures the bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT and paces packets to match, which works better on lossy or long paths. Enable it with net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr.

docs.title: 4 · Closing: FIN, TIME_WAIT and CLOSE_WAIT
docs.text:
• The side that closes first sends FIN and later enters TIME_WAIT for 2×MSL (~60 s on Linux), so late packets from the old connection can't confuse a new one with the same 4-tuple.
  • RST aborts immediately: sent when a port is closed, by firewalls, or by apps that close with unread data.
  • Many TIME_WAIT on a client = it opens a new connection per request. Use keep-alive/pooling; otherwise you can run out of ephemeral ports.
  • Many CLOSE_WAIT = the peer closed but your app never called close(). That's a bug (leaked sockets), not a kernel setting.

docs.title: 5 · Keep-alive and connection reuse
docs.text:
• HTTP keep-alive / connection pools reuse one TCP (and TLS) connection for many requests: no handshake per request. This is the biggest easy win for service-to-service latency.
  • TCP keepalive probes (SO_KEEPALIVE) detect dead peers on idle connections. Default is after 2 hours; many apps tune it.
  • Idle timeouts must line up: if the load balancer drops idle connections after 60 s but the client pool keeps them for 90 s, the client sends on a dead connection and gets a reset (connection reset by peer, 502s). Keep the client idle timeout shorter than the server/LB's.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• 502 / 504 behind an LB often come from idle-timeout mismatches or backends closing keep-alive connections that the LB still uses.
  • Load balancing long-lived connections: gRPC/HTTP/2 keep one TCP connection, so an L4 balancer sends all requests from a client to one pod. Use L7 (per-request) balancing or client-side balancing.
  • SNAT port exhaustion (cloud NAT gateways, many connections to one destination) shows up as connection timeouts. Reuse connections, or add NAT IPs.
  • Useful sysctls: net.core.somaxconn (accept backlog), net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
ss -tan state established | head           # current connections
ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c # count connections per state
ss -ltn                                     # listening sockets + backlog (Recv-Q / Send-Q)
ss -ti dst 1.1.1.1                          # per-connection details: rtt, cwnd, retrans

sudo tcpdump -ni any 'tcp port 443 and host example.com' -c 12 &   # watch the handshake
curl -s -o /dev/null https://example.com

curl -so /dev/null -w 'tcp=%{time_connect}s tls=%{time_appconnect}s ttfb=%{time_starttransfer}s\n' https://example.com
sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control net.core.somaxconn

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Connects take exactly +1 s / +3 s SYN dropped and retried (full backlog, firewall) connection refused Nothing listening → RST connection timed out SYN lost: firewall, security group, routing, NAT connection reset by peer Peer/LB closed it (idle timeout, crash, proxy) Thousands of CLOSE_WAIT App doesn't close sockets Thousands of TIME_WAIT (client) No connection reuse Slow transfers over long distance Small windows, loss → try BBR, tune buffers

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does TCP need a handshake before sending data?

Both sides must agree on starting sequence numbers and confirm the other side is reachable and willing.

2. What's the difference between flow control and congestion control?

Flow control protects the receiver (rwnd, its buffer). Congestion control protects the network (cwnd, estimated from loss or bandwidth/RTT).

3. Your service has 20,000 sockets in CLOSE_WAIT. What do you fix?

The application: it receives the peer's FIN but never closes its socket (leaked connections, missing close() / response body not closed).

4. Why do you get intermittent 502s when the LB idle timeout is 60 s and the backend's keep-alive timeout is 30 s?

The backend closes idle connections first; the LB may send a new request on a connection the backend just closed. Make the backend's timeout longer than the LB's.

5. Why can one gRPC client overload a single pod behind a Kubernetes Service?

kube-proxy balances per TCP connection, and gRPC sends all requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. Use L7 load balancing (mesh, gateway) or client-side balancing.
