docs.title: 6.4 — TLS & certificates deep dive
docs.text:
In short

TLS gives a connection three things: confidentiality (nobody can read it), integrity (nobody can change it) and authentication (you're really talking to shop.example.com). The two sides agree on fresh keys with ECDHE, the server proves its identity with a certificate that chains up to a root CA your device already trusts, and from then on everything is encrypted with fast symmetric ciphers.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) TLS Transport Layer Security Encryption + authentication for a connection Handshake agrees keys, then records are encrypted SSL Secure Sockets Layer TLS's obsolete predecessor Name survives in "SSL certificate"; protocol is dead Symmetric cipher — Same key encrypts and decrypts AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305: fast, used for data Asymmetric crypto — Public/private key pair Used only to agree keys and sign ECDHE Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Key exchange Both sides combine key shares into the same secret Forward secrecy — Old traffic stays safe if the server key leaks later Fresh (ephemeral) keys per connection Certificate (X.509) — Signed statement "this public key belongs to these names" Contains SAN, issuer, validity, public key SAN Subject Alternative Name List of hostnames in a certificate Browser checks the hostname is in it CA Certificate Authority Organisation that signs certificates Must verify you control the domain first Chain / intermediate — Leaf ← intermediate ← root Server sends leaf + intermediates Trust store — Root CAs your OS/browser trusts /etc/ssl/certs, Java cacerts, browser stores ACME Automatic Certificate Management Environment Protocol to get certificates automatically Prove control (HTTP-01/DNS-01), receive cert OCSP / CRL Online Certificate Status Protocol / Certificate Revocation List Ways to say "this cert is revoked" Being replaced by short-lived certificates mTLS mutual TLS Both sides present certificates Service identity in meshes and zero-trust SNI / ECH Server Name Indication / Encrypted Client Hello Hostname in the handshake / encrypted version of it Lets one IP host many sites / hides which one

docs.title: 1 · What does TLS protect, and how does the handshake work?
How does it work?
docs.text:
Chapter 6 showed the 1-RTT TLS 1.3 handshake. Here is what each part achieves:

  1. ClientHello: supported ciphers, an ECDHE key share, SNI (hostname) and ALPN (h2, http/1.1).
  2. ServerHello: the server's key share. Both sides now compute the same shared secret without ever sending it, and derive the session keys. Everything after this point is encrypted.
  3. Certificate + CertificateVerify: the certificate chain, plus a signature over the handshake made with the certificate's private key. That signature proves the server owns the key, not just a copy of the public certificate.
  4. Finished: a MAC over the whole handshake, so a tampered handshake is detected.

Because the key shares are ephemeral, recorded traffic can't be decrypted later even if the server's private key leaks (forward secrecy). TLS 1.3 removed old, weak options (RSA key transport, CBC, SHA-1, renegotiation).

Post-quantum: major browsers, Cloudflare and Go/OpenSSL now offer a hybrid key exchange (X25519MLKEM768) by default, combining classical ECDHE with ML-KEM so recorded traffic stays safe against future quantum computers.

docs.title: 2 · Certificates and the chain of trust
What is in a certificate?
docs.text:
Subject Alternative Name: shop.example.com, www.shop.example.com
Issuer:                   Let's Encrypt R11
Validity:                 2026-11-01 → 2027-01-30
Public key:               EC P-256
Signature:                (made by the issuer's private key)

docs.title: How does the browser decide to trust it?
docs.text:
It builds a path leaf → intermediate(s) → root, verifies each signature, checks the hostname is in the SAN, checks the dates, and requires the root to be in its trust store. The server must send the intermediates. If it forgets them, browsers may still work (they cache intermediates) but curl, Java, Python and mobile apps fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate".

Types: DV (domain validated, what almost everyone uses), OV/EV (organisation checks; browsers no longer show them differently), wildcard (*.example.com, one level only).

docs.title: 3 · Lifetimes, revocation and automation
docs.text:
• Lifetimes are shrinking. Under CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081, the maximum validity of public certificates dropped from 398 to 200 days on 15 March 2026, will drop to 100 days in March 2027 and to 47 days in March 2029. Manual renewal no longer works; automation is mandatory.
  • Revocation (CRL, OCSP) has always been unreliable: browsers soft-fail. The industry answer is short-lived certificates; Let's Encrypt has stopped running OCSP.
  • ACME automates everything: prove domain control with HTTP-01 (a file at /.well-known/acme-challenge/) or DNS-01 (a TXT record, required for wildcards), get the certificate, renew at ~2/3 of its lifetime.

docs.title: 4 · mTLS: certificates for services
docs.text: In normal TLS only the server proves who it is. In mutual TLS the client presents a certificate too. That's how service meshes (Istio, Linkerd), SPIFFE/SPIRE and zero-trust networks give every workload an identity: short-lived certs (hours), rotated automatically, used both for encryption and authorization ("only orders may call payments").

docs.title: 5 · Where TLS terminates
docs.text: Pattern TLS ends at Trade-off Edge termination CDN / LB / ingress Simple; traffic inside is plain unless re-encrypted Re-encryption LB, then new TLS to backend Encrypted end to end, two certificates Passthrough The pod itself (L4 LB) LB can't see HTTP (no path routing, no WAF) Mesh mTLS Sidecar / node proxy Encrypted pod-to-pod without app changes

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• cert-manager + an Issuer/ClusterIssuer + annotations on Ingress/Gateway = certificates that renew themselves. Alert on certmanager_certificate_expiration_timestamp_seconds.
  • Expiry monitoring: blackbox exporter probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry or your synthetic checks. Expired certs are still a top cause of outages.
  • Private CAs for internal services (cert-manager CA issuer, Vault PKI, cloud private CA); distribute the root to clients' trust stores (and Java's separate cacerts!).
  • CAA records limit which CAs may issue for your domain; Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh) show every certificate issued for it.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Handshake details: protocol, cipher, key exchange, chain
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | \
  grep -E 'Protocol|Cipher|Server Temp Key|Negotiated|s:|i:'

# The certificate itself
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | \
  openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

# Days left
echo | openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com 2>/dev/null | \
  openssl x509 -noout -enddate

# Every certificate ever issued for a domain
curl -s 'https://crt.sh/?q=example.com&output=json' | head -c 600; echo

# In Kubernetes with cert-manager
kubectl get certificates,certificaterequests,orders,challenges -A

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Error Meaning / fix certificate has expired Renewal failed → check ACME challenges, cert-manager logs unable to get local issuer certificate Missing intermediate on server, or root not in client trust store hostname mismatch / ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID Name not in SAN (wildcards cover one level) self-signed certificate in chain Private CA not trusted by this client (or a TLS-inspecting proxy) handshake failure / no shared cipher Old client (TLS 1.0/1.1) or wrong SNI HTTP-01 challenge fails Port 80 blocked, redirect loop, wrong ingress class

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why doesn't TLS just use RSA/ECDSA to encrypt all the data?

Asymmetric crypto is slow. It's used once to agree keys and prove identity; the data uses fast symmetric ciphers.

2. What does the CertificateVerify signature prove that the certificate alone doesn't?

That the server has the private key. Anyone can copy a public certificate; only the owner can sign with its key.

3. Your site works in Chrome but curl says 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Why?

The server isn't sending the intermediate certificate. Chrome had it cached; curl didn't. Serve the full chain.

4. Why is the industry moving to 47-day certificates?

Revocation doesn't work reliably, so short lifetimes limit how long a stolen or mis-issued certificate is useful, and force automation.

5. Which ACME challenge do you need for *.example.com?

DNS-01: wildcard certificates require a TXT record under _acme-challenge.example.com.

docs.title: 6.5 — HTTP/2 & HTTP/3 deep dive
docs.text:
In short

HTTP's meaning (methods, headers, status codes) hasn't changed since 1.1. What changed is how it travels. HTTP/2 splits messages into binary frames and runs many streams in parallel over one TCP connection, and HTTP/3 moves that onto QUIC over UDP so a lost packet only stalls one stream, handshakes are faster, and connections survive network changes.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) HOL blocking Head-Of-Line blocking One slow/lost item delays everything behind it At HTTP level in 1.1, at TCP level in h2 Frame — Smallest unit in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, … with a stream id Stream — One request/response pair inside a connection Many streams interleave on one connection Multiplexing — Many streams over one connection Frames from different streams mixed on the wire HPACK / QPACK — Header compression for h2 / h3 Tables of previously sent headers ALPN Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation Picks h2 or http/1.1 during TLS Listed in ClientHello h2c HTTP/2 cleartext HTTP/2 without TLS Used inside clusters (gRPC) QUIC — (originally "Quick UDP Internet Connections") Transport over UDP with TLS 1.3 built in Streams, loss recovery, congestion control in user space Connection ID — QUIC's connection identifier Survives IP/port changes (connection migration) 0-RTT zero round-trip time Sending data in the first flight on resumption Faster, but replayable → only for safe requests Alt-Svc Alternative Service Header advertising another protocol/endpoint Alt-Svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 Server push — h2 feature to send unrequested resources Removed from browsers; use 103 Early Hints

docs.title: 1 · Why HTTP/1.1 wasn't enough
docs.text:
• A connection carries one request at a time. Pipelining existed but never worked well, so browsers opened ~6 TCP+TLS connections per origin.
  • Headers are plain text and repeated on every request (cookies, user agent): kilobytes of overhead.
  • Developers worked around it with domain sharding, sprites and bundling. Many of those hacks are now harmful.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. TLS negotiates h2 via ALPN. Both sides exchange SETTINGS (max concurrent streams, window sizes).
  2. Each request gets an odd stream id. Its headers go in a HEADERS frame (HPACK-compressed), its body in DATA frames.
  3. Frames from many streams are interleaved on the one connection, so a big download doesn't block a small API call.
  4. Per-stream flow control and priorities let both sides control who gets the bandwidth.

The remaining problem: all streams share one TCP byte stream. If one TCP packet is lost, TCP holds back everything after it until it's resent, so all streams stall (TCP-level HOL blocking). On lossy mobile networks h2 can be slower than 1.1 with 6 connections.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
• QUIC runs on UDP and implements reliability, ordering and congestion control itself, per stream. A lost packet only delays the streams whose data was in it.
  • TLS 1.3 is built into QUIC: transport and crypto handshakes are combined into 1 RTT (0-RTT on resumption). Almost the whole header is encrypted.
  • Connection IDs instead of the IP/port 4-tuple: switching from Wi-Fi to 5G keeps the connection alive.
  • Discovery: the first visit uses h2 over TCP; the server says Alt-Svc: h3=":443" (or publishes an HTTPS DNS record), and the browser races QUIC on the next connection. If UDP 443 is blocked, it silently falls back to TCP.

docs.title: 4 · What changes for infrastructure
docs.text: Area Impact Load balancers h2/h3 terminate at the edge; backends often still get HTTP/1.1 or h2. H3 needs UDP 443 open and a UDP-capable LB L4 balancing of h2/gRPC One long connection per client → uneven load. Use L7 balancing or client-side balancing Timeouts Long-lived connections + streaming need idle and stream timeouts tuned separately Observability QUIC is encrypted; tcpdump shows little. Use qlog, server logs, or SSLKEYLOGFILE in tests Old hacks Domain sharding and huge bundles hurt h2/h3; prefer fewer origins and sensible splitting 103 Early Hints Replaces server push: tells the browser to preload CSS/JS while the server is still thinking

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• gRPC is HTTP/2. Inside the cluster it's often h2c; through an ingress you need h2 to the backend (backend-protocol: GRPC on the retired ingress-nginx, appProtocol: kubernetes.io/h2c on Gateway API).
  • Enable HTTP/3 at the CDN or edge first (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Google LB); it's the cheapest win for mobile users.
  • Max concurrent streams (SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS, often 100) caps parallel requests per connection; clients open more connections when they hit it.
  • Watch for HTTP/2 DoS classes (Rapid Reset, CONTINUATION floods): keep proxies patched.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
curl -sI --http2 https://www.cloudflare.com -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n'   # → 2
curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc                              # h3 advertised?
curl -sI --http3-only https://www.cloudflare.com -o /dev/null -w '%{http_version}\n' 2>/dev/null \
  || echo "your curl has no HTTP/3 support"
dig www.cloudflare.com HTTPS +short                                                # h3 hint in DNS
# Chrome: DevTools → Network → right-click columns → enable "Protocol" (h2 / h3)

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: HTTP/1.1 HTTP/2 HTTP/3 Transport TCP TCP QUIC (UDP) Format Text Binary frames Binary frames Parallelism ~6 connections Streams on 1 connection Independent streams Header compression none HPACK QPACK HOL blocking HTTP level TCP level none across streams Handshake (new) TCP + TLS = 2 RTT 2 RTT 1 RTT (0-RTT resume) Negotiation default ALPN h2 Alt-Svc / HTTPS record

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. HTTP/2 multiplexes streams. Why can it still suffer from head-of-line blocking?

Streams share one TCP connection; a lost TCP segment blocks delivery of all later bytes, so every stream waits.

2. How does a browser find out a site supports HTTP/3?

Alt-Svc: h3=":443" on an earlier response, or an HTTPS DNS record. Then it tries QUIC and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

3. Why is 0-RTT data restricted to safe requests?

An attacker can replay the first flight. Replaying a GET is harmless; replaying a payment POST is not.

4. Your gRPC service behind a Kubernetes Service has one hot pod. Why?

gRPC keeps one long-lived HTTP/2 connection; kube-proxy balances connections, not requests.

5. What happens to a QUIC connection when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 5G?

The IP changes but the Connection ID doesn't, so the connection migrates instead of reconnecting.

docs.text: Open your company's site in Chrome DevTools with the Protocol column. Which resources use h2, h3, or http/1.1, and why?

docs.title: 6.6 — Methods, status codes & API styles
docs.text:
In short

Every HTTP exchange is a method ("what do you want to do?") on a URL ("to what?") answered with a status code ("how did it go?"). Knowing which methods are safe and idempotent tells you what can be retried and cached, and knowing the status codes tells you whose fault an error is. API styles like REST, gRPC, GraphQL and WebSockets are different contracts built on these same pieces.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Method (verb) — The action of a request GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, … Safe — Doesn't change server state GET, HEAD, OPTIONS Idempotent — Doing it twice = doing it once GET, PUT, DELETE (not POST, PATCH) Status code — 3-digit result of a request 1xx info · 2xx ok · 3xx redirect · 4xx client · 5xx server REST REpresentational State Transfer Resource-oriented API style URLs are nouns, methods are verbs, JSON bodies OpenAPI — Machine-readable REST contract Generates docs, clients, validation gRPC gRPC Remote Procedure Calls RPC framework over HTTP/2 Protobuf contract, generated stubs, streaming Protobuf Protocol Buffers Compact binary serialization Schema with numbered fields GraphQL — Query language over one endpoint Client asks for exactly the fields it needs WebSocket — Full-duplex connection upgraded from HTTP Upgrade: websocket, then frames both ways SSE Server-Sent Events One-way stream from server over HTTP text/event-stream; used for LLM token streaming Idempotency key — Client-chosen id for a non-idempotent request Server stores the result; a retry returns the same result Rate limiting — Capping requests per client 429 + Retry-After

docs.title: 1 · Methods
docs.text: Method Meaning Safe Idempotent Body Cacheable GET Read a resource ✅ ✅ no ✅ HEAD Like GET, headers only ✅ ✅ no ✅ OPTIONS What's allowed? (CORS preflight) ✅ ✅ no — POST Create / run an action ❌ ❌ yes rarely PUT Replace a resource completely ❌ ✅ yes — PATCH Change part of a resource ❌ ❌ (can be) yes — DELETE Remove a resource ❌ ✅ optional —

docs.title: Why does idempotency matter?
docs.text: Networks fail after the server did the work but before the response arrived. The client can't know whether it happened. Retrying an idempotent request is safe; retrying a POST /payments charges twice. That's why proxies, meshes and SDKs only auto-retry idempotent methods, and why payment APIs (Stripe and others) use an Idempotency-Key header.

docs.title: 2 · Status codes that matter in operations
docs.text:
Code Meaning Usually means 200 / 201 / 204 OK / Created / No Content Success 301 / 308 Moved permanently Old URL, follow Location. 308 keeps the method 302 / 307 Found / temporary redirect Login redirects. 307 keeps the method 304 Not Modified Cache revalidation worked 400 Bad Request Invalid input, or headers/cookies too large 401 Unauthorized (= unauthenticated) Missing / expired token 403 Forbidden Authenticated but not allowed (RBAC, WAF, IP rule) 404 Not Found Wrong path, or wrong Host reaching the default backend 405 Method Not Allowed POST to a GET-only route 408 / 499 Request timeout / client closed (nginx) Client gave up or was too slow 409 / 412 Conflict / Precondition Failed Concurrent edit; If-Match didn't match 413 Content Too Large Body bigger than proxy limit (client_max_body_size) 429 Too Many Requests Rate limited; honour Retry-After 500 Internal Server Error Bug / unhandled exception in the app 502 Bad Gateway Proxy got a bad/no response: backend crashed, reset, wrong port 503 Service Unavailable No healthy backends, overloaded, maintenance 504 Gateway Timeout Backend too slow for the proxy's timeout

Who returned it?

A 502/503/504 is usually generated by the proxy (ingress, LB, mesh), not your app. Check the response headers (Server: envoy, via) and the proxy's own logs before searching the application logs.

docs.title: REST
docs.text: Resources as URLs (/orders/42), methods as verbs, JSON bodies, HTTP status codes and caching used as designed. Described with OpenAPI. Best for public APIs and anything a browser calls.

docs.title: gRPC
docs.text: A .proto file defines services and messages; tooling generates client and server code. Runs on HTTP/2, binary Protobuf, supports streaming in both directions, uses its own status codes (in grpc-status trailers, HTTP status is usually 200). Best for service-to-service calls. Needs L7 load balancing (see 6.3/6.5).

docs.title: GraphQL
docs.text: One endpoint (POST /graphql), a typed schema, and the client asks for exactly the fields it needs, avoiding many round trips. Harder to cache (POST, one URL) and to rate-limit (one query can be very expensive), so use query cost limits.

docs.title: WebSockets and SSE
docs.text:
• WebSocket: starts as HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket, server answers 101 Switching Protocols, then both sides send messages freely. Chat, collaboration, games.
  • SSE: a normal HTTP response that never ends (Content-Type: text/event-stream), the server writes data: … lines. One direction only, works through most proxies, auto-reconnects. This is how most LLM APIs stream tokens.

docs.title: 4 · Good API habits
docs.text:
• Versioning: in the path (/v2/orders) or a header; never break existing clients silently.
  • Pagination: cursor-based (?cursor=…&limit=50) scales better than ?page=500.
  • Errors: one JSON error format everywhere (RFC 9457 "problem details": type, title, status, detail).
  • Timeouts, retries, backoff: every client call needs a timeout; retries only for idempotent requests, with exponential backoff and jitter, and a retry budget so retries don't multiply load during an outage.
  • Rate limits: return 429 with Retry-After; clients must respect it.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• SLOs and alerts are built from status codes: error rate = 5xx / all (4xx are usually the client's fault, but a spike in 401/404 can mean a bad deploy).
  • Ingress limits produce errors that look like app bugs: 413 (body size), 400 (header size), 504 (proxy-read-timeout too short for slow endpoints or streaming).
  • Streaming (SSE, gRPC streams, WebSockets) needs proxy buffering off and long read timeouts, or users see responses arrive all at once or get cut after 60 s.
  • Retries in the mesh plus retries in the app multiply. Configure them in one place.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Methods and codes against a test API
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://httpbin.org/status/503
curl -s -X PUT https://httpbin.org/put -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"a":1}' | head -15
curl -sI -X DELETE https://httpbin.org/get | head -1          # → 405

# Follow redirects and show each hop
curl -sIL http://github.com | grep -E '^HTTP|^location'

# Server-Sent Events: watch a stream arrive line by line
curl -sN https://httpbin.org/stream/3

# gRPC (if you have grpcurl and a server with reflection)
# grpcurl -plaintext localhost:50051 list

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Situation Code Created a resource 201 + Location Success, nothing to return 204 Not logged in / token expired 401 Logged in but not allowed 403 Validation error 400 or 422 Someone else changed it first 409 / 412 Too many requests 429 + Retry-After Backend crashed / refused 502 (from proxy) No healthy backend 503 Backend too slow 504 (from proxy)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Which methods can a proxy safely retry automatically, and why?

Idempotent ones (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS): repeating them doesn't change the result. POST may create a duplicate.

2. What's the difference between 401 and 403?

401: we don't know who you are (missing/invalid credentials). 403: we know who you are and you're not allowed.

3. Users get 504 on a report endpoint that takes 90 s. Where do you look first?

The proxy/ingress/LB read timeout (often 60 s). Raise it for that route, or make the endpoint asynchronous (202 + polling).

4. Why do LLM chat UIs often use SSE rather than WebSockets?

The stream is one-directional (server → client), SSE is plain HTTP, works through proxies and CDNs, and reconnects automatically.

5. Why does gRPC return HTTP 200 even when the call failed?

gRPC reports its own status in the grpc-status trailer at the end of the stream; HTTP status only says the transport worked.

docs.text: Look at last week's 5xx errors in one service. Which were generated by the proxy and which by the app?

docs.title: Chapter 7 — Server side
docs.text:
In short

A request is first answered by a CDN if it can be. Otherwise it reaches a load balancer, which spreads it across identical, stateless app servers behind a reverse proxy. The app reads from a cache, falls back to the database, and pushes slow work to a queue for workers. You scale the stateless part by adding copies and protect the stateful part (data) carefully.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CDN Content Delivery Network Servers near users caching content Serves cached responses from the closest edge LB Load Balancer Spreads traffic over backends L4 by connection, L7 by HTTP request; health checks L4 / L7 Layer 4 / Layer 7 Transport-level vs application-level L4 sees IP:port, L7 sees host, path, headers Reverse proxy / ingress — Front server routing requests to services Routes by host/path, terminates TLS, adds headers Stateless / stateful — Keeps nothing between requests / keeps data Stateless scales by copies; stateful needs care Horizontal / vertical scaling — More machines / bigger machine Horizontal needs stateless apps and a load balancer Cache-aside — App-managed caching pattern Check cache → on miss read DB → fill cache Primary / replica — Write node / read copies of a database Replication copies changes, usually asynchronously Replication lag — Delay before replicas see a write Read-after-write may return old data Queue / worker — Buffer of jobs / process consuming them At-least-once delivery → idempotent jobs, DLQ for failures Idempotent — Safe to run twice with the same result Use idempotency keys for payments and jobs Object storage — Store for files/blobs (S3, GCS) Flat namespace, HTTP API, presigned URLs Circuit breaker — Stops calling a failing dependency for a while Fail fast instead of piling up timeouts

docs.title: 1 · Edge: CDN
docs.text:
What Why A network of servers in hundreds of cities (Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly, Akamai) The closest server is a few ms away instead of 50–150 ms (Chapter 6: round trips!) Caches static files (JS, CSS, images, video) and sometimes API responses The origin never sees most traffic Terminates TLS close to the user, absorbs DDoS, can run small edge functions Faster handshakes, protection

Caching is controlled with HTTP headers like Cache-Control: max-age=3600. A response header such as cf-cache-status: HIT or x-cache: Hit from cloudfront tells you the CDN answered.

docs.title: 2 · Entry: load balancer and reverse proxy
docs.text: Component Layer Job Load balancer (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP LB, HAProxy) L4 (TCP: forwards connections) or L7 (HTTP: reads the request) One public address. Spreads traffic over healthy backends (round robin, least connections). Runs health checks. Often terminates TLS. Reverse proxy / ingress (nginx, Envoy, Traefik, Kubernetes Ingress / Gateway API) L7 Routes by host and path (/api → API service, / → frontend). Adds headers like X-Forwarded-For (the real client IP), compression, rate limits, timeouts.

docs.title: 3 · App tier: stateless servers
docs.text:
• Stateless means a server keeps nothing between requests that it alone knows: no sessions in memory, no files on local disk. Sessions live in Redis or in a signed token (JWT). Files go to object storage.
  • That makes every copy identical and disposable, so you can scale horizontally (add more copies) and kill any copy at any time. That's exactly what Kubernetes and autoscalers do.
  • Vertical scaling (a bigger machine) is simpler but has a ceiling and a single point of failure.

docs.title: 4 · Data tier: cache and database
docs.text:
Cache-aside pattern (the most common):

value = cache.get(key)
if value is None:                 # miss
    value = db.query(...)
    cache.set(key, value, ttl=300)
return value
Component Typical latency (same datacenter) Notes Redis / Memcached ~0.2–1 ms In memory. Hard part: invalidation (when data changes, delete or update the cache entry). Database query (indexed) ~1–10 ms Without an index it's a full table scan, and it gets slower as the table grows.

Database scaling

  • Primary takes all writes. Read replicas receive a copy (usually asynchronous) and serve reads, so a read right after a write may see old data (replication lag).
  • Connection pooling (PgBouncer, or pools in the app): databases handle hundreds of connections, not tens of thousands.
  • Sharding (splitting data across several primaries) comes only when one primary can't keep up.

docs.title: How does cache-aside work?
docs.text: The app asks the cache first. On a hit it returns immediately. On a miss it queries the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns. On writes, it deletes (or updates) the cached key so readers don't see stale data for long.

docs.title: 5 · Async work: queue, workers, object storage
docs.text:
Use when Example The user doesn't need to wait for it Sending an email, resizing an image, generating a PDF, calling a slow third party

Flow: the app puts a job on the queue and immediately replies 202 Accepted. Workers pick jobs up, retry on failure, and send jobs that keep failing to a dead-letter queue. Jobs should be idempotent (safe to run twice), because "at least once" delivery means duplicates happen.

Object storage (S3, GCS) holds files. Clients often upload and download directly with short-lived presigned URLs, so file bytes never pass through your app servers.

docs.title: 6 · Keeping it alive
docs.text: Practice Why Health checks (liveness / readiness) The LB or Kubernetes stops sending traffic to broken instances. Timeouts on every network call A slow dependency must not hang all your threads. Retries with backoff + jitter Survive blips without causing a retry storm. Circuit breakers / rate limits Fail fast and protect overloaded dependencies. Metrics, logs, traces You can't fix what you can't see (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: 502s on every deploy
docs.text:
The alarm

Every rollout of the checkout service produces a burst of 502 Bad Gateway errors for 5–10 seconds. The app logs show nothing unusual; the errors come from the ingress.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

Ingress logs: upstream prematurely closed connection / connect() failed (111: Connection refused) to IPs of pods that are Terminating.

🔍 Clue 2

The pod has no preStop hook, and the app exits immediately on SIGTERM. Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, not one after the other.

🎯 Root cause

When a pod is deleted, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and removes the pod from EndpointSlices at the same time. The ingress/kube-proxy learn about the removal a moment later, so for a few seconds they keep sending requests to a process that has already exited.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Add a preStop sleep (5–10 s), handle SIGTERM gracefully (stop accepting, finish in-flight, then exit), make readiness fail on shutdown, and set terminationGracePeriodSeconds accordingly. Lesson: zero-downtime deploys are a contract between app, Kubernetes and load balancer.

docs.title: 🧭 Go deeper
docs.text: Page What's inside 7.1 — Load balancing L4 vs L7 load balancing, algorithms (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing, EWMA), health checks and readiness, connection draining, sticky sessions, global load balancing, and how Kubernetes Services, Ingress and Gateway API balance traffic. 7.2 — Caching patterns Where caches live (browser, CDN, proxy, in-process, Redis), cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind, TTLs and invalidation, eviction policies, cache stampedes and hot keys, Redis essentials, and how to measure a cache. 7.3 — Databases: storage, transactions & replication How relational databases store and find data (pages, B-tree indexes, WAL), transactions, ACID and isolation levels, MVCC and locks, connection pooling, replication, failover and backups (PITR), sharding, and when to choose NoSQL, plus running databases on Kubernetes. 7.4 — Queues, streams & event-driven systems Why systems use queues, queues vs logs (RabbitMQ/SQS vs Kafka), topics, partitions and consumer groups, delivery guarantees and idempotency, retries and dead-letter queues, ordering, the outbox pattern and CDC, sagas, backpressure and autoscaling consumers with KEDA.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Docker)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 07-server (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces.

A load balancer in front of two app servers, in 2 minutes:

mkdir lb-lab && cd lb-lab
cat > nginx.conf <<'EOF'
upstream app { server app1:80; server app2:80; }
server {
  listen 80;
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://app;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
  }
}
EOF
cat > compose.yaml <<'EOF'
services:
  app1: { image: traefik/whoami }
  app2: { image: traefik/whoami }
  lb:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports: ["8080:80"]
    volumes: ["./nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro"]
EOF
docker compose up -d
for i in 1 2 3 4; do curl -s localhost:8080 | grep Hostname; done   # alternates: round robin
docker compose stop app1 && curl -s localhost:8080 | grep Hostname  # still works
docker compose down

# Is a CDN answering? Look at the cache headers
curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com | grep -iE "cf-cache-status|age|cache-control"

Exercise: while the lab is running, stop app1 and send requests. What does nginx do on the first failed attempt, and how would a health check change that?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
User → CDN (static, cache HIT?) → LB (L4/L7, TLS, health checks) → reverse proxy (host/path routing)
     → stateless app × N (scale out) → cache (hit?) → DB primary (writes) / replicas (reads, lag)
     → slow work: queue → workers (retry, idempotent, DLQ) → object storage (presigned URLs)
Stateless = disposable copies. Stateful = protect it, back it up, scale it carefully.
Always: timeouts, retries with backoff, health checks, observability.

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why should app servers be stateless?

So any instance can serve any request and any instance can be added or killed at any time. That enables horizontal scaling, rolling deploys and self-healing.

2. What's the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?

L4 forwards TCP/UDP connections by IP and port without reading the content. L7 understands HTTP, so it can route by host, path or header, terminate TLS and retry individual requests.

3. A user updates their profile and then immediately sees the old version. What could cause this?

Replication lag (the read went to a replica that hasn't caught up yet) or a stale cache entry that wasn't invalidated on write.

4. Why should queue workers be idempotent?

Most queues deliver "at least once", so a job can run twice (e.g. a worker crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging it). Running it twice must not charge a card twice.

5. Your API calls a payment provider that sometimes takes 30 s. What do you add?

A timeout on the call, retries with backoff (only if the call is idempotent), a circuit breaker, and ideally moving it to an async job so the user's request doesn't wait.

docs.title: 7.1 — Load balancing
docs.text:
In short

A load balancer sits in front of many identical backends, uses health checks to know which ones may get traffic, and an algorithm to choose one for each new connection (L4) or request (L7). Done right, it lets you add servers, deploy without downtime and survive failures, and in Kubernetes this job is split between Services (L4 inside the cluster) and Ingress/Gateway (L7 at the edge).

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) LB Load Balancer Spreads traffic over backends Hardware, software (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy) or cloud L4 LB Layer 4 Balances TCP/UDP connections Sees IP:port only, very fast L7 LB Layer 7 Balances HTTP requests Routes by host/path/header, TLS, retries Round robin — Next backend in turn Simple, ignores load Least connections / least request — Backend with fewest active Better for uneven request costs Consistent hashing — Same key → same backend Cache affinity; few keys move when pool changes EWMA / P2C Exponentially Weighted Moving Average / Power of Two Choices Latency-aware picking Pick 2 random, choose the faster Health check — Probe deciding if a backend gets traffic Active (LB probes) or passive (watch errors) Readiness / liveness — K8s: may get traffic / should be restarted Different questions, different probes Draining — Stop new traffic, let existing finish During deploys and scale-in Sticky sessions — Pin a client to one backend Cookie or source-IP affinity Anycast / GSLB — / Global Server Load Balancing Route users to the nearest region Same IP from many places / DNS-based Gateway API — Kubernetes' successor to Ingress Gateway + HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute, role-oriented

docs.title: 1 · L4 vs L7
docs.text: L4 (TCP/UDP) L7 (HTTP/gRPC) Balances Connections Requests Sees IPs, ports Host, path, headers, cookies, body Features Fast, protocol-agnostic, keeps client IP (NLB) TLS termination, routing, retries, rate limits, WAF Examples AWS NLB, kube-proxy, IPVS, MetalLB ALB, nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, Ingress/Gateway Gotcha Long-lived connections (gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSockets) stick to one backend More CPU, one more TLS hop

docs.title: 2 · Algorithms
docs.text:
• Round robin: fine when every request costs the same.
  • Least connections / least outstanding requests: better when some requests are slow.
  • Power of two choices with EWMA latency (Envoy, Linkerd): picks two at random and sends to the faster; avoids herding onto one "least loaded" node.
  • Consistent hashing (hash $request_uri, ring hash, Maglev): same key always lands on the same backend; good for caches and stateful shards; only ~1/N keys move when a node joins/leaves.
  • Weighted: send 5% to a new version (canary).

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The LB probes each backend (GET /healthz every few seconds). After N failures it's removed; after M successes it's added back.
  2. Passive checks / outlier detection eject backends that return many 5xx even if the probe passes.
  3. On deploy or scale-in, a backend is first marked draining: no new connections, existing ones get time to finish; then it's stopped.

In Kubernetes: the readiness probe decides whether a pod is in the Service's EndpointSlice; the liveness probe restarts a stuck container. A liveness probe that checks the database will restart every pod when the DB blips — keep it shallow. Combine with preStop sleep + graceful SIGTERM handling (3.1) for zero-downtime rollouts.

docs.title: 4 · Sessions and state
docs.text: Sticky sessions (cookie affinity) work but make scaling and deploys uneven and break when a node dies. Prefer stateless app servers with sessions in Redis/DB or a signed token; use stickiness only for real per-node state (WebSockets, local caches).

docs.title: 5 · Kubernetes and global load balancing
docs.text:
• Service (ClusterIP): L4, per connection, via kube-proxy/eBPF (5.3).
  • Service type LoadBalancer: cloud L4 LB → NodePorts or pod IPs.
  • Ingress / Gateway API: L7 controllers (ingress-nginx, Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, cloud controllers). Gateway API adds HTTPRoute/GRPCRoute, traffic splitting, header matching and clean role separation (infra owns Gateways, teams own Routes). The community ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 (no more releases or security fixes), so plan migrations and use Gateway API for new setups.
  • Global: DNS-based (Route 53 latency/failover routing) or anycast L7 LBs (Cloudflare, GCP global LB) send users to the nearest healthy region.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• 502s during deploys = pods killed before the LB stopped sending to them; fix with readiness + preStop sleep + graceful shutdown, and LB deregistration delay.
  • gRPC hot pod = L4 balancing of long-lived HTTP/2; use an L7 proxy, a mesh, or client-side balancing (headless Service).
  • Idle timeouts must line up (client < LB < backend keep-alive), see 6.3.
  • Watch per-backend metrics: one slow pod can dominate p99; outlier detection helps.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# A tiny L7 load balancer with nginx in front of 3 echo servers
docker network create lbdemo
for i in 1 2 3; do docker run -d --rm --name app$i --network lbdemo hashicorp/http-echo -text="app$i"; done
cat > /tmp/nginx.conf <<'EOF'
events {}
http {
  upstream apps { server app1:5678; server app2:5678; server app3:5678; }   # try: least_conn;  hash $remote_addr;
  server { listen 80; location / { proxy_pass http://apps; } }
}
EOF
docker run -d --rm --name lb --network lbdemo -p 8080:80 -v /tmp/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro nginx:alpine
for i in $(seq 6); do curl -s localhost:8080; done          # app1 app2 app3 app1 …
docker stop app2; for i in $(seq 4); do curl -s localhost:8080; done   # passive failover
docker stop lb app1 app3; docker network rm lbdemo

kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> -o wide 2>/dev/null   # who is "ready"

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Choose Raw TCP/UDP, keep client IP L4 (NLB, MetalLB) Path/host routing, TLS, retries L7 (ALB, Envoy, Gateway API) Uneven request cost Least request / P2C EWMA Cache affinity Consistent hashing Canary 5% Weighted routing (HTTPRoute weights) Zero-downtime deploy Readiness + preStop + draining

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can an L4 load balancer leave gRPC traffic unbalanced?

It balances connections; gRPC multiplexes all requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, so one backend gets everything from that client.

2. What's the difference between readiness and liveness probes?

Readiness: should this pod receive traffic now? Liveness: is it stuck and should be restarted?

3. Why is a deep liveness check (that queries the DB) dangerous?

A DB hiccup fails every pod's liveness and Kubernetes restarts them all at once, turning a blip into an outage.

4. When is consistent hashing useful?

When the same key should hit the same backend (cache locality, shards) and you want few keys to move when backends change.

5. Users see 502s for a few seconds during every rollout. What do you check?

Graceful shutdown: readiness turning false before exit, a preStop sleep so endpoints update, SIGTERM handling, and LB deregistration delay.

docs.title: 7.2 — Caching patterns
docs.text:
In short

A cache keeps a copy of expensive results somewhere faster and closer. Every layer, from the browser and CDN to an in-process map and Redis, can answer before the database. The hard parts are always the same: choosing a pattern (cache-aside, write-through…), deciding how stale data may be (TTL, invalidation), and surviving stampedes, hot keys and cache outages.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Hit / miss / hit ratio — Found / not found / % of hits 95% vs 99% hit ratio = 5× fewer DB calls TTL Time To Live How long an entry is valid Expires → next read is a miss Cache-aside lazy loading App reads cache, fills on miss Most common pattern Read-through — Cache library loads from DB itself App only talks to the cache Write-through — Write to cache and DB together Cache always fresh, slower writes Write-behind write-back Write to cache, DB later Fast, risk of loss Invalidation — Removing/updating stale entries Delete on write, events, versioned keys Eviction (LRU/LFU) Least Recently / Frequently Used What to drop when full Redis maxmemory-policy Stampede / thundering herd — Many misses for one key at once All hit the DB simultaneously Hot key — One key with huge traffic Overloads one cache shard Negative caching — Caching "not found" Protects DB from repeated misses Redis REmote DIctionary Server In-memory data store Strings, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams Memcached — Simple distributed memory cache Multi-threaded, key/value only CDN Content Delivery Network Edge caches near users Cache-Control from your origin

docs.title: 1 · Patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Read Write Good for Watch out Cache-aside Cache → miss → DB → fill Write DB, delete key Most apps Race: stale value re-filled after a delete Read-through Cache loads from DB — Libraries/CDNs Same staleness questions Write-through From cache Cache + DB synchronously Read-heavy, need fresh Every write slower Write-behind From cache Cache now, DB async Counters, analytics Data loss if cache dies

Delete, don't update, on writes (in cache-aside): updating the cache from two concurrent writers can leave the older value; deleting forces the next read to load the truth.

docs.title: 2 · TTLs and invalidation
docs.text:
• Short TTL = fresher, more DB load. Long TTL = cheaper, staler. Add jitter (±10%) so thousands of keys don't expire in the same second.
  • Event-driven invalidation: publish "user 42 changed" (outbox/CDC, 7.4) and delete the key everywhere.
  • Versioned keys: product:42:v17; bump the version on change, old keys simply expire.
  • CDN: long TTL + purge API, or hashed asset names (6.1).

docs.title: 3 · Failure modes
docs.text: Problem What happens Fix Stampede A hot key expires, 1,000 requests all miss and hit the DB Request coalescing / single-flight, lock per key, stale-while-revalidate, early refresh Hot key One key gets 100K req/s, one Redis shard melts Local in-process cache in front, key replication, read replicas Cache down Everything falls through to the DB, DB dies too Circuit breaker, rate-limit fallthrough, cache with replicas, warm-up Penetration Requests for non-existent IDs always miss Negative caching, Bloom filter Big values Slow network, memory fragmentation Keep values small, compress, split

docs.title: 4 · Redis essentials
docs.text:
• Single-threaded command execution (I/O threads help networking): one slow command blocks everyone (KEYS *, big SMEMBERS, huge Lua). Use SCAN.
  • Persistence: RDB snapshots and/or AOF log; as a pure cache you may turn them off.
  • Eviction: set maxmemory + maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (or allkeys-lfu) for caches; noeviction makes writes fail when full.
  • HA: replicas + Sentinel, or Redis Cluster (16,384 hash slots across shards); managed: ElastiCache/MemoryDB, Memorystore, Azure Cache. Valkey is the open-source fork many providers now ship.
  • Also useful for: rate limiting, distributed locks (carefully), sessions, leaderboards (sorted sets), queues/streams.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Measure hit ratio, latency, evictions, memory, connected clients (INFO stats, keyspace_hits/misses, evicted_keys).
  • Size memory for the working set plus overhead (~1.5–2× raw data); alert well before maxmemory.
  • A cache is not a database: data must be rebuildable. If losing Redis loses business data, it's a database and needs backups and replication.
  • Plan for cold starts: after a flush or failover, the DB sees full load; warm critical keys or ramp traffic.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
docker run -d --rm --name redis -p 6379:6379 redis:7-alpine
redis-cli SET user:42 '{"name":"Jane"}' EX 300     # value with 300 s TTL
redis-cli TTL user:42; redis-cli GET user:42
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory 50mb
redis-cli CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru
redis-cli --latency -i 1 2>/dev/null & sleep 3; kill $!
redis-cli INFO stats | grep -E 'keyspace_(hits|misses)|evicted_keys'
redis-benchmark -q -n 20000 -t get,set
docker stop redis

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Do Default pattern Cache-aside, delete on write, TTL with jitter Avoid stampede Single-flight / lock / stale-while-revalidate Hot key In-process cache + short TTL in front of Redis Cache eviction policy allkeys-lru / allkeys-lfu Never in production KEYS *, unbounded values Health metrics Hit ratio, p99 latency, evictions, memory

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why delete the key on write instead of updating it in cache-aside?

Concurrent writers can update the cache in the wrong order, leaving an old value; deleting makes the next read fetch the current one.

2. What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?

Many requests miss the same expired hot key at once and all hit the DB. Use request coalescing/locks, stale-while-revalidate or early refresh with jittered TTLs.

3. Your Redis is at 100% CPU on one core while others are idle. Possible causes?

A slow command (KEYS, huge sets, Lua) or a hot key; Redis executes commands on one thread.

4. When is write-behind acceptable?

When losing the last few writes is tolerable (counters, metrics) and write speed matters more than durability.

5. What happens to the database when the cache cluster restarts empty, and how do you prepare?

It gets the full read load (cold cache). Warm critical keys, ramp traffic, and protect the DB with rate limits/circuit breakers.

docs.title: 7.3 — Databases: storage, transactions & replication
docs.text:
In short

A database keeps data in pages on disk and finds rows quickly with indexes, usually B-trees. It makes every change durable by writing it to a write-ahead log (WAL) first, and isolates concurrent transactions with MVCC and locks. It scales and survives failures by replicating that log to other servers. You still need backups, because replication copies mistakes too.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) RDBMS / SQL Relational DB Management System / Structured Query Language Tables + relations + queries PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle Page — Unit of storage (8 KB Postgres, 16 KB InnoDB) Cached in the buffer pool Index (B-tree) — Sorted tree for fast lookups O(log n) page reads instead of a full scan WAL / redo log / binlog Write-Ahead Log Append-only log of changes Written + fsynced before data pages Transaction — Group of changes that succeed or fail together BEGIN … COMMIT / ROLLBACK ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability Transaction guarantees All-or-nothing, rules hold, no interference, survives crash Isolation level — How much concurrent transactions see each other Read committed, repeatable read, serializable MVCC Multi-Version Concurrency Control Readers see a snapshot, writers create new versions Readers don't block writers Deadlock — Two transactions wait for each other DB kills one Query plan / EXPLAIN — How the DB will execute a query Index scan vs seq scan, joins Connection pool — Reusing DB connections PgBouncer, HikariCP, RDS Proxy Replication (sync / async) — Copying the WAL to replicas Durability vs latency trade-off PITR Point-In-Time Recovery Restore to any second Base backup + archived WAL Sharding — Splitting data across databases by key Horizontal write scaling RPO / RTO Recovery Point / Time Objective Max data loss / max downtime Drives backup and HA design

docs.title: 1 · Storage and indexes
docs.text:
• Tables live in fixed-size pages; hot pages are kept in the buffer pool (shared_buffers / innodb_buffer_pool_size), the database's own cache.
  • Without an index, WHERE email = … reads every page (sequential scan). A B-tree index keeps keys sorted in a shallow tree: ~3–4 page reads find one row among millions.
  • Indexes cost: every write updates every index, and they use memory/disk. Index what you filter, join and sort on; check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  • Composite indexes follow left-to-right order: an index on (tenant_id, created_at) helps WHERE tenant_id = ? ORDER BY created_at, not WHERE created_at > ? alone.

docs.title: How does a commit work?
docs.text:
1. Changes are made to pages in memory and described in WAL records.
  2. On COMMIT, the WAL is fsynced to disk (6.3/3.4: that's the slow part). Now the transaction is durable.
  3. Dirty data pages are written to disk later (checkpoints). After a crash, the DB replays the WAL to recover.

That's why disk fsync latency limits commit rate, and why batching writes in one transaction is much faster than thousands of autocommits.

docs.title: 3 · Isolation and MVCC
docs.text:
Level Prevents Default in Read committed Dirty reads PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle Repeatable read + non-repeatable reads (snapshot) MySQL InnoDB Serializable + all anomalies (as if one at a time) Opt-in; may abort with serialization errors → retry

MVCC: an update writes a new row version; readers keep seeing the version from their snapshot. Old versions must be cleaned up (VACUUM in Postgres, purge in InnoDB). Long-running transactions block cleanup → table bloat and slowdowns; watch them.

docs.title: 4 · Replication, failover and backups
docs.text:
• Async replication: commits don't wait for replicas → fast, but a failover can lose the last seconds (RPO > 0). Replicas lag; reads from them may be stale.
  • Sync replication: commit waits for at least one replica → no loss, higher latency.
  • Failover: promote a replica (Patroni, RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora, Orchestrator) and move the endpoint/DNS; apps must reconnect and retry.
  • Backups: replication copies DROP TABLE instantly. Keep base backups + WAL archiving for PITR, and test restores regularly. Define RPO/RTO first.

docs.title: 5 · Scaling and choosing
docs.text:
• Vertical first (bigger instance, better indexes, fewer queries), then read replicas, caching (7.2), partitioning (by time), and finally sharding by tenant/user (Citus, Vitess, application-level) or a distributed SQL DB (CockroachDB, Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB).
  • NoSQL when the access pattern fits: key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), search (OpenSearch), time series (Prometheus, TimescaleDB), vector (pgvector, 10.7). Usually you trade joins/transactions for scale or flexibility.
  • Connections are expensive (Postgres: one process each). Hundreds of pods × pool size can exhaust max_connections → use PgBouncer/RDS Proxy and small app pools.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Databases on Kubernetes: possible with operators (CloudNativePG, Percona, Zalando), local or block PVs, anti-affinity, PodDisruptionBudgets — but managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora) remove most of the operational risk.
  • Migrations in CI/CD: backward-compatible schema changes (expand → migrate → contract), online index builds (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), lock timeouts.
  • Key metrics: connections, replication lag, transaction rate, cache hit ratio, slow queries (pg_stat_statements), locks/deadlocks, disk IOPS and fsync latency, storage growth.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
docker run -d --rm --name pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=pw -p 5432:5432 postgres:17
sleep 5; P="docker exec -i pg psql -U postgres -q"
$P -c "CREATE TABLE users(id serial primary key, email text, created_at timestamptz default now());"
$P -c "INSERT INTO users(email) SELECT 'u'||g||'@x.com' FROM generate_series(1,1000000) g;"
$P -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='u777777@x.com';"   # Seq Scan
$P -c "CREATE INDEX ON users(email);"
$P -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='u777777@x.com';"   # Index Scan, ~1000x faster
$P -c "SHOW transaction_isolation; SHOW shared_buffers; SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn();"
docker stop pg

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Look at Slow query EXPLAIN ANALYZE, missing index, pg_stat_statements Slow commits fsync latency, disk IOPS limits, too many tiny transactions too many connections Pooling (PgBouncer), smaller app pools Stale reads Replica lag; read-your-writes from primary Table bloat Long transactions blocking VACUUM Data deleted by mistake PITR restore (replicas won't help)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is the WAL written before the data pages?

So a committed transaction can always be recovered by replaying the log after a crash, while data pages can be flushed lazily.

2. Why doesn't replication replace backups?

It copies every change, including mistakes and malicious deletes, to replicas within seconds; you need point-in-time backups to go back.

3. A query filters on created_at but the only index is on (tenant_id, created_at). Will it be used efficiently?

Generally no: B-tree composite indexes are used left-to-right; without tenant_id in the filter it can't seek efficiently.

4. What's the trade-off between sync and async replication?

Sync: no data loss on failover but higher commit latency and availability coupling. Async: fast commits but possible loss of recent transactions and stale replica reads.

5. You scale your app from 10 to 100 pods and Postgres starts refusing connections. Why and what's the fix?

Each pod's pool opens N connections; total exceeds max_connections. Use a connection pooler (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy) and smaller per-pod pools.

docs.title: 7.4 — Queues, streams & event-driven systems
docs.text:
In short

A message broker sits between services so a producer can hand off work or announce an event and move on, while consumers process it later at their own pace. Queues (RabbitMQ, SQS) delete messages once handled, logs (Kafka, Kinesis) keep them for replay, delivery is almost always at-least-once — so consumers must be idempotent — and failures go to retries and a dead-letter queue instead of being lost.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Broker — Server storing and delivering messages Kafka, RabbitMQ, SQS, Pub/Sub, NATS Producer / consumer — Writes / reads messages Decoupled in time and scale Queue — Each message handled by one consumer, then removed Work distribution Log / stream — Append-only, retained, replayable Many consumer groups read independently Topic / partition — Named stream / ordered shard of it Order is guaranteed only within a partition Consumer group — Consumers sharing a topic's partitions Max parallelism = number of partitions Offset / ack acknowledgement Position read / "done with this message" Commit after processing At-most / at-least / exactly-once — Delivery guarantees At-least-once + idempotency is the practical default Idempotency — Processing twice has the same effect as once Dedupe by message id, upserts DLQ Dead-Letter Queue Where poison messages go Inspect and replay later Backpressure — Slowing producers when consumers can't keep up Bounded queues, rate limits Outbox / CDC — / Change Data Capture Reliable "DB write + event" Event row in same transaction, relayed later Saga — Multi-step business process across services Each step has a compensating action Consumer lag — Messages waiting to be processed Key metric; drives autoscaling (KEDA)

docs.title: 1 · Why put a queue in between?
docs.text:
• Absorb spikes: 10,000 orders arrive in a minute, workers process 500/s steadily.
  • Decouple: the checkout service doesn't need email, invoicing and analytics to be up.
  • Retry safely: a failed job goes back instead of failing the user's request.
  • Fan-out: one order.created event feeds many independent consumers.

The cost: eventual consistency (things happen "soon", not now), harder debugging (trace across async hops), and new failure modes.

docs.title: 2 · Queue vs log
docs.text: Queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) Log (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar, Redpanda) After consumption Message deleted Message kept (retention: hours…forever) Readers Competing consumers Many independent consumer groups, each with its own offset Replay No Yes: reset offsets, rebuild state Ordering Per queue (FIFO variants) Per partition (by key) Strengths Task distribution, routing, per-message ack, delays Event streaming, high throughput, event sourcing, CDC

docs.title: How does at-least-once work?
docs.text:
1. Consumer reads a message, processes it, then acks/commits the offset.
  2. If it crashes after processing but before the ack, the message is delivered again.
  3. So the handler must be idempotent: store processed message IDs, use upserts (INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING), or design operations that are naturally repeatable ("set status = paid", not "add 10 €").

"Exactly-once" exists only inside specific systems (Kafka transactions between topics); across a DB, an email and a payment API, it's at-least-once + idempotency.

docs.title: 4 · Retries, DLQs and ordering
docs.text:
• Retry transient errors with exponential backoff (delay queues, retry topics); don't hot-loop.
  • After N attempts move the message to a DLQ and alert; one bad message must not block the whole partition (poison pill).
  • Need order per customer? Use the customer ID as the partition key; you get order per key, not globally.
  • More consumers than partitions sit idle — plan partition counts for future parallelism.

docs.title: 5 · Reliable events from a database: outbox and CDC
docs.text:
"Save the order, then publish order.created" fails if the app dies between the two steps (or the publish fails). The outbox: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay (polling or CDC with Debezium reading the WAL, 7.3) publishes it. Consumers dedupe by event ID.

Sagas coordinate multi-service workflows (reserve stock → charge card → ship) with compensating steps (release stock, refund) instead of distributed transactions.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Autoscale consumers on lag, not CPU: KEDA scalers for Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis Streams, Pub/Sub (scale to zero when idle).
  • Alert on: consumer lag growing, DLQ size > 0, oldest message age, broker disk usage and under-replicated partitions (Kafka).
  • Run Kafka on Kubernetes with Strimzi (operator) or use managed (MSK, Confluent Cloud, Event Hubs); KRaft mode replaced ZooKeeper.
  • Graceful shutdown for consumers: stop fetching, finish in-flight messages, commit, then exit (3.1); otherwise every deploy causes redeliveries.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# RabbitMQ with the management UI on http://localhost:15672 (guest/guest)
docker run -d --rm --name rmq -p 5672:5672 -p 15672:15672 rabbitmq:4-management

# Kafka (KRaft, single node) and its CLI
docker run -d --rm --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:latest
sleep 15; K="docker exec -i kafka /opt/kafka/bin"
$K/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic orders --partitions 3
printf 'cust1:order-1\ncust2:order-2\ncust1:order-3\n' | \
  $K/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders --property parse.key=true --property key.separator=:
$K/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --topic orders --from-beginning \
  --group billing --property print.key=true --property print.partition=true --timeout-ms 5000
$K/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --describe --group billing   # offsets + LAG
docker stop kafka rmq

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Use Background jobs Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) + workers Many consumers, replay, high volume Log (Kafka) Order per entity Partition key = entity id Survive duplicates Idempotent handlers (dedupe ids, upserts) DB write + event Outbox / CDC Poison message Retries with backoff → DLQ Scale workers KEDA on lag

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why must consumers be idempotent?

With at-least-once delivery, a crash between processing and ack causes redelivery; the handler must produce the same result twice.

2. You have a topic with 6 partitions and scale consumers to 10. What happens?

Only 6 consumers get partitions; 4 sit idle. Parallelism is capped by the partition count.

3. What's the problem with 'write to DB, then publish to Kafka' in application code?

The two aren't atomic: a crash or publish failure after the commit loses the event (or the reverse order publishes events for data that was rolled back). Use an outbox/CDC.

4. What does a growing consumer lag tell you, and what do you do?

Consumers process slower than producers write. Scale consumers (up to partitions), fix slow handlers, or add partitions.

5. Queue or log for 'replay the last 7 days of events into a new analytics service'?

A log (Kafka) with ≥ 7 days retention; a queue deletes messages once consumed.

docs.title: Chapter 8 — The browser
docs.text:
In short

The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, and lets JavaScript change both. It turns them into styled boxes (style), works out where every box goes (layout) and records how to draw them (paint). The GPU then stacks the layers into a frame (composite). All of this should fit in 16.7 ms, 60 times a second, on a single main thread that JavaScript shares.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) DOM Document Object Model Tree of HTML elements in memory Built by the HTML parser, changed by JS CSSOM CSS Object Model Tree of style rules Built from stylesheets; render-blocking Render tree — Visible nodes with computed styles DOM + CSSOM, minus display:none Layout (reflow) — Computing box geometry Position and size of every box Paint / composite — Recording draw commands / stacking layers on the GPU Composite-only changes (transform/opacity) are cheap Main thread — The renderer's single thread for JS + rendering Long tasks block input and frames Event loop — The scheduler of the main thread Task → microtasks → render, repeat V8 — Chrome's JavaScript engine Bytecode interpreter + optimizing JIT defer / async — Script loading attributes Download in parallel; run after parse / when ready Web Worker — Background JS thread without DOM access Moves heavy work off the main thread LCP / INP / CLS Largest Contentful Paint / Interaction to Next Paint / Cumulative Layout Shift Core Web Vitals Load speed / responsiveness / visual stability SPA / SSR Single-Page Application / Server-Side Rendering Client builds the page / server sends full HTML SSR then hydrates with JS

docs.title: 0 · A browser is many processes
docs.text:
Process Job Browser process Tabs, address bar, network requests, storage, permissions Renderer process (one per site, sandboxed) Parses HTML/CSS, runs JS, does style/layout/paint. Has a main thread, a compositor thread and raster threads. GPU process Talks to the GPU and draws the final frames

Why many processes? Security (a malicious site is locked in its sandboxed renderer) and stability (one crashing tab doesn't take the others down). Chapter 3 isolation, applied.

docs.title: 1 · Parse: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM
docs.text: Step What happens HTML parsing Bytes → characters → tokens (<h1>, text, </h1>) → nodes → the DOM tree. The parser is streaming (it starts before the whole file arrives) and very forgiving of broken HTML. Preload scanner Looks ahead in the HTML for <link>, <script>, <img> and starts downloading them early. CSS parsing Every stylesheet becomes the CSSOM: rules with selectors and properties. CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint until it has the CSS, to avoid a flash of unstyled content.

docs.title: 2 · JavaScript: the main-thread guest
docs.text:
• A plain <script src> is parser-blocking: HTML parsing stops until the script is downloaded and executed, because the script might change the document.
  • defer → download in parallel, run after parsing finishes (in order). async → download in parallel, run as soon as it arrives. type="module" is deferred by default.
  • JS reads and changes the DOM and styles through the DOM API (document.querySelector, element.style, …). Every change can invalidate style, layout or paint.
  • JS runs in V8 (Chapter 4: bytecode + JIT).

docs.title: 3 · Render: style → layout → paint
docs.text:
# Stage What happens 4 Style Match CSS rules to DOM nodes and compute the final value of every property. Nodes with display: none are dropped. Result: the render tree. 5 Layout (reflow) Calculate the geometry: the x, y, width, height of every box, text line breaks. Depends on the viewport size. 6 Paint Record draw commands ("fill rect here, draw text there") for each layer. 7 Composite The compositor thread rasterizes layers into tiles (on the GPU) and stacks them into a frame. Scrolling and transform/opacity animations can be done here without touching the main thread. 8 Display The frame goes to the GPU process and, at the next vsync, to the screen (Chapter 1, step 18).

Remember this: the cost of a change

Changing width/top/font size → layout + paint + composite (expensive). Changing color/background → paint + composite. Changing transform/opacity → composite only (cheap, smooth). That's why good animations use transform.

docs.title: 4 · The event loop and the 16.7 ms budget
docs.text:
The main thread runs a loop: take a task (a click handler, a network callback, a timer), run it to completion, run microtasks (resolved promises), then, about every 16.7 ms, do a rendering step (requestAnimationFrame callbacks → style → layout → paint).

  • A JS task that runs for 200 ms blocks clicks, typing and rendering for 200 ms. That's jank. Tasks over 50 ms are called long tasks.
  • Heavy work goes to a Web Worker (a separate thread without DOM access) or is split into smaller chunks.
  • Layout thrashing: reading layout (offsetHeight) right after writing styles, in a loop, forces layout again and again.

docs.title: How does the event loop work?
docs.text: The main thread repeats: take one task (a click handler, a timer, a network callback) and run it to completion, then run all microtasks (resolved promises), then — if a frame is due — render (rAF → style → layout → paint). A task longer than 50 ms delays input and frames.

docs.title: 5 · Measuring what users feel: Core Web Vitals
docs.text: Metric Measures "Good" LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) When the main content appeared ≤ 2.5 s INP (Interaction to Next Paint) How fast the page reacts to clicks and typing ≤ 200 ms CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) How much things jump around while loading ≤ 0.1

docs.title: 6 · SPA vs server-side rendering
docs.text:
Approach First response Trade-off SPA (React/Vue app, client-side) An almost empty HTML shell + a big JS bundle that builds the DOM Slow first paint on weak devices, smooth navigation after SSR / SSG (Next.js, Nuxt, Astro) Fully rendered HTML from the server or a CDN, then JS hydrates it to make it interactive Fast first paint, more server work

DevOps connection: frontend performance is mostly Chapters 6–7 + this chapter: fewer round trips (HTTP/2, CDN, caching headers), fewer and smaller bytes (compression, code splitting), and less main-thread work.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the release that tripled LCP
docs.text:
The alarm

Field data shows LCP p75 jumping from 1.2 s to 3.8 s right after a frontend release. Lighthouse in CI still looks green; nothing changed on the servers.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

The release added a lazy-loading library and applied loading="lazy" to all images, including the hero image at the top of the page.

🔍 Clue 2

DevTools waterfall: the hero image request now starts only after the JS bundle has run, ~2.4 s after navigation.

🎯 Root cause

The LCP element (the hero image) is no longer discovered by the preload scanner and is deliberately deferred, so the browser downloads it late and the largest paint happens late.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Load the hero eagerly with fetchpriority="high" (and <link rel=preload> if it's in CSS), lazy-load only offscreen images, and add a RUM alert on LCP p75. Lesson: lab tools can miss what real users see; watch field data per release.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Chrome DevTools)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 08-browser (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces.

  1. Open any site → DevTools → Performance → record a page reload. Find the Parse HTML, Evaluate Script, Recalculate Style, Layout, Paint and Composite Layers blocks on the Main and Compositor tracks.
  2. DevTools → Lighthouse → run a report and read LCP, CLS and TBT (total blocking time).
  3. DevTools → More tools → Rendering → enable Paint flashing and Layout shift regions, then scroll and interact.
  4. Compare View Page Source (what the server sent) with the Elements panel (the live DOM after JS ran). For a client-side SPA they're very different.
  5. In the Console:
// Navigation timing: DNS, TCP, TLS, TTFB, DOM ready (Chapter 6 numbers, from the browser's view)
const n = performance.getEntriesByType('navigation')[0];
console.table({ dns: n.domainLookupEnd - n.domainLookupStart, tcp: n.connectEnd - n.connectStart,
  ttfb: n.responseStart - n.requestStart, domContentLoaded: n.domContentLoadedEventEnd, load: n.loadEventEnd });

// Feel a long task: the page freezes for 2 seconds
const t = Date.now(); while (Date.now() - t < 2000) {}

Exercise: in the Performance panel, record while running the 2-second loop and try clicking a button on the page. Find the long task and see when the click was finally handled.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Bytes → HTML parser → DOM          CSS → CSSOM (render-blocking)
<script> blocks parsing (use defer/async) · JS changes DOM/CSSOM via DOM API
DOM + CSSOM → Style (render tree) → Layout (geometry) → Paint (draw commands)
   → Composite (layers on GPU, compositor thread) → frame → vsync → screen
Event loop: task → microtasks → (every ~16.7 ms) rAF → style → layout → paint
transform/opacity = composite only · width/top = layout again
Core Web Vitals: LCP ≤ 2.5 s · INP ≤ 200 ms · CLS ≤ 0.1

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can a plain <script src> in the <head> delay the whole page?

It's parser-blocking: the HTML parser stops, waits for the script to download and execute, and only then continues building the DOM. defer or async avoids this.

2. Which is cheaper to animate, left or transform: translateX()? Why?

transform. Changing left triggers layout and paint on the main thread every frame. transform can be handled by the compositor on the GPU without layout or paint.

3. A button click takes 400 ms to show any effect. Which metric gets worse, and what's the usual cause?

INP (Interaction to Next Paint). Usually a long JavaScript task on the main thread that blocks the event handler or the next rendering step.

4. What's the difference between View Source and the Elements panel?

View Source shows the original HTML bytes the server sent. Elements shows the current DOM, after the parser fixed things up and JavaScript changed it.

5. Why does each site get its own renderer process?

Security and stability. A compromised or crashing page is isolated in its own sandboxed process (Site Isolation) and can't read other sites' memory or bring them down.
