docs.text: Explain the path from HTML bytes to pixels, and why long JavaScript tasks make a page feel slow, in your own words in 5 lines.

docs.title: 8.1 — The rendering pipeline in depth
docs.text:
In short

The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them, computes style and layout (where every box goes), paints layers and composites them on the GPU. Anything that blocks this path — render-blocking CSS, parser-blocking scripts, late fonts and images — delays the first meaningful pixels, and anything that forces layout again and again makes the page janky.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CRP Critical Rendering Path Steps from bytes to first pixels HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, layout, paint DOM / CSSOM Document / CSS Object Model Trees for content / styles Built incrementally while downloading Render-blocking — Resource the browser waits for before painting <link rel=stylesheet> in <head> Parser-blocking — Script that stops HTML parsing <script src> without defer/async Preload scanner — Secondary parser that finds resources early Starts downloads while the main parser is blocked Resource hints — preload, preconnect, dns-prefetch, fetchpriority Tell the browser what matters early Style recalc — Computing final styles for elements Selector matching, cascade, inheritance Layout (reflow) — Computing geometry of every box Expensive on big DOMs Paint — Recording draw operations into layers Text, colours, borders, images Compositing — Combining layers on the GPU transform/opacity changes only need this Layout thrashing — Alternating DOM writes and layout reads Forces many synchronous layouts FOIT / FOUT Flash Of Invisible / Unstyled Text Font-loading behaviours Controlled by font-display Lazy loading — Load offscreen images/iframes later loading="lazy"

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. HTML arrives in chunks and is parsed into the DOM as it streams (TTFB matters, server streaming helps).
  2. The preload scanner looks ahead and starts downloading CSS, JS, fonts and images it finds in the markup.
  3. CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint until it has the CSSOM for stylesheets in <head> (otherwise you'd see unstyled content).
  4. Classic <script src> is parser-blocking: parsing stops until it downloads and runs (it might document.write). It also waits for preceding CSS.
  5. With DOM + CSSOM → style → layout → paint → composite → First Contentful Paint, and later LCP when the biggest element appears.

docs.title: 2 · Unblocking the path
docs.text: Technique Effect <script defer> Download in parallel, run after parsing, in order <script async> Download in parallel, run when ready (any order) — analytics <script type=module> Deferred by default Inline critical CSS, load the rest later Paint above-the-fold content sooner <link rel=preload as=font/image> Start late-discovered critical resources early <link rel=preconnect href=https://cdn…> Do DNS+TCP+TLS to a third-party origin early fetchpriority="high" on the LCP image Download it before less important images loading="lazy" on offscreen images Save bandwidth for what's visible font-display: swap + preload + subsetting Text visible immediately, less layout shift

docs.title: 3 · Style, layout, paint, composite
docs.text:
Change Pipeline work Cost width, top, font size, adding DOM nodes Style → layout → paint → composite High color, background, box-shadow Style → paint → composite Medium transform, opacity (on own layer) Composite only (GPU) Low → smooth 60 fps animations

Layout thrashing: reading el.offsetHeight right after writing a style forces the browser to do layout now; in a loop this means hundreds of layouts per frame. Batch reads, then writes (or use requestAnimationFrame).

Big DOMs (tens of thousands of nodes) make every style/layout pass slower: virtualize long lists.

docs.title: 4 · Images and fonts
docs.text:
• Images are usually the LCP element and most of the bytes: serve AVIF/WebP, the right size per screen (srcset/sizes), from a CDN, with width/height set to avoid layout shift.
  • Fonts: limit families/weights, self-host or preconnect, subset, font-display: swap.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• TTFB is infra's part of rendering: CDN caching of HTML, compression (br/zstd), HTTP/2-3, early hints (103), server-side streaming.
  • Cache headers for hashed static assets (immutable), short/no-cache for HTML (6.1).
  • Image CDNs (or resizing at the edge) turn "upload 5 MB photo" into "serve 60 KB AVIF".
  • Performance budgets in CI (Lighthouse CI) block regressions in JS/CSS size before they ship.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Lighthouse from the command line (Node required)
npx -y lighthouse https://example.com --only-categories=performance --quiet --chrome-flags="--headless" --output=json \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; a=json.load(sys.stdin)['audits']; [print(k, a[k]['displayValue']) for k in ['first-contentful-paint','largest-contentful-paint','total-blocking-time','cumulative-layout-shift']]"

In Chrome DevTools:

  1. Network → reload → look at the waterfall: what starts late? what blocks?
  2. Performance → record a reload → see Parse HTML, Recalculate Style, Layout, Paint; long purple (layout) blocks = thrashing.
  3. Rendering panel → enable "Paint flashing" and "Layout shift regions".
  4. Coverage (Ctrl+Shift+P → Coverage) → how much CSS/JS is unused on load.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Problem Fix Blank screen for long Inline critical CSS, defer scripts, reduce TTFB LCP image late fetchpriority=high, preload, CDN, modern format, right size Janky animation Animate transform/opacity only Layout thrashing Batch reads then writes Text invisible font-display: swap, preload fonts Huge DOM Virtualize lists

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is CSS render-blocking but images aren't?

Without the CSSOM the browser can't know how anything looks or where it goes; painting without it would flash unstyled content. Images can fill in later.

2. What's the difference between defer and async?

Both download in parallel. defer runs after HTML parsing, in document order; async runs as soon as it's downloaded, in any order.

3. Why animate transform instead of left?

left triggers layout and paint every frame; transform can be handled by the compositor on the GPU without layout.

4. What is layout thrashing?

Interleaving DOM writes and layout reads so the browser must recompute layout synchronously many times per frame.

5. What can the infrastructure team do for rendering speed?

Lower TTFB (CDN, caching, streaming), compression, HTTP/2-3, early hints, correct cache headers and image optimization at the edge.

docs.title: 8.2 — JavaScript, the event loop & async
docs.text:
In short

JavaScript runs your code on one call stack per page. Slow things (network, timers, user input) are handled by the browser's Web APIs, which put callbacks into task and microtask queues. The event loop runs one task at a time, drains all microtasks (promises), then lets the page render. So any long task freezes clicks, scrolling and animations until it ends.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Call stack — Frames of currently running functions One at a time; must empty before the next task Heap — Where objects live Garbage collected by V8 Web APIs — Browser features outside JS fetch, timers, DOM events, IndexedDB Task (macrotask) — Unit of work from the task queue Event handler, timer callback, message Microtask — High-priority follow-up work Promise reactions, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver Event loop — Scheduler of the main thread Task → all microtasks → (render) → next task Promise — Object for a future value .then callbacks run as microtasks async / await — Syntax over promises await pauses the function, not the thread Long task — Task > 50 ms Delays input → bad INP rAF requestAnimationFrame Callback before the next paint For animations and DOM writes Web Worker — Background thread without DOM Heavy compute off the main thread Memory leak — Objects kept reachable by mistake Detached DOM nodes, listeners, growing caches libuv — Node.js' event loop + thread pool Same model on the server

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
console.log('1 sync');
setTimeout(() => console.log('4 task (timer)'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 microtask'));
console.log('2 sync');
// prints: 1 sync, 2 sync, 3 microtask, 4 task (timer)
  1. The script itself is a task: lines run on the call stack top to bottom.
  2. setTimeout hands a timer to the Web APIs; when it fires, its callback goes into the task queue.
  3. Promise.then schedules a microtask.
  4. When the stack is empty, the event loop drains all microtasks (3), maybe renders, then takes the next task (4).

docs.title: 2 · The event loop and rendering
docs.text:
• At 60 Hz the browser wants to render every 16.7 ms. Rendering can only happen between tasks.
  • A 300 ms task (big JSON parse, heavy loop, huge React re-render) = 300 ms with no clicks, no scrolling (unless compositor-only), no animation.
  • Microtasks run until the queue is empty: a promise chain that keeps scheduling itself can starve rendering entirely.

docs.title: 3 · Async patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Looks like Notes Callbacks fs.readFile(p, (err, data) => …) Nesting, error handling per callback Promises fetch(u).then(r => r.json()) Chainable, .catch once async/await const r = await fetch(u) Reads like sync code; await yields to the event loop Parallel await Promise.all([a(), b()]) Don't await in a loop when calls are independent Cancel AbortController Abort fetches on navigation/unmount

await doesn't block the thread: the function pauses, other tasks keep running. But CPU work is never async: a for loop over 10 million items blocks whatever you wrap around it.

docs.title: 4 · Keeping the main thread free
docs.text:
• Break up long tasks: process in chunks and yield (await scheduler.yield() where supported, or setTimeout(0)), so input can be handled between chunks.
  • Move heavy work to a Web Worker (parsing, image processing, crypto, search indexing); communicate with postMessage.
  • Do DOM writes in requestAnimationFrame; avoid layout thrashing (8.1).
  • Ship less JS: code-split by route, remove unused libraries, defer third-party scripts (tag managers are frequent offenders).

docs.title: 5 · Memory leaks
docs.text: Common causes: event listeners never removed, intervals never cleared, closures holding big objects, detached DOM nodes still referenced, unbounded in-memory caches. Find them with DevTools Memory → heap snapshots (compare before/after) and the "Detached elements" view.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Node.js is the same model with libuv: a blocking call (sync file I/O, JSON.parse of 50 MB, bcrypt on the main thread) stalls every request on that process. Watch event loop lag / eventLoopUtilization as a metric.
  • Scale Node.js horizontally (more pods / cluster workers), not with more CPU per pod (4.3).
  • Real-user monitoring (RUM) of long tasks and INP shows which releases hurt responsiveness.
  • Third-party scripts (chat widgets, A/B tools, analytics) often dominate main-thread time; govern them like dependencies.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
// Paste in the browser console on any page

// 1. Order of execution
setTimeout(() => console.log('task'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('microtask'));
console.log('sync');

// 2. Feel a long task: try to scroll or click during these 3 seconds
const end = Date.now() + 3000; while (Date.now() < end) {}

// 3. Observe long tasks on this page
new PerformanceObserver(l => l.getEntries().forEach(e => console.log('long task', Math.round(e.duration), 'ms')))
  .observe({ type: 'longtask', buffered: true });

// 4. Same work, chunked, page stays responsive
async function chunked(n) { for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (i % 1e6 === 0) await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r)); } console.log('done'); }
chunked(5e7);

# Node.js: event loop delay while blocking
node -e "const {monitorEventLoopDelay}=require('perf_hooks');const h=monitorEventLoopDelay();h.enable();
setTimeout(()=>{const e=Date.now()+500;while(Date.now()<e){}},100);
setTimeout(()=>console.log('p99 delay ms', h.percentile(99)/1e6),1000)"

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Order What runs 1 Current task (script, event handler, timer callback) 2 All microtasks (promise callbacks, await continuations) 3 Render if due (rAF → style → layout → paint) 4 Next task Problem Fix UI freezes Find long tasks; chunk or move to a Worker Slow independent awaits Promise.all Memory grows Heap snapshots, remove listeners/timers Node latency spikes Event loop lag metric, offload CPU work

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. In what order do setTimeout(f,0), Promise.resolve().then(g) and a sync console.log run?

Sync log first, then g (microtask), then f (task).

2. Why does a 500 ms loop make clicks feel ignored?

The click handler is a task that can only run after the current task finishes; rendering also waits.

3. Does await block the main thread?

No. It pauses that async function and returns control to the event loop; CPU-bound code still blocks.

4. When should you use a Web Worker?

For CPU-heavy work (parsing, image/crypto processing, search) that would otherwise create long tasks on the main thread.

5. What's the server-side equivalent of a long task, and how do you detect it?

A blocking operation on the Node.js event loop; detect with event loop delay/utilization metrics.

docs.title: 8.3 — Web performance & Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
In short

Core Web Vitals turn "is the site fast?" into three user-centred numbers from real visits. LCP measures how fast the main content appears, INP how quickly the page responds to input, and CLS how much things jump around, all at the 75th percentile. Lab tools like Lighthouse help you debug, but field data (CrUX, RUM) is what counts. Much of it depends on infrastructure: TTFB, CDN, caching and compression.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Core Web Vitals — Google's three key UX metrics LCP, INP, CLS LCP Largest Contentful Paint Time until the largest content element renders Good ≤ 2.5 s INP Interaction to Next Paint Slowest typical delay from input to next frame Good ≤ 200 ms (replaced FID in 2024) CLS Cumulative Layout Shift Unexpected movement of visible content Good ≤ 0.1 TTFB Time To First Byte Request start → first response byte Good ≤ 0.8 s FCP First Contentful Paint First text/image painted Good ≤ 1.8 s TBT Total Blocking Time Lab proxy for responsiveness Sum of long-task time over 50 ms p75 75th percentile The value 75% of visits beat Used to pass/fail each metric Lab data — Synthetic test in a controlled setup Lighthouse, WebPageTest Field data / RUM Real User Monitoring Measurements from real visitors CrUX, web-vitals.js, vendor RUM CrUX Chrome UX Report Google's public field dataset Origin/URL level, 28-day window Performance budget — Limits on bytes/metrics Enforced in CI

docs.title: 1 · The three Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
Metric Good Needs improvement Poor Measures LCP ≤ 2.5 s ≤ 4 s > 4 s Loading INP ≤ 200 ms ≤ 500 ms > 500 ms Responsiveness CLS ≤ 0.1 ≤ 0.25 > 0.25 Visual stability

A page "passes" when 75% of visits are in the good range for each. They affect search ranking slightly, but they matter more because they correlate with conversion and bounce rates.

docs.title: LCP = TTFB + resource load delay + resource load time + render delay
docs.text:
• TTFB: server time, DB queries, cold caches, far-away origin, redirects. → CDN/edge caching of HTML, faster backend, 103 Early Hints.
  • Load delay: LCP image discovered late (CSS background, JS-inserted). → put it in HTML, preload, fetchpriority=high.
  • Load time: big image. → AVIF/WebP, right size, image CDN.
  • Render delay: render-blocking CSS/JS, client-side rendering waiting for data. → critical CSS, SSR/streaming, defer JS (8.1).

docs.title: INP = input delay + processing time + presentation delay
docs.text: • Long tasks already running when the user clicks; heavy event handlers; huge re-renders. → break up tasks, less JS, Workers, content-visibility, avoid layout thrashing (8.2).

docs.title: CLS
docs.text: • Images/ads/embeds without reserved size; fonts swapping; content injected above existing content. → width/height or aspect-ratio, reserve slots, font-display + size-adjusted fallbacks, insert below the fold or on user action.

docs.title: 3 · Lab vs field
docs.text:
Lab (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) Field (CrUX, RUM) Who One simulated device/network All your real users Good for Debugging, CI regressions, before release Truth, trends, segmentation (country, device) INP Not measurable (no real interactions) → TBT as proxy Real INP Variance Low (controlled) Real-world spread

Collect field data yourself with the web-vitals library → send to your analytics/observability backend, segment by route, release and device class.

docs.title: 4 · Budgets and process
docs.text:
• Performance budgets: e.g. "JS ≤ 200 KB gzip on the landing page", "LCP p75 ≤ 2.5 s". Enforce with Lighthouse CI in pull requests and alerts on RUM.
  • Release annotations on RUM dashboards show which deploy made INP worse.
  • Third-party governance: every tag must justify its cost.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• You own TTFB: CDN in front of HTML (stale-while-revalidate), origin close to users, warm caches, connection reuse to backends, no redirect chains (http→https→www).
  • Transport: HTTP/2-3, TLS 1.3, Brotli/zstd compression, correct Cache-Control and hashed assets (6.1, 6.5).
  • Edge features: image optimization, Early Hints, edge SSR / caching personalized pages carefully.
  • Observability: put web vitals next to backend latency in the same dashboards; a TTFB jump often points to a backend or cache problem.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Field data from CrUX for any public origin (needs a free Google API key)
# curl -s "https://chromeuxreport.googleapis.com/v1/records:queryRecord?key=$KEY" \
#   -d '{"origin":"https://www.example.com"}' | jq '.record.metrics | map_values(.percentiles.p75)'

# Lab data
npx -y lighthouse https://example.com --preset=desktop --only-categories=performance --view

# TTFB breakdown from the terminal
curl -so /dev/null -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} tcp=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total}\n' https://example.com

<!-- Field data from your own users -->
<script type="module">
  import {onLCP, onINP, onCLS} from 'https://unpkg.com/web-vitals@4?module';
  const send = m => navigator.sendBeacon('/rum', JSON.stringify({name: m.name, value: m.value, id: m.id}));
  onLCP(send); onINP(send); onCLS(send);
</script>

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Metric bad First things to check LCP TTFB, LCP image discovery/priority/size, render-blocking CSS/JS INP Long tasks, heavy handlers, third-party scripts, big re-renders CLS Missing image dimensions, ads/embeds, fonts, injected banners TTFB CDN cache hit ratio, backend latency, redirects, distance

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why can't Lighthouse report INP, and what does it show instead?

INP needs real user interactions over the page's life; Lighthouse shows Total Blocking Time as a lab proxy.

2. LCP is 4 s but TTFB is 3 s. Where do you start?

Server side: caching HTML at the CDN, backend/database latency, redirects, origin distance. The frontend can't fix a 3 s TTFB.

3. What does 'p75 LCP = 2.3 s' mean?

75% of real page loads had LCP at or below 2.3 s; the slowest 25% were worse.

4. A cookie banner pushes the page down after load. Which metric suffers and how do you fix it?

CLS. Reserve its space from the start, overlay it, or show it without moving existing content.

5. Name three infrastructure changes that improve Core Web Vitals.

CDN caching of HTML/assets, HTTP/3 + Brotli compression, image optimization at the edge (also: Early Hints, removing redirect chains).

docs.title: 8.4 — Browser security
docs.text:
In short

Browsers run code from millions of untrusted sites side by side. So they enforce the same-origin policy (a page can't read another origin's data) and isolate sites in separate processes. Most web attacks try to get around that: XSS runs the attacker's script inside your origin, CSRF abuses your cookies from another site, clickjacking frames your page. The defences are mostly headers and cookie flags a platform team can set centrally.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Origin — scheme + host + port https://app.example.com:443 Site — Registrable domain (eTLD+1) + scheme https://example.com; used by SameSite SOP Same-Origin Policy Pages can't read other origins' responses/DOM The browser's core security boundary Site isolation — Each site in its own renderer process Limits Spectre-style leaks between sites XSS Cross-Site Scripting Attacker-controlled script runs in your page Stored, reflected or DOM-based CSP Content Security Policy Header listing allowed script/style/connect sources Blocks injected and inline scripts CSRF Cross-Site Request Forgery Another site triggers a state-changing request with your cookies Prevented by SameSite, tokens, Origin checks SameSite — Cookie attribute: Strict / Lax / None Controls sending cookies on cross-site requests Clickjacking — Your page invisibly framed under a decoy frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options CORS Cross-Origin Resource Sharing Opt-in relaxation of SOP for reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin (6.1) HSTS HTTP Strict Transport Security Always use HTTPS for this site Prevents SSL stripping SRI Subresource Integrity Hash pinning for external scripts integrity="sha384-…" Trusted Types — CSP feature restricting DOM XSS sinks innerHTML only accepts vetted values COOP / COEP Cross-Origin Opener / Embedder Policy Isolation headers Needed for SharedArrayBuffer, stronger isolation

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
JavaScript on https://evil.example can send requests to https://bank.example (forms, images, fetch), but it cannot read the responses, the DOM, cookies or storage of that origin. Everything else in browser security either protects this boundary or carefully relaxes it (CORS for reads, postMessage for windows).

Modern browsers also put each site in its own process (site isolation), so even a renderer bug or Spectre-style side channel can't easily read another site's memory.

docs.title: 2 · XSS and Content Security Policy
docs.text:
XSS = the attacker gets their JavaScript to run on your origin, so the SOP doesn't protect you: it can read the page, call your APIs with the user's session, steal non-HttpOnly tokens.

Kind How Example Stored Malicious input saved and shown to others Comment containing <script> Reflected Input echoed in a response ?q=<script>… in search results DOM-based Client code writes untrusted data into the DOM el.innerHTML = location.hash

Defences (layered):

  1. Encode output for the context (templating frameworks do it by default; avoid innerHTML, dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html).
  2. CSP: Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'nonce-r4nd0m'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none' — blocks inline and foreign scripts even if injection happens. Roll out with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first.
  3. Trusted Types for DOM XSS sinks; HttpOnly cookies so scripts can't read the session.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
The browser automatically attaches cookies to requests for a site — even if the request was started by another site (a hidden form on evil.example posting to bank.example/transfer).

Defences:

  • SameSite=Lax (browser default for cookies without the attribute in Chrome): cookies aren't sent on cross-site POSTs/subrequests, only on top-level GET navigations. Strict = never cross-site. None (+Secure) only when you truly need third-party context.
  • CSRF tokens in forms/headers, or check the Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site headers on state-changing requests.
  • Never change state on GET.

docs.title: 4 · Framing, transport and third parties
docs.text:
• Clickjacking → Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' (or X-Frame-Options: DENY).
  • HSTS → Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload; no mixed content (HTTP resources on HTTPS pages are blocked).
  • Third-party scripts run with your origin's power. Minimize them, pin versions, use SRI for CDN-hosted files, restrict with CSP, and review npm dependencies (lockfiles, audit, provenance) — supply-chain attacks on popular packages are common.
  • Tokens in localStorage are readable by any XSS. Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for sessions (or keep access tokens in memory with short lifetimes).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Set security headers centrally at the CDN/ingress/gateway (HSTS, CSP, frame-ancestors, nosniff, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy) so every app gets them (6.1).
  • CSP report endpoints (report-to) feed violations into your logging; spikes after a deploy show broken or injected scripts.
  • WAF rules catch common injection payloads but are a backstop, not a replacement for encoding.
  • Dependency scanning and SBOMs in CI for frontend packages; pin and verify third-party script hashes.
  • Cookie flags are config: check them in integration tests (Set-Cookie must have HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite).

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Which security headers does a site send?
curl -sI https://github.com | grep -iE 'content-security-policy|strict-transport|x-frame|x-content-type|referrer-policy|permissions-policy|cross-origin'

# Cookie flags
curl -sI https://github.com | grep -i '^set-cookie' | head -3

// Browser console on any site: the SOP in action
fetch('https://example.com').then(r => r.text()).then(console.log).catch(e => console.log('blocked by CORS/SOP:', e.message));
document.cookie;          // HttpOnly cookies do NOT appear here

Online: run your domain through securityheaders.com and Mozilla HTTP Observatory; test CSP with csp-evaluator.withgoogle.com.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Threat Defence XSS Output encoding, CSP (nonces, no inline), Trusted Types, HttpOnly CSRF SameSite=Lax/Strict, CSRF tokens, Origin check, no state change on GET Clickjacking frame-ancestors 'none' Downgrade / sniffing HSTS (+ preload) Compromised CDN script SRI + CSP allow-list Token theft HttpOnly Secure cookies, short-lived tokens

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What exactly does the same-origin policy prevent?

Reading responses, DOM, cookies and storage of another origin; it doesn't prevent sending requests to it.

2. Why is XSS so dangerous even with the SOP in place?

The attacker's script runs on your origin, so the SOP treats it as your code: it can read pages and call APIs as the user.

3. How does SameSite=Lax stop most CSRF?

Cookies aren't attached to cross-site POSTs or subrequests, so a forged form submission from another site arrives without the session.

4. Is CORS a security feature that protects your API?

No. It's a controlled relaxation of the SOP for browser reads; it doesn't stop non-browser clients and isn't authentication.

5. Why roll out CSP in Report-Only mode first?

To see what legitimate scripts/styles would be blocked before enforcing, avoiding breaking the site.

docs.title: Chapter 9 — Modern infrastructure
docs.text:
In short

A container is just a Linux process (Chapter 3) wrapped in namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (what it can use), started from a layered image. Kubernetes keeps comparing the desired state you wrote in YAML with the actual state of the cluster and fixes the difference, forever. CI/CD builds the images and GitOps tells the cluster what should run. Observability shows you whether it actually works.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Container — A process isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups Started from an image by a runtime (containerd/runc) Namespace — What a process can see pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, user, cgroup cgroup control group What a process can use CPU quota, memory limit, I/O, pids OCI image Open Container Initiative Standard container image format Manifest + layers + config, addressed by digest CRI / CNI Container Runtime Interface / Container Network Interface Plugin APIs of Kubernetes kubelet ↔ runtime / pod networking plugins API server / etcd — Kubernetes front door / its database Everything reads/writes cluster state through the API Scheduler / kubelet — Picks a node / runs pods on a node Filter + score nodes / talk to the runtime Controller / reconcile — Loop making actual state match desired state Watch → compare → act → repeat Service / Ingress — Stable virtual IP for pods / HTTP routing into the cluster kube-proxy/eBPF load-balances; ingress routes by host/path CI / CD Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery Automated build-test / automated release Pipelines on every push; rollouts to environments GitOps — Git as the source of truth for deployments An in-cluster agent (Argo CD, Flux) syncs from git IaC Infrastructure as Code Cloud resources defined in code Terraform/OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane plan & apply SLO Service Level Objective A reliability/latency target e.g. 99.9% of requests < 300 ms OTel OpenTelemetry Open standard for metrics, logs, traces SDKs + collector export to any backend

docs.title: 1 · A container is a process with extra walls
docs.text:
Kernel feature What it isolates Examples Namespaces What the process can see pid (own PID 1), net (own network stack and IP), mnt (own filesystem view), uts (hostname), ipc, user (root inside ≠ root outside), cgroup cgroups v2 What the process can use cpu.max (CPU quota → throttling), memory.max (limit → OOM kill), io.max, pids.max Image + overlayfs Its filesystem Read-only layers (one per Dockerfile step) stacked with a thin writable layer on top. Shared between containers. Seccomp, capabilities, AppArmor/SELinux What it is allowed to do Block dangerous syscalls, drop root powers Virtual machine Container Isolation boundary Hypervisor, separate kernel Shared host kernel, namespaces Start time Seconds to minutes Milliseconds Overhead A full OS per VM One process Security isolation Stronger Weaker (shared kernel), hardened with gVisor/Kata/microVMs

An image follows the OCI standard: a manifest + layers (tarballs) + config (entrypoint, env), stored in a registry and identified by an immutable digest (sha256:…).

docs.title: 2 · Kubernetes: a set of control loops
docs.text:
Control plane (the brain):

Component Job kube-apiserver The only front door. Every client (kubectl, controllers, kubelets) talks to it over REST. Authenticates, authorizes, validates, stores. etcd Consistent key-value store holding the entire cluster state. kube-scheduler Picks a node for each unscheduled pod: filter (enough CPU/memory? taints, affinity) then score. kube-controller-manager Many control loops: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods, node health, endpoints, jobs…

Worker nodes (the muscle):

Component Job kubelet Watches the API for pods assigned to its node and makes them real. Runs probes, reports status. Container runtime (containerd + runc) Pulls images and starts containers, via the CRI interface. CNI plugin (Cilium, Calico, …) Gives each pod an IP and connects pod networks across nodes. kube-proxy / eBPF Implements Services: a stable virtual IP that load-balances to the pods behind it.

docs.title: What happens on kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
docs.text:
# Step 5 kubectl sends the Deployment to the API server, which validates it. 6 The API server stores it in etcd. Nothing is running yet, only desired state. 7 The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, the ReplicaSet controller creates Pod objects (status Pending, no node). The scheduler sees them, picks a node for each, and writes the binding back. 8 The kubelet on that node sees a pod assigned to it. 9 It asks the runtime (CRI) to create the pod sandbox. CNI assigns the pod IP. 10 The runtime pulls the image and starts the containers: clone() with new namespaces, put into cgroups, execve the entrypoint (Chapters 3–4!). — Readiness probe passes → the pod is added to the Service's EndpointSlice → traffic starts flowing.

Remember this

Kubernetes never "runs a command once". Every component watches the API and reconciles: "Is actual = desired? If not, take one step closer." Delete a pod of a Deployment and a new one appears. That's the controller doing its job.

docs.title: How does reconciliation work?
docs.text: Each controller watches the API server, compares the desired state (spec) with the actual state (status), and takes one step to close the gap — then repeats on every change and periodically. This is why deleting a pod managed by a Deployment just brings it back.

docs.title: 3 · CI/CD and GitOps
docs.text:
Stage Typical tools Output CI: on every push, test, build and scan GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins An immutable image app:1.4.2 (or @sha256:…) in a registry Promote: update the desired version A commit/PR to the manifests repo (Helm values, Kustomize) Git = the single source of truth CD / GitOps: the cluster pulls changes Argo CD, Flux The cluster converges to what's in git. Drift is detected and corrected. Rollout strategy Rolling update, blue/green, canary (Argo Rollouts) Safe, reversible releases (git revert = rollback)

Cloud resources outside the cluster (VPCs, databases, DNS) are managed the same declarative way with Infrastructure as Code: Terraform/OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane.

docs.title: 4 · Observability: metrics, logs, traces
docs.text:
Signal Answers Tools Metrics How much / how often? (rates, latencies, saturation) Prometheus, Grafana Logs What exactly happened in this request? Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch Traces Where did the time go across services? OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Jaeger

Useful habits: the RED method for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors), and SLOs ("99.9% of requests < 300 ms") that alert on what users feel.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the hotfix that kept disappearing
docs.text:
The alarm

During an incident, an engineer raises a Deployment's memory limit with kubectl edit. The pods restart with the new limit… and two minutes later they're back on the old one and OOMKill again.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

kubectl get deploy -o yaml shows the annotation of the GitOps tool; the Argo CD UI shows the app as OutOfSync → Synced right after the edit.

🔍 Clue 2

The Application has syncPolicy.automated.selfHeal: true.

🎯 Root cause

Argo CD continuously reconciles the cluster to git. The manual edit is drift, and self-heal reverts it to the declared state, exactly as designed.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Make the change in git (a fast-tracked PR), or temporarily pause auto-sync for that app during the incident and commit afterwards. Lesson: with GitOps, git is the only place where changes stick; have a documented break-glass procedure.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (Linux + Docker)
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 09-infra (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) A "container" with nothing but unshare: new PID + mount namespace
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash
ps aux            # you are PID 1 and alone
exit

# 2) A real container is a host process
docker run -d --name web --memory 64m --cpus 0.5 nginx:alpine
PID=$(docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' web); echo $PID
ps -o pid,cmd -p $PID                      # it's right there on the host
sudo ls -l /proc/$PID/ns                   # its namespaces
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/docker-$(docker inspect -f '{{.Id}}' web).scope/memory.max 2>/dev/null   # 67108864 (cgroup v2 + systemd driver)
docker image history nginx:alpine          # the layers
docker rm -f web

# 3) Kubernetes locally with kind, and watch the control loops
kind create cluster
kubectl create deployment hello --image=nginx --replicas=2
kubectl get events -w &                    # Scheduled → Pulling → Created → Started
kubectl delete pod -l app=hello --wait=false && kubectl get pods -w   # new pods appear
kind delete cluster

Exercise: start a container with --memory 32m that tries to use more (docker run --rm --memory 32m python:3-alpine python -c "x=bytearray(100_000_000)"). Check the exit code and docker inspect for OOMKilled. Which kernel feature from Chapter 3 did that?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Container = process + namespaces (see) + cgroups (use) + image layers (overlayfs) + seccomp/caps
Image = OCI manifest + layers + config, by digest, in a registry
K8s control plane: API server (front door) · etcd (state) · scheduler (pick node) · controllers (loops)
K8s node: kubelet (agent) · containerd/runc (CRI) · CNI (pod IP) · kube-proxy/eBPF (Services)
kubectl apply → API → etcd → controllers create pods → scheduler binds → kubelet → CRI pull+start → ready → endpoints
CI builds immutable images → GitOps (Argo CD) syncs desired state from git → rollouts
Observe: metrics (how much) · logs (what) · traces (where) · SLOs

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Is a container a small virtual machine?

No. It's a normal Linux process sharing the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups. A VM runs its own kernel on a hypervisor.

2. A pod is stuck in Pending. Which component hasn't done its job yet, and why might that be?

The scheduler hasn't bound it to a node, usually because no node has enough free CPU/memory for its requests, or because of taints, affinity rules or an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim. kubectl describe pod shows the reason in the events.

3. You delete a pod that belongs to a Deployment and a new one appears. Who created it?

The ReplicaSet controller (in kube-controller-manager). It saw actual replicas < desired replicas and created a new Pod object, which the scheduler and kubelet then made real.

4. What's the difference between push-based CD and GitOps?

In push-based CD the pipeline runs kubectl apply/helm upgrade against the cluster with cluster credentials. In GitOps an agent inside the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) pulls the desired state from git and reconciles continuously, so git is the source of truth and drift is corrected.

5. Your service is slow but CPU and memory look fine. Which signal do you reach for?

Traces, to see which downstream call or span is taking the time across services. Then logs for that specific request.

docs.title: 9.1 — Containers & images
docs.text:
In short

A container image is a stack of read-only, content-addressed layers plus a config, described by a manifest and identified by a digest. You build it from a Dockerfile, push it to a registry, and on each node containerd pulls only the missing layers, stacks them with overlayfs and asks runc to start your process inside namespaces and cgroups (3.5).

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) OCI Open Container Initiative Standards for images, runtimes, distribution Docker, Podman, containerd all follow them Image — Filesystem layers + config (entrypoint, env, user) Immutable; identified by digest Layer — Tarball of filesystem changes Shared and cached between images Manifest / index — List of layers + config / list of per-platform manifests Multi-arch images use an index Digest — sha256: hash of content Same digest = byte-identical image Tag — Human name pointing at a digest Mutable (:latest, :1.4) Registry — Server storing images Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, GAR, Harbor BuildKit / buildx — Modern Docker build engine Parallel stages, cache mounts, multi-platform Multi-stage build — Build in one stage, copy artifacts to a small final stage Smaller, safer images Distroless / scratch — Minimal base images No shell or package manager SBOM Software Bill of Materials List of packages in an image Syft, docker buildx --sbom cosign / Sigstore — Image signing and verification Admission policies verify signatures CRI / containerd / runc Container Runtime Interface kubelet's runtime API / runtime / low-level OCI runtime kubelet → containerd → shim → runc

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
image index (multi-arch)  sha256:aa…
 ├─ manifest linux/amd64  sha256:bb…
 │   ├─ config  (Entrypoint, Env, User, WorkingDir…)
 │   └─ layers  sha256:l1 (base OS) · sha256:l2 (deps) · sha256:l3 (app)
 └─ manifest linux/arm64  sha256:cc…
  • Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer. Layers are hashed; identical layers are stored and downloaded once.
  • On the node, overlayfs stacks the layers read-only and adds one writable layer per container. Deleting a file in a later layer only hides it; the bytes are still in the image.
  • Tags move, digests don't. api:1.4 can be re-pushed; api@sha256:… always means the same bytes.

docs.title: 2 · Builds and caching
docs.text:
• Build cache is per instruction: if an instruction and its inputs haven't changed, the cached layer is reused; once one step changes, all later steps rebuild.
  • So order from least to most frequently changing: base image → OS packages → dependency manifest (package.json, go.mod) → install → source code.
  • BuildKit features: parallel stages, --mount=type=cache for package caches, secrets that don't end up in layers (--mount=type=secret), remote cache in the registry for CI.
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM golang:1.25 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w" -o /app ./cmd/api

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot
COPY --from=build /app /app
USER nonroot
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

docs.title: 3 · Small, secure images
docs.text: Practice Why Multi-stage + distroless/scratch/minimal base Fewer packages = fewer CVEs, smaller pulls Pin base images by digest, rebuild regularly Reproducible, but still get patches Run as non-root, read-only root filesystem Limits damage of a compromise (3.5) No secrets in layers or build args Layers are forever; use runtime secrets Exec-form ENTRYPOINT/CMD Signals reach your app (3.1) .dockerignore Keep .git, node_modules, local files out Scan (Trivy, Grype), SBOM (Syft), sign (cosign) Know what's inside, prove where it came from

docs.title: 4 · The runtime chain
docs.text:
1. kubelet decides a pod should run and calls the CRI (gRPC) on containerd (or CRI-O).
  2. containerd pulls the image, creates the pod sandbox (pause container holding namespaces), asks the CNI plugin to set up networking.
  3. A containerd-shim per pod launches runc, which creates namespaces and cgroups, applies security settings and execves your entrypoint, then exits; the shim stays as parent.
  4. Image pull is often the slowest part of pod start: big images, cold nodes, registry rate limits. Mitigate with smaller images, pre-pulling, registry mirrors, lazy-pulling snapshotters (stargz/SOCI).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull: wrong name/tag, missing pull secret, registry rate limit (Docker Hub), or arch mismatch.
  • Deploy by digest (GitOps tools can pin and update digests) so every node runs exactly the tested bytes.
  • Admission policies (Kyverno, Gatekeeper, Sigstore policy-controller) enforce: allowed registries, signed images, no :latest, non-root.
  • Registry ops: retention policies, vulnerability scanning, replication close to clusters, pull-through caches.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
docker buildx imagetools inspect nginx:alpine | head -20      # index → per-platform manifests
docker pull alpine:3.20 && docker image inspect alpine:3.20 --format '{{.RootFS.Layers}}'
docker history --no-trunc python:3.12-slim | head              # which instruction made each layer
docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock wagoodman/dive:latest nginx:alpine --ci 2>/dev/null | tail -5   # layer efficiency
docker run --rm aquasec/trivy:latest image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL python:3.12-slim 2>/dev/null | tail -15
sudo crictl images 2>/dev/null | head; sudo crictl ps 2>/dev/null | head   # on a Kubernetes node

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Do Fast rebuilds Copy dependency manifests before source; cache mounts Small image Multi-stage + distroless/scratch Same bytes everywhere Reference @sha256: digests Both amd64 and arm64 docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push Know what's inside SBOM + scanner in CI Trust the source cosign sign + verify at admission

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why does changing one line of source code rebuild npm install in a badly ordered Dockerfile?

The COPY . . comes before the install step; any source change invalidates that layer and every layer after it.

2. You RUN rm secret.key in a later step. Is the secret gone from the image?

No. It's still in the earlier layer; anyone with the image can extract it. Use build secrets.

3. What's the difference between a tag and a digest?

A tag is a movable name; a digest is a content hash that always identifies the same image bytes.

4. Which component actually calls clone() to create the container's namespaces?

runc (or another OCI runtime), started by containerd's shim on behalf of the kubelet.

5. Pods take 2 minutes to start on new nodes. Where do you look?

Image pull time: image size, registry throttling/latency, no cache on fresh nodes; use smaller images, mirrors, pre-pulling or lazy pulling.

docs.title: 9.2 — Kubernetes architecture
docs.text:
In short

Kubernetes is a database of desired state (etcd behind the API server) plus many independent controllers that watch it and make reality match. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, and the kubelet on each node starts them through the container runtime. Higher-level controllers (Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs, operators) keep creating, replacing and updating pods for you.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Control plane — Components that manage the cluster API server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager kube-apiserver — The only entry point; REST API Authn → authz (RBAC) → admission → etcd etcd — Consistent key-value store (Raft) Holds all cluster state; back it up kube-scheduler — Picks a node for each pending pod Filter (fits?) then score (best?) Controller — Reconcile loop for a resource type Watch → diff → act (9a) kubelet — Node agent Runs pods via CRI, probes, reports status Pod — Smallest unit: one or more containers sharing net/IPC Has its own IP Deployment / ReplicaSet — Stateless replicas with rolling updates ReplicaSet per version StatefulSet — Stable names + storage per replica Databases, Kafka DaemonSet / Job / CronJob — One pod per node / run to completion / scheduled Agents, batch, periodic tasks Requests / limits — Scheduling reservation / hard cap CPU throttles, memory OOMs (3.2, 3.3) QoS class Quality of Service Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort Eviction order under node pressure Taints / tolerations, affinity — Keep pods off / attract pods to nodes Dedicated nodes, spreading CRD / operator Custom Resource Definition Extend the API / controller for an app kind: PostgresCluster managed automatically Admission webhook — Validate or mutate objects on create/update Policies (Kyverno), sidecar injection

docs.title: 1 · The declarative model
docs.text:
You don't tell Kubernetes what to do, you tell it what you want (replicas: 3, image, resources). Controllers continuously compare spec (desired) with status (actual) and act (9a diagram). Consequences:

  • Delete a pod of a Deployment → a new one appears. Edit a pod by hand → it may be replaced.
  • Everything is eventually consistent: kubectl apply returns immediately; the system converges over seconds.
  • Components never call each other; they watch the API server. That's why the API server and etcd health are critical.

docs.title: 2 · What happens after kubectl apply
docs.text:
1. API server: authenticates you, checks RBAC, runs admission (defaults, policies, mutating webhooks), validates and stores the Deployment in etcd.
  2. Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates 3 Pods (status Pending, no node).
  3. Scheduler filters nodes (enough requested CPU/memory? taints tolerated? affinity? volume zone?), scores the rest (spread, bin-packing), and binds each pod to a node.
  4. kubelet on that node sees the pod: pulls the image, creates the sandbox, CNI assigns an IP, mounts volumes, starts containers (9.1).
  5. Probes: startup → readiness → pod becomes Ready and is added to Service EndpointSlices; traffic starts (7.1).

docs.title: 3 · Scheduling and resources
docs.text:
• The scheduler only looks at requests, not actual usage. Requests too low → overpacked nodes, throttling/OOM; too high → wasted money.
  • Taints/tolerations: keep general pods off special nodes (GPU, spot). Node affinity: require/prefer certain nodes. Pod (anti-)affinity and topology spread constraints: spread replicas across nodes and zones.
  • QoS: Guaranteed (requests = limits for all), Burstable, BestEffort (none). Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first.
  • PriorityClasses + preemption let critical pods evict less important ones.
  • Autoscaling: HPA (replicas by metrics), VPA (right-size requests), Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter (add/remove nodes).

docs.title: 4 · Extending Kubernetes: CRDs and operators
docs.text: A CRD adds a new resource type (Certificate, KafkaTopic, PostgresCluster); an operator is a controller that reconciles it, encoding operational knowledge (backups, failover, upgrades). Most of the ecosystem — cert-manager, Argo CD, Strimzi, CloudNativePG, KServe — is built this way.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Troubleshooting order: kubectl get pod (status) → describe (events) → logs --previous → node and cluster events.
  • Protect the control plane: etcd backups, API rate limits (APF), avoid controllers or CI jobs that list everything every second.
  • Upgrades: control plane first, then nodes; respect version skew; use PodDisruptionBudgets so drains don't take down all replicas.
  • Multi-tenancy: namespaces + RBAC + ResourceQuotas + LimitRanges + NetworkPolicies + Pod Security Admission.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# A local cluster
kind create cluster --name lab 2>/dev/null || true
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system                      # control plane as pods (kind/kubeadm)
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -15   # the whole chain from section 2
kubectl get rs,pods -l app=web -o wide
kubectl delete pod -l app=web --wait=false; kubectl get pods -l app=web -w   # reconciliation (Ctrl+C)
kubectl api-resources | head -20; kubectl get crd 2>/dev/null | head
kubectl auth can-i create deployments --as=system:serviceaccount:default:default
kind delete cluster --name lab

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Pod status Usually means Pending Can't schedule: resources, taints, affinity, PVC zone ContainerCreating Image pull, volume mount, CNI ImagePullBackOff Name/tag/credentials/rate limit CrashLoopBackOff App exits; check logs --previous OOMKilled Memory limit hit Running but not Ready Readiness probe failing Evicted Node pressure (disk/memory)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Which component writes to etcd?

Only the API server; everything else reads and writes through it.

2. A pod stays Pending forever. What do you check?

kubectl describe pod events: insufficient CPU/memory requests, untolerated taints, unsatisfiable affinity, unbound PVC or zone mismatch.

3. Why did a pod you deleted come back?

Its ReplicaSet controller saw fewer pods than desired and created a replacement.

4. What does the scheduler use to decide if a pod fits: requests or actual usage?

Requests.

5. What's an operator?

A controller plus CRDs that automate running a specific application (create, scale, backup, upgrade, failover) the way a human operator would.

docs.title: 9.3 — Kubernetes networking
docs.text:
In short

Kubernetes asks for a simple model: every pod has its own IP and can reach every other pod without NAT. A CNI plugin does the plumbing. Services give groups of pods a stable virtual IP and DNS name, and Gateway API / Ingress bring external HTTP traffic in. NetworkPolicies decide who may talk to whom, and a service mesh can add mTLS, retries and telemetry.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CNI Container Network Interface Plugin API for pod networking Called by the runtime when a pod starts Pod CIDR — IP range for pods (per node) e.g. 10.244.3.0/24 on node 3 Overlay — Pod traffic wrapped in node-to-node tunnels VXLAN / Geneve / IPIP Native routing — Pod IPs routed directly (no tunnel) BGP (Calico), cloud routes, VPC CNI eBPF dataplane — Kernel programs for forwarding and policy Cilium; can replace kube-proxy Service (ClusterIP) — Stable virtual IP + port for pods DNAT to an endpoint (5.3) EndpointSlice — List of ready pod IPs behind a Service Updated by readiness NodePort / LoadBalancer — Expose a Service on node ports / via a cloud LB For external access Headless Service — clusterIP: None DNS returns pod IPs directly CoreDNS — Cluster DNS svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local (6.2) Ingress / Gateway API — L7 entry into the cluster Gateway + HTTPRoute is the modern API NetworkPolicy — Pod-level firewall rules Label selectors, enforced by CNI Service mesh — Proxies (sidecar or node/ambient) for service-to-service traffic mTLS, retries, traffic splitting, metrics

docs.title: How does a pod get on the network?
docs.text:
1. kubelet asks the runtime to create the pod sandbox (its own network namespace, 3.5).
  2. The runtime calls the CNI plugin: create a veth pair (one end eth0 in the pod, the other in the host), assign an IP from the node's pod CIDR (IPAM), add routes.
  3. Across nodes, the CNI makes pod IPs reachable: routes (Calico BGP, cloud route tables), cloud-native IPs (AWS VPC CNI gives pods VPC IPs), or an overlay tunnel (Flannel VXLAN, Calico/Cilium in tunnel mode).
CNI Approach Notable Cilium eBPF, routing or overlay kube-proxy replacement, L7 policy, Hubble observability, mesh Calico BGP routing / overlay, iptables or eBPF Mature NetworkPolicy, on-prem friendly AWS VPC CNI / Azure CNI / GKE dataplane Pods get cloud IPs Direct LB targeting, watch IP exhaustion Flannel Simple VXLAN overlay No NetworkPolicy by itself

docs.title: 2 · Services and DNS
docs.text:
• A Service selects pods by labels; EndpointSlices list the ready ones.
  • ClusterIP is virtual: kube-proxy (iptables/IPVS/nftables) or an eBPF dataplane rewrites 10.96.12.7:80 → a pod IP (5.3). Load balancing is per connection.
  • DNS: orders (same namespace), orders.shop, orders.shop.svc.cluster.local → ClusterIP; headless Services return pod IPs (StatefulSets: kafka-0.kafka.shop.svc…).
  • externalTrafficPolicy: Local keeps the client IP for NodePort/LB traffic; internalTrafficPolicy / topology-aware routing keep traffic in the same node/zone to save latency and cross-AZ cost.

docs.title: 3 · Getting traffic in: Ingress and Gateway API
docs.text:
Ingress Gateway API Resources Ingress (+ controller-specific annotations) GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, TLSRoute… Roles One object for everything Infra team owns Gateways; app teams own Routes Features Host/path routing, TLS + header matching, weighted traffic splitting, cross-namespace refs, portable across implementations Status Frozen; community ingress-nginx retired (2026) The recommended standard

Implementations: Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, Kong, cloud controllers (GKE, AWS LB Controller).

docs.title: 4 · NetworkPolicies and meshes
docs.text:
• NetworkPolicy: once a policy selects a pod for ingress/egress, everything not allowed is denied. Start with default-deny per namespace, then allow: DNS egress (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-dns), app-to-app flows, egress to specific CIDRs. Cilium/Calico add L7 and FQDN policies.
  • Service mesh (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium mesh): automatic mTLS between workloads (6.4), retries/timeouts/circuit breaking, traffic splitting, golden metrics per call. Sidecar mode (proxy per pod) vs ambient/node mode (shared node proxy + optional L7 waypoints) trade isolation against resource cost.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Debug in layers: DNS → Service → EndpointSlice (any ready pods?) → pod IP directly → NetworkPolicy → node routing/CNI → MTU (5.1).
  • Service with no endpoints = selector doesn't match labels, or pods not Ready.
  • Cross-AZ traffic is a hidden cost; use topology-aware routing for chatty services.
  • Observability: Hubble (Cilium), mesh dashboards, or flow logs show who talks to whom and what was dropped.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kubectl create deployment echo --image=hashicorp/http-echo -- /http-echo -text=hello -listen=:8080
kubectl expose deployment echo --port 80 --target-port 8080
kubectl get svc echo; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=echo -o wide
kubectl run -it --rm net --image=nicolaka/netshoot --restart=Never -- bash -c '
  cat /etc/resolv.conf; dig +short echo.default.svc.cluster.local;
  curl -s echo; ip addr show eth0 | grep inet; ip route'

# Default-deny then watch it fail
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny }
spec: { podSelector: {}, policyTypes: [Ingress] }
EOF
kubectl run -it --rm t --image=curlimages/curl --restart=Never -- curl -s -m 3 echo || echo "blocked (if your CNI enforces policies)"
kubectl delete networkpolicy default-deny; kubectl delete deploy,svc echo

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Check could not resolve host CoreDNS pods, NetworkPolicy blocking DNS, ndots (6.2) Service times out EndpointSlice empty? readiness? targetPort? Works pod→pod same node, not cross-node CNI routes/overlay, security groups, MTU Client IP is a node IP externalTrafficPolicy: Local / proxy protocol 502 from Gateway Backend Service/port, readiness, timeouts Random drops at scale conntrack table, SNAT ports (5.3)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What are the three rules of the Kubernetes network model?

Every pod gets its own IP; pods can reach all other pods without NAT; agents on a node can reach all pods on that node.

2. What does the CNI plugin do when a pod starts?

Creates the pod's interface (veth), assigns an IP, sets routes, and makes the IP reachable from other nodes.

3. A Service exists but curl to it times out. First thing to check?

Its EndpointSlice: if empty, the selector doesn't match or no pods are Ready.

4. Why prefer Gateway API over Ingress for new setups?

It's the maintained standard with richer, portable features (traffic splitting, header matching, role separation), and the community ingress-nginx controller has been retired.

5. After applying a default-deny NetworkPolicy, nothing can resolve DNS. Why?

Egress to kube-dns (port 53) is now denied too; add an explicit allow rule for DNS.

docs.title: 9.4 — CI/CD & GitOps
docs.text:
In short

CI turns every change into a tested, scanned, signed artifact (an image digest), and CD moves that artifact through environments. With GitOps, each environment's desired state lives in git. An agent inside the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) continuously pulls and reconciles it. Deployments become reviewed, auditable, reversible with git revert, and can roll out gradually with canary or blue-green.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CI Continuous Integration Build + test every change Pipeline on each push/PR CD Continuous Delivery / Deployment Always releasable / automatically released Promotion through environments Artifact — The thing you deploy Image digest, Helm chart, binary Pipeline — Ordered jobs in CI GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Tekton IaC Infrastructure as Code Infra defined in code Terraform/OpenTofu, Pulumi, Crossplane GitOps — Git = source of truth, pulled by an agent Argo CD, Flux reconcile cluster to git Drift — Live state ≠ git Detected and (optionally) auto-corrected Helm / Kustomize — Templating / overlay tools for manifests Per-environment configuration Rolling / blue-green / canary — Deployment strategies Gradual replace / switch / small % first Progressive delivery — Automated canary with metric analysis Argo Rollouts, Flagger Feature flag — Turn code paths on/off at runtime Decouple deploy from release SLSA Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts Framework for build integrity Provenance, hermetic builds DORA metrics DevOps Research and Assessment Delivery performance Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, recovery time

docs.title: A good pipeline
docs.text:
1. Fast feedback first: lint, unit tests, type checks (minutes).
  2. Build once: produce one image per commit, tagged with the git SHA, pushed by digest. Never rebuild for another environment.
  3. Verify: integration tests (ephemeral environments, Testcontainers), security scans (dependencies, image, IaC, secrets), SBOM generation.
  4. Sign and attest: cosign signature + build provenance (SLSA), so the cluster can verify the image came from your pipeline.
  5. Speed: cache dependencies and Docker layers, run jobs in parallel, only build what changed in monorepos.

docs.title: 2 · Delivery: pushing vs pulling
docs.text:
Push-based CD GitOps (pull) Who applies CI job runs kubectl apply/helm upgrade Agent in the cluster syncs from git Credentials CI needs cluster admin credentials Cluster only needs read access to git/registry Drift Not noticed Detected, can self-heal Audit / rollback CI logs, re-run job Git history, git revert Multi-cluster Script it ApplicationSets / Flux Kustomizations

Typical GitOps flow: app repo CI builds api@sha256:… → opens a PR (or a bot such as Argo CD Image Updater/Renovate does) to the config repo updating the digest in overlays/staging → merge → Argo CD syncs staging → tests pass → promote the same digest to production via another PR (or with a promotion tool like Kargo).

docs.title: 3 · Deployment strategies
docs.text:
Strategy How Pros Cons Recreate Stop all old, start new Simple Downtime Rolling (K8s default) Replace pods gradually (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) No extra capacity, no downtime Old and new run together; slow rollback Blue-green Run new version fully, switch traffic at once Instant switch and rollback Double capacity during switch Canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% with checks Limits blast radius Needs traffic splitting + metrics Feature flags Deploy dark, enable per user/percentage Release without deploy Flag debt, complexity

Progressive delivery: Argo Rollouts/Flagger shift traffic step by step (via Gateway API, mesh or ingress) and query Prometheus/Datadog; if error rate or latency breaches thresholds, they roll back automatically.

Database changes must be backward compatible across a rollout (expand → migrate → contract, 7.3), because old and new versions run at the same time.

docs.title: 4 · Measuring delivery: DORA
docs.text:
Metric Elite-ish target Deployment frequency On demand (many per day) Lead time for changes < 1 day from commit to production Change failure rate Low (single-digit to ~15%) Failed deployment recovery time < 1 hour

Small, frequent, reversible changes improve all four at once.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Secrets in GitOps: never plain in git; use External Secrets Operator (from Vault/cloud secret managers), Sealed Secrets or SOPS.
  • Environment config: Kustomize overlays or Helm values per environment; keep differences small and explicit.
  • Policy as code: Kyverno/Gatekeeper/Conftest in CI and at admission (signed images, resource limits, no privileged pods).
  • Pipeline security: least-privilege tokens, OIDC to cloud (no long-lived keys), pinned actions by SHA, protected branches and required reviews.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Argo CD in a kind cluster, syncing a public example app
kind create cluster --name gitops
kubectl create ns argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
kubectl -n argocd rollout status deploy/argocd-server --timeout=300s
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata: { name: guestbook, namespace: argocd }
spec:
  project: default
  source: { repoURL: https://github.com/argoproj/argocd-example-apps, path: guestbook, targetRevision: HEAD }
  destination: { server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, namespace: default }
  syncPolicy: { automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true } }
EOF
sleep 30; kubectl get applications -n argocd; kubectl get deploy
kubectl scale deploy guestbook-ui --replicas=5; sleep 20; kubectl get deploy guestbook-ui   # self-heal back to git
kind delete cluster --name gitops

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Use Same bits in every env Build once, deploy by digest, promote No cluster creds in CI GitOps pull (Argo CD / Flux) Undo a bad deploy git revert in config repo (or rollout undo) Limit blast radius Canary + automated analysis Release ≠ deploy Feature flags Secrets External Secrets / Sealed Secrets / SOPS Track improvement DORA metrics

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why 'build once, promote everywhere' instead of rebuilding per environment?

So production runs exactly the bytes that were tested; rebuilding can pull different dependencies or base images.

2. What's the main security advantage of pull-based GitOps?

CI doesn't need cluster credentials; the cluster pulls from git and only needs read access.

3. Someone runs kubectl edit in production. What does Argo CD with selfHeal do?

It detects drift from git and reverts the live object to the git state.

4. When is blue-green better than canary?

When you need an instant, all-at-once switch and instant rollback, and can afford double capacity briefly (or can't split traffic finely).

5. Why must DB migrations be backward compatible during rolling or canary deploys?

Old and new app versions run simultaneously against the same database.

docs.title: 9.5 — Observability: metrics, logs, traces & SLOs
docs.text:
In short

Observability means answering "what is wrong and why?" from the outside. Metrics tell you that something changed, traces show where in a request time or errors come from, and logs explain what exactly happened. OpenTelemetry is one standard way to produce all three. SLOs with burn-rate alerts make sure you get paged for what users actually feel.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Metric — Numeric time series with labels http_requests_total{route="/cart",code="500"} Counter / gauge / histogram — Metric types Only goes up / goes up and down / distribution in buckets Cardinality — Number of distinct label combinations High cardinality (user_id) explodes cost Log — Timestamped event record Structured (JSON) beats free text Trace / span — A request's path / one operation in it Spans share a trace id (traceparent, 6.1) Sampling — Keeping only some traces Head-based or tail-based (keep errors/slow) Profile — Where CPU/memory is spent in code Continuous profiling (Pyroscope, Parca) OTel OpenTelemetry Vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, protocol (OTLP), collector Instrument once, send anywhere Exemplar — A trace id attached to a metric sample Jump from a latency spike to an example trace RED / USE Rate, Errors, Duration / Utilization, Saturation, Errors Checklists for services / resources What to put on dashboards SLI Service Level Indicator Measured good events / total events e.g. % requests < 300 ms and not 5xx SLO Service Level Objective Target for an SLI over a window 99.9% over 30 days Error budget — Allowed unreliability = 1 − SLO 0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43 minutes Burn rate — How fast the budget is being consumed Alert when burning 14× faster than allowed

docs.title: 1 · The signals and when to use each
docs.text:
Signal Answers Cost Example Metrics Is something wrong? Trends, alerts Low (aggregated) p99 latency of /checkout jumped Traces Where in the call chain? Medium (sampled) 900 ms of 1 s spent in inventory → postgres Logs What exactly happened? High (volume) deadlock detected on table orders Profiles Which code uses the CPU/memory? Low–medium 40% CPU in JSON serialization

Connect them: put trace ids in logs, use exemplars on metrics, and the same resource labels (service.name, k8s.pod.name, deployment.environment) everywhere.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. SDKs / auto-instrumentation (Java agent, Python, Node, .NET, Go, eBPF-based) create spans for incoming/outgoing HTTP, gRPC, DB calls, and record metrics and logs, propagating traceparent across services.
  2. Apps export via OTLP to an OpenTelemetry Collector: usually an agent per node (DaemonSet) plus a central gateway.
  3. The collector processes: batching, memory limits, adding Kubernetes metadata, dropping or redacting sensitive attributes, tail sampling (keep all errors and slow traces, 5% of the rest).
  4. It exports to backends: Prometheus/Mimir (metrics), Loki/OpenSearch (logs), Tempo/Jaeger (traces), or a vendor (Datadog, Grafana Cloud, New Relic, Honeycomb…). Switching backends is a config change, not re-instrumentation.

docs.title: 3 · Metrics with Prometheus
docs.text:
• Prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints (or receives OTLP / remote write) and stores time series.
  • RED per service: rate(http_requests_total[5m]), error ratio, histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])).
  • USE per resource: CPU utilization, run-queue/throttling (saturation), errors; same for memory, disk, network.
  • Kubernetes: cAdvisor (container usage), kube-state-metrics (object state: restarts, desired vs available replicas), node-exporter (host).
  • Cardinality is the #1 cost/performance problem: never put user IDs, request IDs or raw URLs in labels.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Choose an SLI users feel: "fraction of /checkout requests that succeed and take < 500 ms".
  2. Set an SLO: 99.9% over 30 days → error budget = 0.1% ≈ 43 minutes of full outage (or many small bad periods).
  3. Alert on burn rate, with multiple windows: page if the last 1 h and 5 min burn > 14.4× (2% of the monthly budget gone in an hour); ticket if 6 h burn > 6×. This catches fast outages quickly and slow degradations without noisy alerts.
  4. Use the budget: plenty left → ship faster; exhausted → focus on reliability.

Alert on symptoms (SLO burn, user-facing errors), not on every cause (CPU 80%); causes go on dashboards for investigation. Every page should be actionable and link to a runbook.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Standardize service names, labels and log format across teams (OTel semantic conventions); provide auto-instrumentation via the OTel Operator so teams get traces without code changes.
  • Control cost: sample traces, drop debug logs at the collector, cap cardinality, set retention per signal.
  • On-call hygiene: few, high-quality alerts; postmortems that are blameless and produce fixes; track MTTR (DORA, 9.4).
  • Correlate deploys: annotate dashboards with releases (9.4); most incidents start with a change.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Grafana's all-in-one OTel stack: OTLP in, Grafana + Prometheus + Loki + Tempo out (UI on :3000)
docker run -d --rm --name lgtm -p 3000:3000 -p 4317:4317 -p 4318:4318 grafana/otel-lgtm

# Send a test span over OTLP/HTTP
NOW=$(date +%s%N); TID=$(openssl rand -hex 16); SID=$(openssl rand -hex 8)
curl -s -X POST localhost:4318/v1/traces -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"resourceSpans\":[{\"resource\":{\"attributes\":[{\"key\":\"service.name\",\"value\":{\"stringValue\":\"demo\"}}]},\"scopeSpans\":[{\"spans\":[{\"traceId\":\"$TID\",\"spanId\":\"$SID\",\"name\":\"checkout\",\"kind\":2,\"startTimeUnixNano\":\"$NOW\",\"endTimeUnixNano\":\"$((NOW+250000000))\"}]}]}]}"
echo "open http://localhost:3000 → Explore → Tempo → search service.name=demo"

# PromQL to try in Explore → Prometheus
#   rate(prometheus_http_requests_total[5m])
#   histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(prometheus_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
docker stop lgtm

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Question Signal / query Are users affected? SLO burn rate, error ratio, p99 latency Which service is slow? Trace waterfall, service graph Why did this request fail? Logs filtered by trace id Which code burns CPU? Continuous profiling Is the node/pod saturated? USE: CPU throttling, memory, PSI, network What changed? Deploy annotations, git history

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why shouldn't you use user_id as a Prometheus label?

Each distinct value creates a new time series; millions of users = millions of series, exploding memory, storage and query cost.

2. What's the difference between an SLI and an SLO?

The SLI is the measurement (ratio of good events); the SLO is the target for it over a time window.

3. Your SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. How much full downtime does the error budget allow?

0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43.2 minutes.

4. Why alert on burn rate instead of 'error rate > 1% for 5 minutes'?

Burn rate ties alerts to the budget and user impact: fast burns page quickly, slow burns open tickets, and brief harmless blips don't wake anyone.

5. What does tail-based sampling give you that head-based sampling doesn't?

The decision is made after the trace completes, so you can keep all errors and slow traces while dropping most normal ones.

docs.title: Chapter 10 — AI infrastructure
docs.text:
In short

An LLM is a huge file of weights plus code that does matrix multiplications. To answer a prompt, you may add relevant documents (RAG) and process the prompt in one parallel step (prefill). Then the answer is generated one token at a time (decode). Each step reads all the weights and a growing KV cache from the GPU's HBM memory. An inference server batches many users together to keep the very expensive GPU busy. Everything from Chapters 1–9 is still underneath.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text:
Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) LLM Large Language Model Neural network that generates text Predicts the next token, appends it, repeats GPU Graphics Processing Unit Massively parallel processor Thousands of lanes + Tensor Cores doing matrix math HBM High Bandwidth Memory The GPU's own memory Holds weights and KV cache, read at TB/s Prefill / decode — The two phases of generation Whole prompt at once / one token per step KV cache Key-Value cache Saved attention state of past tokens Avoids recomputation, grows with context × users TTFT / TPOT Time To First Token / Time Per Output Token Latency metrics Queue + prefill / one decode step RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation Answering with your documents Embed → vector search → put chunks in the prompt CUDA / NCCL Compute Unified Device Architecture / NVIDIA Collective Communications Library GPU programming platform / multi-GPU communication Kernels on the GPU / all-reduce over NVLink & IB

The full A–Z list is in the 📖 AI glossary.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: longer context, collapsing throughput
docs.text:
The alarm

To support long documents, the team raises --max-model-len of a vLLM deployment from 8k to 128k tokens. Throughput drops by 70%, latency explodes and logs fill with preempted sequences, although GPU memory isn't fuller than before.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

vLLM's startup log: the number of KV-cache blocks is unchanged, but maximum concurrency for 131072 tokens per request dropped to ~1.5×.

🔍 Clue 2

Most requests are still short, but a few long ones grab huge parts of the KV cache, and the scheduler preempts and recomputes others to make room.

🎯 Root cause

GPU memory after the weights is the KV cache. It's per token (~128 KB/token for an 8B model in FP16), so a few very long sequences consume what dozens of normal ones would use, and batching collapses.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Route long-context requests to a separate pool, set --max-num-seqs/--max-num-batched-tokens deliberately, use FP8 KV cache and prefix caching, or use a larger/more GPUs (tensor parallel). Lesson: in LLM serving, capacity planning means KV-cache planning.
