docs.text: Page What you'll learn 10.1 AI fundamentals What an LLM is, tokens, embeddings, attention, MoE, the model lifecycle 10.2 GPU hardware Inside a GPU, HBM and the roofline, number formats, NVLink, scale-up vs scale-out 10.3 Software stack CUDA, cuBLAS/cuDNN/NCCL, drivers, containers, MIG/MPS, DCGM 10.4 Distributed training Parallelism, all-reduce, clusters, checkpoints, gang scheduling 10.5 Inference & serving KV cache paging, continuous batching, quantization, speculative decoding, P/D disaggregation 10.6 AI platform on Kubernetes GPU Operator, DRA, Kueue, JobSet/LWS, inference gateway, autoscaling, cost 10.7 Applications RAG, vector DBs, agents, MCP, AI gateways, guardrails, evals

docs.title: 1 · Why GPUs?
docs.text:
CPU (Chapter 2) GPU Cores Tens of big, smart cores (branch prediction, out-of-order) Thousands of small, simple lanes grouped in SMs (streaming multiprocessors) Good at Complex, branchy, sequential logic The same math on huge arrays in parallel Special units Vector instructions (AVX) Tensor Cores: dedicated matrix-multiply units for FP16/BF16/FP8 Memory DDR RAM, ~100 GB/s range HBM stacked on the package, several TB/s

A transformer layer is mostly big matrix multiplications, which is exactly what a GPU is built for.

docs.title: 2 · What happens to one prompt
docs.text:
"Why is the sky blue?" → tokenizer → [10445, 374, 279, 13180, 6437, 30] → embeddings
→ N transformer layers (attention + MLP) → probabilities for the next token → sample "The"
→ append, run again → "sky" → … until <end> or max tokens
Phase What it does Bottleneck User-visible metric Prefill Processes all prompt tokens at once, in parallel Compute (tensor cores) TTFT: time to first token Decode Generates one token per step, each step depending on the previous one Memory bandwidth: all weights are read for every step TPOT / ITL: time per output token

Tokens are streamed back to the client as they're generated (Server-Sent Events over HTTP, Chapter 6).

docs.title: 3 · The memory math
docs.text:
The first question for any model: does it fit?

weights ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter
  FP16/BF16 = 2 bytes · FP8/INT8 = 1 byte · INT4 = 0.5 bytes

  7B  × 2 B =  ~14 GB   → fits one 24 GB GPU
  70B × 2 B = ~140 GB   → does NOT fit one 80 GB GPU → quantize (FP8 ≈ 70 GB, INT4 ≈ 35 GB) or split across GPUs

On top of the weights comes the KV cache: for every token in every active request, each layer stores its attention keys and values so they don't have to be recomputed. It grows with context length × number of concurrent requests and is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

Chapter 3 connection: vLLM's PagedAttention manages the KV cache in fixed-size blocks, like the OS manages memory in pages. That avoids fragmentation and lets many more requests share the GPU.

docs.title: 4 · The inference server
docs.text:
Feature Why Continuous batching Instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, new requests join and finished ones leave at every decode step. GPU utilization goes way up. KV cache management Paging, prefix caching (reuse the cache for a shared system prompt), eviction. Quantization FP8/INT4 weights: less memory, more bandwidth per token, small quality cost. Parallelism Tensor parallel: split each layer across GPUs in one node (needs fast NVLink). Pipeline parallel: different layers on different GPUs/nodes. Across nodes you need InfiniBand/RoCE. OpenAI-compatible API /v1/chat/completions, so clients and gateways work unchanged.

Common engines: vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, plus Triton Inference Server for general models. Ollama / llama.cpp for laptops and CPUs.

docs.title: 5 · The software stack: Chapters 3–4 again
docs.text:
Your app → inference engine (Python) → PyTorch → CUDA libraries (cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL)
        → CUDA runtime (user space .so) → ioctl() syscalls → nvidia.ko kernel driver (ring 0) → GPU
  • CUDA kernels are small programs that run on thousands of GPU lanes at once. Libraries ship heavily optimized ones (matrix multiply, attention).
  • NCCL handles GPU-to-GPU communication (all-reduce, all-gather) over NVLink or the network.
  • The user-space CUDA libraries and the kernel driver must be version-compatible. That's a classic source of "works on one node, not the other".

docs.title: 6 · RAG: giving the model your documents
docs.text: Step When What Index Offline Split documents into chunks → an embedding model turns each chunk into a vector → store in a vector DB (pgvector, Qdrant, Milvus…) with an ANN index (e.g. HNSW). Retrieve Per request Embed the question → find the top-k most similar chunks (cosine similarity). Generate Per request Put those chunks into the prompt as context → the LLM answers using them.

docs.title: 7 · On Kubernetes (Chapter 9)
docs.text:
Piece Job NVIDIA GPU Operator Installs and manages the driver, container toolkit, device plugin and DCGM exporter on GPU nodes. Device plugin Advertises nvidia.com/gpu as a schedulable resource. Pods request it: resources.limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1. GPU node pools Separate, tainted nodes so only GPU workloads land there. Sharing MIG (hardware partitions on supported GPUs) or time-slicing for small models. Autoscaling Scale on queue length, KV cache usage or tokens/s, not CPU. Model loading (tens of GB) makes cold starts slow, so cache weights on the node.

Metrics that matter: TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s, request queue length, KV cache utilization, GPU utilization and memory (DCGM), and cost per million tokens.

docs.title: 8 · Training vs inference (briefly)
docs.text: Training also stores gradients and optimizer states (several times the weight memory), runs on many GPUs at once (data/tensor/pipeline parallel), synchronizes with NCCL all-reduce over very fast networks, and writes large checkpoints to storage. Inference is the part most platform teams operate day to day.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
🧪 Ready-made lab

Run this chapter's experiments with one command: ./labs/run.sh 10-ai (scripts). No setup? Open in Codespaces. 

# 1) No GPU needed: run a small model locally (Ollama)
ollama run llama3.2:1b "Explain the KV cache in one sentence"
curl -s http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"llama3.2:1b","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}],"stream":false}'

# 2) With an NVIDIA GPU: look at it, then serve a model with vLLM
nvidia-smi                                   # GPUs, memory, utilization, driver/CUDA version
pip install vllm
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct        # OpenAI-compatible server on :8000
curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hi"}]}'

# 3) The memory math in Python
python3 -c "
for p in (7, 13, 70):
    print(f'{p}B: FP16 {p*2} GB · FP8 {p} GB · INT4 {p/2:.0f} GB')"

Exercise: in the vLLM logs, find how much GPU memory went to the weights and how many KV cache blocks it could allocate with the rest. Send 20 requests in parallel and watch throughput (tokens/s) vs. latency per request.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Prompt → tokens → PREFILL (all at once, compute-bound → TTFT)
       → DECODE (1 token/step, reads all weights, bandwidth-bound → TPOT) → stream tokens (SSE)
Memory: weights (params × bytes) + KV cache (context × concurrency) must fit in HBM
Too big? quantize (FP8/INT4) or shard (tensor parallel over NVLink, nodes over InfiniBand)
Server: continuous batching · PagedAttention (KV in pages) · prefix caching · OpenAI API
Stack: app → engine → PyTorch → cuBLAS/cuDNN/NCCL → CUDA runtime → nvidia.ko → GPU
RAG: chunk → embed → vector DB → top-k → into the prompt
K8s: GPU Operator · nvidia.com/gpu · tainted GPU pools · scale on queue/KV, not CPU

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is decoding usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute?

Each decode step produces one token per request, but it still has to read all model weights (and the KV cache) from HBM. There's little math per byte read, so the GPU waits for memory. Batching many requests together reuses each weight read for more tokens.

2. Can a 70B model in FP16 run on a single 80 GB GPU?

No. The weights alone are ~140 GB. Options: quantize (FP8 ≈ 70 GB, still tight with KV cache; INT4 ≈ 35 GB) or split the model across several GPUs with tensor parallelism.

3. What is the KV cache, and why does it limit concurrency?

It stores the attention keys and values of all previous tokens of each active request so they aren't recomputed every step. It grows with context length and the number of concurrent requests, and it has to fit in GPU memory next to the weights.

4. Why scale an LLM service on queue length or KV cache usage instead of CPU?

The work happens on the GPU. CPU usage stays low even when the GPU is saturated and requests are queuing, so CPU-based autoscaling would never react.

5. In RAG, what does the embedding model do, and what does the vector DB do?

The embedding model turns text (chunks and questions) into vectors that capture meaning. The vector DB stores the chunk vectors and quickly finds the ones closest to the question's vector, which are then added to the prompt.

docs.title: 10.1 — AI fundamentals for infra people
docs.text:
In short

A model is a function made of billions of numbers (parameters). An LLM turns text into tokens, tokens into vectors, pushes them through a stack of transformer layers (attention + MLP), gets a score for every possible next token, picks one, appends it and runs again. Everything in AI infrastructure exists to store those numbers, move them fast and do that math cheaply.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) AI Artificial Intelligence Software that performs tasks that normally need human intelligence Today mostly means machine-learned models ML Machine Learning Programs that learn behaviour from data instead of hand-written rules Adjust numbers (parameters) until outputs match examples NN Neural Network A model made of layers of simple math units Each layer multiplies inputs by weights and applies a non-linearity LLM Large Language Model A huge neural network trained on text to continue text Predicts the next token, appends it, repeats GPT Generative Pre-trained Transformer The family name of decoder-only transformer LLMs Pre-trained on text, then generates token by token Token — A piece of text (word, part of word, symbol) The unit the model reads and writes BPE Byte-Pair Encoding The usual tokenizer algorithm Repeatedly merges the most frequent character pairs into tokens Embedding — A vector of numbers that represents a token or text Similar meanings → nearby vectors Parameter / weight — One learned number inside the model Billions of them = the model's "knowledge" Transformer — The neural-network architecture behind modern LLMs Stacks of attention + MLP layers Attention — The mechanism that lets a token look at other tokens Query·Key scores decide how much of each Value to mix in Q / K / V Query / Key / Value Three vectors computed for every token Q asks, K is matched against Q, V is the content passed along RoPE Rotary Position Embedding How position (word order) is encoded Rotates Q and K by an angle that depends on the position MLP / FFN Multi-Layer Perceptron / Feed-Forward Network The per-token neural network inside each layer Expands, applies a non-linearity, projects back MoE Mixture of Experts An MLP split into many experts plus a router Only the top-k experts run for each token Logits — Raw scores for every possible next token Softmax turns them into probabilities Context window — Max tokens the model can handle at once Prompt + output must fit SFT Supervised Fine-Tuning Training on example prompt → answer pairs Teaches the model to follow instructions RLHF Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback Training on human preferences A reward model scores answers, the LLM is tuned to maximize it DPO Direct Preference Optimization Simpler preference training Learns directly from "A is better than B" pairs LoRA / QLoRA Low-Rank Adaptation / Quantized LoRA Cheap fine-tuning Trains small adapter matrices next to frozen weights (QLoRA: base in 4-bit) VLM Vision-Language Model A model that reads images and text Image encoder output is fed in as extra tokens ASR / TTS Automatic Speech Recognition / Text-to-Speech Speech → text / text → speech Audio models, usually streaming KV cache Key-Value cache Stored K and V of past tokens Avoids recomputing them at every step (10.5)

docs.title: 0 · What is an LLM, and how does it work?
What is it?
docs.text: An LLM (Large Language Model) is a neural network with billions of parameters that has learned, from a huge amount of text, how text usually continues. It doesn't search a database. It predicts.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Training (once): show it trillions of tokens. At every position it guesses the next token, compares the guess with the real one, and nudges its parameters a tiny bit. Repeat billions of times. The result is a weights file.
  2. Inference (every request): load the weights into GPU memory. Turn your prompt into tokens, run them through the network, get the most likely next token.
  3. Loop: append that token to the input and run again, one token at a time, until a stop token or the length limit.

docs.title: 1 · What is a "model", physically?
docs.text: Thing What it is Infra meaning Parameters / weights Billions of numbers learned during training Size on disk and in GPU memory. 8B params × 2 bytes = ~16 GB Architecture The code that says how the numbers are used (layers, sizes) config.json: number of layers, hidden size, heads, vocab size, context length Weights file *.safetensors (Hugging Face), *.gguf (llama.cpp/Ollama) Downloaded from a model hub or object storage, often tens to hundreds of GB Tokenizer Rules for splitting text into tokens tokenizer.json, ships with the model Model card / license Intended use, limits, license Can you legally run it commercially?

docs.title: 2 · Tokens: the unit of everything
docs.text:
• The tokenizer (usually BPE: byte-pair encoding) splits text into frequent pieces: "unbelievable" → ["un", "believ", "able"].
  • Each piece maps to an integer ID in a fixed vocabulary (tens of thousands to ~200k entries).
  • Rule of thumb for English: 1 token ≈ 4 characters ≈ ¾ of a word. Turkish is agglutinative and usually needs more tokens per word.
  • Context window = how many tokens (prompt + answer) the model can handle at once: from 8k to 1M+ tokens.
  • Everything is priced and measured in tokens: API pricing, throughput (tokens/s), latency per token, KV cache size.

docs.title: 3 · Embeddings: meaning as coordinates
docs.text: Each token ID is looked up in an embedding table and becomes a vector (e.g. 4,096 numbers). Training arranges these vectors so that things with similar meaning end up close together. The same idea, applied to whole sentences by a separate embedding model, powers semantic search and RAG (10.7).

docs.title: 4 · The transformer, layer by layer
docs.text: Part What it does Plain-language version Positional encoding (e.g. RoPE) Adds word-order information "This token is the 5th one" Self-attention Each token computes a query (Q), a key (K) and a value (V). Q·K scores decide how much of each other token's V to mix in "Which earlier words matter for understanding this one?" Multi-head attention Several attention "heads" in parallel, each learning different relationships Grammar, references, topic… MLP / feed-forward A big per-token neural network, about ⅔ of all parameters Where most "knowledge" is stored Residual + normalization Keeps signals stable through many layers Plumbing × N layers The block repeats 30–100+ times Deeper = more capable, more compute

docs.title: How does attention work?
docs.text:
1. Every token computes three vectors: a Query ("what am I looking for?"), a Key ("what do I contain?") and a Value ("what do I pass on?").
  2. The current token's Query is compared with the Key of every earlier token (a dot product) → one score per token.
  3. Softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1.
  4. The token's new representation is the weighted sum of the Values. In the example below, "it" ends up carrying mostly the meaning of "the cat".

Modern LLMs are decoder-only: each token can only attend to tokens before it. That's what makes generation one token at a time possible, and why keys and values of past tokens can be cached (the KV cache, 10.5).

Mixture of Experts (MoE): the MLP is split into many "experts" and a small router sends each token to only a few of them. The model has many total parameters (all must sit in memory) but only a fraction are active per token (less compute). Infra consequence: memory sized for total, compute sized for active.

docs.title: 5 · From scores to text: sampling
docs.text:
The last layer produces a logit (score) for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax turns them into probabilities, then:

Setting Effect Greedy (temperature 0) Always take the most likely token: deterministic, can be repetitive Temperature < 1 sharper and safer, > 1 more random and creative Top-p / top-k Only sample from the most likely few tokens Max tokens / stop sequences When to stop generating

docs.title: 6 · The model lifecycle
docs.text: Stage What happens Compute profile Pre-training Learn to predict the next token on trillions of tokens of text Thousands of GPUs for weeks to months (10.4) Post-training Instruction tuning (SFT), preference tuning (RLHF, DPO), reinforcement learning for reasoning Large, but much smaller than pre-training Fine-tuning Adapt to your domain. LoRA / QLoRA train small adapter matrices instead of all weights One to a few GPUs Distillation / quantization Make a smaller or lower-precision version that's cheaper to run Offline jobs Inference Serve the model to users 24/7, latency-sensitive, where most money is spent over time (10.5)

docs.title: 7 · Model types you'll meet
docs.text: Type Input → output Typical infra LLM (decoder) text → text Big GPUs, KV cache, streaming Embedding model (encoder) text → vector Small, high-throughput, batchable Reranker (query, document) → relevance score Small, used in RAG Multimodal / VLM image + text → text LLM + vision encoder Diffusion text → image/video GPU-heavy per request, no KV cache Speech audio ↔ text (ASR / TTS) Streaming, real-time

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
for s in ["The weather is very nice today.", "Bugün hava çok güzel."]:
    ids = enc.encode(s)
    print(len(ids), "tokens:", [enc.decode([i]) for i in ids])
EOF

# 2) Read a model's architecture without downloading the weights

  python3 -c "import json,sys; c=json.load(sys.stdin); print({k:c[k] for k in ['num_hidden_layers','hidden_size','num_attention_heads','num_key_value_heads','vocab_size','max_position_embeddings']})"

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Model = architecture (config.json) + weights (safetensors/gguf) + tokenizer
Text → tokens (BPE, ~4 chars each in English) → IDs → embeddings (vectors)
→ N × [ self-attention (Q,K,V: what matters?) + MLP (knowledge, ~2/3 of params) ]
→ logits → softmax → sample (temperature, top-p) → append → repeat
Decoder-only → past K/V can be cached (KV cache)
MoE: total params in memory, only active params computed per token
Lifecycle: pre-train → post-train (SFT, RLHF/DPO) → fine-tune (LoRA) → quantize → serve

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is everything in LLM infrastructure measured in tokens?

The model processes tokens, not characters or words. Compute per request, latency per step, KV cache memory and API cost all scale with the number of input and output tokens.

2. A MoE model has 120B total parameters but only 5B active per token. What do you size memory and compute for?

Memory for all 120B (every expert must be loaded), compute for roughly 5B per token. That's why MoE models are cheap to run per token but still need lots of GPU memory.

3. Why can past keys and values be cached in a decoder-only model?

Each token only attends to earlier tokens, and earlier tokens never change once generated. So their K and V vectors stay valid and can be reused for every following step.

4. What does temperature 0 mean?

Greedy decoding: always pick the most likely next token. Output becomes deterministic (given the same inputs and setup).

5. What's the difference between fine-tuning with LoRA and full fine-tuning, from an infra point of view?

LoRA trains small adapter matrices while the base weights stay frozen, so it needs far less GPU memory and produces small files. Many LoRA adapters can even be served on top of one shared base model.

docs.title: 10.2 — GPU & accelerator hardware
docs.text:
In short

A data-center GPU is thousands of small math lanes (with special Tensor Cores for matrix math) fed by a few hundred GB of very fast HBM memory. Eight of them sit in one server, connected all-to-all with NVLink through NVSwitch (scale-up). Servers talk to each other with one NIC per GPU over InfiniBand or RoCE Ethernet (scale-out). For LLMs the limit is usually how fast bytes move, not how fast math happens.

docs.title: 1 · What is a GPU, and how does it work?
What is it?
docs.text: A CPU has a few dozen powerful cores built for complicated, sequential work. A GPU has 100+ SMs, each with many simple lanes and a few Tensor Cores, built to do the same simple math on huge arrays at the same time. Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplications, which is exactly that.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The CPU launches a kernel (a GPU function) with thousands of thread blocks.
  2. The blocks are spread across the SMs. Inside an SM, threads run in warps of 32 that execute the same instruction together (SIMT).
  3. Data flows HBM → L2 → shared memory/registers → Tensor Cores. Fast kernels reuse each byte as many times as possible once it's on-chip.
  4. Results are written back to HBM. The next kernel (next layer) starts.

docs.title: 2 · Number formats (precision)
docs.text:
Format Bytes Where it's used FP32 4 Classic training, optimizer states TF32 4 (stored), 19-bit math Tensor Core mode for "FP32" matmuls BF16 2 Default for training and serving: FP32's range, less precision FP16 2 Inference, older training FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2) 1 Training and inference on Hopper and newer FP4 (NVFP4 / MXFP4) 0.5 Inference on Blackwell and newer INT8 / INT4 1 / 0.5 Quantized weights for inference

Fewer bytes per number = more numbers per second through the same memory bus, and each step down roughly doubles Tensor Core throughput.

docs.title: 3 · Compute-bound or memory-bound? The roofline
docs.text:
Arithmetic intensity = FLOPs done per byte read from memory.

GPU "ridge point" ≈ peak FLOPS / memory bandwidth
  e.g. ~1,000 TFLOPS BF16 / ~3.35 TB/s ≈ 300 FLOPs per byte

LLM decode, batch 1: each 2-byte weight is used for ~2 FLOPs → ~1 FLOP/byte → hugely memory-bound
LLM decode, batch 64: each weight is reused 64× → ~64 FLOPs/byte → still memory-bound, much better
LLM prefill (long prompt): each weight reused for every prompt token → compute-bound

That gives a useful upper bound: max tokens/s for one stream ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes of weights. An 8B model in BF16 (16 GB) on a 3.35 TB/s GPU can't decode faster than ~200 tokens/s per stream, no matter how many FLOPS it has. Batching is how you get more total tokens/s out of the same bandwidth (10.5).

docs.title: 4 · Generations at a glance (approximate)
docs.text:
Generation Example HBM per GPU NVLink per GPU New formats Ampere A100 40/80 GB 600 GB/s TF32, BF16 Hopper H100 / H200 80 / 141 GB 900 GB/s FP8, Transformer Engine Blackwell B200 / B300, GB200/GB300 NVL72 ~180–288 GB 1.8 TB/s FP4 Rubin (2H 2026) Vera Rubin NVL72 288 GB HBM4 3.6 TB/s —

Numbers move fast. Always check the vendor datasheet for the exact SKU (SXM vs PCIe versions differ a lot).

docs.title: 5 · Scale-up vs scale-out: what's the difference?
What is it?
docs.text:
Every AI cluster has two networks:

  • Scale-up: GPUs inside one NVLink domain (8 GPUs in a server, or 72 in an NVL72 rack) talk over NVLink + NVSwitch at TB/s. They can read each other's memory almost like local memory.
  • Scale-out: everything beyond that domain goes over the network: one 400–800 Gb/s NIC per GPU, InfiniBand or RoCE Ethernet, arranged as a rail-optimized fat-tree (GPU #3 of every server is on "rail 3", and so on).

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A GPU writes data for a GPU in another server.
  2. With GPUDirect RDMA, its NIC reads it straight from HBM, no CPU copy.
  3. Leaf and spine switches forward it. The fabric is designed to be lossless and non-blocking.
  4. The remote NIC writes it straight into the remote GPU's HBM.

Rule of thumb: keep the most communication-heavy parallelism (tensor parallel) inside the scale-up domain. Use the scale-out network for less chatty parallelism (data parallel, pipeline parallel) (10.4).

docs.title: 6 · Power, cooling, and the rest of the server
docs.text:
• A modern 8-GPU server draws 10 kW or more. A rack-scale NVL72 system draws over 100 kW and is liquid-cooled. Power and cooling, not GPUs, are often the real data-center bottleneck.
  • The server also has 2 CPUs (to feed data, run the driver and the framework), PCIe switches linking GPUs, NICs and NVMe drives, and often a DPU for storage and north-south traffic.

docs.title: 7 · Not only NVIDIA
docs.text:
Vendor Chips Software AMD Instinct MI300 series and newer (large HBM) ROCm, HIP (CUDA-like), PyTorch support Google TPU generations (pods with their own interconnect) JAX, PyTorch/XLA, available on Google Cloud AWS Trainium (training) / Inferentia (inference) Neuron SDK Intel Gaudi SynapseAI / PyTorch

DevOps connection: hardware choice decides your software stack (CUDA vs ROCm vs XLA vs Neuron), your Kubernetes device plugins/DRA drivers, and your capacity planning (power, cooling, network) — not just your benchmark numbers.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself (on a machine with an NVIDIA GPU)
docs.text:
nvidia-smi                                  # GPUs, memory used, utilization, power, driver/CUDA version
nvidia-smi topo -m                          # how GPUs, NICs and CPUs are connected (NV#, PIX, SYS…)
nvidia-smi nvlink --status 2>/dev/null      # NVLink links and speeds
nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,CLOCK,POWER | less
lspci | grep -iE "nvidia|mellanox"          # GPUs and NICs on the PCIe bus
ibv_devinfo 2>/dev/null | head              # RDMA-capable NICs (InfiniBand / RoCE)

# Measure matmul TFLOPS and memory bandwidth with PyTorch
python3 - <<'EOF'
import torch, time
x = torch.randn(8192, 8192, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.time()
for _ in range(50): y = x @ x
torch.cuda.synchronize(); dt = time.time() - t
print(f"matmul: {50 * 2 * 8192**3 / dt / 1e12:.0f} TFLOPS")
a = torch.empty(2 * 1024**3, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda")
torch.cuda.synchronize(); t = time.time()
for _ in range(20): b = a.clone()
torch.cuda.synchronize(); dt = time.time() - t
print(f"copy bandwidth: {20 * 2 * a.numel() / dt / 1e12:.2f} TB/s")
EOF

Exercise: divide the measured bandwidth by the size of an 8B BF16 model (16 GB). That's the theoretical max tokens/s for a single stream on this GPU.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
GPU = 100+ SMs × (CUDA cores + Tensor Cores) + HBM (80–288 GB, TB/s)
Work: kernel → thread blocks → warps of 32 (SIMT) · data: HBM → L2 → shared mem → Tensor Cores
Formats: FP32 4B · BF16/FP16 2B · FP8 1B · FP4/INT4 0.5B → fewer bytes = faster
Roofline: ridge ≈ FLOPS / bandwidth (~300 FLOP/B) · decode ≈ 1 FLOP/B × batch → memory-bound
Max tokens/s per stream ≈ bandwidth ÷ weight bytes
Server: 2 CPU + PCIe switches + 8 GPU + NVSwitch (scale-up) + 8 NIC (scale-out) · ~10 kW
Scale-up: NVLink/NVSwitch, NVL72 · Scale-out: IB/RoCE, rail-optimized, GPUDirect RDMA

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why are LLMs usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than FLOPS during decode?

Each decode step reads every weight once but only does ~2 FLOPs per weight per sequence. That's far below the ~300 FLOPs/byte the GPU needs to be compute-bound, so it waits on HBM.

2. What's the theoretical max decode speed of a 70B FP8 model on one GPU with 4.8 TB/s?

70 GB of weights ÷ 4.8 TB/s ≈ 15 ms per token → ~70 tokens/s for a single stream (ignoring KV cache reads). Batching raises total throughput, not single-stream speed.

3. What's the difference between NVLink and InfiniBand?

NVLink is the scale-up link between GPUs inside a server or rack (TB/s, memory-like). InfiniBand (or RoCE) is the scale-out network between servers (hundreds of Gb/s per NIC).

4. What does GPUDirect RDMA save?

Copies through the CPU and system RAM. The NIC reads from and writes to GPU memory directly, which lowers latency and frees the CPU.

5. Why does every GPU get its own NIC in an AI server?

Collective operations (like all-reduce) make all GPUs send data at the same time. One NIC per GPU, each on its own "rail", gives every GPU full network bandwidth without sharing.

docs.title: 10.3 — GPU software stack & sharing
docs.text:
In short

Your PyTorch code calls CUDA libraries (cuBLAS for matmul, cuDNN/FlashAttention for attention, NCCL for multi-GPU communication), which launch kernels through the user-space driver (libcuda.so), which talks to the kernel driver (nvidia.ko) via ioctl syscalls, which programs the GPU. In containers the image brings the libraries, the host brings the driver, and the two must be compatible. One GPU can be given whole, sliced in hardware (MIG), shared by processes (MPS) or time-shared.

docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) CUDA Compute Unified Device Architecture NVIDIA's GPU programming platform Language extensions + runtime + driver to run code on the GPU Kernel (GPU) — A function that runs on the GPU Launched by the CPU with a grid of thread blocks PTX Parallel Thread Execution A portable GPU "assembly" JIT-compiled by the driver to the exact GPU SASS — (Streaming ASSembler) The real machine code of a specific GPU generation What the SMs actually execute Compute capability — GPU generation number (e.g. 8.0, 9.0, 10.0) Decides which features and networks cuDNN CUDA Deep Neural Network library Kernels for convolution, attention, normalization Called by frameworks automatically CUTLASS CUDA Templates for Linear Algebra Subroutines C++ templates to build custom GEMM kernels Used by libraries and engines for fused kernels FlashAttention — A fast, memory-efficient attention kernel Tiles the computation so it stays in on-chip SRAM NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library Multi-GPU / multi-node communication All-reduce, all-gather over NVLink / InfiniBand TensorRT — NVIDIA's inference optimizer/compiler Fuses layers and picks the fastest kernels for a model Triton (language) — A Python-like language for writing GPU kernels Used by torch.compile to generate fused kernels torch.compile — PyTorch's compiler Captures the model graph and generates optimized kernels CUDA Graphs — Record a sequence of kernel launches once, replay it Removes CPU launch overhead per step UMD / KMD User-Mode Driver / Kernel-Mode Driver libcuda.so / nvidia.ko User-space half and kernel half of the driver NVML NVIDIA Management Library API for GPU status and control What nvidia-smi uses DCGM Data Center GPU Manager Fleet-level GPU monitoring and docs.title: 1 · What is CUDA, and how does a kernel launch work?
What is it?
docs.text: CUDA is the platform that lets normal programs run code on NVIDIA GPUs: a C++ extension for writing kernels, a runtime to manage memory and launches, and libraries with pre-optimized kernels. Almost nobody writes raw CUDA for AI; frameworks call the libraries for you.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. y = model(x) in PyTorch → PyTorch picks an operation, e.g. a matrix multiply.
  2. It calls cuBLAS, which picks the best GEMM kernel for these sizes and this GPU.
  3. The kernel launch goes through the CUDA runtime (libcudart) and driver API (libcuda.so), which place a command in a queue (stream) shared with the GPU.
  4. The driver uses ioctl syscalls on /dev/nvidia* (Chapter 3!) when it needs the kernel module, e.g. to allocate memory or map buffers.
  5. The GPU's front-end reads the queue, spreads thread blocks over the SMs, results land in HBM.
  6. Launches are asynchronous: the CPU queues work and moves on. torch.cuda.synchronize() waits for the GPU to finish.

Why torch.compile and CUDA Graphs matter: a model step can be thousands of tiny kernels. Fusing them (fewer reads/writes of HBM) and replaying them as a graph (fewer CPU launches) is often a big speed-up.

docs.title: 2 · Versions and compatibility (the classic headache)
docs.text:
Piece Where it lives Rule Kernel driver nvidia.ko + libcuda.so Host (node image) The driver version decides the maximum CUDA version it can run (nvidia-smi shows "CUDA Version: X") CUDA runtime + libraries (cudart, cuBLAS, cuDNN, NCCL) Your container image (or pip wheels like torch) Must be ≤ what the host driver supports (with some forward-compat exceptions) GPU architecture (compute capability) Hardware Your binaries must include SASS for it, or PTX the driver can JIT

Typical errors: CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version (driver too old), no kernel image is available for execution on the device (binary not built for this GPU generation).

docs.title: 3 · GPUs in containers
docs.text:
1. The container image contains the CUDA runtime and libraries (e.g. a PyTorch image) but not the driver.
  2. When the container starts, the NVIDIA Container Toolkit (via a runtime hook or a CDI spec) mounts /dev/nvidia* device files and the host's libcuda.so and tools into the container.
  3. Inside, the app sees the GPU as if it were local. Isolation is still namespaces + cgroups (Chapter 9) plus device permissions.

On Kubernetes the GPU Operator installs the driver, the toolkit and the device plugin / DRA driver on every GPU node (10.6).

docs.title: 4 · Sharing a GPU: what are the options, and how do they work?
docs.text: Method How it works Isolation Best for Whole GPU One workload gets the full device Full Large models, training MIG The GPU is split in hardware into up to 7 instances, each with its own SMs, L2 slice and memory Strong (memory + fault isolation) Many small inference models, multi-tenant MPS A server process merges several processes' work into one GPU context, so their kernels run concurrently Weak (shared memory space, one fault can affect all) Cooperative processes from one team Time-slicing The GPU switches between processes in turns None (memory is shared, no limits) Dev/test, bursty low-usage workloads

docs.title: 5 · Monitoring and health
docs.text:
Tool What it gives you nvidia-smi (NVML) Utilization, memory, power, temperature, processes, clocks DCGM + DCGM exporter Prometheus metrics: SM activity, tensor pipe activity, memory bandwidth, NVLink traffic, XID errors, ECC dcgmi diag Active health tests before you put a node into service dmesg / kernel logs XID errors (e.g. memory faults, fallen-off-the-bus)

"GPU utilization 100%" in nvidia-smi only means a kernel was running, not that the SMs were busy. Use DCGM's SM activity and tensor pipe active metrics to see real usage.

DevOps connection: treat the driver + toolkit version as part of the node image, pin and roll it like a kernel upgrade, and gate new nodes with dcgmi diag before they join the pool.

Exercise: in the strace output, find the openat("/dev/nvidia…") calls and count the ioctls needed just to create one tensor on the GPU.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
PyTorch → cuBLAS / cuDNN / FlashAttention / NCCL → CUDA runtime (libcudart)
       → driver API (libcuda.so, from host) → ioctl on /dev/nvidia* → nvidia.ko → GPU
Kernels launch async into streams · torch.compile fuses · CUDA Graphs replay
Host driver sets max CUDA version · image ships runtime + libs · binaries need SASS/PTX for the GPU
Containers: NVIDIA Container Toolkit / CDI mounts devices + libcuda.so
Sharing: whole GPU > MIG (hw slices) > MPS (shared context) > time-slicing (no isolation)
Monitor: nvidia-smi (NVML) · DCGM exporter (SM/tensor activity, XID) · dcgmi diag

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Your pod fails with \"CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version\". Where is the problem?

The host's driver is older than the CUDA runtime inside the image needs. Either upgrade the node driver (GPU Operator / node image) or use an image built for an older CUDA version.

2. Why doesn't a CUDA container image contain the GPU driver?

The driver includes a kernel module (nvidia.ko) that must match the host kernel and is loaded on the host. The toolkit mounts the matching user-space part (libcuda.so) from the host into the container at start-up.

3. When would you choose MIG over time-slicing?

When workloads from different teams or tenants share a GPU and need guaranteed memory and fault isolation with predictable performance. Time-slicing gives no isolation and no memory limits.

4. nvidia-smi shows 100% utilization but throughput is low. What do you check?

DCGM metrics like SM activity, tensor pipe activity and memory bandwidth. 100% "utilization" only means some kernel was running in the sample period; it may be tiny, memory-bound or waiting.

5. What does NCCL do, and on which hardware paths?

It implements collective communication (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter…) between GPUs, choosing NVLink/NVSwitch inside a node and InfiniBand/RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA between nodes.

docs.title: 10.4 — Distributed training
docs.text:
In short

Training repeats one loop billions of times: forward (predict), loss (how wrong), backward (which way to nudge each parameter) and optimizer step (nudge). A big model doesn't fit on one GPU, so the work is split across thousands of GPUs with several kinds of parallelism. Collectives like all-reduce keep them in sync over NVLink and InfiniBand. Jobs are scheduled all at once (gang scheduling) and protected with frequent checkpoints.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Forward / backward pass — Compute predictions / compute gradients Backward walks the layers in reverse (backpropagation) Loss — One number measuring how wrong the predictions are For LLMs: cross-entropy of the real next token Gradient — Direction and size to change each parameter Computed by backpropagation for every parameter Optimizer (Adam/AdamW) Adaptive Moment Estimation The rule that updates parameters from gradients Keeps 2 running averages per parameter (m, v) Batch / global batch — Examples processed per step / across all GPUs Bigger batch = fewer, larger steps Mixed precision — Compute in BF16/FP8, keep master weights in FP32 Speed of low precision, stability of high precision Activation checkpointing — Don't store all activations; recompute in backward Trades ~30% more compute for much less memory DP Data Parallel Every GPU has a full model copy, different data Gradients averaged with all-reduce each step FSDP layer's matrices split across GPUs Partial results exchanged every layer → needs NVLink PP Pipeline Parallel Layers split into stages on different GPUs Micro-batches flow through stages like an assembly line EP Expert Parallel MoE experts placed on different GPUs Tokens sent to their experts with all-to-all CP / SP Context / Sequence Parallel Long sequences split across GPUs Each GPU handles part of the tokens, attention exchanges K/V Collective — A communication pattern among many GPUs All-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast, all-to-all All-reduce — Everyone contributes a tensor, everyone gets the sum Ring/tree algorithms in NCCL NCCL NVIDIA Collective Communications Library The library implementing collectives Uses NVLink inside nodes, RDMA between nodes Gang scheduling — Start all pods/processes of a job together or none Prevents half-started jobs holding GPUs forever Slurm Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management Classic HPC batch scheduler sbatch / docs.title: 1 · What is the training loop, and how does it work?
What is it?
docs.text: Training is optimization: find parameter values that make the loss small on the training data.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Forward: run a batch of token sequences through the model, get predictions for every next token.
  2. Loss: compare predictions with the real next tokens (cross-entropy).
  3. Backward: backpropagation computes a gradient for every parameter.
  4. Sync (if distributed): average gradients across data-parallel GPUs (all-reduce).
  5. Optimizer step: AdamW updates every parameter a little.
  6. Repeat for millions of steps. Every N steps, checkpoint.

docs.title: 2 · Memory accounting: why one GPU isn't enough
docs.text:
Per parameter, with mixed precision and AdamW:

Item Bytes per parameter BF16 weights 2 BF16 gradients 2 FP32 master weights 4 Adam first moment (m) 4 Adam second moment (v) 4 Total (before activations) ~16

A 70B model → ~1.1 TB just for this state, plus activations. An 80–288 GB GPU can't hold it, so the state must be sharded (FSDP/ZeRO) and the work split (TP/PP).

Compute: training FLOPs ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. Example: 8B parameters × 15T tokens × 6 ≈ 7×10²³ FLOPs. At ~1,000 TFLOPS peak and 40% MFU, that's ~500,000 GPU-hours: about 3 weeks on 1,000 GPUs.

docs.title: 3 · Parallelism: what are the kinds, and how do they work?
docs.text:
Kind What gets split Communication Where it should run DP The data; each GPU has a full copy All-reduce gradients once per step Anywhere (scale-out OK) FSDP / ZeRO Weights, grads, optimizer state All-gather weights per layer, reduce-scatter grads Anywhere, more traffic than DP TP Each matrix inside a layer Every layer, forward and backward Inside the NVLink domain PP The layers into stages Activations between stages Across nodes, watch for pipeline "bubbles" EP MoE experts All-to-all token routing Inside or across nodes CP / SP The sequence (long contexts) K/V exchange in attention Inside fast domains

Big runs combine them ("3D/4D parallelism"): e.g. TP=8 inside each server × PP=4 across servers × DP over the rest.

docs.title: 4 · Collectives: what is all-reduce, and how does it work?
What is it?
docs.text: All-reduce takes one tensor from every GPU and gives every GPU the element-wise sum (or average). It's how data-parallel GPUs agree on the same gradients.

docs.title: How does it work? (ring algorithm)
docs.text:
1. Each GPU splits its gradient into N chunks and the GPUs form a ring.
  2. Reduce-scatter (N−1 steps): each GPU sends one chunk to its neighbour and adds the chunk it receives. At the end, each GPU owns one fully summed chunk.
  3. All-gather (N−1 steps): the finished chunks are passed around until every GPU has all of them.
  4. Each GPU sends ~2× the gradient size in total, independent of the number of GPUs, so the ring uses bandwidth optimally. NCCL also uses tree and other algorithms for latency.

docs.title: 5 · The cluster around the GPUs
docs.text:
Part What matters Network (10.2) Rail-optimized, non-blocking IB/RoCE. One slow link slows every step, since collectives wait for the slowest GPU. Storage Datasets streamed from object storage or a parallel FS. Checkpoints can be TBs each, so write them asynchronously and in parallel. Scheduling Gang scheduling (all-or-nothing), topology-aware placement (keep a job's nodes close in the network), quotas and priorities between teams. Slurm in HPC, Kueue/JobSet/KAI/Volcano on Kubernetes. Failures At thousands of GPUs, a GPU, NIC or node fails every few hours. Detect it (XID errors, NCCL timeouts, stragglers), replace the node, restart from the last checkpoint. Observability Loss curve, tokens/s, step time, MFU, per-GPU utilization, NCCL bandwidth.

DevOps connection: a training cluster is a batch system, not a web service. What matters is goodput: the fraction of GPU-hours that actually advanced the model, after failures, restarts, queueing and slow nodes.

docs.title: 6 · Fine-tuning: the small-scale version
docs.text:
Most teams don't pre-train. They fine-tune an open model:

Method Hardware Notes LoRA 1–8 GPUs Train small adapters, base weights frozen QLoRA 1 GPU Base model in 4-bit, adapters in BF16 Full fine-tune Multi-node All weights updated, needs FSDP

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# 1) Data-parallel training with 2 processes on a CPU (no GPU needed): see ranks and all-reduce
cat > ddp_demo.py <<'EOF'
import os, torch, torch.distributed as dist
dist.init_process_group("gloo")
rank, world = dist.get_rank(), dist.get_world_size()
model = torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel(torch.nn.Linear(10, 1))
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
for step in range(3):
    x = torch.randn(32, 10) + rank            # each rank gets different data
    loss = ((model(x) - 1) ** 2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()   # backward() all-reduces gradients
    print(f"rank {rank}/{world} step {step} loss {loss.item():.3f} weight[0]={model.module.weight[0,0].item():.4f}")
dist.destroy_process_group()
EOF
torchrun --nproc_per_node=2 ddp_demo.py   # the weights stay identical on both ranks

# 2) A raw all-reduce
cat > allreduce_demo.py <<'EOF'
import torch, torch.distributed as dist
dist.init_process_group("gloo")
t = torch.tensor([float(dist.get_rank())])
dist.all_reduce(t)
print(f"rank {dist.get_rank()}: {t.item()}")   # every rank prints 6.0 (0+1+2+3)
EOF
torchrun --nproc_per_node=4 allreduce_demo.py

# 3) The memory and compute math
python3 -c "
p=70e9; print('training state TB:', p*16/1e12)
print('GPU-hours for 8B x 15T tokens @ 1000 TFLOPS, 40% MFU:', 6*8e9*15e12/(1e15*0.4)/3600)"

# 4) A Slurm job skeleton for multi-node training (for reference)
#SBATCH --nodes=4 --gpus-per-node=8 --ntasks-per-node=1 --exclusive
srun torchrun --nnodes=$SLURM_NNODES --nproc_per_node=8 \
     --rdzv_backend=c10d --rdzv_endpoint=$(hostname):29500 train.py

Exercise: in the DDP demo, remove DistributedDataParallel (use the plain model) and run again. Do the weights on the two ranks still match? Why not?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Loop: forward → loss → backward (gradients) → all-reduce → optimizer step → repeat · checkpoint every N
Memory: ~16 bytes/param (BF16 w+g, FP32 master, Adam m+v) + activations → shard it
Compute: FLOPs ≈ 6 × params × tokens · MFU 35–55% is good
DP (copy model) · FSDP/ZeRO (shard state) · TP (split matrices, inside NVLink) · PP (split layers) · EP (experts) · CP (sequence)
All-reduce (ring): reduce-scatter + all-gather · ~2× data per GPU regardless of N
Cluster: rail-optimized IB/RoCE · parallel FS / object store · gang scheduling (Slurm, Kueue, KAI) · restart from checkpoints

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why is tensor parallelism usually kept inside one server (or NVLink domain)?

TP exchanges partial results in every layer, forward and backward. That needs the TB/s bandwidth and low latency of NVLink; over the network it would make every step wait.

2. Roughly how much memory does full training state need for a 13B model with AdamW and mixed precision?

About 16 bytes per parameter → ~208 GB, before activations. That's more than one GPU, so you'd use FSDP/ZeRO across several GPUs.

3. What is gang scheduling and why does distributed training need it?

Starting all processes of a job together or not at all. If only some ranks start, they block waiting for the others while holding expensive GPUs, and two such jobs can deadlock the cluster.

4. One node in a 512-GPU job has a slow NIC. What happens to the whole job?

Every collective waits for the slowest participant, so every step slows down to that node's speed. Straggler detection and replacing the node matter.

5. Your 1,000-GPU run checkpoints every 3 hours and a node fails every 4 hours on average. Why is that bad?

Each failure loses up to 3 hours × 1,000 GPUs of work plus restart time, and failures happen almost as often as checkpoints. Checkpoint more often (asynchronously) to raise goodput.

docs.title: 10.5 — Inference & serving deep dive
docs.text:
In short

Serving an LLM means turning GPU memory bandwidth into tokens per second for many users at once. At the same time, time to first token and time per output token must stay low. The main tools: a KV cache managed like virtual memory, continuous batching to keep the GPU full, and quantization and speculative decoding to make each step cheaper. At scale add prefix caching, KV-aware routing and separate prefill and decode pools.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Inference / serving — Running a trained model for users An engine loads weights, accepts requests, streams tokens Prefill — Processing the whole prompt All prompt tokens in parallel, builds the KV cache Decode — Generating output tokens One token per request per step TTFT Time To First Token Latency until the first output token Queueing + prefill TPOT / ITL Time Per Output Token / Inter-Token Latency Time between output tokens One decode step for this request E2E latency End-to-End Total request time TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1) Throughput — Total tokens/s (or requests/s) of a deployment Grows with batch size, until latency SLOs break Goodput — Throughput that meets the latency SLO What actually counts for users SLO Service Level Objective A latency/availability target e.g. p95 TTFT < 1 s, p95 TPOT < 50 ms KV cache Key-Value cache Stored attention K and V of past tokens Grows with context length × concurrent requests GQA / MQA Grouped-Query / Multi-Query Attention Fewer K/V heads than Q heads Shrinks the KV cache several times PagedAttention — KV cache stored in fixed-size blocks A block table maps logical to physical blocks (like page tables) Continuous batching — Rebuild the batch at every decode step New requests join, finished ones leave immediately Chunked prefill — Split long prompts into chunks Mixes prefill chunks with decode steps so decodes don't stall Prefix caching — Reuse KV of a shared prompt prefix System prompt / chat history computed once Quantization — Store weights (and maybe KV/activations) in fewer bits FP8, INT8, INT4 (AWQ, GPTQ), FP4 Speculative decoding — Draft several tokens cheaply, verify in one big pass Output identical to normal decoding, fewer slow steps MTP Multi-Token Prediction Extra heads that predict several next tokens Built-in draft for speculative decoding P/D disaggregation Prefill/Decode disaggregation Prefill and decode on different workers KV cache transferred between them over RDMA KV-aware routing — Send a request where its prefix KV already is Router tracks which pod holds which prefixes EPP Endpoint Picker The routing brain in the Gateway API Inference Extension Scores pods by KV cache hit, queue, load NIXL NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library Fast KV-cache transfer library Moves KV between GPUs/nodes/storage tiers Multi-LoRA — Many fine-tuned adapters on one base model Adapter chosen per request, base weights shared SSE Server-Sent Events HTTP streaming format data: {...} chunk per token(s) OpenAI-compatible API — /v1/chat/completions, /v1/completions, /v1/embeddings De-facto standard request/response format

docs.title: 1 · What happens to one request?
docs.text:
1. The client sends POST /v1/chat/completions with stream: true.
  2. The gateway authenticates, applies quotas, picks the model. The router picks a replica (ideally one that already has this prompt prefix cached).
  3. The engine's scheduler queues the request, then admits it into the running batch when there's KV cache space.
  4. Prefill: the prompt is tokenized and processed in one big parallel pass. The KV cache is filled. The first token comes out → TTFT.
  5. Decode: every step, the engine runs the whole batch for one more token per request → TPOT. Each token is streamed back as an SSE chunk.
  6. On a stop token or max_tokens, the request leaves the batch and its KV blocks are freed (or kept for prefix reuse).

docs.title: 2 · Metrics that matter
docs.text:
Metric Driven by Users feel it as TTFT Queue time + prompt length (prefill compute) "It starts answering quickly" TPOT Batch size, model size, memory bandwidth "It types fast" (~20–50 ms/token feels fluent) Throughput (tokens/s per GPU) Batch size, KV cache capacity, optimizations Cost per million tokens Goodput Throughput within SLOs The real capacity number to plan with

The core trade-off: bigger batches → higher throughput but higher TPOT. Capacity planning = find the largest batch (concurrency) where p95 TTFT and TPOT still meet the SLO.

docs.title: 3 · What is the KV cache, and how does paging work?
What is it?
docs.text:
For every token in a request, every layer stores its attention Key and Value vectors so they don't have to be recomputed at every decode step.

KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per value
Llama-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 dim, BF16): 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 ≈ 128 KB per token
→ 8,000-token conversation ≈ 1 GB · 50 such users ≈ 50 GB of KV cache, on top of 16 GB of weights

docs.title: How does paging work? (PagedAttention)
docs.text:
1. GPU memory left after the weights is cut into fixed-size blocks (e.g. 16 tokens each).
  2. Each request has a block table mapping its logical blocks to physical blocks, exactly like an OS page table (Chapter 3).
  3. Blocks are allocated on demand as the request grows, so no memory is reserved for tokens that may never be generated.
  4. Requests with the same prefix can point to the same physical blocks (copy-on-write), which is how prefix caching works.
  5. When memory is full, the scheduler preempts (pauses) a request or offloads blocks to CPU RAM/SSD.

docs.title: 4 · What is continuous batching, and how does it work?
What is it?
docs.text: Instead of starting a fixed batch and waiting for its longest request to finish, the engine re-forms the batch at every decode step.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. Run one decode step for every active request (+1 token each).
  2. Remove requests that just finished, free their KV blocks, return them to users.
  3. Admit waiting requests into the free space. Their prompts are processed with chunked prefill, mixed into decode steps so existing users don't stall.
  4. Repeat. The GPU never sits half-empty waiting for one long answer.

docs.title: 5 · Making each step cheaper
docs.text: Technique What it saves Trade-off Quantization (FP8 / INT8 / INT4 / FP4 weights, FP8 KV cache) Memory and bandwidth per token → more tokens/s, bigger batches Small accuracy loss, must evaluate FlashAttention / fused kernels / CUDA Graphs HBM traffic and CPU launch overhead None (engine default) Prefix caching Prefill of repeated system prompts, RAG context, chat history Memory to hold cached blocks Speculative decoding / MTP Number of slow decode steps Extra draft compute; best at low batch sizes GQA / MLA (model architecture) KV cache size Chosen at training time

docs.title: How does speculative decoding work?
docs.text:
1. A draft (a small model, or extra MTP heads on the big model) quickly proposes the next k tokens.
  2. The big target model checks all k in one forward pass (like a tiny prefill, cheap because decode is bandwidth-bound and has spare compute).
  3. The longest prefix that matches what the target would have produced is accepted. The first mismatch is replaced by the target's token.
  4. Output is identical to normal decoding; you just get several tokens per big step.

docs.title: 6 · Scaling out: replicas, sharding, disaggregation
docs.text:
Situation What you do Model fits one GPU, more traffic More replicas behind a load balancer Model doesn't fit one GPU Tensor parallel inside a node (TP=2/4/8), pipeline/expert parallel across nodes for very large or MoE models Many requests share prefixes KV/prefix-aware routing so requests land where their KV already is (round robin destroys cache hits) Long prompts hurt everyone's TPOT P/D disaggregation: prefill pool and decode pool, KV transferred over RDMA, each pool scaled on its own load KV cache doesn't fit Tiered KV: HBM → CPU RAM → local SSD → shared storage Many fine-tuned variants Multi-LoRA: one base model, adapters loaded per request

On Kubernetes this is the job of the Gateway API Inference Extension (InferencePool + an endpoint picker), llm-d (CNCF project for distributed vLLM/SGLang serving on Kubernetes) and NVIDIA Dynamo (an engine-agnostic distributed serving framework). See 10.6.

docs.title: 7 · The engines
docs.text:
Engine Strengths vLLM Widest model and hardware support, PagedAttention, OpenAI-compatible, the community default SGLang Very fast prefix caching (RadixAttention), structured outputs, strong for agent workloads TensorRT-LLM NVIDIA-optimized kernels and FP8/FP4, highest performance on NVIDIA when tuned Triton Inference Server Multi-framework server for any model type (not only LLMs) llama.cpp / Ollama CPUs, laptops, edge devices, GGUF quantized models

DevOps connection: an LLM endpoint is stateful in disguise. Its KV cache makes "which pod" matter, warm-up after a restart is slow (loading tens of GB of weights), and autoscaling needs LLM signals (queue length, KV utilization, TTFT), not CPU.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# 1) KV cache math for any model config
python3 - <<'EOF'
layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bytes_ = 32, 8, 128, 2      # Llama-3-8B, BF16
per_tok = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_
print(f"{per_tok/1024:.0f} KB/token · 8k context = {per_tok*8192/1e9:.2f} GB · 50 users = {per_tok*8192*50/1e9:.0f} GB")
EOF

# 2) Serve a small model with vLLM (GPU) and watch the engine's own metrics
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct --max-num-seqs 64 &
curl -N localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"model":"Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct","stream":true,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Count to 10"}]}'
curl -s localhost:8000/metrics | grep -E "num_requests_running|num_requests_waiting|kv_cache_usage|time_to_first_token" | head

# 3) Load test: throughput vs latency at different concurrency
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct --dataset-name random \
  --random-input-len 1000 --random-output-len 200 --num-prompts 200 --max-concurrency 8
#   repeat with --max-concurrency 64 and compare tokens/s, TTFT and TPOT

Exercise: run the benchmark at concurrency 1, 8, 32 and 128. Plot output tokens/s against p95 TPOT. Where would you set the limit for a 50 ms TPOT SLO?

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
Request: gateway → router (prefix-aware) → queue → PREFILL (TTFT) → DECODE steps (TPOT) → SSE stream → free KV
E2E ≈ TTFT + TPOT × (output tokens − 1) · throughput ↑ with batch, TPOT ↑ too → plan on goodput
KV/token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes (8B ≈ 128 KB) · paged in blocks, shared prefixes, offload tiers
Continuous batching + chunked prefill keep the GPU full
Cheaper steps: quantization (FP8/INT4/FP4) · FlashAttention · prefix caching · speculative decoding / MTP
Scale: replicas → TP for big models → KV-aware routing → P/D disaggregation (llm-d, Dynamo, Inference Gateway)
Engines: vLLM · SGLang · TensorRT-LLM · Triton · llama.cpp/Ollama

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Users complain the first word takes 4 seconds to appear but then text flows fast. Which metric and which phase?

High TTFT: either queueing (not enough capacity, or bad routing) or slow prefill (very long prompts). Prefix caching, chunked prefill, more replicas or P/D disaggregation help.

2. Why does round-robin load balancing hurt LLM serving?

It ignores where each conversation's KV cache (prefix) lives, so requests keep landing on pods that must recompute the prefill. KV-aware routing sends them to the pod that already has the prefix.

3. How much KV cache does a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads of dimension 128 need for 100 concurrent 4k-token requests in BF16?

2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 128 KB/token → × 4,096 tokens × 100 requests ≈ 54 GB.

4. Does speculative decoding change the model's answers?

No. Accepted tokens are exactly those the target model would have produced; the draft only lets several of them be confirmed in one forward pass.

5. Why split prefill and decode onto different GPUs?

They stress different resources (compute vs memory bandwidth). Mixed together, long prefills stall everyone's decode steps. Separate pools can be sized and scaled independently and tuned for their bottleneck.

docs.title: 10.6 — AI platform on Kubernetes
docs.text:
In short

Kubernetes becomes an AI platform by adding a few layers. The GPU Operator prepares GPU nodes, and DRA (or the older device plugin) lets pods claim GPUs. Kueue/KAI queue jobs fairly with gang scheduling, and JobSet/LeaderWorkerSet run multi-pod training and inference. An inference gateway routes requests to model servers that autoscale on LLM signals. The platform team's goal: high GPU utilization, fair sharing, fast cold starts, clear cost.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) GPU Operator — Operator that manages the whole GPU node stack Installs driver, container toolkit, device plugin / DRA driver, DCGM exporter, MIG manager NFD / GFD Node Feature Discovery / GPU Feature Discovery Labels nodes with their hardware e.g. nvidia.com/gpu.product=H100-SXM Device plugin — The classic way to expose devices Advertises a count (nvidia.com/gpu: 8) as an extended resource DRA Dynamic Resource Allocation The new device API (GA since v1.34, resource.k8s.io/v1) Pods claim devices by attributes; the scheduler matches and allocates ResourceSlice — DRA object published by a driver Lists the devices on a node with their attributes DeviceClass — DRA object defined by admins Names a kind of device and its selection rules ResourceClaim / Template — What a pod asks for "1 GPU with ≥80 GB" or "2 GPUs on the same NVLink" Taints / tolerations — Keep normal pods off GPU nodes GPU nodes are tainted; only GPU workloads tolerate it Kueue — Kubernetes-native job queueing LocalQueue → ClusterQueue with quotas, borrowing, preemption KAI Scheduler — NVIDIA's open-source AI-aware scheduler Hierarchical queues, gang scheduling, GPU sharing Gang scheduling — All pods of a job start together or none Avoids deadlocks and half-started jobs JobSet — A group of Jobs managed as one unit Multi-pod distributed training with shared lifecycle LWS LeaderWorkerSet Groups of pods (leader + workers) as one replica Multi-node inference of models too big for one node KubeRay — Operator for Ray clusters Ray Train / Ray Serve on Kubernetes KServe — Model serving platform on Kubernetes InferenceService CRDs, autoscaling, canaries Gateway API Inference Extension — Kubernetes SIG project for LLM routing InferencePool + an endpoint picker (EPP) scoring pods by KV cache and load llm-d — CNCF project for distributed LLM inference vLLM/SGLang + inference gateway + P/D disaggregation + KV-aware routing KEDA Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling Autoscaler driven by external metrics Scales on queue length, KV usage, Prometheus queries HPA Horizontal Pod Autoscaler Built-in autoscaler Scales replicas on CPU/memory or custom metrics Model cache — Keep model weights close to GPUs Node-local NVMe, shared PVC, or OCI image volumes DCGM exporter Data Center GPU Manager exporter GPU metrics for Prometheus Utilization, memory, power, XID errors per GPU/pod OpenCost — Kubernetes cost allocation Cost per namespace/team, including GPUs

docs.title: 1 · Preparing GPU nodes: what does the GPU Operator do?
What is it?
docs.text: An operator that turns a plain node with an NVIDIA card into a ready-to-use GPU node, and keeps it that way.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. NFD/GFD detect the GPU and label the node (product, memory, MIG capability, driver version).
  2. The driver container installs nvidia.ko for the node's kernel (or uses a pre-installed driver).
  3. The container toolkit configures containerd so containers can get GPUs (via CDI).
  4. The device plugin or DRA driver advertises the GPUs to Kubernetes.
  5. DCGM exporter exposes per-GPU metrics, MIG manager applies MIG layouts from a node label.
  6. A validator runs a test workload; only then is the node ready for GPU pods.

Platform tip: keep GPU nodes in separate, tainted node pools per GPU type, and treat driver versions like kernel versions (pin, roll out gradually, dcgmi diag before joining).

docs.title: 2 · Asking for a GPU: device plugin vs DRA
What is DRA?
docs.text: Dynamic Resource Allocation replaces "give me n of nvidia.com/gpu" with a claim that describes which device you need, similar to how PersistentVolumeClaims describe storage. Core DRA is GA since Kubernetes v1.34 (resource.k8s.io/v1), and NVIDIA's DRA driver for GPUs now lives in the Kubernetes SIGs organization.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. The DRA driver on each node publishes ResourceSlices: every GPU with its attributes (model, memory, MIG profile, NVLink domain…).
  2. An admin defines DeviceClasses (e.g. gpu.nvidia.com).
  3. A pod references a ResourceClaim (or a template) with requests and selectors, e.g. "1 GPU with ≥80 GB".
  4. The scheduler finds a node whose devices satisfy the claim, allocates them and writes the result to the claim.
  5. The kubelet asks the driver to prepare the device and the container starts with it.
# Classic device plugin
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
---
# DRA (resource.k8s.io/v1)
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata: { name: single-gpu }
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu
        exactly:
          deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: vllm }
spec:
  resourceClaims:
  - name: gpu
    resourceClaimTemplateName: single-gpu
  containers:
  - name: vllm
    image: vllm/vllm-openai
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: gpu

docs.title: 3 · Sharing GPUs fairly: how do Kueue and gang scheduling work?
What is it?
docs.text: The default scheduler places pods one by one and has no idea that 64 pods belong to one training job, or that team A owns half the GPUs. Kueue (and AI schedulers like KAI or Volcano) add queues, quotas and all-or-nothing admission.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A Job/JobSet is created with a label kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: training. Kueue keeps it suspended.
  2. It sits in the namespace's LocalQueue, which points to a ClusterQueue that owns a quota (e.g. 64 GPUs of flavor "H100").
  3. When the whole job fits the quota (borrowing unused quota from other queues if allowed), Kueue admits it and unsuspends it, so all pods are created together.
  4. If a higher-priority job needs the GPUs, Kueue can preempt borrowed capacity.
# (API version depends on your Kueue release)
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterQueue
metadata: { name: gpu-cq }
spec:
  namespaceSelector: {}
  resourceGroups:
  - coveredResources: ["nvidia.com/gpu"]
    flavors:
    - name: h100
      resources:
      - name: "nvidia.com/gpu"
        nominalQuota: 64
---
apiVersion: kueue.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: LocalQueue
metadata: { namespace: team-a, name: training }
spec: { clusterQueue: gpu-cq }

docs.title: 4 · Workload types and their Kubernetes building blocks
docs.text: Workload Building blocks Notes Distributed training / fine-tuning JobSet, PyTorchJob (Kubeflow Trainer), Kueue, topology-aware placement Gang scheduling, checkpoints to object storage Batch inference / evals Job / JobSet + Kueue, or Ray Throughput-oriented, can use spot capacity Online LLM serving (one node) Deployment + vLLM/SGLang, Inference Gateway / KServe Readiness after model load, KV-aware routing Online serving (multi-node model) LeaderWorkerSet (one replica = leader + workers) TP inside nodes, PP across Distributed serving at scale llm-d or NVIDIA Dynamo P/D disaggregation, KV cache tiers, KV-aware routing (10.5) Notebooks / dev JupyterHub, time-sliced or MIG GPUs Idle culling to free GPUs

docs.title: 5 · Model weights: the cold-start problem
docs.text:
A 70B model is ~140 GB. Pulling that from object storage on every pod start means minutes of cold start.

Approach How Node-local cache DaemonSet or init container pre-pulls weights to local NVMe Shared volume ReadOnlyMany PVC on a fast parallel filesystem OCI artifacts / image volumes Ship weights as OCI artifacts, reuse the registry and node image cache Fast loaders Streaming loaders (e.g. safetensors streaming) to start serving sooner

docs.title: 6 · Autoscaling LLM servers
docs.text:
Signal Why Queue length / waiting requests Direct sign of missing capacity KV cache utilization When near 100%, new requests wait or get preempted TTFT / TPOT p95 The SLO you actually promised ~~CPU utilization~~ Meaningless: the work is on the GPU

Use KEDA or HPA with Prometheus metrics from the engine (/metrics), keep a minimum warm replica count (cold starts are slow), and scale prefill and decode pools separately when disaggregated.

docs.title: 7 · Observability and cost
docs.text:
• DCGM exporter → Prometheus → Grafana: SM activity, tensor activity, memory, power, XID errors, per pod.
  • Engine metrics: running/waiting requests, KV usage, TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s.
  • Cost: GPU-hours per namespace/team (OpenCost/Kubecost), cost per million tokens per model, idle GPU-hours.

DevOps connection: the classic platform metrics change meaning. "Utilization" means SM/tensor activity, "capacity" means KV cache and tokens/s, "deploy time" includes loading 100+ GB of weights, and a 10% utilization gain on GPUs is often worth more than everything else in the cluster combined.

# 1) Install the GPU Operator (on a cluster with NVIDIA GPU nodes)
helm repo add nvidia https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia && helm repo update
helm install gpu-operator nvidia/gpu-operator -n gpu-operator --create-namespace
kubectl get pods -n gpu-operator

# 2) A GPU smoke test

  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"gpu-test","image":"nvidia/cuda:12.6.3-base-ubuntu24.04","command":["nvidia-smi"],"resources":{"limits":{"nvidia.com/gpu":1}}}]}}'

# 3) DRA objects (on a DRA-enabled cluster)

# 4) Kueue: install, then watch admissions

kubectl get workloads -A        # one Workload per queued job: admitted or pending, and why

Exercise (no GPU needed): install Kueue on a kind cluster with a fake quota on cpu, submit three Jobs that each need 60% of the quota, and watch only one get admitted at a time.

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text:
GPU node: GPU Operator = driver + toolkit (CDI) + device plugin/DRA driver + DCGM exporter + MIG manager · tainted pools
Ask for GPUs: limits nvidia.com/gpu: N (count)  →  DRA: ResourceSlice → DeviceClass → ResourceClaim → scheduler allocates
Fair sharing: Kueue LocalQueue → ClusterQueue (quota, borrow, preempt) · gang admission · KAI / Volcano
Workloads: JobSet (training) · LWS (multi-node serving) · KServe / Inference Gateway / llm-d (online serving)
Cold start: cache weights on node NVMe / PVC / OCI artifacts · keep warm replicas
Autoscale on queue length, KV usage, TTFT/TPOT — not CPU
Watch: DCGM (SM/tensor activity, XID) · engine metrics · GPU-hours and $/1M tokens per team

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What can DRA express that nvidia.com/gpu: 1 can't?

Attributes and relationships: a specific model or memory size, a MIG profile, several GPUs on the same NVLink domain, shared claims between pods. The device plugin only exposes a count.

2. A 64-GPU training job gets 40 pods scheduled and the rest stay Pending. What's wrong, and what fixes it?

No gang scheduling: the default scheduler placed pods one by one. The 40 running pods hold GPUs while waiting for the others. Kueue (or KAI/Volcano) admits the job only when all 64 GPUs are available.

3. Why should GPU nodes be tainted?

So that ordinary pods (web apps, sidecars, system jobs) don't land on very expensive GPU nodes and take CPU/memory that GPU workloads need. Only pods that tolerate the taint and request GPUs go there.

4. Your LLM Deployment scales up but new pods take 8 minutes to become Ready. What do you change?

Cache model weights close to the node (local NVMe pre-pull, shared PVC, OCI artifacts), use a streaming loader, keep a minimum number of warm replicas and scale earlier (on queue length rather than on SLO violations).

5. What does the endpoint picker in the Gateway API Inference Extension do that a normal Service doesn't?

It chooses a model server pod per request based on LLM-specific signals: prefix/KV cache locality, queue length, KV cache usage, LoRA adapters loaded. A Service just load-balances connections.
