docs.title: 14.4 — Accounts, landing zones & disaster recovery
docs.text:
In short

A landing zone is the foundation every workload lands on. It's an organization of many accounts/projects (per team and environment), so mistakes and breaches stay small. It adds single sign-on, organization-wide guardrails nobody can switch off, shared networking, and central logging and security. Disaster recovery is a deliberate choice of how much data (RPO) and time (RTO) you can lose, proven by regular game days.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Organization — Top container for all accounts AWS Organizations, GCP Organization, Azure Management Groups OU Organizational Unit Folder of accounts sharing policies Prod, NonProd, Security, Sandbox Account / project / subscription — Isolation and billing boundary Separate IAM, quotas, resources SCP / Org Policy Service Control Policy Guardrail on everything in an OU "Deny leaving eu-* regions", even for admins IAM Identity Center — SSO into many accounts Permission sets → short-lived roles Account vending — Automated creation of new accounts Control Tower AFT, Terraform Hub-and-spoke — Central network hub, workload VPCs as spokes Transit Gateway, Shared VPC, Virtual WAN Log archive — Central, immutable audit logs Org-wide CloudTrail, write-once bucket RPO Recovery Point Objective Max acceptable data loss "≤ 5 minutes of transactions" RTO Recovery Time Objective Max acceptable downtime "Back within 1 hour" Pilot light / warm standby — DR with minimal / scaled-down copy Cheaper than active-active, slower Active-active — Two+ regions serving traffic Lowest RTO/RPO, hardest data story Game day — Planned failure exercise Practise failover, measure real RTO

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
An account (AWS), project (GCP) or subscription (Azure) is a hard boundary: IAM, quotas, resource limits and billing are per account. One shared account means one leaked key or one bad terraform destroy can reach everything. A typical structure:

  • Management account: billing, organization, SSO. No workloads, very few people.
  • Security and Log archive accounts: org-wide audit logs (write-once), security tooling and findings; workload admins can't touch them.
  • Shared services / Network: transit hub, egress, DNS, CI runners, artifact registries.
  • Workload accounts: per team (or product) × environment (payments-prod, payments-staging), so prod is separate from experiments.
  • Sandbox accounts: free experimentation with budgets and auto-cleanup.

docs.title: 2 · Guardrails and access
docs.text:
• People log in through SSO (IAM Identity Center, Entra ID, Google Workspace) with MFA and get short-lived role sessions via permission sets; no IAM users with passwords or keys (11).
  • Guardrails (SCPs, Org Policies, Azure Policy) apply to everyone in an OU, including account admins:
    • only approved regions (data residency)
    • can't disable CloudTrail/GuardDuty or delete the log archive
    • no public S3 buckets, no IAM user keys
    • require encryption, require tags
  • Detective controls (AWS Config, Security Hub, Policy Analyzer) find what preventive rules can't block.
  • Account vending: new accounts are created by code with the baseline already applied: SSO, logging, networking, budgets.

docs.title: 3 · Shared networking
docs.text:
• Hub-and-spoke: workload VPCs (spokes) attach to a hub (Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN, GCP Shared VPC / NCC, Azure Virtual WAN) that holds central egress, inspection firewalls, on-prem VPN/Direct Connect and shared DNS (5.4).
  • IP address planning up front: non-overlapping CIDRs per account and region (IPAM), or you can't connect them later.
  • Private endpoints for cloud APIs reduce NAT costs and exposure (13).

docs.title: 4 · Disaster recovery strategies
docs.text:
Strategy What runs in the DR region Typical RPO Typical RTO Cost Backup & restore Nothing; backups copied there Hours (last backup) Hours–days $ Pilot light Data replicated; core infra defined in IaC, scaled to zero Minutes Tens of minutes–hours $$ Warm standby Small but working copy of the whole stack Seconds–minutes Minutes $$$ Active-active Full stack serving traffic in both ≈ 0 (with careful data design) ≈ 0–minutes $$$$

Choose per service, based on business impact: the payment system may need warm standby, the internal wiki needs backups. Remember what disasters actually look like: much more often a bad deploy, a deleted table or ransomware than a whole region going down. Backups with point-in-time recovery in another account protect against the common ones.

docs.title: 5 · Proving it: runbooks and game days
docs.text:
1. Write the runbook: who decides to fail over, the exact steps (DNS/traffic switch, promote replica, scale up), how to fail back.
  2. Automate as much as possible (IaC for the DR region, scripts for promotion).
  3. Run game days: restore a production backup into a fresh account; fail over a service; measure the real RTO and RPO.
  4. Fix what broke (expired credentials, missing quotas in the DR region, hard-coded endpoints), and repeat each quarter.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• The landing zone is a platform product (16.4): teams request an account and get a ready, compliant environment in minutes.
  • IaC everything in the landing zone too (Control Tower + AFT, Terraform modules, Cloud Foundation Toolkit), so it can be rebuilt and audited.
  • Quotas and capacity in the DR region must be reserved or at least requested in advance; GPUs especially (10).
  • Dependencies count: your DR plan fails if the IdP, DNS provider, container registry or CI system is only in the failed region.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# AWS Organizations: what does my org look like? (needs org read permission)
aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[].Id' --output text
aws organizations list-organizational-units-for-parent --parent-id $(aws organizations list-roots --query 'Roots[0].Id' --output text) \
  --query 'OrganizationalUnits[].Name'
aws organizations list-policies --filter SERVICE_CONTROL_POLICY --query 'Policies[].Name'

# A classic guardrail SCP: deny everything outside two EU regions (except global services)
cat > region-guardrail.json <<'EOF'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"DenyOutsideEU","Effect":"Deny",
 "NotAction":["iam:*","organizations:*","sts:*","support:*","cloudfront:*","route53:*","budgets:*"],
 "Resource":"*","Condition":{"StringNotEquals":{"aws:RequestedRegion":["eu-central-1","eu-west-1"]}}}]}
EOF
python3 -m json.tool region-guardrail.json > /dev/null && echo "valid JSON"

# DR drill: restore an RDS snapshot into a new instance and time it
# time aws rds restore-db-instance-from-db-snapshot --db-instance-identifier drill-$(date +%s) --db-snapshot-identifier <snapshot>

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Goal Do Limit blast radius Account per team × env, prod separate People access SSO + MFA + short-lived roles, no IAM users Rules nobody can bypass SCPs / Org Policies on OUs Audit Org-wide trail to an immutable log-archive account Connect VPCs Hub-and-spoke, planned non-overlapping CIDRs Survive deletes & ransomware PITR + cross-account, locked backups Survive a region Pilot light / warm standby / active-active per service Know it works Quarterly game days with measured RTO/RPO

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why use separate accounts for prod and dev instead of one account with tags?

Accounts are hard isolation boundaries for IAM, quotas and blast radius; tags and naming conventions don't stop a dev-side mistake or compromised key from touching prod.

2. What can an SCP do that IAM policies in the account can't?

It sets a ceiling for everyone in the account, including its administrators, so rules like "never disable CloudTrail" or "only EU regions" can't be bypassed locally.

3. What's the difference between pilot light and warm standby?

Pilot light keeps data replicated and infrastructure ready but compute mostly off; warm standby runs a small working copy of the whole stack, so it recovers faster but costs more.

4. Which disasters are more common than a full region outage, and what protects against them?

Bad deployments, accidental deletes, data corruption and ransomware. Point-in-time recovery, versioning, and immutable backups in a separate account protect against them.

5. Why run game days?

Untested DR plans fail on details (expired credentials, missing quotas, hard-coded endpoints); exercises reveal them and measure the real RTO and RPO.

docs.title: Chapter 15 — Kubernetes in depth: running it in production
Chapter 15 — Kubernetes in depth: running it in production
docs.text:
In short

Chapter 9 showed how Kubernetes works. Running it in production is about the details that decide uptime. That means the right workload controller with correct probes, requests and graceful shutdown, plus config and persistent volumes that follow pods. It also means packaging with Helm or Kustomize, autoscaling pods and nodes, reading pod status quickly, and upgrading every few months without drama.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Day 2 — Operating after the initial install Upgrades, scaling, backups, incidents Workload controller — Object that manages pods for you Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, CronJob Probe — Kubelet health check startup, readiness, liveness PDB PodDisruptionBudget Min available pods during voluntary disruptions Protects against drains taking too many PV / PVC PersistentVolume / Claim Storage object / a pod's request for it Bound 1:1, provisioned by CSI CSI Container Storage Interface Plugin standard for storage drivers Creates, attaches, mounts cloud disks Helm — Package manager for Kubernetes Charts = templates + values, releases Kustomize — Template-free overlays base + patches per environment Operator — Controller + CRD encoding operational knowledge Manages complex apps (DBs, Kafka) HPA / VPA Horizontal / Vertical Pod Autoscaler Replica count / resource size automation Based on metrics KEDA Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling Scales on external events, to zero Queue length, Kafka lag, cron Karpenter — Node autoscaler that picks instance types Provisions just-in-time nodes Velero — Backup/restore of cluster resources and volumes Object storage + snapshots

docs.title: 1 · Pick the right controller
docs.text:
Controller For Key behaviour Deployment Stateless services Rolling updates via ReplicaSets, maxSurge/maxUnavailable StatefulSet Databases, brokers, anything with identity Stable names (db-0), ordered start, one PVC per pod DaemonSet One pod per node Log shippers, CNI, node exporters, CSI node plugins Job / CronJob Run to completion / on schedule Retries (backoffLimit), concurrencyPolicy, TTL cleanup

Bare pods are never used in production: nothing recreates them.

docs.title: 2 · The settings that decide uptime
docs.text:
1. Requests and limits: requests for scheduling and guaranteed share; memory limit to contain leaks; CPU limits often omitted to avoid throttling (3.2).
  2. Probes: readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts (be conservative), startup protects slow boots (15.1).
  3. Graceful shutdown: handle SIGTERM, a short preStop sleep, enough terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
  4. Spread: ≥ 2 replicas, topologySpreadConstraints across zones and nodes, a PodDisruptionBudget.
  5. Security context: non-root, read-only filesystem, no privilege escalation (11).

docs.title: 3 · State, config and packaging
docs.text:
• Config through ConfigMaps and Secrets (External Secrets/CSI from Vault or a cloud secret manager), storage through PVCs and StorageClasses (15.2).
  • Package apps with Helm charts or Kustomize overlays and deliver with GitOps (9.4); use operators for complex stateful software (15.3).

docs.title: 4 · Scale, troubleshoot, upgrade
docs.text:
• Autoscaling in two layers: HPA/KEDA/VPA for pods, Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler for nodes (15.4).
  • Troubleshoot by status: Pending = scheduling, ImagePullBackOff = registry, CrashLoopBackOff = the app or its limits, Running but failing = probes, Services, network (15.5).
  • Upgrade regularly: Kubernetes ships ~3 minor versions a year and each gets ~14 months of patches; managed providers force upgrades when versions expire (15.5).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Most production outages on Kubernetes come from configuration, not Kubernetes bugs: missing readiness probes, no PDB, requests copied from a template, a single replica, missing shutdown handling.
  • Make the good defaults part of the platform (16.4): a chart or template with probes, PDB, spread, security context and resource defaults.
  • Enforce them with policy (Kyverno/Gatekeeper, 11) and check them in CI (kube-linter, kubeconform, Polaris).

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the deploy that dropped 2% of requests
docs.text:
The alarm

Every deployment of the orders service causes a burst of 502 errors for about 30 seconds. Rollouts "succeed" and the pods look healthy.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

The errors come from the ingress controller: "upstream connection refused / reset" to pod IPs that are terminating.

🔍 Clue 2

The app exits immediately on SIGTERM. There's no preStop hook, and the readiness probe only checks that the port is open, so new pods receive traffic before their connection pools and caches are ready.

🎯 Root cause

Endpoint removal is asynchronous: the ingress and kube-proxy still send requests for a few seconds after a pod gets SIGTERM. The app died instantly, and new pods were marked Ready too early.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Add preStop: sleep 5, handle SIGTERM by stopping new work and draining in-flight requests, set a meaningful readiness endpoint (dependencies warm), use maxUnavailable: 0 and a PDB. Lesson: "zero-downtime deploys" are a property of your pods' lifecycle, not of Kubernetes itself.

docs.text: Page What's inside 15.1 — Workloads, probes & scheduling Deployments and rollout settings, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs, the three probes and how to design them, graceful shutdown, requests and QoS, affinity, taints, topology spread, priority and PDBs. 15.2 — Configuration & persistent storage ConfigMaps and Secrets, env vs mounted files, External Secrets, PVs, PVCs, StorageClasses, access modes, CSI drivers, volume binding and zones, expanding and snapshotting volumes, StatefulSets and running databases. 15.3 — Helm, Kustomize & operators Helm charts, values, releases and hooks, Kustomize bases and overlays, choosing between them, CRDs and the operator pattern, well-known operators, and how these fit into GitOps. 15.4 — Autoscaling pods and nodes metrics-server and custom metrics, HPA behaviour and tuning, KEDA and scale to zero, VPA and right-sizing, Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter, consolidation, spot, and capacity headroom. 15.5 — Troubleshooting, upgrades & backups A systematic method by pod status, exit codes, events, kubectl debug, node problems, DNS and network checks, version skew and upgrade process, deprecated APIs, etcd and Velero backups.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# A local cluster with 3 nodes (kind)
cat > kind.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes: [{role: control-plane}, {role: worker}, {role: worker}]
EOF
kind create cluster --name day2 --config kind.yaml

# A production-shaped deployment: replicas, probes, PDB, spread
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine --replicas=3
kubectl set resources deployment web --requests=cpu=50m,memory=64Mi --limits=memory=128Mi
kubectl create pdb web --selector=app=web --min-available=2
kubectl get pods -o wide                     # spread over workers?

# Drain a node and watch the PDB keep 2 pods available
kubectl drain day2-worker --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data &
kubectl get pods -o wide -w
kind delete cluster --name day2

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Checklist item Why ≥ 2 replicas + topology spread Survive node/zone loss Readiness + startup probe No traffic before ready SIGTERM handling + preStop No dropped requests on deploy Requests from real usage, memory limit Good packing, contained leaks PDB Safe drains and upgrades Non-root, read-only FS Smaller blast radius Packaged (Helm/Kustomize) + GitOps Reproducible, reviewable Regular upgrades + Velero backups Supported versions, recoverable

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. When do you use a StatefulSet instead of a Deployment?

When pods need stable identity and their own storage: stable names, ordered start/stop and one PVC per replica (databases, brokers, clustered apps).

2. What's the difference between a readiness and a liveness probe?

Readiness decides whether a pod receives traffic (removed from Service endpoints when failing); liveness decides whether the container is restarted.

3. Why can pods drop requests during a rolling update even though Kubernetes waits for readiness?

Endpoint removal propagates asynchronously after SIGTERM; if the app exits immediately, load balancers still route a few requests to it. A preStop delay and graceful draining fix it.

4. What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?

Voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades, autoscaler consolidation) evicting too many pods at once; it doesn't protect against crashes or node failures.

5. Why must Kubernetes clusters be upgraded regularly?

Minor versions are supported for only about 14 months; managed services force upgrades, APIs get removed, and security fixes only come for supported versions.

docs.title: 15.1 — Workloads, probes & scheduling
docs.text:
In short

A production workload is a controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job) plus a pod template. Requests and placement rules decide where it runs. Startup and readiness probes decide when it gets traffic, and liveness decides when it's restarted. SIGTERM handling, preStop and the grace period decide whether it shuts down without dropping a single request.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) ReplicaSet — Keeps N identical pods Created and managed by a Deployment maxSurge / maxUnavailable — Rolling update speed Extra pods allowed / pods allowed down Startup probe — "Has it finished booting?" Other probes wait until it succeeds Readiness probe — "Can it take traffic now?" Fail → removed from Service endpoints Liveness probe — "Is it stuck?" Fail → container restarted QoS class Quality of Service Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort Decides eviction order under pressure Node affinity — Prefer/require nodes by labels zone, instance-type, gpu=true Pod (anti-)affinity — Place near / away from other pods Co-locate cache, separate replicas Taint / toleration — Node repels pods / pod accepts the taint Dedicated GPU or system nodes Topology spread — Even distribution over a topology key maxSkew: 1 across zones PriorityClass — Importance of pods Higher priority can preempt lower Grace period — Time between SIGTERM and SIGKILL terminationGracePeriodSeconds, default 30

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Changing a Deployment's pod template creates a new ReplicaSet; the controller scales it up and the old one down in steps limited by maxSurge (extra pods above desired) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed to be missing). A new pod counts as available only after it's Ready for minReadySeconds.

spec:
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 0 }   # never below capacity
  minReadySeconds: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300                            # mark failed if stuck

kubectl rollout status|history|undo follows and reverts. For canary/blue-green use Argo Rollouts or Flagger (9.4, 16.2).

docs.title: 2 · Other controllers
docs.text:
• StatefulSet: pods name-0..N with stable DNS via a headless Service and one PVC each from volumeClaimTemplates; ordered or parallel start; partitioned rolling updates for careful upgrades (15.2).
  • DaemonSet: one pod per (matching) node, rolled node by node; tolerate taints to run on every node.
  • Job: runs pods until completions succeed, retries up to backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, indexed jobs for parallel work, ttlSecondsAfterFinished for cleanup.
  • CronJob: creates Jobs on a schedule (timeZone supported); set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid for jobs that mustn't overlap and startingDeadlineSeconds.

docs.title: 3 · Designing probes
docs.text:
Probe Good check Bad check Startup Same endpoint as readiness, generous failureThreshold × periodSeconds (e.g. 30 × 5 s) Missing for slow JVM apps → killed by liveness while starting Readiness Can serve requests: initialized, critical caches warm, not draining Checks every downstream dependency → whole fleet goes unready when the DB blips Liveness Process is wedged (deadlock, event loop stuck): a cheap in-process check Calls the DB, or same as readiness with tight timeouts → restart storms under load

Many services need no liveness probe at all: a crashed process restarts anyway. Add one only for known "alive but stuck" failure modes.

docs.title: 4 · Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
When a pod is deleted, two things happen in parallel: the kubelet sends SIGTERM (after running preStop), and the endpoint controller removes the pod from Services, which takes a moment to reach kube-proxy and ingress controllers. So:

  1. preStop: exec sleep 5 (or a native sleep action) keeps the pod serving until endpoints are updated.
  2. On SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests, close connections, flush.
  3. Keep total time below terminationGracePeriodSeconds; after it the container is SIGKILLed (exit 137).
  4. Make sure the app is PID 1 or uses an init (tini, exec in the entrypoint) so it actually receives the signal (3.1).

docs.title: 5 · Placement: requests, affinity, taints, spread
docs.text:
• Requests are what the scheduler packs on; QoS follows from requests/limits: Guaranteed (requests = limits), Burstable, BestEffort (none, evicted first).
  • nodeSelector / node affinity for hardware or zones; taints keep general pods off special nodes (nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule), pods that belong there tolerate them.
  • topologySpreadConstraints with topology.kubernetes.io/zone and kubernetes.io/hostname keep replicas apart; prefer them over pod anti-affinity at scale.
  • PriorityClasses: critical system and production pods can preempt batch work when capacity is short.
  • PodDisruptionBudget (minAvailable or maxUnavailable) protects against drains, upgrades and consolidation removing too many at once.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Bake these into your service template/chart: probes, preStop, PDB, spread, security context, sensible defaults (16.4).
  • Load-test during a rolling deploy and during a node drain; 0 errors is the bar.
  • Alert on kube_deployment_status_replicas_unavailable, restart counts and rollouts stuck past progressDeadlineSeconds.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name wl
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: web } }
  strategy: { rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: web } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 20
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - { maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname, whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway, labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: web } } }
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          resources: { requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 32Mi }, limits: { memory: 64Mi } }
          startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }, periodSeconds: 2, failureThreshold: 15 }
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /, port: 80 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
          lifecycle: { preStop: { sleep: { seconds: 5 } } }
EOF
kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.28-alpine && kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl rollout history deploy/web && kubectl rollout undo deploy/web
kubectl get pod -l app=web -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}{end}'
kind delete cluster --name wl

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Setting Default to maxUnavailable 0 for user-facing services startupProbe For anything booting > 10 s readinessProbe Always, local readiness only livenessProbe Only for known hang modes, cheap check preStop 5–10 s sleep Grace period > preStop + longest request Spread Zone + hostname, maxSkew: 1 PDB maxUnavailable: 1 (or 25%)

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. What do maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 0 mean for a 4-replica Deployment?

During the rollout up to 1 extra pod may exist (5 total), and the number of available pods never drops below 4: a new pod must be ready before an old one is removed.

2. Why can a liveness probe that checks the database make an outage worse?

If the database slows down, every pod fails liveness and is restarted at the same time, losing caches and connections and adding load exactly when the system is struggling.

3. Why is a startup probe useful?

It gives slow-starting apps time to boot without loosening liveness and readiness probes; those only start once the startup probe succeeds.

4. What happens between kubectl delete pod and the container stopping?

The pod is marked terminating; in parallel the endpoint is removed from Services and the kubelet runs preStop then sends SIGTERM; after the grace period any remaining process gets SIGKILL.

5. What's the difference between a taint and node affinity?

A taint on a node repels pods that don't tolerate it (node chooses); node affinity on a pod attracts it to nodes with certain labels (pod chooses). Dedicated nodes usually use both.

docs.title: 15.2 — Configuration & persistent storage
docs.text:
In short

The same image runs in every environment because configuration is injected at runtime. It comes from ConfigMaps and Secrets (as env vars or files), ideally synced from a real secret manager. Data that must outlive a pod lives on a PersistentVolume that the pod claims through a PVC. A StorageClass and its CSI driver create it as a cloud disk in the right zone and attach it wherever the pod runs.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) ConfigMap — Key-value config object Mounted as files or env vars Secret — Config for sensitive values base64 in the API; encrypt etcd at rest External Secrets Operator ESO Syncs secrets from Vault/cloud managers ExternalSecret → Kubernetes Secret Secrets Store CSI — Mounts secrets directly from a manager No Kubernetes Secret object needed PV PersistentVolume A piece of storage in the cluster Backed by a cloud disk, NFS, local disk PVC PersistentVolumeClaim A request for storage Size + access mode + class StorageClass — How to provision volumes Provisioner, parameters, reclaim policy Access modes RWO / ROX / RWX / RWOP Who can mount it Block disks are RWO (one node) CSI Container Storage Interface Standard storage driver API Controller (create/attach) + node (mount) plugins WaitForFirstConsumer — Delay provisioning until a pod is scheduled Disk created in the pod's zone Reclaim policy — What happens to a PV when the PVC is deleted Delete or Retain VolumeSnapshot — Point-in-time copy of a volume Via CSI snapshot support

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
envFrom:
  - configMapRef: { name: app-config }        # every key becomes an env var
volumeMounts:
  - { name: tls, mountPath: /etc/tls, readOnly: true }
volumes:
  - name: tls
    secret: { secretName: app-tls }            # every key becomes a file
  • Env vars are read once at process start; changing the ConfigMap does nothing until the pod restarts.
  • Mounted files are updated by the kubelet within about a minute (not with subPath); the app must re-read them.
  • To roll pods on config change, put a hash of the config in a pod annotation (Helm checksum/config, Kustomize configMapGenerator name suffixes) or use Reloader.
  • Secrets are only base64-encoded; protect them with RBAC (get secrets is powerful), encryption at rest with a KMS provider, and avoid printing env vars in logs (11).
  • Better: keep the source of truth in Vault / AWS Secrets Manager / GCP Secret Manager and sync with External Secrets or mount with the Secrets Store CSI driver, authenticating with workload identity (no static keys).

docs.title: 2 · Volumes, claims and classes
docs.text:
1. A pod references a PVC (claimName: data).
  2. The PVC asks for 50Gi, ReadWriteOnce, class gp3.
  3. The StorageClass names a provisioner (ebs.csi.aws.com, pd.csi.storage.gke.io) and parameters (type, IOPS, encryption, KMS key).
  4. With volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer, provisioning waits until the scheduler picks a node, so the disk is created in that node's zone.
  5. The CSI controller creates the disk, a PV is bound to the PVC; the CSI node plugin attaches and mounts it into the pod.
Access mode Meaning Typical backend RWO Read-write by one node Block disks (EBS, PD) RWOP Read-write by one pod Block disks, strict single writer RWX Read-write by many nodes NFS/EFS/Filestore, CephFS ROX Read-only by many nodes Shared datasets

docs.title: 3 · Living with volumes
docs.text:
• Zones: an RWO disk exists in one zone; a pod using it can only run there. If that zone loses capacity, the pod stays Pending. Replication across zones is the application's job (database replicas) or a regional disk.
  • Expansion: allowVolumeExpansion: true, then edit the PVC size; filesystems grow online on most CSI drivers. Shrinking is not supported.
  • Snapshots: VolumeSnapshot objects with a VolumeSnapshotClass; restore by creating a PVC with dataSource.
  • Reclaim policy: Delete removes the disk when the PVC goes away; use Retain for important data, so a deleted namespace doesn't delete your database.
  • Ephemeral storage: emptyDir (node disk or memory), counted against ephemeral-storage requests; exceeding it gets the pod evicted.

docs.title: 4 · StatefulSets and databases
docs.text:
StatefulSets give each replica a stable name and its own PVC (data-db-0, data-db-1), which stays even if the pod is rescheduled. That's the foundation, but running a database also needs replication setup, failover, backups, upgrades and monitoring. Options:

  • Managed database outside the cluster (RDS, Cloud SQL): simplest, usually the right default (14.2).
  • Operators that encode this knowledge (CloudNativePG, Percona, Strimzi for Kafka, Redis operators) when you need databases in the cluster (15.3).
  • Hand-written StatefulSets for databases: rarely a good idea.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• One image, many environments: config differences belong in overlays/values (15.3), never in separate images.
  • Monitor volumes: kubelet_volume_stats_used_bytes / capacity_bytes alerts before disks fill; IOPS limits on cloud disks (14.2).
  • Back up PVs with CSI snapshots or Velero (15.5), and rehearse restores.
  • Don't put secrets in Helm values in git; reference external secrets instead (or encrypt with SOPS/Sealed Secrets).

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name st
# Config as a file that updates live
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=GREETING=hello
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: cfg }
spec:
  containers:
    - name: c
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo env=$GREETING file=$(cat /cfg/GREETING); sleep 5; done"]
      envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: app-config } }]
      volumeMounts: [{ name: cfg, mountPath: /cfg }]
  volumes: [{ name: cfg, configMap: { name: app-config } }]
EOF
sleep 10; kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=GREETING=merhaba -o yaml --dry-run=client | kubectl apply -f -
sleep 70; kubectl logs cfg --tail=2             # file changed, env did not

# Dynamic provisioning with kind's default StorageClass
kubectl get storageclass
kubectl create -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data }
spec: { accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], resources: { requests: { storage: 1Gi } } }
EOF
kubectl get pvc data                            # Pending until a pod uses it (WaitForFirstConsumer)
kind delete cluster --name st

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Need Use Plain settings ConfigMap (files if you want live reload) Credentials External Secrets / CSI from a secret manager Restart on config change Checksum annotation, generator suffix, Reloader Disk for one pod PVC RWO, class with WaitForFirstConsumer Shared files RWX (EFS/Filestore/NFS) Protect important data reclaimPolicy: Retain + snapshots Database Managed service, or a mature operator

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. You change a ConfigMap used via envFrom. Why doesn't the app see the new value?

Environment variables are set when the container starts; they aren't updated in a running process. Restart the pods (e.g. via a config checksum annotation) or mount the ConfigMap as files.

2. Why are Kubernetes Secrets not enough on their own?

They're only base64-encoded, readable by anyone with get secrets, and stored in etcd unencrypted unless configured. Use encryption at rest, tight RBAC and ideally an external secret manager.

3. What does WaitForFirstConsumer solve?

It delays creating the disk until the pod is scheduled, so the volume is created in the same zone as the node; otherwise the disk could land in a zone where the pod can't run.

4. Why can a pod with an RWO PVC get stuck in Pending after a zone failure?

The disk lives in the failed zone and can only attach to nodes there; the scheduler can't place the pod anywhere else.

5. Why use Retain as the reclaim policy for important volumes?

With Delete, deleting the PVC (or its namespace) also deletes the underlying disk; Retain keeps the disk so the data can be recovered.

docs.title: 15.3 — Helm, Kustomize & operators
docs.text:
In short

Helm packages an application as a chart of templates rendered with values and tracks installs as releases; Kustomize starts from plain YAML and applies overlays per environment without templates. Both just produce manifests, typically applied by GitOps. Operators go further: a CRD adds a new API type (PostgresCluster) and a controller keeps running in the cluster, reconciling that resource into StatefulSets, backups and failovers, which encodes a human operator's knowledge as software.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Chart — Helm package Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates/ Values — Inputs to a chart Defaults overridden by -f prod.yaml / --set Release — One installation of a chart Name + namespace + revision history Hook — Job run at install/upgrade phases pre-upgrade DB migration OCI registry Open Container Initiative Store charts like images helm push chart.tgz oci://… Base / overlay — Kustomize shared config / per-env patches overlays/prod patches base Generator — Creates ConfigMaps/Secrets with hash suffix Triggers rollouts on change CRD CustomResourceDefinition Adds a new resource type to the API Schema, versions, validation CR Custom Resource An instance of a CRD kind: Certificate Operator — Controller for a CRD with domain knowledge Reconcile loop: observe → diff → act Finalizer — Blocks deletion until cleanup is done Operator removes it when finished Crossplane — Operators for cloud resources Kubernetes API for databases, buckets

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
helm install shop ./chart -f values-prod.yaml renders templates/*.yaml with Go templates and the merged values, sends the manifests to the API server, and stores the release (rendered manifest + values) as a Secret in the namespace. helm upgrade computes a 3-way diff (old manifest, new manifest, live state) and applies it; helm rollback goes back to a stored revision.

# templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicas }}
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}@{{ .Values.image.digest }}"
          resources: {{- toYaml .Values.resources | nindent 12 }}
  • Good for distributing software (cert-manager, ingress controllers, Prometheus) and internal "service charts" with many options.
  • Pitfalls: templating YAML with whitespace is fragile; huge values files become an untyped API (use values.schema.json); hooks and CRD upgrades need care; never helm install by hand into prod: render and deliver with GitOps.

docs.title: 2 · Kustomize
docs.text:
base/            deployment.yaml service.yaml kustomization.yaml
overlays/dev/    kustomization.yaml  (replicas: 1, image tag, small resources)
overlays/prod/   kustomization.yaml  (replicas: 6, HPA, PDB patch, prod ConfigMap)

kubectl apply -k overlays/prod (or kustomize build) merges strategic patches / JSON patches onto the base. No templates: every file is valid YAML you can read. Generators add a content hash to ConfigMap names, so changes roll pods automatically. It's built into kubectl and supported natively by Argo CD and Flux.

docs.title: 3 · Which one?
docs.text:
Situation Choose Installing third-party software Its Helm chart (pin the version) Your own services, few env differences Kustomize, or one internal Helm chart for all services Many teams, one golden service template Internal Helm chart with a schema Tweaking a third-party chart's output Helm + Kustomize post-render (Argo CD/Flux support it) Logic-heavy config (loops, functions) cdk8s, Jsonnet/Tanka, or CUE/KCL, carefully

Whatever you choose, render in CI, validate (kubeconform, policy checks), diff, and let GitOps apply.

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
1. A CRD registers a new type with an OpenAPI schema, e.g. postgresql.cnpg.io/v1 Cluster.
  2. You apply a custom resource: instances: 3, storage: 100Gi, backup: s3://….
  3. The operator's controller watches these resources and reconciles: creates pods/PVCs, configures replication, schedules backups, performs failover and rolling minor upgrades, updates .status.
  4. Deleting the CR runs cleanup guarded by finalizers.

Well-known operators: cert-manager (TLS certificates), CloudNativePG / Percona (databases), Strimzi (Kafka), Prometheus Operator (monitoring), External Secrets (15.2), Argo Rollouts (progressive delivery), Crossplane (cloud resources as Kubernetes objects, 14.3).

Before adopting one, check: maturity and maintainers, upgrade path of the operator itself, CRD version migrations, what happens if the operator is down (workloads should keep running), backup/restore story, RBAC it needs.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• A golden service chart (probes, PDB, HPA, security context, monitoring) is one of the highest-leverage platform artifacts (16.4).
  • Pin chart versions and image digests; promote the same rendered artifacts across environments (9.4).
  • Track deprecated API versions in charts before cluster upgrades (pluto, kubent, 15.5).
  • Operators are production software you run: monitor them, upgrade them, read their release notes.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name pkg
# Helm: scaffold, render, install, upgrade, roll back
helm create demo && helm template demo ./demo --set replicaCount=2 | grep -A3 "kind: Deployment"
helm install demo ./demo && helm upgrade demo ./demo --set replicaCount=3
helm history demo && helm rollback demo 1 && kubectl get deploy demo

# Kustomize: base + overlay
mkdir -p k/base k/prod
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine --dry-run=client -o yaml > k/base/deploy.yaml
printf "resources: [deploy.yaml]\n" > k/base/kustomization.yaml
cat > k/prod/kustomization.yaml <<'EOF'
resources: [../base]
replicas: [{ name: web, count: 5 }]
images: [{ name: nginx, newTag: 1.28-alpine }]
configMapGenerator: [{ name: web-config, literals: [MODE=prod] }]
EOF
kubectl kustomize k/prod | grep -E "replicas|image|name: web-config"

# An operator: cert-manager and a self-signed certificate
helm install cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace --set crds.enabled=true --wait
kubectl get crd | grep cert-manager
kind delete cluster --name pkg

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Command Use helm template … -f values.yaml See exactly what will be applied helm upgrade --install --atomic Upgrade or install, roll back on failure helm history / rollback Revisions and undo helm diff upgrade (plugin) Preview changes kubectl kustomize dir Render an overlay kubectl get crd / kubectl explain <kind> Discover custom APIs kubectl get <cr> -o yaml → .status What the operator thinks

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Where does Helm store information about a release?

In the release's namespace, as a Secret per revision containing the rendered manifest, values and metadata; that's what helm history and rollback use.

2. What's the main difference between Helm and Kustomize?

Helm renders templates with values (and manages releases); Kustomize patches plain YAML bases with overlays, without templates or release tracking.

3. Why add a checksum of the ConfigMap to the pod template annotations?

So a config change changes the pod template, triggering a rolling update; otherwise pods keep running with old config.

4. What is the operator pattern?

A CRD defines a new resource type and a controller continuously reconciles those resources to the desired state, automating operational tasks like provisioning, failover, backups and upgrades.

5. What should you check before running an operator in production?

Maturity and maintenance, how the operator and its CRDs are upgraded, the RBAC it needs, behaviour when the operator is down, and its backup/restore and failure handling.

docs.title: 15.4 — Autoscaling pods and nodes
docs.text:
In short

Kubernetes scales in two layers. Pod autoscalers change how many replicas run (HPA, KEDA) or how big they are (VPA). When new pods don't fit, node autoscalers (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) add machines and later consolidate them away. It only works well with realistic requests, fast-starting pods and a little headroom, because new nodes take minutes.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) metrics-server — Cluster-wide CPU/memory usage Source for kubectl top and resource HPA HPA Horizontal Pod Autoscaler Adjusts replica count desired = ceil(current × metric / target) Utilization target — % of the request to aim for averageUtilization: 70 Custom / external metrics — Non-CPU signals RPS, latency, queue depth via adapters Stabilization window — Wait before scaling down/up Avoids flapping (behavior) KEDA Kubernetes Event-Driven Autoscaling Scalers for 60+ event sources Can scale to and from zero VPA Vertical Pod Autoscaler Recommends/sets requests Off / Initial / Recreate / InPlaceOrRecreate Cluster Autoscaler CA Scales node groups Reacts to pending pods Karpenter — Provisions nodes directly Picks instance type per pending pods Consolidation — Removing/replacing underused nodes Evicts pods respecting PDBs Overprovisioning — Low-priority placeholder pods Reserve headroom for fast scale-up Cooldown — Delay between scaling actions Prevents oscillation

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Every ~15 s the HPA controller reads metrics and computes:

desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetric / targetMetric)

With 4 pods at 140% of their CPU request and a target of 70%: ceil(4 × 140/70) = 8. Then minReplicas/maxReplicas and the behavior policies apply.

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 50
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 } }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:   { policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }] }
    scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300 }
  • Utilization is relative to requests: no requests → no CPU-based HPA; inflated requests → the HPA never scales.
  • CPU is a proxy. For I/O-bound or queue-driven work, scale on requests per second, in-flight requests or queue length (Prometheus Adapter, KEDA).
  • Don't combine HPA and VPA on the same CPU/memory metric.

docs.title: 2 · KEDA: event-driven and scale to zero
docs.text: KEDA watches external sources (Kafka lag, SQS/RabbitMQ queue length, Prometheus queries, cron, HTTP traffic) and feeds them to an HPA it manages; it also handles 0 ↔ 1 activation, which the HPA alone can't. Ideal for workers, batch consumers and dev environments.

docs.title: 3 · VPA: right-sizing
docs.text:
VPA watches actual usage and recommends requests (target, lower/upper bounds). Modes:

  • Off: recommendations only; read them (kubectl describe vpa) or feed a dashboard (Goldilocks). The safe default.
  • Initial: sets requests when pods are created.
  • Recreate / InPlaceOrRecreate: updates running pods; in-place resize (pods change resources without restart, beta and enabled by default since Kubernetes 1.33) reduces disruption.

Right-sized requests are the base of everything else: correct HPA math, good bin packing, lower cost (13).

docs.title: 4 · Node autoscaling
docs.text:
Cluster Autoscaler Karpenter Model Scales predefined node groups (ASG/MIG) Creates individual nodes from NodePools Instance choice Fixed per group Chooses from many types per pending pods Speed Group API + boot Direct fleet API + boot (usually faster) Cost optimisation Scale-down of empty/underused nodes Consolidation: delete or replace with cheaper nodes Clouds All major AWS natively, Azure (AKS NAP), others via providers

Both react to pending pods; new nodes need 1–3 minutes (boot, join, pull images, CNI ready). Consolidation evicts pods, so PDBs and graceful shutdown (15.1) matter. Use karpenter.sh/do-not-disrupt or disruption budgets for jobs that mustn't be interrupted.

docs.title: 5 · Headroom and spot
docs.text:
• Overprovisioning: a Deployment of low-priority "pause" pods reserves capacity; real pods preempt them instantly, and the autoscaler then replaces the evicted placeholders with new nodes in the background.
  • Spot nodes for stateless and batch workloads: diversify instance types, handle the interruption notice (node termination handler / Karpenter interruption queue), keep a baseline on on-demand (13).
  • Scale-up is only as fast as your slowest step: big images, slow startup, init containers, cold caches. Measure "pending → ready" time.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Load-test the scaling path: from 1× to 5× traffic in 2 minutes, watch HPA events, pending pods, node launches and error rates.
  • Alert on HPA at maxReplicas, pods pending > 5 min, and nodes not becoming ready.
  • Set ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges per namespace so one team's autoscaler can't consume the cluster.
  • Scale predictable peaks ahead of time (KEDA cron scaler, scheduled minReplicas).

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name as
# metrics-server for kind (insecure TLS to kubelets is fine for a lab)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/latest/download/components.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system patch deploy metrics-server --type=json -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'

kubectl create deployment php --image=registry.k8s.io/hpa-example
kubectl set resources deploy php --requests=cpu=200m && kubectl expose deploy php --port=80
kubectl autoscale deploy php --cpu-percent=50 --min=1 --max=10
kubectl run load --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- sh -c "while true; do wget -q -O- http://php; done"
kubectl get hpa php -w            # watch replicas climb; Ctrl-C after a few minutes
kubectl delete pod load; kubectl get hpa php -w   # and slowly come back down (stabilization window)
kind delete cluster --name as

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause HPA shows <unknown> No metrics-server / adapter, or no requests Never scales up Requests far above usage, target too high Flapping No stabilization window, metric too noisy Scaled pods stay Pending No node autoscaler, quota, or constraints (zone PVC, taints) Slow to absorb spikes Node boot + image pull; add headroom, smaller images Cost keeps rising Requests too high, consolidation blocked by PDBs/annotations

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. 5 pods run at 90% of their CPU request; the target is 60%. How many replicas will the HPA want?

ceil(5 × 90 / 60) = ceil(7.5) = 8 replicas (within min/max).

2. Why does CPU-based HPA depend on correct requests?

Utilization is measured as a percentage of the request. If requests are much higher than real usage, utilization never reaches the target and the HPA doesn't scale (and nodes are wasted).

3. What can KEDA do that the HPA alone can't?

Scale on many external event sources out of the box and scale workloads to zero and back up when events arrive.

4. How does Karpenter differ from Cluster Autoscaler?

Instead of growing predefined node groups, it looks at pending pods and launches the best-fitting instance types directly, and actively consolidates by removing or replacing nodes with cheaper ones.

5. Why keep headroom even with fast autoscalers?

New nodes take minutes to boot, join and pull images; without spare capacity, sudden spikes hit before new capacity is ready.

docs.title: 15.5 — Troubleshooting, upgrades & backups
docs.text:
In short

Kubernetes tells you what's wrong if you read it in order. The pod status points to the failing layer, events explain why, logs (including --previous) show the app's side, and kubectl debug lets you look inside. Healthy clusters also need upgrades every few months within the supported version skew, after removing deprecated APIs. And backups (etcd, Velero, snapshots) that you have actually restored.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Events — Short-lived records of what controllers did kubectl events, kept ~1 h by default Exit code — Container's process result 0 ok, 1 app error, 137 SIGKILL/OOM, 143 SIGTERM OOMKilled Out Of Memory Kernel killed the container for exceeding its memory limit cgroup memory.max (3.3) CrashLoopBackOff — Container keeps exiting; restarts are delayed exponentially 10 s → 5 min ImagePullBackOff — Image can't be pulled; retries with backoff Name/tag, auth, registry limits Ephemeral container — Debug container added to a running pod kubectl debug -it pod --image=… EndpointSlice — List of ready pod IPs for a Service Empty = no ready pods match Node conditions — Ready, MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, PIDPressure Pressure → evictions Version skew — Allowed version gaps between components kubelet up to 3 minors older than API server Deprecated API — API version scheduled for removal Must migrate manifests before upgrading etcd snapshot — Backup of the cluster's state store Self-managed clusters; managed ones do it for you Velero — Backs up Kubernetes objects + volumes To object storage, restore to any cluster

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -o wide                       # 1. status, restarts, node, IP
kubectl describe pod <pod>                     # 2. conditions, last state, exit code, EVENTS at the bottom
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous   # 3. what the app said before it died
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp    # 4. the wider picture (nodes, PVCs, scheduler)
kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot --target=<container>   # 5. look from inside

Work from the outside in: is it scheduled? Is the image there? Does the process stay up? Is it ready? Can traffic reach it?

docs.title: 2 · Status by status
docs.text: Status Typical causes Check / fix Pending Not enough CPU/memory for requests; taints without tolerations; affinity/spread unsatisfiable; PVC in another zone or unbound; quota exceeded Events: 0/6 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint…; fix requests, add capacity, check node autoscaler ImagePullBackOff / ErrImagePull Typo in name/tag, private registry without credentials, architecture mismatch (arm64 vs amd64), registry rate limits describe message; test pull on the node; imagePullSecrets or node IAM; pull-through cache CrashLoopBackOff App error at startup, missing config/secret, wrong command, liveness killing a slow start, dependency unreachable logs --previous, exit code, try the command in kubectl debug --copy-to with a shell OOMKilled (exit 137) Memory limit too low or a leak; JVM/Node heap not matching the limit describe → Last State: OOMKilled; raise the limit, set heap to ~75% of limit, profile Running but not Ready Readiness probe failing, app still warming up, dependency down describe probe failures; kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc> Ready but unreachable Service selector/port mismatch, NetworkPolicy, DNS, ingress config kubectl port-forward, curl from a debug pod, nslookup svc.ns.svc.cluster.local (9.3, 6.2) Evicted Node DiskPressure/MemoryPressure, ephemeral storage exceeded Node conditions, container logs filling disk, ephemeral-storage requests Terminating forever Finalizers waiting on something, node gone kubectl get pod -o yaml → finalizers; investigate the owner before forcing

docs.title: 3 · Nodes and the cluster
docs.text:
• kubectl get nodes + describe node: conditions, allocatable vs allocated, taints.
  • kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=busybox gives a shell with the host filesystem at /host (journal, kubelet and containerd logs) without SSH.
  • Control plane health: API server latency and errors, etcd leader changes and fsync latency (12), webhook timeouts (a broken admission webhook can block all deployments).
  • CoreDNS problems show up as timeouts everywhere: check its pods, cache hit rate and ndots behaviour (6.2).

docs.title: 4 · Upgrades
docs.text:
Kubernetes releases about 3 minor versions per year; each gets roughly 14 months of patches. Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) eventually upgrade you automatically or charge for extended support.

  1. Read the changelog and the deprecation guide for every minor you cross; scan manifests and Helm releases for removed APIs (pluto, kubent, API server metrics apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis).
  2. Upgrade add-ons first if needed (CNI, CSI, ingress, cert-manager, operators) to versions supporting the target.
  3. Upgrade the control plane one minor at a time (1.32 → 1.33 → 1.34), never skipping.
  4. Upgrade nodes: surge new nodes and drain old ones (PDBs and graceful shutdown make it painless, 15.1), or blue/green node pools.
  5. Do it in staging first, keep upgrades routine (every quarter) rather than heroic (every two years).

Version skew: kubelets may be up to 3 minor versions older than the API server, never newer; kubectl ±1.

docs.title: 5 · Backups
docs.text:
• etcd holds all cluster state. Managed control planes back it up for you; on self-managed clusters take regular etcdctl snapshot save backups, encrypt them and store off-cluster.
  • Velero backs up Kubernetes objects (per namespace or label) and volumes (CSI snapshots or file-level copies) to object storage and restores them into the same or another cluster: for disasters, migrations and "someone deleted the namespace".
  • GitOps makes stateless parts reproducible from git (9.4); backups are mainly for state and for things created outside git.
  • Test restores into a fresh cluster on a schedule (14.4).

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Put the method into a runbook with copy-paste commands and link it from alerts.
  • Ship events and logs to your logging system; events disappear after an hour.
  • Track upgrade debt as a metric: versions behind latest, months until end of support.
  • Use kubectl plugins and tools that speed things up: k9s, stern (multi-pod logs), kubectl-neat, krew.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
kind create cluster --name ts
# 1. Pending: request more CPU than exists
kubectl run big --image=nginx:alpine --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"big","image":"nginx:alpine","resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"64"}}}]}}'
# 2. ImagePullBackOff: a tag that doesn't exist
kubectl run typo --image=nginx:does-not-exist
# 3. CrashLoopBackOff: a command that exits
kubectl run crash --image=busybox:1.37 -- sh -c "echo starting; exit 3"
# 4. OOMKilled: allocate more than the limit
kubectl run oom --image=polinux/stress --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"oom","image":"polinux/stress","args":["--vm","1","--vm-bytes","200M"],"resources":{"limits":{"memory":"64Mi"}}}]}}'
sleep 40; kubectl get pods
for p in big typo crash oom; do echo "== $p"; kubectl describe pod $p | grep -E "Reason|Exit Code|Warning" | head -4; done
kubectl logs crash --previous
kubectl debug node/ts-control-plane -it --image=busybox:1.37 -- chroot /host sh -c "crictl ps | head -5"
kind delete cluster --name ts

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Exit code Meaning 0 Completed normally 1 / 2 Application error / misuse 126 / 127 Not executable / command not found 137 SIGKILL: OOMKilled or killed after grace period 139 SIGSEGV: segmentation fault 143 SIGTERM: asked to stop Need Command Why not scheduled describe pod → Events Why it died logs --previous, Last State Who receives traffic get endpointslices Shell without one in the image kubectl debug -it pod --image=netshoot --target=c Node logs without SSH kubectl debug node/X -it --image=busybox

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. A pod is Pending. Where do you look first and what are common causes?

The events in kubectl describe pod: insufficient CPU/memory for its requests, taints without tolerations, unsatisfiable affinity/spread, an unbound PVC or one in another zone, or a namespace quota.

2. A container shows exit code 137. What happened?

It was killed with SIGKILL, most often by the OOM killer for exceeding its memory limit (Reason: OOMKilled), or because it didn't stop within the termination grace period.

3. Why use kubectl logs --previous for a CrashLoopBackOff?

The current container may have just restarted and logged nothing useful; --previous shows the output of the instance that crashed.

4. A Service returns connection errors but the pods are Running. What do you check?

Whether the pods are Ready and appear in the Service's EndpointSlices, whether the selector and target port match, NetworkPolicies, and DNS resolution from a debug pod.

5. Why can't you jump from Kubernetes 1.31 directly to 1.34?

The control plane must be upgraded one minor version at a time to keep components within the supported skew and allow storage/API migrations; removed APIs must also be migrated at each step.

docs.title: Chapter 16 — DevOps practices: how good teams ship and operate software
Chapter 16 — DevOps practices: how good teams ship and operate software
docs.text:
In short

DevOps is not a job title or a tool. It's a way of working in which the people who build software also ship and run it. Changes are small and flow through automated pipelines many times a day, and deploying is separated from releasing so every step is reversible. Production is observed, incidents become blameless learning, and a platform makes the right way easy. DORA metrics show that speed and stability go together.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) DevOps Development + Operations Shared ownership of building and running software Culture + automation + feedback CALMS Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing A lens to assess DevOps adoption Tools alone ≠ DevOps SRE Site Reliability Engineering Operations as a software problem SLOs, error budgets, toil reduction (9.5) Platform engineering — Building internal self-service platforms Golden paths, developer portals (16.4) DORA metrics DevOps Research and Assessment Delivery performance measures Deploy frequency, lead time, change fail rate, recovery time Lead time for changes — Commit → running in production Hours for top performers Change failure rate — % of deploys causing a failure Needs rollback/hotfix/incident Toil — Manual, repetitive, automatable work SRE goal: < 50% of time Trunk-based development — Everyone integrates to main daily Short branches, feature flags (16.1) Feature flag — Runtime switch for behaviour Deploy ≠ release (16.2) Postmortem — Written analysis after an incident Blameless, action items (16.3) Team Topologies — Model of team types and interactions Stream-aligned, platform, enabling, complicated-subsystem

docs.title: 1 · What DevOps changes
docs.text:
Before: developers "throw code over the wall" to operations, releases are big, rare and scary, and the people paged at night didn't write the code. After:

  • You build it, you run it: teams own services end to end, including on-call.
  • Small batches: a 50-line change is easy to review, test, deploy and roll back; a 3-month release is not.
  • Automate the path to production: build, test, security checks, deploy (9.4), infrastructure (14.3).
  • Fast feedback: tests in minutes, metrics in seconds, users' reactions in hours.
  • Learning culture: incidents are investigated to improve the system, not to find someone to blame.

docs.title: 2 · Measuring it: DORA
docs.text:
Metric Measures Elite teams (roughly) Deployment frequency How often you deploy to production On demand, many per day Lead time for changes Commit → production Less than a day Change failure rate Deploys that cause failures Low (around 5–15%) Failed deployment recovery time Time to restore after a bad deploy Less than an hour

DORA's research across many years and thousands of teams shows that throughput and stability correlate positively: teams that deploy more often also fail less and recover faster, because small changes are safer. Measure these per team as trends, never as targets for individuals.

docs.title: 3 · DevOps, SRE and platform engineering
docs.text:
• DevOps is the philosophy: shared ownership, flow, feedback, learning.
  • SRE is a concrete implementation for reliability: SLOs, error budgets that decide when to slow down, limits on toil, blameless postmortems (9.5, 16.3).
  • Platform engineering scales it: instead of every team becoming experts in Kubernetes, Terraform and observability, a platform team provides paved roads as a product (16.4).
  • The "DevOps engineer" role in practice is a mix of all three: building pipelines and infrastructure, enabling teams and running production.

docs.title: 4 · The practices in this chapter
docs.text:
1. Git workflows & code review (16.1): trunk-based development, small PRs, fast reviews, versioning.
  2. Safe releases (16.2): feature flags, progressive delivery, database migrations without downtime.
  3. Incidents (16.3): on-call, severity, incident command, postmortems.
  4. Platform engineering (16.4): golden paths, developer portals, platform as a product.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Everything in Chapters 9, 11, 13, 14 and 15 is the technical side; this chapter is the way of working that makes those tools pay off.
  • In interviews, expect questions like "how do you deploy safely?", "walk me through an incident you handled", "how would you measure your team's delivery?", "how do you reduce toil?"
  • Change starts small: shorten one pipeline, add one flag, write one blameless postmortem, automate one ticket type.

docs.title: 🚨 Incident story: the Friday release train
docs.text:
The alarm

The team ships a monthly release every last Friday. This month's release has 140 merged PRs. 20 minutes after deploy, checkout conversion drops by 30% and nobody can tell which change caused it.

Try to diagnose it yourself first, then open the clues one by one.

🔍 Clue 1

Rolling back means reverting all 140 changes, including a database migration that already dropped a column. The rollback fails.

🔍 Clue 2

Several features were developed on long-lived branches merged in the last week; integration testing happened for the first time in staging two days before release.

🎯 Root cause

Big-batch releases. Too many changes at once make failures likely, diagnosis slow and rollback impossible; a destructive migration in the same release removed the escape hatch.

🛠️ Fix and lesson

Hotfix forward this time, then move to trunk-based development with daily integration, deploy each merge to production behind feature flags, split migrations into expand/contract steps, and track DORA metrics. Lesson: releasing more often is how you make releases boring and safe.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Measure two DORA metrics from your own git history (rough, but eye-opening)
# Deployment frequency proxy: tags (or merges to main) per week over the last 90 days
git log --since="90 days ago" --tags --simplify-by-decoration --pretty="%ad" --date=format:%G-W%V | sort | uniq -c | tail -12

# Lead time proxy: hours from first commit of a PR branch to its merge into main
git log --merges --first-parent main --since="30 days ago" --pretty="%H %ct" | while read m t; do
  first=$(git log --reverse --pretty=%ct $m^1..$m^2 2>/dev/null | head -1); [ -n "$first" ] && echo $(( (t-first)/3600 ))
done | sort -n | awk '{a[NR]=$1} END{if(NR) print "median lead time (h):", a[int((NR+1)/2)], " PRs:", NR}'

# Batch size: lines changed per merge (smaller is safer)
git log --merges --first-parent main --since="30 days ago" --pretty=%H | head -20 | while read m; do
  git diff --shortstat $m^1 $m; done

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Principle Practice Small batches Short branches, small PRs, deploy each merge Automate CI/CD, IaC, policy as code, self-service Reversible Flags, canary, expand/contract, rollback tested Feedback Fast tests, SLOs, dashboards, alerts on symptoms Shared ownership You build it, you run it, sustainable on-call Learn Blameless postmortems with completed action items Measure DORA trends per team, developer experience surveys

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Is DevOps a role, a tool or something else?

Primarily a culture and set of practices: shared ownership of building and running software, small automated changes and fast feedback. Tools and roles support it but don't create it.

2. What are the four DORA metrics?

Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and failed deployment recovery time.

3. Why do small, frequent deployments improve stability?

Each change is easier to review and test, failures are rarer and smaller, it's obvious which change caused a problem, and rolling back affects little.

4. How do DevOps, SRE and platform engineering relate?

DevOps is the philosophy of shared ownership and flow; SRE implements reliability with SLOs, error budgets and toil limits; platform engineering scales both by giving teams self-service golden paths.

5. Why should DORA metrics not be used to rank individuals?

They describe a team's system of work; using them as personal targets invites gaming (e.g. tiny meaningless deploys) and destroys their value as honest feedback.

docs.title: 16.1 — Git workflows & code review
docs.text:
In short

High-performing teams use trunk-based development: everyone works on short-lived branches (hours, not weeks) that merge into a protected main through small pull requests with required automated checks and a fast human review, so main is always releasable. Unfinished work hides behind feature flags instead of long branches, commits follow a convention, and releases get semantic versions and generated changelogs.

docs.title: 📖 Key terms & abbreviations
docs.text: Term Stands for What it is How it works (one line) Trunk / main — The single integration branch Always green, always deployable Trunk-based development TBD Integrate into main at least daily Short branches or direct commits + flags GitFlow — develop/release/hotfix branches Suits versioned, shipped software; slows SaaS PR / MR Pull / Merge Request Proposed change + review + checks GitHub / GitLab Branch protection — Rules on main Required reviews, checks, no force-push Merge queue — Tests PRs in merge order before landing Keeps main green at high volume CODEOWNERS — Files → required reviewers Auto-requests the right team Squash merge — One commit per PR on main Clean, revertible history Conventional Commits — type(scope): summary feat, fix, chore, BREAKING CHANGE SemVer Semantic Versioning MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH Breaking / feature / fix Monorepo / polyrepo — One repo for many projects / one per project Trade-offs in tooling and coupling Signed commits — Cryptographically verified authorship SSH/GPG/Sigstore gitsign (11)

docs.title: How does it work?
docs.text:
Trunk-based GitFlow Branches main + short feature branches (≤ 1–2 days) main, develop, feature, release, hotfix Integration Continuous, daily At the end of features / releases Unfinished work Behind feature flags (16.2) Stays on a branch Releases From main, any time (or release branches cut from main) Release branches, merges back to develop and main Fits SaaS, services deployed continuously Software with several supported versions (mobile apps, libraries, on-prem products)

Long-lived branches cause merge hell: conflicts, surprise interactions and big-bang integration at the worst moment. DORA research links trunk-based development with higher delivery performance.

docs.title: 2 · Protecting main
docs.text:
• Required status checks: build, unit tests, lint, type checks, security scans (secrets, dependencies, IaC, 11).
  • Required reviews: at least one approval; CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths (infra, auth, payments); dismiss stale approvals on new pushes.
  • No direct pushes, no force-push, linear history (squash or rebase merges).
  • Merge queue when many PRs land: each is tested against the latest main plus PRs ahead of it, so main never breaks from "green separately, red together".
  • Signed commits and protected tags for supply chain integrity (11).

docs.title: 3 · Small PRs and good reviews
docs.text:
• Size: under ~400 changed lines gets real review; 2,000-line PRs get "LGTM". Split by layer, use stacked PRs or flags.
  • Description: what and why, how it was tested, risks, screenshots, links to the ticket.
  • Reviewers look for: correctness, readability, tests, security, operability (logs, metrics, failure handling), backward compatibility.
  • Speed matters: aim for a first review within a few hours; waiting PRs drive people towards big batches.
  • Automate the nitpicks: formatters and linters in CI, so humans discuss design, not whitespace.
  • Kindness: comment on the code, not the person; separate "must fix" from "nit/optional".

docs.title: 4 · Commits, versions and changelogs
docs.text:
feat(checkout): retry payment provider on 503 with backoff
fix(api): return 404 instead of 500 for unknown order id
feat(auth)!: drop support for API keys v1

BREAKING CHANGE: v1 API keys are no longer accepted.
  • Conventional Commits make history searchable and allow tools (release-please, semantic-release, changesets) to compute the next SemVer version and write the changelog automatically: fix → patch, feat → minor, !/BREAKING CHANGE → major.
  • Services deployed continuously often use build numbers or commit SHAs plus image digests; libraries and APIs need SemVer so consumers know what's safe.
  • Tag releases, and make every deployed artifact traceable to a commit (9.4).

docs.title: 5 · Monorepo or polyrepo?
docs.text:
Monorepo Polyrepo Pros Atomic cross-project changes, shared tooling, easy refactors, one source of truth Clear ownership boundaries, simple per-repo CI, independent permissions Cons Needs build tooling (Bazel, Nx, Turborepo, Pants), CI must test only what changed Cross-repo changes are painful, version drift, duplicated tooling Fits Many tightly related services/libraries, strong platform team Independent teams/products, open-source components

Either works with good tooling; pick based on coupling and team structure, not fashion.

docs.title: 🔧 DevOps connection
docs.text:
• Branch protection, required checks and CODEOWNERS are configuration as code too (Terraform GitHub provider, repository rulesets).
  • CI speed is a developer-experience metric: a 40-minute pipeline produces bigger PRs. Cache, parallelize, test only what changed.
  • Infra repos follow the same rules: PR, plan output, review, apply after merge (14.3).
  • Pre-commit hooks (pre-commit, lefthook) catch secrets and formatting before they reach CI.

docs.title: 🧪 Try it yourself
docs.text:
# Practise a clean trunk-based flow locally
mkdir tbd && cd tbd && git init -q -b main && echo "v1" > app.txt && git add . && git commit -qm "chore: initial commit"
git switch -c feat/greeting
echo "hello" >> app.txt && git commit -qam "feat(app): add greeting"
echo "hello, world" > app.txt && git commit -qam "fix(app): full greeting text"
git switch main && git merge --squash feat/greeting -q && git commit -qm "feat(app): add greeting (#12)"
git log --oneline --graph

# Interactive rebase to clean up before opening a PR (on your own branch only)
#   git rebase -i main
# Find which commit broke something
#   git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.4.0; git bisect run ./test.sh

# Who should review a path? (GitHub CODEOWNERS syntax)
printf "/infra/   @acme/platform\n/payments/ @acme/payments @acme/security\n" > CODEOWNERS && cat CODEOWNERS

docs.title: 🃏 Cheat sheet
docs.text: Practice Default Branch lifetime < 2 days PR size < 400 lines, one purpose Checks on main Build, tests, lint, security — required Reviews ≥ 1, CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths, first response < 4 h Merge style Squash, linear history, merge queue at scale Commit style Conventional Commits Versioning SemVer for libraries/APIs, digests for services

docs.title: ❓ Test yourself
docs.text:
1. Why do long-lived feature branches hurt delivery?

They delay integration, so conflicts and interactions appear late and all at once; reviews get huge, and releases become big, risky batches.

2. How do you merge unfinished work daily without exposing it to users?

Put it behind a feature flag (or keep it unreachable) so the code is integrated and deployed but not released (16.2).

3. What problem does a merge queue solve?

Two PRs that pass CI separately can break main when combined; the queue tests each PR against main plus the PRs ahead of it before merging.

4. Under SemVer, what does a change from 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 signal?

A breaking change: consumers may need to change their code or configuration to upgrade.

5. When does GitFlow still make sense?

For software where several versions are maintained and shipped in discrete releases (mobile apps, libraries, on-prem products) rather than deployed continuously.
